AG-001.summary: Sabotage derailed the Paris–Tourcoing express near Arras during the strikes of November–December 1947, killing 16 people and injuring about 30. The government and President Vincent Auriol called those strikes insurrectional. The government blamed the Communists. Interior Minister Jules Moch instructed prefects to take all police measures needed to clear illegally occupied premises. The perpetrators were never identified. The causes of the derailment were never clearly established.
AG-001.records:
The government: blamed the Communists.
The Interior Ministry: a later review that contradicted the insurrection thesis.
The newsreels: Actualités françaises of 11 December 1947 linked the derailment to the strike wave.
Historians: among them Robert Mencherini, who cites a study suggesting that former Resistance militants meant to strike a train carrying riot police.
AG-001.gap: The government fixed the political attribution before any investigative finding. The Interior Ministry's own later assessment contradicted the insurrection thesis. That assessment never became a public finding on the derailment.
AG-001.joining: In the source checked, no authority named an attacker. Historians later reexamined the record and concluded that the causes of the derailment were never clearly established.

AG-002.summary: The Western Allies introduced the Deutsche Mark in the western zones and West Berlin in June 1948. On 24 June 1948 Soviet forces closed the road, rail and canal links to the western sectors of Berlin. The closure cut off food and coal and left the city without electricity. The United States began an airlift on 26 June and Britain on 28 June. The Soviets offered to lift the blockade if the Deutsche Mark was withdrawn from West Berlin. The Allies refused. The blockade was lifted on 11 or 12 May 1949 (the Office of the Historian gives both dates).
AG-002.records:
US Military Government and Robert Murphy, the Political Adviser in Berlin: food needs of 2,000 tons a day for the western sectors, an airlift planned at about 225 tons a day at the start, and General Clay's austerity orders on food and electric power for US personnel.
The Department of the Army and the State Department: doubted on 23 June that the timing was right for a unilateral US protest.
The Soviet occupation authorities: the closures.
AG-002.gap: The blockade was a single, overt and continuous act of coercion against a city's supply, designed to be noticed, so the aggregation gap was absent. The problem lay in response. Murphy framed that response as leaving the Soviets 'the dilemma either of permitting supplies to come through from the west or of feeding the Berlin population.'
AG-002.joining: The occupying powers recorded the closures and supply effects at once. Murphy recommended a joint Western protest citing Marshal Zhukov's 1945 commitment to supply the western sectors with food and fuel. The airlift replaced the cut services.

AG-003.summary: From 1948 the Soviet Union jammed Western broadcasts, chiefly the BBC External Services, the Voice of America (VOA) and Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL). By 1984 Bulgaria and Poland also jammed VOA and RFE/RL. By then Czechoslovakia jammed RFE/RL. Soviet spending on jamming was estimated at $250–300 million a year. Every International Telecommunication Convention since 1947 required stations to operate without causing harmful interference to other members' radio services. The UN General Assembly condemned intentional interference by 'some countries' in December 1950 (resolution 424 (V), adopted 49–5). Jamming was suspended from 1963 to 1968 and eased in the 1970s. It intensified again in 1980 after the invasion of Afghanistan and the Polish crisis.
AG-003.records:
The targeted broadcasters (BBC, VOA, RFE/RL): among them staff studies by RFE/RL of jamming against its programs (1965–1982).
The Deutsche Bundespost's Fernmeldetechnisches Zentralamt: sent RFE/RL direction-finding maps of jamming for 1954/55, 1957 and 1965 (letter of 19 November 1981).
The USIA Office of Research: 'Jamming of Western Radio Broadcasts to the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe' (1983).
The ITU: could mediate, conciliate or make technical accommodations only when the parties invited it.
The International Frequency Registration Board of the ITU: enforcement and interpretation of the radio regulations.
The UN General Assembly: three resolutions in 1950, on which the Soviet Union abstained or voted against.
The Soviet government: defended jamming as protection against subversive broadcasts.
AG-003.gap: Jamming was continuous, and its noise signals carried identification markers, usually in Morse code, so the aggregation gap was absent. The gap lay in authority. The ITU could act only if the parties invited it, and its recommendations could be rejected without penalty. The USSR treated jamming as a state's right to shield its population from subversive broadcasts.
AG-003.joining: Western governments and broadcasters named the jamming states. The UN General Assembly condemned 'some countries' in 1950 in a nonbinding resolution that did not name the Soviet Union. No forum with binding authority ruled. During the negotiation of the 1975 Helsinki Final Act the United States sought an anti-jamming provision. The USSR did not agree to it.

AG-004.summary: On 18 September 1948 Hungarian authorities arrested Paul Ruedemann and George Bannantine, American managers of the Hungarian-American Oil Company (MAORT), a Standard Oil (New Jersey) subsidiary. Hungarian staff had been arrested earlier. On 25 September the government took over the company's management by a decree whose stated purpose was 'to prevent wilful sabotage of the production of crude oil.' The Interior Ministry published a 'Grey Book' presenting the postwar decline in oil output as sabotage against the people's democracy, combining verifiable data with confessions written under duress. The Americans were expelled to Austria and withdrew their confessions in Vienna. Simon Papp, the former MAORT chief geologist and managing director, was sentenced to death, commuted to life imprisonment, released in 1955 and rehabilitated by the Hungarian Academy of Sciences in 1987.
AG-004.records:
MAORT: the production and reservoir records, which showed output rising until 1943 and falling afterward. A 2009 Hungarian industry history ascribes that curve to natural geological decline, after wartime sequestration accelerated exploitation and the Red Army held the fields until 1947.
The Ministry of Interior and the police: the interrogation record. They published the Grey Book.
The court: received the indictment.
The US Legation and the State Department: recorded the arrests and described the confessions as 'wholly false'.
Standard Oil (New Jersey): prepared a memorandum refuting the sabotage charges. The United States delivered it with its note to the Hungarian foreign ministry on 30 November 1948.
AG-004.gap: The one institution with an interest in a sabotage finding did the joining. The state security apparatus combined genuine production statistics, auditors' reports taken out of context, false witness statements and coerced confessions. It set aside the technical record of reservoir depletion held by the company and the United States. No independent body could test the claim.
AG-004.joining: The Hungarian Interior Ministry and the court joined the records into an attack claim in September-December 1948. They named the American managers and Hungarian staff as saboteurs. Only later reassessment undid the claim: the Americans' public retraction in Vienna in October 1948, the US note of 30 November 1948, Béla Kissh's 1984 University of Maryland history of MAORT, the Hungarian Academy of Sciences' rehabilitation of Papp in 1987, and a 2009 Hungarian industry history that describes the indictment as built largely on assumptions presented as facts.

AG-005.summary: From 20 to 27 September 1950 a Navy ship sprayed Bacillus globigii and Serratia marcescens over San Francisco in six Army-sponsored tests of the vulnerability of port cities to biological attack. Edward Nevin developed a urinary-tract infection two days after the tests ended, was readmitted to Stanford Hospital on 11 October and died of endocarditis on 1 November. Ten other Stanford patients had similar Serratia infections. A Defense Department report recorded Army scientists' judgment that the outbreak appeared coincidental. The test was not acknowledged until newspapers linked it to Nevin's death in December 1976. In March 1977 the Army told a Senate subcommittee of this test and 238 others conducted between 1949 and 1969. In 1983 the Ninth Circuit held that the government could not be sued.
AG-005.records:
The Army and the Navy: the classified test record, including results from sampling stations around the bay.
Stanford Hospital physicians: the clinical record of the eleven patients, which they published as an unexplained outbreak.
Army scientists: aware of the cluster, they judged it coincidental in a Defense Department report.
AG-005.gap: Classification kept the exposure record away from the clinicians. The only party holding both records judged the link coincidental. The military had no medical monitoring plan because it considered the bacteria harmless.
AG-005.joining: Newspapers joined the records in December 1976. The Army gave a Senate subcommittee its account in March 1977. In 1981 Nevin's family sued. The government argued that the death was a coincidence and that it was immune for a planning decision. The family lost at trial and in the Ninth Circuit (1983). The Supreme Court declined to hear the case.
AG-005.harm_found_later: Whether the test caused the infections was argued in court three decades later by scientists. Among them was Matthew Meselson, who testified for the family that the Serratia in Nevin's blood was likely the sprayed strain.

AG-006.summary: On 16 June 1950 the party newspaper Neues Deutschland reported that an extraordinary commission had established that United States aircraft dropped large quantities of Colorado potato beetles over the German Democratic Republic. The same report carried the Council of Ministers' proposal to the governments of the Soviet Union, Poland and Czechoslovakia for joint countermeasures. In July 1950 the GDR propaganda chief Gerhart Eisler published the brochure Halt, Amikäfer. The Deutsches Historisches Museum states that the accusations were invented.
AG-006.records:
An extraordinary government commission: the finding about aircraft.
The Council of Ministers: turned the finding into a proposal to three neighboring governments.
Eisler's brochure: assembled the material for publication.
American authorities on the Western side: asked Bonn for countermeasures.
A press unit of the West German Ministry for All-German Affairs: agreed with American intelligence officers in early August 1950 to produce cardboard decoy beetles marked with an F for Freiheit. The beetles were mailed to the councils of every GDR municipality or dropped from balloons.
AG-006.gap: The beetle finds were dispersed across fields and gathered by local collection campaigns that included schoolchildren. A government commission with a political purpose did the joining. The sources consulted do not show that any underlying field report recorded aircraft. No independent body reviewed the finding.
AG-006.joining: A state commission joined the beetle finds into an attack claim and named the United States. The Council of Ministers carried the claim into interstate diplomacy. The Deutsches Historisches Museum's account of the brochure states that the accusations were invented. The responses of the Soviet, Polish and Czechoslovak governments were not established.

AG-007.summary: North Korea, China and the Soviet Union accused the United States of biological warfare in a first campaign from May to July 1951 and in a major campaign from 22 February 1952 to the end of the war. Three bodies endorsed the charges. A commission of the International Association of Democratic Lawyers visited North Korea and China in March 1952. A Chinese government commission reported on 7 April 1952. An International Scientific Commission convened by the World Peace Council, chaired by Joseph Needham, was in North Korea and China from 23 June to 31 August 1952; its report ran to 669 pages. China and North Korea refused investigation by the International Committee of the Red Cross, the World Health Organization and a UN General Assembly commission. Soviet documents published in 1998 include a message to Mao of 2 May 1953 stating that the accusations were fictitious. The memoir of Wu Zhili, head of the Chinese People's Army Health Division, published posthumously in 2013, states that they were fabricated.
AG-007.records:
The accusing governments' staff and commissions: the incident records.
The Needham commission: conducted no field investigations of its own. It accepted the material Chinese government staff presented, without independent corroboration.
The ICRC: applied for access on 4 March 1952 and repeated its requests on 28 and 31 March. It ended the effort on 30 April.
UN Secretary-General Trygve Lie: transmitted a WHO offer of epidemic-control assistance three times in March 1952. Both countries rejected it.
The Soviet Union: vetoed two US draft Security Council resolutions in July 1952, the first calling for an ICRC investigation and the second stating that the charges must be presumed false if investigation was refused.
The General Assembly: approved a five-state commission (Brazil, Egypt, Pakistan, Sweden, Uruguay) on 23 April 1953 by 51 votes to 5 with 4 abstentions. On 28 July 1953 its president reported that the commission could not accomplish its task because China and North Korea refused assistance.
AG-007.gap: The only bodies admitted to the sites were commissions chosen or convened by the accusing side. China and North Korea refused access to every neutral body with authority to investigate. The records that would settle the matter sat in the accusers' party archives.
AG-007.joining: The accusers joined their own records into a public attack claim. No international body adjudicated. Milton Leitenberg and the Cold War International History Project joined the archival record from 1998, with further Russian releases in 2015 and 2016. Their work showed the claim to be fabricated. China and North Korea have officially maintained the charges.

AG-008.summary: Microwave beams aimed at the US Embassy in Moscow from nearby Soviet buildings were detected from 1953, with two new sources from May 1975. On 6 February 1976 window screening was installed. In 1976 the State Department commissioned a retrospective cohort study from Abraham Lilienfeld of Johns Hopkins. It compared 1,827 Moscow staff with 2,561 staff at eight other Eastern European posts and reported in 1978 that it had found nothing that convincingly implicated microwave exposure in adverse health effects. A 2012 review by J. Mark Elwood noted the study's limited exposure information, its many uncorrected comparisons and its short follow-up. Elwood concluded that the original findings were supported and that contrary reinterpretations rested on misinterpretation of the results.
AG-008.records:
The US government: the measurements of the signal.
The State Department: personnel and medical records and death certificates.
The Lilienfeld team: traced 94 percent of Moscow staff but received questionnaires from only 51 percent. No records showed where employees had worked or lived in Moscow, and the study staff could not obtain the basic intensity measurements before the report was written.
AG-008.gap: The record of the signal and the medical record of the staff were kept for different purposes. The medical files held no exposure data. When the records were joined after 1976, exposure could be assigned only to employees who returned questionnaires.
AG-008.joining: The State Department joined the records through a commissioned academic study. The signal came from Soviet buildings near the embassy, so no attacker needed naming. The open question was harm. The study did not establish it, and later critics disputed it.
AG-008.harm_found_later: Any harm to embassy staff and families could be assessed only by retrospective epidemiology that lacked individual exposure measurements.

AG-009.summary: From October 1959 the State Department received many reports of flights over Cuba, some reportedly dropping incendiaries on sugar cane fields. A leaflet flight over Havana on 21 October 1959 carried leaflets bearing the typed name of Comandante Pedro Luis Díaz Lanz. In February 1960 a small aircraft that had left Florida was destroyed with its two occupants, apparently while trying to bomb a Cuban sugar mill. Fidel Castro charged that the raids came from the United States. A State Department memorandum of 24 February 1960 recorded that, apart from the Díaz Lanz flight and the destroyed plane, the Department had no proof that the flights came from US territory, that 'we must now accept this possibility,' and that the matter should go to the Cabinet so that several enforcement agencies would act together.
AG-009.records:
The Cuban government and press: public charges. After the 21 October flight the newspaper Revolución headlined 'aircraft reported from US' and gave the impression of an air bombing, contrary to official police statements.
The US Embassy in Havana: its investigation (despatch 712, 12 November 1959) attributed the two deaths and about 50 injuries reported that night to government fire and grenades thrown from cars.
The State Department: reports of the flights and the February 1960 memorandum.
The enforcement agencies: Customs and the Coast Guard (Treasury), the FBI and the Immigration and Naturalization Service (Justice), the Federal Aviation Agency and the Department of Defense, which the memorandum asked to coordinate enforcement.
The Operations Coordinating Board: 'expressed doubt that enough action was being taken to prevent the illegal flights.'
AG-009.gap: Enforcement against flights from US airfields was divided among Treasury, Justice, the FAA and Defense. The State Department had no proof of origin for most reported flights, and the charges came from a hostile government. A plane destroyed with its occupants supplied the first proof of US origin beyond the Díaz Lanz flight.
AG-009.joining: The State Department's Bureau of Inter-American Affairs asked for Cabinet attention so that the enforcement agencies would act jointly. Stevenson drafted that memorandum, Deputy Assistant Secretary Lester Mallory initialed it, and Under Secretary Dillon approved it on 24 February 1960. The Operations Coordinating Board urged the Department to 'canalize' executive action. Havana named the United States. In the records checked, Washington named no organizer publicly.

AG-010.summary: In February 1959 transatlantic cables off Newfoundland suffered twelve breaks. The cable companies notified the US government. On 26 February the US Navy's USS Roy O. Hale stopped the Soviet fishing trawler Novorossisk, and a boarding party examined it under the 1884 cable convention. A Soviet note handed to US Ambassador Llewellyn Thompson in Moscow denied that the trawler had damaged any cable, called the reports of damage 'a complete invention' and said the detention had been undertaken 'with provocative aims in mind'.
AG-010.records:
The cable companies: the outages and, later, the repair findings, which showed that three of the twelve breaks were man-made cuts.
The boarding party: recorded that the trawler had been present over the cables at the time of the damage.
The State Department: relied on the 1884 convention, which permits inspection of the documents of ships suspected of damaging cables willfully or negligently.
The Soviet government: kept its own account and denied any damage.
AG-010.gap: The repair findings on the nature of the breaks came after the boarding. The convention allowed inspection of documents and gave no means of establishing intent. The officer who led the boarding party said the trawler 'probably quite likely' had something to do with the break. He said he did not know whether the damage was accidental or intentional. Fishing trawlers damaged cables regularly, so every break had a ready non-hostile explanation.
AG-010.joining: The companies' notice and the Navy boarding tied the outages to one vessel under the treaty's inspection right. Winkler reports that the party found nothing directly showing deliberate state action, and that it confirmed the Novorossisk had been over the cables when they were damaged. The sources checked record no formal US finding of deliberate Soviet cutting. The incident soon slipped from public attention.

AG-011.summary: The French ship La Coubre, bringing arms from Belgium, exploded in Havana harbor on 4 March 1960, killing a number of French crew members and 75 Cuban dock workers. On 5 March Prime Minister Fidel Castro attributed responsibility for the explosion to the United States. The State Department called the charge 'unfounded and irresponsible,' and the United States delivered a protest note on 15 March. The sources checked record no joint or neutral inquiry into the cause.
AG-011.records:
The Cuban government: Castro's public attribution to the United States.
The US chargé in Havana: offered condolences and assistance on 5 March.
The State Department: a press statement denying the charge, the Secretary's protest to the Cuban chargé d'affaires on 7 March, and the note of 15 March.
The US Embassy country team: called the accusation a 'fabricated, irresponsible charge' and part of a 'deliberate attempt to precipitate a crisis in Cuban-American relations' (telegram of 8 March 1960).
AG-011.gap: The physical record stayed in Cuban hands. The cargo came from Belgium and the ship from France. Each government used the event for its own account. The records checked show no joint or neutral inquiry.
AG-011.joining: Cuba fixed the attribution politically within a day. The United States rejected it within days and treated the charge as a sign of Cuban intent to provoke a crisis. No neutral body joined the records in the sources checked.

AG-012.summary: Express train no. 12 from Strasbourg to Paris derailed near Blacy (Marne), between Vitry-le-François and Loisy-sur-Marne, on the afternoon of 18 June 1961. Senator Jacques Duclos gave the toll as 27 dead. The official inquiry excluded any responsibility of SNCF staff, and official statements rejected sabotage. Six months later Duclos asked the minister of public works and transport why OAS involvement had been ruled out while the inquiry had reached no conclusion. He noted that the Vitry-le-François stationmaster had received an OAS letter before the derailment threatening to blow up the track.
AG-012.records:
The official inquiry: excluded staff fault. It had no conclusions after six months.
The official statements: rejected sabotage.
The Vitry-le-François stationmaster: had received the OAS letter ('Nous ferons sauter la voie d'ici peu').
SNCF staff: reported sabotage found on the morning of 19 June on the line to which trains had first been said to be diverted. They doubted the laboratory conclusions on a shattered rail fragment sent to Paris.
SNCF staff delegates: refused any account of the inquiry for more than six months.
The Senate: Duclos's written question.
AG-012.gap: According to Duclos, the inquiry set sabotage aside quickly and did not pursue the threat letter held at the station. In his account, the staff observations and the laboratory work on the rail fragment stayed with separate bodies, and staff representatives were kept out of the inquiry.
AG-012.joining: Duclos's parliamentary question set the threat letter, the staff observations and the uncompensated victims side by side six months after the event. In the sources checked, no authority joined the records into an attribution.
AG-012.harm_found_later: Six months after the derailment the victims had received no compensation.

AG-013.summary: In the night of 11–12 June 1961 the Befreiungsausschuss Südtirol (BAS) blew up 37 high-voltage pylons, eight railway pylons and two high-pressure lines in South Tyrol. BAS left leaflets demanding self-determination. Italian police mistreated many of those detained, and two detainees, Franz Höfler and Anton Gostner, died in custody. BAS members were tried in the first Milan criminal trial. The UN General Assembly had called on Austria and Italy in 1960 to settle their dispute on the basis of the 1946 Gruber–De Gasperi Agreement, and it repeated that call in Resolution 1661 (XVI) of 28 November 1961.
AG-013.records:
The BAS: the leaflets.
The Italian police: arrests and interrogations, with mistreatment documented in detainees' letters published by the Dolomiten on 9 January 1962.
The Milan court: the first Milan criminal trial.
The South Tyrolean People's Party (SVP): its leader Silvius Magnago condemned the attacks as dangerous to the negotiations.
The Austrian government: its foreign minister Bruno Kreisky raised the torture allegations at the United Nations on 23 November 1961.
The UN General Assembly: resolutions of 1960 and 28 November 1961.
The Italian government: set up the Commission of Nineteen partly in response.
AG-013.gap: The attacks were simultaneous and announced by leaflets. Recognition was therefore immediate. The mistreatment of detainees turned the prosecution itself into a contested record. Austria carried that record to the United Nations.
AG-013.joining: The BAS signaled its authorship. Italian courts tried the members within Italian reach. Austria took the underlying dispute to the United Nations. Historians still dispute the effect of the attacks. Rolf Steininger argues that autonomy came in spite of the Feuernacht. Hans Karl Peterlini notes that the Commission of Nineteen was itself a product of the attacks.

AG-014.summary: Operation Mongoose began with a directive of 30 November 1961. In 1963 the CIA proposed a new program of sabotage and harassment against Cuba, which the 5412 Special Group approved on 24 May 1963. A CIA plan of 11 October 1962 ranked 33 land targets in order of economic importance, among them power plants, aqueducts, flour mills, piers, refineries and radio and television stations. A sabotage team was sent against the Matahambre copper mine during the Missile Crisis. Its members were captured on 5 and 14 November 1962, according to the Cuban account of Fabián Escalante. The planning and approval records became public through later declassification.
AG-014.records:
The CIA: the plans and target lists. William Harvey's plan of 11 October 1962 and Desmond FitzGerald's Special Affairs Staff in 1963.
The 5412 Special Group: the approvals. On 19 June 1963 the program was presented to 'Higher Authority', who showed a particular interest in external sabotage, and the meeting was told that a first operation could take place in July.
Fabián Escalante's account: the Cuban record of the captured Matahambre team, published later.
Cuba: in 1999 filed a claim for human damages against the US government in the People's Provincial Court of the City of Havana and transmitted it to the UN as A/54/122.
AG-014.gap: The victim state could name the attacker, and the planners expected it to. The April 1963 proposal stated that 'U.S. attribution will be claimed' even without losses, and that involvement could become known through confessions of captured personnel. The June 1963 meeting accepted 'a considerable noise level'. The confirming records stayed in classified US files, so Cuban charges came only from an adversary government.
AG-014.joining: The planning record became public through declassified documents published in Foreign Relations of the United States. The National Security Archive's 2019 briefing book joined CIA and White House records with Escalante's Cuban account of the Matahambre raid. In 1975 the Senate Select Committee (Church Committee) published an interim report on alleged assassination plots with a section on Cuba. Cuba's 1999 claim aggregated incidents unilaterally and has no US counterpart.

AG-015.summary: United States forces sprayed herbicides over South Vietnam from 1961 to 1971 in Operation Ranch Hand, in part to destroy crops as a tactic for decreasing enemy food supplies. The flight records were incomplete and contained errors. Under contract to the National Academy of Sciences, Jeanne Mager Stellman and colleagues rebuilt the spray record and published it in Nature in April 2003. The revision added more than seven million liters to the 1974 inventory and nearly doubled the dioxin estimate. By linking flight paths to hamlet records, it found 3,181 hamlets sprayed directly with at least 2.1 million and perhaps as many as 4.8 million people present.
AG-015.records:
The Air Force HERBS file: flight paths for missions from August 1965 to December 1971, with Army helicopter missions from 1968. Its error rate was about 10 percent.
The Defense Department: added a Services-HERBS file in 1985 from further record searches.
The 12th Air Commando Squadron: the Ranch Hand operational records, from which the 2003 authors identified some 200 missions before August 1965.
The National Archives: operational project folders for about half of the projects.
The Hamlet Evaluation System: hamlet locations and populations. It was established in June 1967 and filled in by US district advisors and Vietnamese district chiefs.
The corrected file: 9,141 missions. Spraying in Laos is documented without coordinates for part of it.
The 1974 National Academy of Sciences report: worked without the Hamlet Evaluation System files, which were not made available to it in time. It also worked from a '202 Tasks Realized' document that the 2003 authors found to contain many errors.
AG-015.gap: The spray records were kept as operational logs. The 2003 authors found that analyzing spraying by the purpose recorded in the HERBS file was inaccurate. Population records sat in a separate pacification reporting system. The impetus to join them came from the Institute of Medicine. The Agent Orange Act of 1991 asked the Institute to review the scientific findings on herbicide exposure and veterans' disease, and the Institute recommended that the Department of Veterans Affairs develop historical reconstruction methods. The 2003 paper describes itself as the result of that recommendation.
AG-015.joining: Academic researchers under contract to the National Academy of Sciences joined the mission and hamlet records, and published in Nature in 2003, more than thirty years after the last mission. The sprayer was known throughout, so the joining established scale and exposure. No authority has used the joined record to attribute harm to individual Vietnamese civilians.
AG-015.harm_found_later: Civilian exposure became estimable only through reconstruction from military flight logs and pacification data. 1,430 further sprayed hamlets could not be assigned populations. The Institute of Medicine had relied as authoritative on a 1988 reference that attributed the four highest dioxin values in the record to Agent Purple. The 2003 authors disputed that attribution.

AG-016.summary: Cuba accused the United States of biological warfare twelve times from 1962, among them over a 1981 dengue outbreak that killed 158 people. In 1997 it alleged that a US aircraft had released the crop pest Thrips palmi over the island in 1996, destroying 20,000 tons of potato, cucumber and other crops on a state farm. Cuba circulated its case at the UN (A/52/128, 28 April 1997) and brought it under the Biological Weapons Convention. The formal consultative meeting of states parties, the first test of the treaty's procedure for an alleged biological attack, ended inconclusively in August 1997. Its chair, Ian Soutar, said a US plane had crossed Cuba and an infestation had occurred, but the meeting could not establish a formal causal link between the two events. A 1999 report by Raymond Zilinskas of the Monterey Institute's Center for Nonproliferation Studies found that all twelve allegations were probably false.
AG-016.records:
Cuba: its records of the overflight and the infestation, in an annex circulated at the UN ("Information about the appearance in Cuba of the Thrips palmi plague").
The US government: the record of the flight, which it said was a narcotics-eradication mission to Colombia. Its delegation head, Donald Mahley, called the charges baseless.
The consultative meeting: received both accounts.
AG-016.gap: Only the accusing state held the outbreak record, and only the accused held the flight record. The meeting did not investigate on site. At that time delegates saw no need for a field investigation.
AG-016.joining: Cuba joined its records into an attack claim. The meeting received both accounts and declined to find a causal link. It asked diplomats from Brazil, Canada, Iran, the Netherlands, Nigeria and Russia to clarify the matter and report by the end of 1997. An independent assessment of all Cuba's allegations came in 1999 from an academic nonproliferation center. No attacker was named.

AG-017.summary: Mudiad Amddiffyn Cymru (MAC), led from 1966 by John Jenkins, bombed tax offices and the pipelines that carried water from Welsh reservoirs to English cities. On 27 May 1968 an explosion damaged a support carrying an emergency pipeline from Lake Vyrnwy to Liverpool, about 20 yards below the dam at Llanwddyn. Two days earlier a bomb had exploded at the Welsh Office's Crown Buildings in Cardiff. The Secretary of State for Wales told the Commons there had been four such explosions in Wales in twelve months. Jenkins was arrested on 2 November 1969 and sentenced at Flintshire Assizes to concurrent ten-year terms.
AG-017.records:
Liverpool Corporation: owner of the Vyrnwy pipeline. Its officials investigated the damage with local police.
Cardiff City police and the Regional Crime Squad: the Cardiff bomb.
Special Branch.
The Welsh Office and Parliament.
AG-017.gap: Separate bodies investigated each explosion. In May 1968 MPs complained of no apparent progress and asked that the Regional Crime Squad be given complete charge, assisted by Special Branch from Scotland Yard, as 'a national matter'. The Secretary of State replied that how the police did their work was a matter for the police. Authorship was contested: Gwynfor Evans of Plaid Cymru suggested that government secret service agents might be responsible. The cost fell on the English water undertaking, and a Liverpool MP asked why Liverpool ratepayers should bear it. According to Delayed Gratification, MAC's cell structure left the police without leads.
AG-017.joining: Two men died in a premature explosion at Abergele on the eve of the July 1969 investiture. A woman who had seen Jenkins with an operative then went to the police, according to Jenkins, and police identified him. His conviction attributed the campaign to MAC. Jenkins said the authorities would not have broken MAC's cover without the informer.

AG-018.summary: United States aircraft operating from Thailand seeded clouds over the Ho Chi Minh Trail during each southwest monsoon from 20 March 1967 to 5 July 1972, to increase rainfall on enemy lines of communication. The program was held in a special channel with very limited access. Its code names were changed when they became known. The Defense Department briefed a Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee chaired by Senator Claiborne Pell in a top-secret session on 20 March 1974. The transcript was made public on 19 May 1974.
AG-018.records:
The Defense Department: 2,602 sorties and 47,409 seeding units expended, including units over North Vietnam in 1967 and 1968, at an annual cost of about 3.6 million dollars.
The Defense Intelligence Agency: estimated that rainfall rose in limited areas up to 30 percent above that predicted.
The remote sensors on the trail: recorded the drop in logistics traffic cited as the effect.
Secretary of Defense Melvin Laird: told the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on 18 April 1972 that "we have never engaged in that type of activity over North Vietnam," and wrote to the committee in January 1974 that he had since learned that such activities were conducted there in 1967 and 1968.
An interagency study chaired by Herman Pollack of the State Department: no conclusions on the military aspects of weather modification. The study was refused information on the military use of weather modification.
AG-018.gap: No recorder on the ground could distinguish seeded rain from the monsoon. The Defense Department told the Senate that the results could not be precisely quantified for lack of ground stations. Inside the United States government the program sat in a special channel. The deputy assistant secretary of defense responsible for East Asia learned of it from a Jack Anderson column. The State Department's interagency study was refused information on it. The Secretary of Defense gave the Senate an inaccurate denial in 1972.
AG-018.joining: The Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee on Oceans and International Environment, chaired by Senator Pell, obtained the Defense Department briefing on 20 March 1974, seven years to the day after the first operational mission. The subcommittee made the transcript public on 19 May 1974. The Senate had adopted Pell's Resolution 71, calling for an international agreement against environmental modification as a weapon, on 11 July 1973 by 82 votes to 10. The UN adopted the Environmental Modification Convention in 1976. The attacking state named itself, under congressional pressure.
AG-018.harm_found_later: No record attributes any flood, crop loss or other civilian harm in Laos, Cambodia or Vietnam to the seeding. The Defense Department's own estimate of effect rested on modeled rainfall and sensor counts of enemy traffic.

AG-019.summary: During the North Yemen civil war, an air raid killed about 120 people at Ketaf on 5 January 1967, many of them women and children, amid reports of poison gas. A raid on Gahr on 10 or 11 May 1967 killed 75. An ICRC medical team, delayed by the bombing of its convoy, reached Gahr four days after the raid. It examined four survivors and an exhumed body and concluded that death was caused by pulmonary edema from inhaling a toxic gas. A supplementary report by Dr. Lauppi of Bern judged that conclusion perfectly justified. The ICRC sent its report to the parties at the start of June. Its public statement of 2 June 1967 did not point to the responsible party, because it could not obtain conclusive proof. The United States, whose information attributed the gas attacks to the UAR (Egypt), chose to stay in the background because of sensitive intelligence and propaganda implications.
AG-019.records:
ICRC delegates and doctors: the clinical and site record.
The ICRC: in its protest to the UAR over the bombing of its convoy, it identified UAR-marked aircraft as the source of that attack.
The US government: intelligence it did not publish, which it said fully justified the ICRC's concern.
AG-019.gap: The only neutral recorder on site established the cause of death. It could not obtain conclusive proof of the attacker, so it kept its public statement general. The government holding the attribution record kept it secret for political reasons.
AG-019.joining: In the sources checked, nobody with authority joined the ICRC's clinical finding to the intelligence record in public, and no international body named the attacker. The State Department suggested in July 1967 that the ICRC publish its report or send it to the UN, while keeping its own intelligence out of public view. It noted that attacks had resumed on 2–3 July and that a 15 July attack at Hajjah reportedly killed 150 people.

AG-020.summary: Oleg Lyalin, an officer of the KGB's sabotage department (Department V), was posted to London under Soviet trade-delegation cover. MI5 recruited him in the spring of 1971. He defected on 3 September 1971, after a drunk-driving arrest at the end of August. He described plans to flood the London Underground, disrupt British Rail timetables, sabotage the Fylingdales early-warning station and disrupt BBC and Post Office communications. He identified a submarine landing site at Hayburn Wyke on the Yorkshire coast, arms caches and recruited agents. Ministers agreed on 21 September 1971 to act. On 24 September the government expelled 90 Soviet officials and barred 15 more from returning (Operation FOOT).
AG-020.records:
MI5: surveillance of Lyalin from February 1971 and a five-volume debriefing dossier.
The Foreign Office: initially incredulous. The FOOT memorandum, sent by the Foreign and Home Secretaries to the Prime Minister at the end of July 1971, estimated at least 120 Soviet intelligence officers in Britain.
The Home Office: worried about trade with the USSR.
MI6: feared retaliation against its agents in Moscow.
The police: the drunk-driving arrest on Tottenham Court Road.
The preparations themselves: reconnaissance and recruited clerks, among them one in the Greater London Council's motor licensing department with access to the list of MI5 and Special Branch vehicles. They had produced nothing that a service operator would record as an incident.
AG-020.gap: Sabotage preparation against civilian services leaves no disruption to report. The counter-espionage records tracked people and contacts, and recognition depended on a single insider. Much of the record remains closed. MI5's file on Lyalin is sealed, and three related Foreign Office files (FCO 168/4587–4589) were withheld as of September 2025.
AG-020.joining: MI5 joined Lyalin's account with its surveillance record. Prime Minister Edward Heath and senior ministers agreed on 21 September 1971 to proceed despite the risks of Soviet retaliation and lost trade. The expulsion was presented as a measure against Soviet intelligence officers. The sabotage targets became known mainly through later journalism and Richard Kerbaj's book The Defector (2025).

AG-021.summary: On 22 July 1970 the Palermo–Turin express, called the Treno del Sole in one account and the Freccia del Sud in another, derailed about 750 meters from Gioia Tauro station. The derailment, which came during the revolt over the siting of Calabria's regional capital, killed six people and injured dozens (54 or 72, according to the account). The railway police excluded a deliberate cause, but experts appointed by the Palmi prosecutor found a damaged rail and concluded that the cause was likely malicious. Four railway employees were charged before the case was archived with no one held responsible. In 1993 Giacomo Lauro stated that a bomb had caused the derailment. On 27 February 2001 the Corte d'Assise of Palmi confirmed its link to the Reggio revolt.
AG-021.records:
Emilio Santillo, the Reggio Calabria police chief: immediately blamed the unbolting of a bogie on the ninth carriage.
Railway police: two reports, the first a month after the crash and the second on 9 September 1971. They excluded a deliberate origin and blamed the drivers for lifting a 60 km/h speed restriction.
The expert panel appointed by the Palmi prosecutor: found a rail with its inner foot partly removed over about 180 cm. It concluded that the cause was likely malicious.
Four railway employees: charged with culpable disaster and manslaughter. The judge found that they had not committed the act, and the case was archived.
Five anarchists from Reggio: died in a road crash at Ferentino on 26 September 1970 on their way to Rome. The inquiry into their deaths was shelved.
AG-021.gap: By keeping the event in the accident category, the operator's own police placed suspicion on railway staff. The prosecutor's expert finding produced no suspect. Explosive attacks on rail lines in the region followed on 22 and 27 September and 10 October 1970 without changing the classification of the July derailment. Recognition waited 23 years for an insider witness.
AG-021.joining: Giacomo Lauro said in 1993 that a bomb had caused the derailment and later that he had supplied the explosives, paid by the Comitato d'azione per Reggio capoluogo. On 11 November 1994 he named Vito Silverini, Giovanni Moro and Vincenzo Caracciolo as the bombers. Carmine Dominici, a leading figure in Avanguardia Nazionale in Reggio from 1967 to 1976, confirmed his account. The Corte d'Assise of Palmi confirmed the link to the Reggio revolt on 27 February 2001. According to Il Dispaccio, none of the people Lauro named was convicted.
AG-021.harm_found_later: For more than two decades the records listed the six deaths as a railway accident. The only prosecution was of railway employees, for culpable disaster.

AG-022.summary: The 300 MW Tandragee-Maynooth interconnector, opened in 1970 with 20 of its 50 km in Northern Ireland, was attacked repeatedly by the Provisional IRA from the early 1970s. An October 1988 background paper by the Department of Economic Development's Electricity Division listed about two dozen dated incidents from July 1971 to April 1982, mostly tower bombings. It also listed the hijacking and destruction of engineers' vehicles and a bomb under the Northern Ireland Electricity Service office at Camlough. The line had been out of service since the mid-1970s. Its restoration needed three towers rebuilt and about two miles of conductor restored to the border, at an NIE cost estimated at £0.75 million against savings of £2.5 million a year.
AG-022.records:
Northern Ireland Electricity (NIES/NIE): the incident and repair record, with the cost and savings estimates.
RUC: supplied the security assessment. It held that repair crews would in all probability face intimidation and that a restored line would again become a PIRA target.
Department of Economic Development: compiled the incident appendix in a background paper.
Electricity Supply Board, in the Republic: the southern record. The 1988 paper gave no cost estimate for it.
Parliament: received terrorist-related criminal-damage compensation figures as annual totals by year of settlement. The published figures gave no breakdown by type of property.
AG-022.gap: The record was split by the border (NIE and ESB) and by function (engineering, policing, compensation). The joined incident list existed only as an internal departmental appendix prepared for a policy decision. Because the compensation statistics aggregated all terrorist-related criminal damage, the cost of attacks on utilities could not be separated.
AG-022.joining: The Department of Economic Development joined the NIE and RUC records in 1988 and concluded that 'there is no effective means of protecting a long line over open country from terrorist attack'. The attacker was named as PIRA throughout. NIE accepted that the RUC could not recommend restoration, while keeping the question under review. The campaign's effect, a severed link and an isolated grid, was public; its cost and incident count were not.
AG-022.harm_found_later: The economic harm of the outage (foregone savings of about £2.5 million a year to NIE) appeared only in the internal costing. No compensation or incident statistic shows it.

AG-023.summary: A Yugoslav Airlines (JAT) DC-9 flying from Stockholm via Copenhagen to Zagreb and Belgrade broke up over Czechoslovakia, killing 27 of the 28 aboard. One flight attendant, Vesna Vulović, survived. The investigation found that 'the cause of the accident was total destruction of the aircraft by explosion of the explosive placed in carried luggage,' and the bombing was officially attributed to Croatian nationalists. In 2009 two German journalists argued that the plane had probably been shot down by the Czechoslovak air force. In October 2024 the Swedish TV4 program Kalla fakta reported that the Yugoslav security service had named seven Croatian nationalists as responsible, three of them still alive in Sweden.
AG-023.records:
Czechoslovak investigation: found the probable cause to be an explosive device in checked luggage, which exploded in the forward cargo hold.
Czech civil aviation authority: its files, released only gradually.
Yugoslav State Security Service (UDBA): documents naming Josip Senić of the Croatian Revolutionary Brotherhood among those responsible. They were never made public in Yugoslavia.
Kvällsposten, a Swedish newspaper: an anonymous telephone warning about the bomb. It came from a man who admitted the call in the 2024 documentary.
Swedish prosecutors: said in 2024 that the crime had been time-barred in Sweden since 1997.
Czech accident-investigation institute and Czech police: each holds part of the record.
AG-023.gap: Four states on both sides of the Cold War divide were involved: the investigation, the intelligence on suspects and the departure airports lay in Czechoslovakia, Sweden, Denmark and non-aligned Yugoslavia. The Yugoslav security-service files stayed closed. The gradual release of Czech files left room for journalists in 2009 to argue that the bomb story covered a mistaken shoot-down.
AG-023.joining: In January 2009 the ARD radio correspondent Peter Hornung and the aviation journalist Tim van Beveren argued that the bomb story had been spread by Czechoslovak and Yugoslav intelligence. They made the argument after about 18 months of interviews and file research. Hornung said his thesis rested on indications, since key documents had been destroyed. In October 2024 Kalla fakta, drawing on UDBA documents, named seven suspects. The Swedish chief prosecutor said prosecution might be possible in the victims' countries of citizenship. Vladimír Plos, head of the Czech accident-investigation institute, referred the case to the Czech police. No court joined the records.

AG-024.summary: During the American bombing of North Vietnam in 1972, Hanoi reported repeated attacks on the dike system that protects the Red River delta. It claimed 173 raids against the dikes since April, with direct hits at 149 locations. On 28 July the Nixon administration, answering Soviet accusations of a deliberate campaign, released a CIA report. The report found that bombing had caused accidental minor damage at 12 locations and that the dikes were not the intended targets. The French geographer Yves Lacoste combined firsthand observation in the delta with mapping of the damage. He argued that the strikes followed a strategy meant to produce an apparently natural disaster in the flood season while making deliberate intent impossible to prove.
AG-024.records:
North Vietnamese authorities: damage recorded site by site, with published counts of raids and hits.
CIA: assessed the damage for the Nixon administration. The administration made the assessment public.
Lacoste: damaged points recorded on the ground. He mapped them against the delta's physical and human geography.
AG-024.gap: The two parties counted the same campaign at different scales, 149 locations against 12. The American assessment classified each hit as accidental. The significance of a given breach depended on the segment and the flood season, which a count of hits does not capture. The United States held the strike records and the damage assessment and was also the accused party.
AG-024.joining: Lacoste, an academic outsider with no authority over any of the records, joined the dispersed damage reports with the geography of the delta and argued that the pattern showed a deliberate strategy. According to Bowd and Clayton, his exposé shaped opposition to the war and the wider debate on political lying. The American assessment of July 1972 classified the damage as minor and accidental.

AG-025.summary: Under the name New World Liberation Front (NWLF), bombers claimed about 70 bombings in the San Francisco Bay Area between 1974 and 1978 and were believed responsible for 26 more elsewhere in Northern California. Among their targets, alongside business offices, hotels, clubs and politicians, utility companies were a favorite. In August 1978, for example, the NWLF claimed a molotov cocktail attack on a Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E) facility in Berkeley. In June 1983 Ronald Huffman was federally indicted for conspiring to commit 16 bombings between 1973 and 1978 against politicians, power stations and oil companies.
AG-025.records:
Utilities and other targets: the damage.
The news organizations and television stations: the claims. Among them was KPIX newsfilm of the claimed attack on a PG&E facility on Grove Street in Berkeley, 15 August 1978.
FBI: an inquiry into ties between Huffman and the group, reported in January 1980.
A grand jury and federal prosecutors: the 1983 indictment.
Later compilers: counts that differ. They give about 70 claimed bombings in the Bay Area, 30 over seven years according to John Wolf, and 16 in the indictment.
AG-025.gap: Each attack was claimed and so recognized, but the claim label joined the incidents under one name without establishing who made them. The counts of the campaign differ between sources by more than half. Authorship was tied to an individual only years later.
AG-025.joining: The attackers' own claims had joined the incidents under a name that did not identify their authors. The federal indictment of June 1983 joined 16 bombings to Huffman.

AG-026.summary: A bomb exploded at LaGuardia Airport at about 6:30 p.m. on 29 December 1975, killing 11 people and injuring about 75. It was most likely in a coin-operated public locker next to the TWA and Delta baggage claim area. A caller to UPI claimed the bombing for the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO), whose spokesmen denied any role. The FAA reported that no claim had been validated. The FBI and NYPD questioned the Croatian nationalist Zvonko Bušić, who hijacked a TWA flight from LaGuardia in September 1976. A federal grand jury examined his ties to the bombing without filing charges. The case remains an open, unsolved homicide.
AG-026.records:
NYPD: led the investigation under Deputy Chief Edwin Dreher. Dreher took the case file home when he retired in 1983.
FBI: its role was first described as 'informal' because there were no indications of terrorist activity. Its New York field office later supplied hundreds of agents.
ATF: examined debris with the NYPD and FBI.
Army ordnance specialists: began reconstructing the device in January 1976.
FAA: issued an alert to airlines and airports that night. It judged that the incident revealed no weakness in existing security procedures.
Port Authority: the property on which jurisdictional questions arose at the scene.
A government and industry review group led by the FAA Administrator: in place from 30 December 1975. Its records are at the Ford Presidential Library.
A federal grand jury.
UPI: the anonymous claim.
AG-026.gap: Under NYPD leadership, the FBI, the ATF, the FAA and the Port Authority each held part of the scene and the record. The FBI's early role was informal because nothing pointed to terrorism. With no validated claim, leads spread across 38 states and three countries. The task force of 120 investigators shrank to several detectives, and the case file left official custody with the retiring commander.
AG-026.joining: In 1983 an FBI agent reassigned to the case found nothing of substance linking Bušić or anyone else to the bombing. The records were never joined into an attribution. When the journalist Elon Green asked the agencies about the case in 2026, none replied; he reassembled it from archival and press records.

AG-027.summary: On 6 October 1976 a bomb brought down a Cubana DC-8 after take-off from Barbados, killing all 73 aboard. Two Venezuelans who reportedly worked for the Caracas security firm of the Cuban exile Luis Posada Carriles, Freddy Lugo and Hernán Ricardo Lozano, were arrested. A Venezuelan judge issued warrants for them, for Posada and for Orlando Bosch, head of the exile coalition CORU. Declassified CIA and FBI records published in 2005 showed advance reporting of exile plans to bomb a Cubana airliner.
AG-027.records:
Venezuelan courts: the warrants and the prosecution of Posada and Bosch, who were arrested in Caracas.
CIA: a report of 22 June 1976 on 'possible plans of Cuban exile extremists to blow up a Cubana airliner'. The agency had been in occasional contact with Posada as an informant until June 1976.
FBI's legal attaché in Caracas: several contacts with one of the Venezuelans who placed the bomb. The attaché gave him a US visa five days before the bombing.
FBI: a report of 7 October 1976 saying a source had all but admitted that Posada and Bosch engineered the bombing. A cable of 21 October said sources reported that CORU was responsible.
Secretary of State Kissinger: received an 18 October 1976 report saying a CIA source had heard Posada say in late September, 'We are going to hit a Cuban airliner.'
AG-027.gap: Because the attack was obvious and single, it was recognized at once. The prior warnings sat in US intelligence files, whose declassified versions give no indication that the CIA alerted Cuban authorities. The US agencies' identification of the likely planners also stayed in classified reporting. The prosecutions ran in Venezuela, from whose prison Posada escaped in 1985.
AG-027.joining: The National Security Archive published the CIA, FBI and State Department records in 2005, while Posada was detained in Miami and seeking asylum.

AG-028.summary: From 1977 ETA attacked the Lemóniz nuclear plant, under construction near Bilbao for the private utility Iberduero, as well as the utility's towers and transformers. A bomb at the plant killed two workers, Andrés Guerra and Alberto Negro, and a 1979 bomb in the turbine area killed Ángel Baños, a contractor's employee. ETA kidnapped chief engineer José María Ryan on 29 January 1981, demanded that the plant be dismantled, and killed him. His body was found on 6 February. On 5 May 1982, the day the Basque public company formed to manage the plant was constituted, ETA killed project director Ángel Pascual Múgica. Work on the nearly finished plant was abandoned in 1984 under the National Energy Plan of the González government.
AG-028.records:
Iberduero: losses of over $400 million claimed for 1981 on the halted project.
The press: nearly 100 ETA bomb attacks on Iberduero transformers and installations by May 1982. These caused blackouts and $30 million in repair costs.
ETA: communiqués, including the 'sentence' on Ryan and the announcement of a 'new front' against Iberduero's senior staff linked to Lemóniz.
Basque Government: received managing control of the plant without ownership, under an agreement signed on 22 March 1982.
The central government: the 1984 energy plan and compensation to Iberduero.
AG-028.gap: There was no gap in recognition: ETA claimed its attacks and announced its aims. The accounts diverge on the outcome. The project was formally abandoned under the government's 1984 energy plan, while a 2024 El Español column calls Lemóniz the most visible monument of an ETA victory.
AG-028.joining: ETA's communiqués attributed the attacks. The state's response in 1982 moved management of the plant from the utility to a Basque public company. The central government's 1984 energy plan ended the project. In the sources checked, no official body attributed the project's end to the campaign.
AG-028.harm_found_later: According to a study by Josu Ugarte cited in El Español, electricity consumers paid the more than €2.1 billion cost of the abandoned plant through their bills, under a compensation commitment to Iberduero that ran until 2016.

AG-029.summary: On the evening of 8 January 1977 three bombs exploded in Moscow, one in a Metro carriage and two at grocery stores on 25th October Street, killing seven people and injuring 37. After a KGB investigation, the Supreme Court of the USSR convicted three Armenians, Stepan Zatikyan, Akop Stepanyan and Zaven Bagdasaryan, of sabotage on 24 January 1979 and sentenced them to death. On 31 January the court announced that the case had been heard 'in open session' and that the sentence had been carried out. Andrei Sakharov warned of 'a deliberate frame-up or a judicial mistake' and asked for a new inquiry. The Moscow Helsinki Group recorded that the trial was closed and that Zatikyan was said to have been outside Moscow at the time.
AG-029.records:
KGB Moscow City and Region administration: opened the case on 8 January 1977.
KGB Investigation Department: took the case over in November 1977.
Armenian KGB: its operative group captured the suspects in early November 1977, after they abandoned a bag of explosive devices at Moscow's Kursk Station on 30 October. Its chairman reported 750 victims and witnesses questioned, 140 expert examinations and more than 100 searches.
Supreme Court judgment: fingerprints on items in the bag, a handwritten circuit diagram, and damage to the Moscow Metro assessed at 23,649 rubles.
Izvestia: a letter of 8 February 1979 giving '44 people including seven dead' as victims and attacking Sakharov.
The samizdat Chronicle of Current Events and the Moscow Helsinki Group (Document No. 81): recorded that relatives were not told of the trial. They also recorded that witnesses known to the Chronicle did not identify the objects shown to them and that Zatikyan was said to have an alibi.
AG-029.gap: One security service held the whole official record, released almost none of it and was itself suspected by critics. The trial was closed although announced as open. The only independent record was samizdat, which had no access to the case file.
AG-029.joining: The KGB and the Supreme Court joined the records into a conviction and named three Armenian nationalists. Sakharov's letter to Brezhnev of 30 January 1979, asking for the executions to be halted and a new inquiry ordered, received no official answer.

AG-030.summary: An anthrax epidemic first recognized in Nkai District, Matabeleland, in November 1978 spread through much of the country during the war, affecting cattle and people. J. C. A. Davies published the human case series in the Central African Journal of Medicine between 1982 and 1985. Meryl Nass, an American physician living in Zimbabwe, argued in 1992 that the epidemic had been spread deliberately. A 2016 reanalysis, which estimated 17,199 human cases and 171,990 infected cattle, left both a natural and a deliberate hypothesis open.
AG-030.records:
District hospitals: the human cases. They included over 500 at Nkai Hospital from January 1979 to October 1980, 712 at Beatrice Road Infectious Diseases Hospital in Salisbury from January 1980 to June 1982, and five fatal meningitis cases among 18 at Parirenyatwa General Hospital.
Davies's case series: the text reports 10,738 cases and about 200 deaths. The provincial tables total 17,068 cases and 101 deaths.
The 2016 authors: found no surviving bovine anthrax records for 1978 to 1980. They found only scattered figures, such as more than 5,000 cattle deaths in Lupane.
Stuart Hargreaves, head of veterinary services in Rhodesia and then Zimbabwe: ascribed the rise in cases to broken fences and halted vaccination.
Special Branch of the police and the Selous Scouts: separately, documents that record a poisoning program from 1977. One, dated 24 June 1977, records 809 deaths from poisoned items.
Gould and Folb: the Special Branch officer who ran the program told them that he could not verify the kill claims.
AG-030.gap: Human cases were recorded hospital by hospital in wartime, under a government whose security forces ran a covert poisoning program. The cattle cases belonged to a veterinary service whose records for the key years did not survive. The security service kept its record of the poisoning program apart from both. Nass's claim of deliberate spread was published fourteen years after the epidemic began; the 2016 reanalysis came thirty-eight years after it began.
AG-030.joining: Individual researchers joined the health, veterinary and security records, which no official inquiry brought together. Nass did so in 1992, toward a deliberate-release claim. In 2002 Chandré Gould and Peter Folb reported a former Special Branch officer's account that anthrax had once been deployed and called for a thorough investigation. Wilson and colleagues in 2016 kept both hypotheses and noted that nothing further had been offered in support of the deliberate one. In 2017 Glenn Cross judged the epidemic highly consistent with natural occurrence, propagated almost certainly by wartime conditions. No authority has named an attacker for the epidemic.
AG-030.harm_found_later: The cattle losses cannot be recovered, because the veterinary record for the epidemic years is gone and the 2016 cattle estimate rests on an assumed ratio of human cases to infected carcasses. The poisoning program's deaths survive only in its own partial documents, whose kill claims its commander could not verify.

AG-031.summary: Five Dutch children in Haarlem and Maastricht were hospitalized after eating Jaffa oranges injected with mercury. Dutch police found 14 poisoned oranges in a batch of 220. A group calling itself the Arab Revolutionary Army-Palestinian Command claimed credit in a letter to the Dutch health ministry, saying the aim was to damage the Israeli economy and "not to kill innocent people". A separate letter attributed to the PLO said "oppressed Palestinian workers" had poisoned the fruit. Threat letters went to 18 European countries where Israeli produce was sold. The West German health ministry banned sales of Israeli citrus pending an investigation.
AG-031.records:
Dutch police: the count of poisoned fruit.
Dutch hospitals: the five poisoning cases.
West German health ministry: several consumer complaints. It issued the sales ban.
One of the largest Dutch supermarket chains: sent all its Jaffa oranges for laboratory inspection.
Some buyers: returned fruit with puncture marks.
Israeli Citrus Marketing Board: worked with the Israeli embassy and the Dutch authorities. It argued that the injection had occurred in the Netherlands because injected fruit would have rotted before reaching Europe.
AG-031.gap: Almost nothing kept the records apart: the claim letters reached governments within days of the clinical cases, and puncture marks made the contamination visible to buyers. The Israeli Citrus Marketing Board argued the question of where along the chain the fruit was injected. The sources consulted do not record how it was settled.
AG-031.joining: By writing to the Dutch health ministry and to 18 countries, the claimants joined the records themselves. Publicity closed the gap within days.

AG-032.summary: In a West Berlin speech in September 1981, Secretary of State Alexander Haig charged that Soviet-backed Laotian and Vietnamese forces were waging toxin warfare. The charge covered Hmong fighters and villages in Laos, as well as Khmer Rouge forces and villages in Cambodia. Haig set out the charge in a detailed report to Congress the following March. Secretary George Shultz repeated it in November 1982 in a further report to Congress and to UN member states. A UN group of experts could not reach a final conclusion in 1981 and reported in December 1982 that the accusations could not be proven, while citing circumstantial evidence suggestive of possible use. Matthew Meselson, who obtained samples from American officials in 1983, found large amounts of hollowed-out pollen native to Southeast Asia and no significant excess of mycotoxins on yellow-rain-covered leaves. He proposed that the material was bee feces, an explanation a 1989 field study of bee defecation flights supported. The United States never withdrew the charge.
AG-032.records:
US Embassy in Bangkok: reported Hmong accounts to the Secretary of State in a telegram of 2 September 1978 ('Hmong Refugees Escape Description'). Its later telegrams to the Defense Intelligence Agency and the State Department carried interview summaries, sample reports and the quarterly reports of a CBW field team chief through 1985.
Meselson and Julian Perry Robinson: reviewed the record. They found that the investigation had not used reliable methods of witness interrogation or of forensic laboratory investigation, that contrary findings had been dismissed or withheld, and that there had been no independent review.
Outside scientists: received the documents through Freedom of Information Act releases from 1986.
AG-032.gap: Witness accounts and laboratory results came from different bodies and were judged inside the accusing government, without independent review. The contrary findings were set aside. Meselson's team found that the original interviewers had asked leading questions. The team attributed most of the reported illness to dysentery and nutritional deficiencies in the refugee camps.
AG-032.joining: The State Department joined refugee testimony and a selection of laboratory results into a public attack claim naming the Soviet Union. The claim was undone by academic scientists working from samples and from documents released under the Freedom of Information Act. No authority adjudicated; the allegation was left standing on the official record.

AG-033.summary: The TRC found that the short-term strategy for Angola adopted by South Africa's State Security Council in March 1979 called for attacks on roads, bridges, rail networks and airfields in the south. It found that the attacks were to be of such a nature that the targets could not be used again for the rapid deployment of Angolan forces. The TRC also found that this strategy rendered the Benguela railway, which linked southern Angola with the central African interior, inoperative for ten to fifteen years. The SADF attacked petroleum facilities as well, including the Luanda oil refinery (30 November 1981) and storage tanks at Huambo (1987). On 21 May 1985 a 4 Reconnaissance commando unit was intercepted attempting to sabotage the Cabinda Gulf Oil complex. Its commander, Captain Wynand du Toit, was captured. The TRC cited UNICEF estimates that at least 100,000 Angolans died in 1980–85, mainly from war-related famine, and that 333,000 Angolan children died of unnatural causes between 1981 and 1988.
AG-033.records:
Angolan government: the economic cost of war damage, estimated at US$12 billion for 1987 alone.
UNICEF: mortality estimates.
Angolan forces: captured du Toit.
Angolan sources: described the mission's aim as blowing up the Cabinda oil facilities.
State Security Council and SADF: strategy documents and operations, with few archival holdings surviving on the surrogate operations.
TRC.
AG-033.gap: The damage figures in the sources checked, the Angolan government's US$12 billion for 1987 and UNICEF's mortality estimates, do not separate SADF operations from UNITA's insurgency. UNICEF's categories, 'war-related famine' and 'unnatural causes', name no attacker. The strategy that tied the sabotage together sat in South African security documents. The Cabinda raid shows the opposite case: one target and a captured officer exposed the operation at once. The accounts of the mission's purpose still differed, one describing it as an operation to confirm the existence of ANC and SWAPO bases.
AG-033.joining: When du Toit was captured in May 1985, the Cabinda attempt was attributed to South Africa immediately. In 1998 the TRC joined the 1979 SSC strategy to the record of destroyed railways and fuel installations. It placed UNICEF's mortality figures beside them without apportioning the deaths among the parties.
AG-033.harm_found_later: Deaths from the collapse of transport, food distribution and health services exist only as UNICEF reconstructions: 100,000 deaths in 1980–85 and 333,000 child deaths in 1981–88. No source checked attributes a share of them to the infrastructure campaign.

AG-034.summary: In December 1979 the Ethiopian government launched its principal counterinsurgency campaign in the southeast. An RRC reconnaissance team visited Harerghe in February–March 1980 and released its findings three months later, when the government began appealing in June 1980 for relief for 'victims of drought.' The report attributed the destruction of water facilities (pumping machines taken away and 40 supply points destroyed) to Somalis in the war of 1977/8. It did not mention the destruction of infrastructure and wells by the Ethiopian army. UN missions in May–June and July 1980 recommended food aid through the RRC and support for villagization. In November 1980 the RRC itself reported the food supply situation in Bale, Harerghe and Sidamo as 'normal.'
AG-034.records:
RRC Early Warning and Planning Service: the reconnaissance report of June 1980 and the food supply forecast of November 1980.
Two UN missions and the UN Coordinating Committee for Relief and Rehabilitation: each held part of the record.
ICVA mission (dated early 1981 in Africa Watch's text and January 1982 in its footnote): noted 'tight security dispositions' in the villages. It did not question the official explanation of protection from 'bandits'.
UNHCR: assistance rising from $100,000 in 1979 to $2.7 million in 1980 and $7.3 million in 1981.
Victoria Brittain, a journalist: interviewed refugees in Somalia in May 1980. The refugees all denied that drought was the reason for their flight and spoke of violence and destruction by the Ethiopian army.
AG-034.gap: According to Africa Watch, the government denied the existence of the war between 1978 and 1988 and never allowed independent access to war zones. By the same account, it blamed displacement in vague terms on the 1977/8 war and on drought. The national recorder classified displacement under drought and attributed water losses to the previous enemy. The UN and voluntary agencies worked inside that classification. A journalist in Somalia held the refugees' account.
AG-034.joining: In its 1991 report Africa Watch joined the RRC documents, the UN mission reports, the timing of military operations and the refugee testimony, attributing the displacement to counterinsurgency by the Ethiopian army.
AG-034.harm_found_later: The harm from destroyed wells and forced relocation into villages is recorded only as drought relief and villagization statistics. No count separates it.

AG-035.summary: A suitcase holding about 23 kg of explosive, left in the second-class waiting room of Bologna Centrale station, exploded on 2 August 1980, killing 85 people and injuring more than 200. On 13 January 1981 officers and collaborators of the military intelligence service SISMI planted a suitcase with the same explosive and a fake dossier, 'Terrore sui treni,' on the Taranto–Milan train. The aim was to point investigators toward an international plot by two foreign right-wing extremists. On 23 November 1995 the Court of Cassation confirmed the life sentences of the NAR members Valerio Fioravanti and Francesca Mambro for the bombing. It also confirmed the misdirection convictions of Licio Gelli, head of the P2 lodge, the SISMI officers Pietro Musumeci and Giuseppe Belmonte, and Francesco Pazienza. Luigi Ciavardini's conviction became final in 2007. In 2022 the Bologna Corte d'Assise sentenced Paolo Bellini to life imprisonment and found that Gelli and the intelligence official Federico Umberto D'Amato had contributed to the attack.
AG-035.records:
Bologna prosecutors and the DIGOS police: issued 28 arrest warrants against far-right militants by late August 1980.
The telephone claims of responsibility: first in the name of the Nuclei Armati Proletari, then in the name of the neo-fascist NAR. The claims were later contradicted.
SISMI: the planted suitcase and fake dossier.
The courts: first-instance conviction 1988, acquittal on appeal 1990, annulment 1992, retrial 1994 and final judgment 1995, with Ciavardini passing through the juvenile courts to 2007. Gilberto Cavallini was sentenced to life at first instance in 2020, and Bellini was acquitted in 1992 and convicted in 2022.
Raymond Hill, a British informant: reported that a neo-fascist had announced an imminent attack about four months before the bombing. The police held this lead from 1985 and lost it through a transcription error in the name.
Harald Polzer, a tourist: an amateur film shot at the station.
The association of victims' families: its lawyers took part in the Bellini trial.
AG-035.gap: The bombing was recognized as an attack quickly. The gap concerned attribution, which an intelligence service widened deliberately by injecting false records into the investigation. An informant's report pointing to the neo-fascist milieu was lost under a misspelled name. Courts and the head of state put forward competing attributions. The question of who ordered the attack stayed open for four decades.
AG-035.joining: The courts joined the records over successive trials. On 23 November 1995 the Court of Cassation confirmed the core convictions and the misdirection convictions. The 2022 first-instance judgment against Bellini relied on the tourist's film and on the retraction by his former wife, Maurizia Bonini, of the alibi she had given him. In July 2021 she testified that she recognized him in the film. The judgment's written reasons, reported in April 2023, described a covert intelligence network centered on Gelli and D'Amato. In 1991 President Francesco Cossiga blamed Palestinians for the bombing.

AG-036.summary: The 1983–85 famine in northern Ethiopia was officially ascribed to drought. Africa Watch's 1991 report found that widespread drought occurred only some months after the famine was already under way. It found that the government's counterinsurgency strategy was 'the prime culprit'. In the report's account, the strategy's elements were offensives into the surplus-producing districts of Tigray, the bombing of marketplaces, and bans on the movement of petty traders and migrant laborers, which stopped surplus grain from reaching deficit areas. Hausien, the most important market in northeast Tigray, was bombed repeatedly until it was destroyed in June 1988, when an estimated 1,800 marketgoers were killed. The report estimated a minimum of 400,000 famine deaths in the north and attributed something over half of that mortality to human rights abuses.
AG-036.records:
Relief and Rehabilitation Commission, a government body: figures for those 'in need', based on village reports in government-held areas and gross estimates elsewhere, with a Tigray total of exactly one million in 1983. It kept publishing bulletins while all famine news was suppressed in the domestic media from June to September 1984.
FAO: satellite imagery of vegetation and ground surveys. The report notes that these cannot evaluate war, trade disruption or taxation.
UN and other institutions: a commonly quoted figure of one million famine deaths. The report says it has 'absolutely no scientific basis'.
Relief agencies on both sides of the front line: their caseloads. They included the Relief Society of Tigray (REST), working with the TPLF.
AG-036.gap: Relief agencies measured caseloads; the RRC and FAO measured crops, rainfall and need. The UN quoted a death figure without an inquiry. Each recorder counted within its own category. None of these categories registers a bombed market or a trade ban as a cause of hunger. According to Africa Watch, the government denied the existence of the war between 1978 and 1988 and never allowed independent access to the war zones. In Africa Watch's account, the main national recorder belonged to the government whose army was causing the shortages.
AG-036.joining: In 1991, after the government's fall, Africa Watch joined production and price records with the timing and location of military offensives as well as of restrictions.
