It named the Ethiopian government. It worked mainly from interviews with refugees and other Ethiopians abroad and from secondary sources. The report called for an investigative commission of the new government to complete the record. Africa Watch also stated that a proper demographic investigation of 1983–85 famine mortality was no longer possible. In the sources checked, no official body adopted the finding.
AG-036.harm_found_later: According to Africa Watch, the commonly quoted one million deaths had no scientific basis. The share attributable to government abuses, over half of at least 400,000, exists only in Africa Watch's reconstruction.

AG-037.summary: On the night of 31 May–1 June 1980 two MK Special Operations teams placed limpet mines on fuel tanks at Sasol I and Natref in Sasolburg and at Sasol II in Secunda. They destroyed eight tanks, with damage estimated at R66 million. On 18–19 December 1982 four limpet mines planted by Rodney Wilkinson, who worked at the site, exploded at the Koeberg nuclear power station, then under construction, two in each of the two containment buildings. They damaged electrical cables and other equipment. The ANC claimed the attack in a statement from Dar es Salaam on 19 December. The Minister of Minerals and Energy, Piet du Plessis, insisted there was 'absolutely no danger of radio-active pollution'. The enriched uranium stored on site was beyond the reach of the bombs.
AG-037.records:
Police: detained Sasol employee Patrick Chamusso after the 1980 attack, although he had no part in it.
The cabinet and State Security Council: met urgently after Koeberg.
Eskom: its former chief executive, Ian McRae, said its investigations showed a possible link to the Baader-Meinhof group, which could not be confirmed.
SASRIA: the political-risk insurance pool formed by South African insurers in February 1979, with the state as reinsurer of last resort.
ANC: communiqués. One claimed a July 1982 fire at Koeberg that plant management rejected.
The press: damage and delay estimates.
TRC Amnesty Committee: amnesty to Wilkinson and Heather Gray, 31 May 1999. It also issued decision AC/2001/003 on the Special Operations Unit, including the Sasol attacks.
AG-037.gap: Claimed, conspicuous attacks on single sites left little to join. The records diverged on cost and on the bomber: in 1982 the Koeberg damage was projected at R450–500 million with up to ten months' delay, while a 1999 report gave almost R500 million and 18 months. The bomber's identity became public only in 1995.
AG-037.joining: ANC claims attributed the attacks at once. The parliamentary opposition called for an independent inquiry into Koeberg. The TRC amnesty process in 1999–2000 added operational detail and found the Sasol attacks politically motivated and directed at what were considered legitimate targets.

AG-038.summary: During Mozambique's civil war the oil pipeline from Beira to Zimbabwe, the Beira railway and the Cahora Bassa transmission network to South Africa were attacked repeatedly, with RENAMO as the visible author. South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission later found that SADF Special Forces operatives blew up the fuel storage tanks at Beira in March 1982. It also found that South Africa took over responsibility for RENAMO in March 1980, supplying it through the SADF's Directorate of Special Tasks (DST), and that a parallel operation (Drama) recruited and trained Zimbabweans for sabotage of infrastructure. The TRC cited official records showing that the pipeline was ruptured in attacks 37 times between 1982 and 1987, with an estimated loss of over ten million liters of fuel. It reported that RENAMO sabotaged the Beira railway on average once a week between February 1986 and September 1987. The Commission found the Cabora Bassa network so frequently sabotaged that it was inoperative for more than a decade.
AG-038.records:
Mozambican authorities: official records of pipeline ruptures and fuel lost.
Hidroeléctrica de Cahora Bassa: owner of the HVDC link to the Apollo station near Johannesburg. It recorded a long-term service interruption from 1985 to 1997.
The Gorongosa diaries, found in 1985: continued SADF involvement with RENAMO after the 1984 Nkomati Accord, including secret visits by South Africa's Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs.
SADF and DST files: the SADF liaison point told the TRC that DST had destroyed them when it closed in the early 1990s. The military archives held one file on Drama and a file on Operation Mila recording monthly supply drops to RENAMO through 1983.
AG-038.gap: The pipeline operator, the railway, the power utility and the Mozambican state each logged incidents under RENAMO's name. The sponsor's part sat in compartmented military files outside any civilian recorder's reach. After the Nkomati Accord, as Craig Williamson told the TRC, an official project became a covert one. The TRC found that the cabinet and the State Security Council appear to have been kept unaware of the continuing support. No institution with access to both the damage records and the operational files existed until the TRC, by which time most of the files had been destroyed.
AG-038.joining: The Gorongosa diaries tied South Africa to RENAMO in 1985. Foreign Minister Pik Botha later confirmed their authenticity to the TRC. From SANDF submissions, testimony, information from a former DST aide and the surviving files, the TRC named SADF Special Forces for the 1982 Beira tank attack and DST as the office running RENAMO. In its report of October 1998 it set these findings beside the Mozambican damage counts.
AG-038.harm_found_later: The sources checked count ruptures, liters lost, weekly railway sabotage and years of outage. None estimates the harm to the people in Mozambique and Zimbabwe who depended on the corridor's fuel and power.

AG-039.summary: A bomb of about 15 to 20 kilograms of explosive went off at about 9:50 p.m. on 21 February 1981 at the RFE/RL building in Munich, next to the Czechoslovak service. It caused more than $2 million in damage and injured four employees and, by one account, two neighbors. Stasi and Hungarian records opened after the end of communist rule show that Carlos's group planned the attack at a meeting in Budapest on 14 October 1980, in a safe house provided by Hungarian intelligence. They also show that the explosives were to come from a Romanian intelligence officer and that senior Securitate officers congratulated Carlos afterward. Romanian secret police archives reportedly indicate that Ceaușescu ordered the bombing.
AG-039.records:
West German police: the scene, including a Ford with French plates and five hand grenades abandoned about 200 meters away.
RFE/RL: the damage and injury record.
Hungarian state security: found Johannes Weinrich's notes in a flat used by the group. It sent copies to the Stasi in April 1981.
Stasi: files on the group, including a top-secret report of 28 April 1981 on a detainee in Munich who had known of the planned attack.
AG-039.gap: Within two months of the attack the planning record existed, held by Warsaw Pact services that had sheltered the perpetrators. The West German investigators held the scene. The two halves of the record stayed apart until the archives opened after 1989.
AG-039.joining: After the archives opened, German prosecutors and writers working from them, among them Richard Cummings for RFE/RL, joined the scene record with Stasi and Hungarian files. Helmut Voigt was put on trial in 1994 for his support of the Carlos group. Weinrich was arrested in Yemen and extradited to Germany in 1995 to face charges that included the RFE/RL attack. Cummings wrote in 2020 that no one had been prosecuted for the bombing.

AG-040.summary: Project Coast, a secret chemical and biological warfare program of the South African Defence Force, was established in 1981, renamed Project Jota in 1992 and officially ended in 1995. Its alleged uses against opponents entered the public record only after apartheid. Among them was the state's case that three police officers poisoned the Reverend Frank Chikane in 1989 with paraoxon obtained from a project researcher, André Immelman. These alleged uses became public through documents seized after the 1997 arrest of the project officer, Wouter Basson, through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's hearing of 8 June to 31 July 1998, and through Basson's criminal trial. The Pretoria High Court acquitted Basson on 11 April 2002. The Health Professions Council of South Africa found him guilty of professional misconduct on 18 December 2013.
AG-040.records:
Stocks of drugs and chemical agents: allegedly dumped at sea on 23 January 1993.
National Intelligence Agency: after Basson's arrest, seized trunks of project documents found at an associate's home. It made them available to the TRC and the Attorney-General.
Clinicians: recorded harm without being told its cause.
Peter Folb, a pharmacologist: between 1985 and 1987 wrote to the Minister of Health and to General Neethling of the police, asking what teargas the security forces were using, because it was harming civilians. Neither replied.
AG-040.gap: Harm caused by the program was recorded by doctors without the agent's identity. The only record that could link it was secret and partly destroyed. A clinician's request to join the records went unanswered.
AG-040.joining: At its 1998 hearing the TRC joined testimony with surviving documents. After the criminal court acquitted Basson in 2002, the state's appeals failed. In 2013, after a six-year hearing, the HPCSA found that he had acted unethically in his duties as a chemical warfare expert. Chandré Gould and Peter Folb compiled the joined record for UNIDIR in 2002.
AG-040.harm_found_later: Victims of the program's covert uses became known through operators' testimony at the TRC and the trial. The court accepted that the operators had killed or tried to kill their targets but rejected their testimony implicating Basson as given under duress to save themselves from prosecution. Whether the police officers poisoned Chikane remains unknown, according to Gould and Folb.

AG-041.summary: During the Iran–Iraq War both belligerents attacked merchant ships. A tally from Lloyd's Shipping Intelligence Unit and Center for Defense Information figures counted 451 attacks from 1981 to 1987, 179 of them in 1987. In 1987 Iran laid moored contact mines: the reflagged Kuwaiti tanker Bridgeton, part of the first US-escorted convoy, struck one on 24 July. On 10 August the Texaco Caribbean struck another in the anchorage off Fujairah, the first mine encountered outside the Gulf. On 21 September 1987 US Army helicopters attacked and captured the Iranian vessel Iran Ajr, which was found to have mines on board.
AG-041.records:
Lloyd's Shipping Intelligence Unit: attack counts for 1981–1986.
Center for Defense Information: attack counts for 1986–1987. The two sources differed slightly for 1986.
Ship-attack summaries in United Nations Security Council documents: a separate series. O'Rourke compiled it as 340 ships attacked in 1984–1987 and 169 in 1987.
Shipowners and flag states: damage and casualties.
The US Navy: mine strikes.
AG-041.gap: The series disagreed: O'Rourke calls the UN count 'somewhat discrepant' and notes that 'other sources vary considerably'. He reports that some counts of deaths were two or three times as high as his UN-based figure. In the UN-based series he places 129 attacks under other or unknown weapons. Moored mines left no attacker on any record until a minelayer was caught.
AG-041.joining: When the Iran Ajr was captured with mines on board, the 1987 mining was tied to Iran at once. Navy specialists matched the serial numbers of nearby unexploded mines to those aboard. O'Rourke reports that the mining campaign 'apparently tapered off or ended in September'. In the sources checked the attack series were never reconciled into one authoritative count.
AG-041.harm_found_later: Counts of seafarers killed varied by a factor of two or three, and the UN-based series lists 47 attacks for which no casualty information was reported. The human cost of the campaign against shipping therefore remains a reconstruction.

AG-042.summary: Two members of Carlos's group, Magdalena Kopp and Bruno Breguet, were arrested in Paris on 16 February 1982. After their arrest a bomb on the Paris–Toulouse express 'Le Capitole' killed five people and wounded 28 (29 March 1982). On 31 December 1983 bombs on a Marseille–Paris TGV and at the Marseille railway station killed five more. At the later trial the prosecution alleged that Carlos had written two letters claiming the New Year's Eve 1983 attacks. On 15 December 2011 a Paris court convicted three defendants of organizing four attacks in 1982 and 1983: Carlos in person, Johannes Weinrich and Ali Kamal al-Issawi in absentia. The four attacks had killed 11 people and injured more than 140. Christa-Margot Fröhlich, living in Germany, which would not extradite her, was acquitted.
AG-042.records:
French police and investigating magistrates: an initial investigation in the 1980s and the Kopp and Breguet case.
AFP: received a telephone claim for the Marseille station bombing in the name of the 'Organisation of Armed Arab Struggle'. It also received the claim for the Capitole bombing in the name of the 'International Terrorist Friends of Carlos'.
The East German Stasi: treated Carlos as a guest of the state and kept top-secret files on the group under the code name 'Separat'.
Hungarian intelligence: provided the group a safe house in Budapest in October 1980 before moving to expel it in 1981.
The Romanian secret police: archives used in the prosecution, together with the Hungarian and East German ones.
Jean-Louis Bruguière, the anti-terrorism judge: ordered the trial.
AG-042.gap: Several attacks were claimed, and recognition was immediate. Judicial attribution waited until the main suspect was in French custody in 1994, after years in which the group had operated with support from East German and Hungarian security services. Germany's refusal to extradite one co-defendant kept part of the case outside French reach.
AG-042.joining: French investigating magistrates pursued the case from the 1980s. After French agents captured Carlos in Khartoum in 1994 with the help of the Sudanese government, Judge Bruguière ordered a trial. The 2011 judgment named Carlos, Weinrich and al-Issawi on a record that included files from Hungarian, East German and Romanian secret-police archives. The defense called these files unreliable.

AG-043.summary: Seven people in five communities in the Chicago area died after taking Extra-Strength Tylenol capsules laced with cyanide. The first deaths were those of 12-year-old Mary Kellerman in Elk Grove Village on 29 September 1982 and of three members of the Janus family in Arlington Heights. The deaths fell in separate municipalities, each with its own fire, police and emergency services. Two off-duty fire lieutenants and a village nurse connected the first deaths to Tylenol within about a day. Cyanide-laced capsules were found at both scenes. The manufacturer recalled an estimated 31 million bottles nationwide. James Lewis was convicted of extortion for a letter demanding $1 million from Johnson & Johnson, but no one was ever charged with the murders.
AG-043.records:
Fire and police departments of each municipality: records of their own response (Elk Grove Village, Arlington Heights, Elmhurst and others).
The Cook County Medical Examiner: a bulletin flagging multiple deaths with no known cause.
Helen Jensen, Arlington Heights village nurse: found a bottle with six capsules missing and a Jewel-Osco receipt at the Janus home. She insisted the pills were the cause.
Elmhurst detectives: collected bottles from the home of victim Mary McFarland.
Chicago's mayor: ordered Tylenol off store shelves.
Johnson & Johnson: cooperated with investigators.
The Illinois task force: formed by Attorney General Ty Fahner and the Illinois State Police, it held the investigative file. Arlington Heights police still held the file in 2023.
AG-043.gap: Because the victims were spread across five communities, each death entered a different local record as a sudden unexplained death, and no single body received all of them. David Williams, the Illinois State Police commander, later described the case as at first 'almost too big' because it spanned five cities. Sgt. Joe Murphy of the Arlington Heights police acknowledged 'communication breakdowns' as the case passed between investigators.
AG-043.joining: Lt. Philip Cappitelli of the Arlington Heights Fire Department was off duty and listening to a police radio when he heard of three deaths at one address. From his mother-in-law he learned that a coworker's 12-year-old daughter had died in Elk Grove Village. He called Lt. Richard Keyworth of the Elk Grove Village Fire Department. The two had colleagues read them the response reports, noted Tylenol at both scenes and passed the link to their chiefs, who informed law enforcement. Investigators then found cyanide-laced capsules at both locations. The Attorney General's task force handled more than 1,000 leads; no murderer was named.

AG-044.summary: At about 1:30 a.m. on 31 May 1982 the anarchist group Direct Action bombed BC Hydro's Cheekeye–Dunsmuir substation near Qualicum Beach on Vancouver Island. The attack used about 350 pounds of stolen dynamite and destroyed four shunt reactors, with damage put at about $4.5 million to $5 million. The group's statement ended, 'This is the best contribution we can make towards protecting the Earth.' On 14 October 1982 the group bombed a Litton Systems plant in Toronto that made guidance components for the US cruise missile, injuring ten people. On 20 January 1983 police disguised as a highway maintenance crew arrested the group's five members near Squamish.
AG-044.records:
BC Hydro: damage and repair, with work halted for more than two months.
The police: found no leads after the substation bombing despite a $125,000 reward.
Direct Action: its own communiqués.
A Globe and Mail reporter: noticed similarities between the Litton communiqué and the Vancouver newsletter Resistance.
The RCMP: surveillance and arrest.
The courts: sentences from six years to life.
AG-044.gap: The bombing had a single target and a public claim. Recognition was immediate. Attribution of the claim to persons stalled after the substation bombing and advanced only after a second attack, when a journalist matched the text of a communiqué to a local newsletter.
AG-044.joining: After a journalist joined the Litton communiqué to the newsletter, the police traced the newsletter's post office box holder. RCMP surveillance then led to the January 1983 arrests of Ann Hansen, Brent Taylor, Doug Stewart, Gerry Hannah and Julie Belmas.

AG-045.summary: From 1982 Renamo, a South African-supported rebel movement, attacked Mozambique's primary health care network, attacking health units, kidnapping and killing health workers and destroying transport. Cliff and Noormahomed (Social Science & Medicine, 1988) described these attacks as 'an integral part of South African destabilization of Mozambique'. They linked the disruption of health services to higher mortality, famine and epidemics, while finding the primary health care system 'remarkably resistant to destruction.' On 28 August 1985 Zimbabwean and Mozambican government forces stormed Renamo's Gorongosa headquarters, capturing notebooks of thousands of decoded radio messages. Mozambique's security services studied the notebooks to show that South Africa had kept supporting Renamo after the 1984 Nkomati Accord.
AG-045.records:
Mozambique's health services: attacks on health units, health workers and transport. Cliff and Noormahomed assembled these records.
Renamo: radio traffic between its commander-in-chief and regional and local groups, recording its operations. The traffic was captured as the Cadernos de Gorongosa (1983–1985).
South Africa: an undertaking in the 1984 Nkomati Accord to end support for the rebels.
AG-045.gap: Each attack hit a single health unit and was recorded as one incident of insurgent violence. The pattern of deliberate targeting of a health system, and the external sponsor, became visible only when the national record was assembled and when the insurgent's own archive fell into government hands.
AG-045.joining: Public health researchers joined the health-service records into the argument that health was a target of destabilization (1988). Mozambican security services studied the captured notebooks to show continued South African support. Historian Michel Cahen later presented the notebooks, available for consultation in Lisbon, as a research source (2021).
AG-045.harm_found_later: Deaths from disrupted preventive programs were recorded as disease deaths. Their link to the campaign rests on later analysis.

AG-046.summary: Shortly before midnight on 18 January 1982 at least five Soviet-made rockets were fired at the Superphénix fast-breeder reactor at Creys-Malville, then under construction. One contemporary report described a hole 14 inches deep in the 3.5-foot concrete containment wall. A second report counted four hits causing little damage. No one was injured. On 19 January an anonymous caller told Agence France-Presse that a 'pacifist-ecologist' had carried out the attack to delay construction. In a 2003 book the Geneva anti-nuclear activist Chaïm Nissim said he was the author of the attack, which was by then long time-barred.
AG-046.records:
The French authorities: did not make full damage details public.
The commission of inquiry: announced by the Mitterrand government.
AFP: the anonymous claim.
ARMOS, the local opposition association: said it did not advocate this form of protest.
Other antinuclear groups: condemned the attack while sympathizing with its motives.
Nissim: later, his own account.
AG-046.gap: The act was obvious and hit a single target, so it was classified as an attack at once. Attribution waited 21 years: the perpetrator lived in Geneva, about 50 km away across the Swiss border, and the claim named no organization.
AG-046.joining: Nissim had never been publicly identified when he disclosed his own role in 2003, by which time prosecution was long time-barred. In the sources checked, no authority joined the records into an attribution.

AG-047.summary: In early 1984 mines laid in or near Corinto, Puerto Sandino and El Bluff damaged ships of several flags. Among them were the Panamanian freighter Los Caribes (7 March), the Soviet tanker Lugansk (20 March), on which five crew were gravely injured, and the Japanese freighter Terushio Maru. By early April the Nicaraguan government counted 11 explosions in about 40 days, 2 dead and at least 20 injured, and its army reported three government fishing boats destroyed. Anti-Sandinista rebels claimed the mining. The US government denied involvement until CBS News and the Wall Street Journal reported on 6 April 1984 that the CIA was directing it from a mother ship. In 1986 the ICJ found that the mines had been laid by persons in the pay and acting on the instructions of the CIA, under the supervision and with the logistic support of US agents. It also found that US agents had participated in planning, directing and supporting attacks on oil installations, including the attack on Corinto of 10 October 1983.
AG-047.records:
Ship crews and the Corinto port administrator: three inbound ships in a month refused to enter and unloaded at Caldera, Costa Rica.
The Nicaraguan government and army: explosion, casualty and damaged-ship counts, seven ships by early April, and a complaint to the UN Security Council.
The Soviet government: a formal protest over the Lugansk, holding the US government responsible.
Lloyd's of London: according to local shipping agents in early April 1984, it had neither declared Nicaragua a theater of war nor raised rates.
The Nicaraguan Democratic Force (FDN): announced that the ports would continue to be mined.
The CIA: a report of more than 80 pages to Senate committee members in March 1984. It contained only a short reference to the mining.
The House Intelligence Committee: Director Casey apparently disclosed details to it.
The Senate Intelligence Committee: its chairman and vice-chairman charged that they had not been fully informed as the law required.
The ICJ: the proceedings and the 1986 judgment.
AG-047.gap: Nicaragua had the explosions and casualties, but its accusation against Washington was treated as a party's claim. Shipping agents and the insurance market registered damage and risk without a war-zone designation. The rebels' claim supplied a plausible non-state author, and the US government pointed to rebel announcements of the mining. The oversight channel that could have joined the operation to the damage received a short reference buried in a long CIA report. The chairman and vice-chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee charged that they had not been fully informed as the law required. No public warning to shipping existed, so no maritime notice recorded the minefields.
AG-047.joining: CBS News and the Wall Street Journal reported the CIA's direction of the mining on 6 April 1984, displacing the rebel explanation. The CIA declined comment. Senate Intelligence Committee chairman Barry Goldwater wrote to CIA Director Casey that the mining was 'an act violating international law' and 'an act of war,' and vice-chairman Daniel Patrick Moynihan resigned his post in protest. Nicaragua filed its application at the ICJ on 9 April 1984. In its judgment of 27 June 1986 the Court attributed the mining to the United States. It held, by fourteen votes to one, that by failing to make known the existence and location of the mines the United States had breached customary international law.
AG-047.harm_found_later: The ICJ recorded that the mines caused personal and material injury and created risks causing a rise in marine insurance rates. The refused and diverted ships imposed a cost on shippers, as well as on Nicaraguan coffee and cotton exports. In the sources checked that cost appears only in general terms.

AG-048.summary: Sendero Luminoso repeatedly bombed the transmission lines that carried power to Lima from Junín, Pasco and Huánuco, the sole source of electricity for the capital's seven million people. On one night in May 1983 police blamed Sendero for 40 bomb attacks that felled 10 electricity poles and blacked out Lima. A US Defense Intelligence Agency summary of 14 December 1988 reported that Sendero had bombed at least a dozen towers southeast of Lima on 7 December, its third such attack since 22 November. The summary added that the attacks had caused continuous outages, rationing cuts of up to 20 hours a day in some districts and shortages of drinking water. During the May 1989 'armed strike' guerrillas dynamited bridges and power pylons. They cut supplies of food, power and export minerals from the three provinces to Lima.
AG-048.records:
The national police: attack counts per night, and about 500 detained after the May 1983 blackout.
The US Defense Intelligence Agency: the summary of 14 December 1988.
The Senate commission chaired by Enrique Bernales: 2,117 'acts of terrorism' nationwide in 1989 and 1,656 in 1991, 672 of them in Lima. The vast majority were attributed to Sendero.
The foreign press: news reports.
AG-048.gap: The blackouts were public and attributed to Sendero. Recognition was immediate. The records kept the infrastructure dimension apart: the police and the Senate commission counted undifferentiated 'acts of terrorism'. The intelligence summary noted the water shortages in passing, and no consolidated count of towers, outage hours and water interruptions was located.
AG-048.joining: Attribution was never in doubt in the sources checked: the police blamed Sendero in 1983, and US intelligence attributed the 1988 tower attacks to it. No body that joined the infrastructure records was found.
AG-048.harm_found_later: The loss of drinking water and services in Lima during rationing appears only incidentally in intelligence and press records. No source located estimates the harm of the blackouts to health or livelihoods.

AG-049.summary: On 17 July 1983 the Indian newspaper Patriot, which the KGB had helped set up in 1967, published an anonymous letter claiming that AIDS resulted from US military experiments. Literaturnaya Gazeta revived the claim on 30 October 1985. The retired East German biophysicist Jakob Segal gave it pseudo-scientific form, with support from East German foreign intelligence (HVA) whose extent historians dispute. By late 1987 the story had appeared in more than 200 periodicals in 80 countries. The State Department-chaired Active Measures Working Group rebutted it. After Secretary of State George Shultz raised the matter on 23 October 1987, the Soviet Academy of Sciences disavowed the claim in Izvestia. In 1992 the head of Russian foreign intelligence, Yevgeny Primakov, confirmed the KGB's role.
AG-049.records:
The KGB and the HVA: the campaign record. About 90 percent of HVA files were destroyed or disappeared in 1989–90.
The Stasi: registered the operation as 'Denver' in July 1986.
The Active Measures Working Group: an interagency committee chaired by the State Department with CIA and USIA members. It monitored placements, contacted editors and challenged Soviet officials.
Scientific records: evidence against the claimed origin. The Soviet AIDS specialist Viktor Zhdanov reported a 1974 infection traced to blood transfusions, and the State Department cited findings that AIDS may have existed in human populations since at least 1959.
AG-049.gap: The campaign supplied a fabricated join between a natural epidemic and a foreign laboratory. The rebuttal fell to a foreign-ministry working group whose own error the campaign exploited: USIA searched for the original letter only back to January 1984. In November 1986 a State Department spokesman said no such article had appeared in Patriot. Literaturnaya Gazeta answered by reproducing it.
AG-049.joining: The attack claim was manufactured by intelligence services. The correction came from a foreign-ministry working group and from the accusing state's own academy of sciences. After the Cold War it also came from the perpetrator's successor service. Soviet media continued to repeat the claim after the academy's disavowal.

AG-050.summary: Between 21 March and 3 April 1983, 943 cases of an acute illness were recorded in the West Bank. Of these, 660 (70 percent) were girls aged 12 to 17. The outbreak began at a girls' secondary school. Jordan, Iraq and Syria told the UN Security Council that the girls had been poisoned. Israeli medical authorities found no organic cause, and a WHO inquiry could identify no specific cause. CDC, asked through the US Department of State, reported in MMWR on 29 April 1983 that clinical, epidemiological and toxicological analyses indicated a psychogenic illness induced by stress, possibly triggered by the odor of low concentrations of hydrogen sulfide near the first school.
AG-050.records:
Israeli medical authorities: the clinical inquiry, which found no organic cause.
WHO: an inquiry, reported to the Security Council (S/15756).
Franz Altherr, an ICRC physician: reportedly found no indication of poisonous agents.
CDC physicians: assembled clinical, epidemiological and toxicological analyses.
Jordan, Iraq and Syria: poisoning allegations submitted to the Security Council. Iraq named a yellow substance containing sulfur.
AG-050.gap: The clinical record lay with the health authorities of the occupying power, while the poisoning claims were made at the UN by states hostile to it. Neither side's account could therefore settle the question for the other. Israel asked international bodies for independent assessments.
AG-050.joining: CDC joined the clinical, epidemiological and toxicological records and classified the event as psychogenic. WHO found no specific cause and no reason to challenge the Israeli findings. No attacker was named. In August 1983 Israel's ambassador to the UN wrote that the Security Council had remained silent after these reports.

AG-051.summary: Early on Tuesday 11 December 1984 the Communist Combatant Cells (CCC) blew up NATO fuel pipelines in Belgium at five locations at once. The pipelines were to be used by NATO forces in a crisis, and no one was hurt. The group claimed the attacks within a series against NATO-related targets. Its threat to strike NATO headquarters outside Brussels was taken seriously by police. Justice Minister Jean Gol said, 'We can't protect every inch of the NATO pipeline.'
AG-051.records:
NATO: fuel pipelines for its forces in a crisis. It tightened security at headquarters.
Belgian police and justice officials: dragnet operations and the investigation.
The CCC: claims of responsibility.
The Brussels court of assizes: the 1988 sentences of the group's leaders.
AG-051.gap: The gap was narrow: the attacks were simultaneous, claimed and aimed at a named alliance asset. The problem lay in protection of a long linear asset with many exposed points.
AG-051.joining: The CCC joined the incidents by claiming them. The group carried out 14 attacks in Belgium in 1984 and 1985. Its four leaders, Pierre Carette, Bertrand Sassoye, Didier Chevolet and Pascale Vandegeerde, were arrested in Namur on 16 December 1985. On 21 October 1988 the Brussels court of assizes sentenced them to life imprisonment. Two firefighters died in the group's bombing of the VBO building in Brussels.

AG-052.summary: On 18 March 1984 two masked men broke into the Nishinomiya home of the president of Ezaki Glico and abducted him. He escaped three days later. The extortion campaign that followed extended to Morinaga and, by the National Police Agency's count, more than 30 companies. From 7 October 1984 the perpetrators placed 18 cyanide-laced Morinaga products at 16 supermarkets and other locations. In February 1985 more cyanide-laced sweets were found in Tokyo and Nagoya. The case ended unsolved: the NPA conceded in February 2000, as the statute of limitations on the last crimes expired, that it would arrest no suspects.
AG-052.records:
Each prefectural police force: its own file on crimes in its area, Hyogo for the kidnapping in Nishinomiya and Osaka for the confinement. The crimes spread to Kyoto, Aichi and Tokyo.
The National Police Agency: designated the series as NPA-Designated Case No. 114.
The police: released an extortion tape on 11 October and supermarket security-camera footage of a suspect on 15 October 1984.
The targeted companies: received the threats.
The stores and the police: recorded the poisoned items found on shelves.
AG-052.gap: Because the attackers announced themselves, recognition was immediate. The joining problem concerned the investigation: the crimes crossed several prefectures, each with its own police force. A senior NPA official, Yuji Aiura, later blamed caution and poor coordination between the NPA and prefectural police. Aiura added that the items left at crime scenes were mass-produced and their buyers could not be traced.
AG-052.joining: From 1984 the NPA joined the prefectural files under its designation. By 2000 about 1.3 million officer deployments, some 28,300 public tips and questioning of about 125,000 people had been recorded. No perpetrator was named. NPA chief Setsuo Tanaka said, 'It is extremely regrettable that we could not apprehend suspects.'

AG-053.summary: Between 9 July and 15 August 1984 at least 17 merchant ships were damaged by explosions attributed to mines in the Gulf of Suez and the Red Sea. Inspectors discounted two further claimed strikes because they found only internal damage. A CIA memorandum of 28 August counted nineteen damaged ships. Egypt and Saudi Arabia sought international mine countermeasures support in early August. Over several weeks 26 ships from six countries searched the Red Sea. On 12 September HMS Gavington found a Soviet-made bottom influence mine at the western edge of the southbound traffic lane leaving Suez. US and British analysts attributed the mining to the Libyan roll-on/roll-off ship Ghat. Qadhafi denied responsibility. A telephoned claim by 'Islamic Jihad' to have laid 190 mines was discounted.
AG-053.records:
Masters, owners and damage inspectors: each casualty, recorded separately. They distinguished external mine damage from internal damage.
The Suez Canal authorities: the documentation required for every shipment, foremost the Ghat's changing crew lists, which Mobley says gave the strongest direct indication of Libya's responsibility. The Ghat's declared cargo of 'agricultural machinery' for Assab was in fact 950 tons of military materiel.
UK bodies and the CIA: the UK naval attaché in Cairo, the UK embassies in Addis Ababa, Amman and Tehran, the UK Joint Intelligence Committee and Defence Intelligence Staff, and the CIA each held fragments. These were a Soviet assistant military attaché's remark in Amman that Libya was laying Soviet mines, a US report that mining with 110 or 150 mines had been discussed in Libya in late May, Iranian leaders' denials, and the ship's port call at Assab.
The Royal Navy's after-action report and the Admiralty Research Establishment at Portland: the mine exploitation results, including an activation clock set to 8 days, 19 hours.
AG-053.gap: On 9 July the first strike damaged a single Soviet-flagged ship. It was followed by 18 days without incidents, so it stood as an isolated casualty. Mobley reports that the inquiry was slowed by the delay in engaging the intelligence and military establishments in London and Washington, which then had to analyze ship movements that had taken place well before collection could be focused on the area. Only a few position points existed for the Ghat south of the canal. The light damage led analysts to expect mines with about 100-kg warheads, but the mine recovered carried 750 kg. Among the minehunting navies, a British briefing complained of a 'considerable delay' before other nations learned of the recovered mine and called coordination 'less than ideal'.
AG-053.joining: Egypt joined the canal records first: on 19 August Defence Minister Abu Ghazala told a US congressional delegation that he was '100 percent sure' Libya was responsible. He cited the timing of the Ghat's passage and the substitution of Libyan military officers for regular crew. The CIA memorandum of 28 August judged a Libyan ship the most likely minelayer but called the case 'not conclusive'. A draft of the UK Joint Intelligence Committee first stressed Iran until Ministry of Defence coordinators pushed toward Libya. UK Defence Intelligence Staff analysis placed the Ghat in the Gulf of Suez about nine days before the strikes there began, matching the recovered mine's arming delay of just under nine days. Attribution remained an intelligence assessment built on circumstantial records. In the sources checked, no international body named Libya.

AG-054.summary: At Iran's request Secretary-General Javier Perez de Cuellar appointed toxicologists from Australia, Spain, Switzerland and Sweden. Their report of 26 March 1984 concluded that mustard gas and the nerve agent tabun had been used in the war and did not identify Iraq as the source. A mission that visited Iran from 26 February to 3 March 1986 found unanimously that Iraqi forces had used chemical weapons against Iranian forces on many occasions. On 21 March 1986 the members of the Security Council strongly condemned Iraq by name (S/17932). After the attack on the Kurdish town of Halabja in 1988, in which about 5,000 Kurds were killed, the US State Department blamed Iran. Security Council resolution 612 of May 1988 blamed nobody. The Iran account was carried into a 1990 Strategic Studies Institute study. On 17 January 2010 the Iraqi High Tribunal sentenced Ali Hassan al-Majid to death for the Halabja attack.
AG-054.records:
Iran: called for the inquiry and held the casualty records.
The 1984 specialists: a report of 28 pages stating that the extent of use could not be determined within the time and resources available to them.
The 1986 team: examined sites, weapons components and numerous casualties and drew on the earlier missions of 1984 and 1985. It found that the attacks were continuing on a more intense scale.
The US State Department: its own account of Halabja, blaming Iran. US officials said the account undercut Iran's propaganda advantage at a time when Washington was pressing for an arms embargo on Iran.
The Security Council: its position in resolution 612, adopted without debate or explanation of votes in a meeting of about five minutes.
AG-054.gap: Because the missions were mandated to establish facts, the 1984 report recorded use without a user. The Council's practice varied between condemning Iraq by name in 1986 and blaming nobody in 1988. At Halabja a statement by a government then pressing for an arms embargo on Iran introduced a second suspect. Later works deflected Iraq's responsibility by relying on that account.
AG-054.joining: The Secretary-General's missions joined the battlefield medical records from 1984, and the Council named Iraq in 1986. Attribution for Halabja was settled only by a national criminal court, after the fall of the regime: the Iraqi High Tribunal convicted Ali Hassan al-Majid of crimes against humanity 22 years after the attack.

AG-055.summary: A DC-8 chartered by the Multinational Force and Observers, carrying 248 soldiers of the US 101st Airborne Division home from peacekeeping duty in the Sinai, crashed on take-off from Gander, killing all 256 aboard. Callers claiming to speak for Islamic Jihad contacted Reuters in Beirut and the US consulate in Oran. Within 36 hours an FBI team in Gander accepted a declaration that 'terrorism was not involved.' Five of the nine members of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board (CASB) found ice contamination of the wings the most probable cause. Four dissented and attributed the crash to an explosion. A review by former Supreme Court justice Willard Estey found the icing finding unsupported by the record and advised against further investigation.
AG-055.records:
The CASB: flight recorders, wreckage laid out in a grid in a Gander hangar, and the probable-cause report of 28 October 1988.
The RCMP Central Forensic Laboratory: found no explosive residue.
RCMP officers: took sworn statements from five witnesses who saw flames before the aircraft fell.
The US Army: joined the RCMP and the CASB in a second site examination from 5 January to 7 February 1986. Its recovered weapons included no military ammunition or explosive devices.
The autopsy radiographs: showed no blast or fragmentation injury patterns.
A consultant for the airline's representatives: attributed two fuselage holes to a pre-impact explosion.
A former Army customs inspector in Cairo: said he could not check the cargo because he had no pass for the tarmac.
The FBI: said Canadian authorities kept its agents from the site.
The anonymous callers: claims of responsibility.
AG-055.gap: The safety board held nearly all the physical records. The FBI, which might have tested the terrorism hypothesis, said it was kept from the site. The board then split on what the same fragments showed, and the dissent became public.
AG-055.joining: The CASB majority settled the event as non-hostile (icing), while the minority left the hostile hypothesis open. Estey found the icing finding unsupported and declined to recommend a new inquiry. In the United States, a House Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing in December 1990. Representative Robin Tallon and 103 other members of Congress asked President Bush for an investigation in 1992. No authority named an attacker.

AG-056.summary: The Caño Limón–Coveñas pipeline is owned by the Cravo Norte Association of Ecopetrol and Occidental and operated by Ecopetrol. The ELN and FARC have bombed it since soon after it began operating in December 1985. Portafolio reported in 2019 that it had been bombed a little over 1,500 times in 30 years. The volume spilled has never been settled. In 1997 the Defensoría del Pueblo analyzed 636 bombings of the country's main pipelines in 1986–96. It estimated the oil spilled in Colombia at 11 times the Exxon Valdez spill. Environment Minister Eduardo Verano De La Rosa, writing around 1998, counted 717 attacks on oil infrastructure and about two million barrels spilled. A December 2002 State Department report to Congress stated that the pipeline had been hit over 940 times since 1986, with over 11 million barrels spilled. In January 2019 an Ecopetrol spokesperson cited about 3.5 million barrels since 1985, while the same article gave 3.7 million.
AG-056.records:
Ecopetrol: counts of bombings, 89 on this line in 2018. It kept a separate count of illegal taps, 1,107 'válvulas ilícitas' across its pipelines in 2018.
The Defensoría del Pueblo: a 1997 report on 636 bombings and on contamination of named streams. It cited Ecopetrol's security coordinator's estimate that only 25 to 30 of every 100 barrels spilled were recovered.
The Ministry of the Environment: about 2,600 km of rivers and streams and 1,600 ha of wetlands affected in 70 municipalities of 13 departments. It gave farmland as 60,000 ha in one passage and 6,000 ha in another.
The US State Department: a December 2002 report under P.L. 107-206, giving 170 attacks in 2001 and 400,000 barrels spilled that year.
AG-056.gap: The ledgers each count a different unit: attacks on the line, attacks on all pipelines or all oil infrastructure, barrels spilled, barrels recovered. The theft taps are counted apart from bombings, although both release crude. In the sources checked, no agency assesses cumulative environmental damage across incidents. The Defensoría stated in 1997 that pollution problems were generally not followed up.
AG-056.joining: Across the sources checked, the cumulative spill totals run from about 2 million to over 11 million barrels. No institution has reconciled the ledgers. The Defensoría attributed most bombings to the ELN, followed by the FARC, so attribution was rarely the problem.
AG-056.harm_found_later: Damage to rivers, wetlands, fisheries and drinking-water sources accumulates across hundreds of incidents and exists only as incompatible estimates. The Defensoría documented a 1996 spill into the La Gritona stream in Cubará, Boyacá, whose water supplied a village aqueduct.

AG-057.summary: After Chernobyl and during protests against the Wackersdorf reprocessing plant and other nuclear sites, militants brought down high-voltage pylons by explosives, sawing or loosening their bolts. The militants, from the autonomist and anarchist scene, also damaged Bundesbahn signals and overhead lines across West Germany. The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) counted more than 150 actions against pylons in 1986, with about 200 masts damaged or destroyed, and more than 80 in 1987. In December 1986 the Bundestag Legal Affairs Committee recommended an Act to Combat Terrorism. The Act created a new offense of destroying important work equipment (§ 305a StGB) and placed it in the catalog of the terrorist-organization offense (§ 129a StGB).
AG-057.records:
The BfV, section on criminal damage with use of force: the pylon attacks (995 cases in 1986).
The BfV, category of 'terrorist acts': 318 in 1986, defined by the § 129a catalog of serious offenses such as murder, arson and causing explosions. It also recorded 153 dangerous interferences with rail, air or road traffic.
The BfV, damage figures: none for about 40 percent of the attacks it classed as terrorist in 1986.
The Bundestag Legal Affairs Committee: a report of 3 December 1986 with a different count. It gave 101 attacks on energy-supply installations in the preceding ten months, 92 of them on pylons.
The BfV's terrorism figures from 1987: a new line for attacks on energy-industry installations (89 in 1987, counted together with disruptions of other public utilities, and 27 in 1988). The 1987 report stated that its counting had changed because of the amendment of § 129a.
The BfV, property offenses: pylon damage, still listed separately (more than 80 in 1987, 20 in 1988, and 14 actions against pylons, power lines and substations in 1989).
AG-057.gap: Each sawn pylon was a local property offense. The terrorism category excluded sawing and unbolting, because it followed the criminal-code catalog. The catalog covered explosions and arson but left out damage done with saws and wrenches. Counts from different bodies for overlapping periods do not match. Attribution rested on claim letters and published sabotage instructions. The BfV wrote only that left-wing extremists 'come into consideration' as perpetrators of most of the actions.
AG-057.joining: Within the year the BfV joined the incident reports into national counts and linked them to instructions circulated in left-wing extremist publications. The committee majority used such counts to move the category by statute, so that attacks on energy installations became catalog offenses for terrorism proceedings. The SPD and Green minority objected to the extension. In its view the extension would draw people who were not terrorists in the proper sense into § 129a proceedings, with their checkpoints, searches, easier pretrial detention and monitoring of correspondence between detained suspects and defense counsel. The majority answered that these effects were intended.

AG-058.summary: The TRC's report records that Security Branch members staged explosions to build the credibility of informers and agents inside Umkhonto we Sizwe (MK). In 1987/88 J. H. le Roux and other Security Branch members set off a controlled explosion near an unused railway line at Factoria, Krugersdorp, and made sure the media reported it. The explosion was staged for an informer who had received MK orders to commit an attack. In other 'credibility operations' planned by the SIU, attacks on a power station and a railway line in Johannesburg were carried out with MK slogans painted at the scene. Brigadiers W. Schoon and H. Muller authorized them, and further attacks on the railways followed.
AG-058.records:
The press: reported the Factoria explosion as the police intended.
MK: the informer could then report success to it.
The Security Branch units that staged the attacks: the record of authorship.
The ANC: two lists of armed actions given to the TRC, one acknowledged and one of 'armed actions for which target category and/or responsibility is uncertain'.
The TRC Amnesty Committee: applications such as le Roux's (AM4148/96).
AG-058.gap: Outside records classified the blasts by their appearance: MK slogans and press coverage arranged by the police. The only record of authorship lay inside the units that staged the attacks. While the conflict lasted, no institution had the means or the incentive to test the attribution. The ANC's own list of uncertain actions made no distinction between civilian casualties caused by 'operational difficulties', state 'false flag operations' and acts of MK members interpreting ANC policy in their own way.
AG-058.joining: Perpetrators disclosed the operations to the TRC in amnesty applications. The ANC told the TRC that some explosions at Wimpy Bars and supermarkets in the late 1980s, generally believed to be its work, may have been state 'false flag operations'. The Commission asked the ANC for information on its uncertain cases and received no response. It found on a balance of probabilities that the uncertain operations it examined had been carried out by ANC members.

AG-059.summary: From 16 December 1988 the Provisional IRA attacked the cross-border Belfast-Dublin line with bombs and hoax calls. The attacks included a 400 lb radio-controlled device, found and defused on 28 December 1988. They also included explosions at Kilnasaggart Bridge, Silverwood Bridge and Craigmore Viaduct. On 17 February 1989 a secondary device in the same campaign injured a British Army explosives officer. In an April 1989 Dáil adjournment debate the Irish government stated that the line had been closed for some 45 days since 16 December. It added that passengers were being bussed between Newry and Dundalk and that union representatives estimated about 400 railway jobs at risk. On 4 July 1990 Ray Burke, Minister for Justice and Communications, told the Seanad that the line had suffered 87 disruptions and 29 bombs, exploded or defused, in about 18 months.
AG-059.records:
Northern Ireland Railways: reported devices on the line to the authorities.
The Irish government: a dated incident list compiled for the Dáil debate, covering bombs, hoax calls, bomb scares and closures, with hours closed. The list is held in a Department of Foreign Affairs file.
Burke's 1990 statement: counted 87 'disruptions' alongside 29 bombs. It said that his department kept in contact with the British through the Anglo-Irish Secretariat.
The Northern Ireland Office Principal Secretariat: a memo of 10 July 1990 analyzing Burke's statement. On confirmation from its own sources, the memo called his reference to an injured teenager at Lurgan misleading, since there had been no casualties.
AG-059.gap: The attacker was known and the line visibly closed, so recognition was not delayed. The records were split by the border and by category (bomb, hoax, scare, closure). The joined count existed as a political statement by one government that the other checked against its own reporting.
AG-059.joining: The Irish government joined the incident record for parliamentary use in 1989 and 1990 and kept the British informed through the Anglo-Irish Secretariat. The Northern Ireland Office checked the Irish statement and corrected one claim. PIRA was named throughout, and on 16 April 1989 it issued a statement advising rail employees to stay away from the line.

AG-060.summary: On 2 March 1989 an anonymous caller told the United States embassy in Santiago that he had poisoned Chilean fruit with cyanide. The FDA judged the threat a hoax and on 6 March asked Customs to lift the hold on most Chilean fruit. After a second call on 8 March, the FDA's Philadelphia laboratory found cyanide at about 0.51 parts per million in a sample of two grapes from the ship Almeria Star on 12 March. Imports of Chilean fruit were suspended from 13 to 17 March. A Chilean Exporters Association study of June 1990 put the loss at 333 million dollars, a figure the General Accounting Office did not verify.
AG-060.records:
The US embassy: received both threat calls.
Customs: the detained fruit.
FDA inspectors: by 12 March they had examined about 1,200 of some 365,000 crates on the Almeria Star and analyzed about 75 suspicious samples.
The Philadelphia laboratory: the positive result. It completed its worksheets on 15 March, three days after the tests, and retained part of the sample.
The FDA's Cincinnati laboratory: a later analysis, which fell below its detection limit.
The FDA: notified other importing countries, including Canada and Japan.
The Chilean Exporters Association: the loss estimate.
The General Accounting Office: reviewed the file at Senator Jesse Helms's request. It reported on 6 September 1990 that both tests were widely used and accepted, that it found no serious deficiencies in the chain of custody, and that its consultants considered a false positive extremely unlikely.
AG-060.gap: The threat calls, the laboratory finding and the trade loss sat with different institutions working to different thresholds. They were a consular report of a threat first classified as a hoax, a regulatory finding on two grapes, and a commercial loss across an export season. The supply-chain record that could show where contamination occurred was held in another country by an interested party. Chile could contest the FDA's decision only through diplomacy and litigation.
AG-060.joining: Within a day the FDA joined the calls and the laboratory result and suspended imports. In September 1990 the GAO reviewed the record and upheld the FDA's handling. No perpetrator was identified; the caller had said his purpose was to draw attention to the poor living conditions of Chilean workers. About 2,400 growers and shippers sued the FDA under the Federal Tort Claims Act for 240 million dollars and lost. The FDA had argued that the discretionary function exemption barred the claims. The Supreme Court declined to hear the case.
AG-060.harm_found_later: The losses fell on Chilean growers and workers, between 20,000 and 50,000 of whom lost their jobs by one contemporary estimate. Their claims against the FDA failed in court.

AG-061.summary: Witches' broom, a fungal disease of cacao endemic in northern Brazil, was found on a farm in southern Bahia on 22 May 1989. It spread through the region, and cocoa output fell from about 406,000 tonnes a year in 1984-85 to about 123,000 tonnes in 1999-2000. Brazil, formerly the second-largest producer, became an importer. In June 2006 Veja published the account of Luiz Henrique Franco Timóteo, a PDT militant at the time. He said that he and four friends from the PT, described as CEPLAC employees, had planned the contamination in late 1987. On his account he brought infected branches from the north from 1989 to 1992 to break the political power of the cocoa landowners. The named men denied involvement. CEPLAC's director-general said Timóteo should be investigated by the Federal Police. No one was found guilty.
AG-061.records:
CEPLAC, the federal cocoa agency: its technicians found the first outbreak during routine inspection and tracked the epidemic as a plant-health problem.
Veja's account: technicians found infected branches tied to cacao trees, and sabotage was a hypothesis that was never proven.
Federal Police: a four-hour statement from Timóteo in 2006.
Senate: a speech that quoted his confession.
A Brazilian genome project: began studying the fungus in 2001.
AG-061.gap: The plant-health agency recorded an epidemic of a known pathogen whose wind-borne spread provided a natural explanation. Within that record, the observation of infected branches tied to trees remained an unproven hypothesis. The allegation came seventeen years later, from a self-declared participant, inside a partisan dispute that made each side's account suspect.
AG-061.joining: Veja, a news magazine, joined the confession with the 1989 outbreak record in June 2006. CEPLAC's director-general called it a police matter. According to a 2023 opinion column in Poder360, the investigation closed without identifying culprits and no one was found guilty. The attack claim remains contested.
AG-061.harm_found_later: The collapse of the cocoa economy cost more than 200,000 jobs, according to the Veja account. The loss was recorded as agricultural decline. No procedure ever attributed it to any person.

AG-062.summary: AT&T's long-distance network failed on the afternoon of 15 January 1990. About 70 million calls went uncompleted during the nine-hour recovery. AT&T traced the failure to faulty code in new software loaded in mid-December into all 114 of its 4ESS switches. In AT&T's account, a switch returning to service after a fault sent messages that caused neighboring switches to fail in a chain reaction. Police and telephone-company security, who knew that hackers were entering switching systems, suspected hackers. Bruce Sterling argued that the crash gave the 1990 crackdown on hackers "its sense of edge and its sweaty urgency."
AG-062.records:
AT&T engineering: the switch-level record. Its director of technology development, Larry Seese, described it in the trade press ("The fault was in the code").
The telephone-company security units and police: reports on hacker groups, some from informants.
The press: AT&T's public explanation and apology.
AG-062.gap: Within days the operator classified the failure as internal. The security and police record had been built from reports on hackers, a category that the switch-level explanation did not displace.
AG-062.joining: AT&T joined its own records and attributed the crash to its software. No attacker was named. In May 1990 the Secret Service and Arizona's Organized Crime and Racketeering Bureau carried out the Operation Sundevil raids. On 8 May officers served 27 search warrants. The raids made three arrests. The link to the crash is Sterling's argument, which no official finding in the sources reviewed makes.

AG-063.summary: Security Council resolution 687 (1991) made Iraq liable for 'any direct loss, damage, including environmental damage' from the invasion and occupation of Kuwait. The UN Compensation Commission processed the claims. Its 'F4' panel awarded funds for monitoring and assessment of environmental and public-health damage, then decided the substantive claims. In the third instalment (2003) the panel found Kuwait's freshwater lenses at Umm Al-Aish and Raudhatain contaminated. It found the sources to be seawater used to fight the oil-well fires, together with contaminants leaching from oil lakes and oil recovery pits. The panel recommended about $41.5 million against about $185 million claimed. Of roughly $25 billion in public-health claims by five states, awards covered only limited items, such as Kuwait's costs for treating post-traumatic stress disorder and mine and ordnance injuries.
AG-063.records:
Kuwait: groundwater contamination recorded through monitoring data. It amended its claim on that basis.
The claimant governments: monitoring and assessment programs funded by earlier UNCC awards.
Iraq: counter-explanations for the aquifers, naming pre-1990 over-pumping, mismanagement and the siting of the oil recovery pits.
The F4 panel of commissioners: assessed causation and quantum and reported to the Governing Council.
AG-063.gap: The act and its author were never in doubt. The harm was the problem: water and health damage had to be separated from pre-existing conditions and other sources. The record lacked pre-invasion baselines: 'the absence of pre-invasion data on TPH levels makes it difficult to assess the full significance of postinvasion data'. The monitoring methods raised 'issues regarding quality assurance, data comparability and data interpretation.' Where other factors contributed, the panel apportioned the damage and reduced the award accordingly. A UNCC lawyer later wrote that 'insufficiency of evidence was frequently an insurmountable problem for the environmental and public health claims.'
AG-063.joining: The UNCC, a Security Council subsidiary body with authority to decide liability, joined claimant monitoring records into findings on causation and quantum between the early 2000s and June 2005. Under its rule, Iraq was 'not exonerated' where other factors contributed, though 'due account' would be taken of them. Iraq was named from the start. The open questions were causation and quantum.
AG-063.harm_found_later: Most of the public-health harm claimed by five states was not compensated with the records available. The reconstruction that a claims body was created to perform left the greater part of that harm outside the record of attributed damage.

AG-064.summary: After the 1991 uprising the Iraqi government built dams, dikes and canals that kept Tigris and Euphrates water out of the southern marshes. These included the Third River, officially the Saddam River, opened on 7 December 1992, and at least four further drainage canals completed in 1993 and 1994. The government described the works as promoting the economic, social and cultural revival of the area. The United Nations Environment Programme announced in 2001, from satellite imagery, that most of the marshlands had been lost. Human Rights Watch reported in January 2003 that the Marsh Arab population, about 250,000 in 1991, had fallen to fewer than 40,000 in the homeland.
AG-064.records:
UNEP: compared NASA satellite images and reported a loss of about 90 percent between 1992 and 2000, about 85 percent in its August 2001 release. It attributed part of the decline to upstream damming since the 1970s and the immediate cause to drainage works of the early 1990s, and found that most reclaimed land had remained barren since the works were completed in 1993 and 1994.
UN Special Rapporteur Max van der Stoel: found "extremely little evidence" of successful reclamation and "indisputable evidence of widespread destruction and human suffering". The refugees he interviewed in 1994 named the drainage as the principal reason for flight.
Human Rights Watch: captured Iraqi documents, including a secret "Plan of Action for the Marshes" of 30 January 1989 and a drainage document that the opposition group SCIRI said it took from a captured government engineer. It also held refugee interviews.
United Kingdom: released Royal Air Force photographs of destroyed settlements in November 1993.
United States: released aerial photographs in 1999.
AMAR Foundation: commissioned an imagery study, which found in 1994 that the al-'Amara marshes had shrunk to 67 percent of their 1984/85 extent.
The refugee figures: of about 95,000 refugees from southern Iraq in Iran, some 40,000 came from the marshlands.
The Iraqi government: neither released its own data nor allowed international NGOs access.
AG-064.gap: Each component was a public works project with an agricultural justification, recorded as engineering. Some of the water loss had an independent cause in upstream dams. Hydrological, humanitarian and human rights records sat with different bodies in different countries. The state that held the primary data neither published it nor permitted access. The Special Rapporteur's recommendation of February 1993 that human rights monitors be placed in the area was reiterated every year until his resignation in 1999.
AG-064.joining: UNEP joined satellite imagery across three decades and gave the loss a figure in 2001, a decade after the works began. Human Rights Watch joined the UNEP findings with captured documents, refugee testimony and aerial photographs in January 2003. It judged the drainage "motivated primarily by political rather than economic concerns," naming the government.
AG-064.harm_found_later: The harm to a population that lived on fishing, cultivation, buffalo breeding and reed gathering appears in no agricultural or health series. It had to be reconstructed from refugee testimony and displacement estimates, which range from at least 100,000 to as many as 190,000 internally displaced.

AG-065.summary: After the 1991 Gulf War, UN Security Council sanctions restricted Iraq's oil exports and with them its imports of food and medicine. The 1999 Child and Maternal Mortality Survey (ICMMS), conducted by UNICEF with field staff provided by the Iraqi government, showed a large and sustained rise in under-five mortality. UNICEF's executive director said there would have been 500,000 fewer child deaths in 1991–98 had the fall in mortality of the 1980s continued. Dyson and Cetorelli (BMJ Global Health, 2017) showed that three surveys conducted after 2003 put under-five mortality for 1995–2000 near 40 per 1,000, with no such rise. They concluded that the ICMMS data 'were evidently rigged.'
AG-065.records:
The international team independent of Iraqi authorities (1991): Ascherio et al. (NEJM 1992) surveyed 271 clusters and estimated a threefold rise in under-five mortality between January and August 1991, attributing it to the war and trade sanctions. Dyson and Cetorelli later judged that it probably overstated 1991 mortality.
FAO (1995): a smaller survey in Baghdad, in which Dyson and Cetorelli judge that deception also seems to have occurred.
The census of 1997 in the center and south: its child mortality questions led a US Census Bureau official to doubt the high estimates.
UNICEF (1999): the ICMMS.
Later surveys (2004–2011): the Iraq Living Conditions Survey and the 2006 and 2011 Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys.
A working group of the UN Independent Inquiry Committee (2005): questioned the rise and suggested that the government might have tampered with the ICMMS data.
AG-065.gap: The harm claim was joined early and with international authority. The raw survey data stayed with the producers. UNICEF, according to Dyson, has neither acknowledged the error nor made the ICMMS data publicly available. A test against independent surveys became possible only after the government fell in 2003.
AG-065.joining: Demographers Tim Dyson and Valeria Cetorelli joined the post-2003 survey series with the earlier results in 2017. Dyson called the rigging of the 1999 survey 'an especially masterful fraud'. He suggested that it occurred at the fieldwork or data-entry stage at the Iraqi government's behest, with the aim of heightening international concern to end sanctions. The ICMMS results had been cited in political argument for years, including by Tony Blair in his 2010 testimony to the Chilcot Inquiry. The reanalysis accepted a slight rise in child mortality in 1991. Its target was the claim of a large and sustained rise.

AG-066.summary: Retreating Iraqi troops set fire to more than 600 Kuwaiti oil wells in 1991. The act was deliberate, visible and attributed from the start. What stayed open was the health effect on troops, firefighters and residents, which separate military, advisory and academic bodies assessed over three decades.
AG-066.records:
US Army: estimated cancer and noncancer risks from the smoke with EPA's standardized methodology. It concluded that 'the potential for significant long-term adverse health effects' for exposed personnel was minimal.
Private firefighting companies: employed 110 firefighters at the well heads in 28-day periods without breathing protection.
Presidential Advisory Committee on Gulf War Veterans' Illnesses (1996): noted that 'no cases of illnesses resembling those reported by Gulf War veterans were reported' among the firefighters.
Gulf War veterans: reported symptoms to health authorities.
UN Compensation Commission: created by the Security Council in 1991 to compensate losses resulting directly from the invasion and occupation. It awarded $52.4 billion and made its last payment in January 2022.
AG-066.gap: The attack itself raised no question of recognition. The harm record was split among exposure assessments, veterans' reports, firefighters' employers and researchers, each tied to one exposure. Smoke, nerve agents and other exposures were studied separately, and joining them required epidemiology years later.
AG-066.joining: The Presidential Advisory Committee (December 1996) joined the Army's exposure assessment with the firefighter comparison. It concluded that 'it is unlikely exposure to oil-well fire smoke is responsible for symptoms' reported by veterans. A 2022 study led by Robert Haley (UT Southwestern, Environmental Health Perspectives) found sarin 'largely responsible' for Gulf War illness, while not ruling out other chemical exposures for a small number of cases.
AG-066.harm_found_later: Illness among veterans could be identified only through later epidemiological reconstruction. Its distribution among exposures, the smoke included, has been disputed for three decades.

AG-067.summary: During the siege of Sarajevo the city went without running water, electricity and gas for long periods. A document shown at the Mladić trial recorded 140 days without electricity in downtown Sarajevo in 1993. Civilians were shelled and sniped while fetching water. A report published by the Sarajevo Canton Memorial Fund quotes Mladić addressing the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly on 12 May 1992, as cited from an ICTY judgment. As the report quotes him, he said that 'we are not going to say that we are going to destroy the power supply pylons or turn off the water supply' and that 'we have to wisely tell the world, it was they who were shooting, hit the transmission line and the power went off'. In the Galić trial (2003) the majority found a water queue in Dobrinja deliberately targeted. Judge Nieto-Navia's dissent found no evidence that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps (SRK) obstructed repairs of the utility networks. The dissent also recorded a UN representative's view that certain local Bosnian leaders delayed repairs to attract international sympathy.
AG-067.records:
Utility companies on both sides of the line: outage and repair records. The wartime director of the power transmission company in Ilidža testified for Mladić's defense in 2014 that electricity to Sarajevo 'was never cut off, except in case of a breakdown'.
UN Military Observers: charged with monitoring both sides. The Galić dissent states that they concentrated on the SRK and were understaffed.
UNHCR: civilians' dependence on aid, such as about 100,000 wholly dependent in June 1995.
ICTY prosecutors, defense and chambers: each built its own account.
The 2016 Karadžić judgment summary: terror-campaign findings on sniping and shelling only.
AG-067.gap: An outage presented as a breakdown or an unrepaired line sits in the utility's engineering record. A shell at a water point sits in the military-observer and criminal record. Each cut could be explained by fighting near the lines, by refusal of both sides to guarantee repair crews' safety, or by the other side's delay. According to the Galić dissent, one electricity cut lasted three months because both sides refused to guarantee repair crews' safety. Many UN assessments relied in part on press accounts. The deliberate-deprivation charge required joining engineering, humanitarian and military records that were kept for other purposes.
AG-067.joining: ICTY prosecutors joined utility deprivation into the Mladić indictment, which alleged that the Bosnian Serb leadership deprived Sarajevo's civilians of electricity, water and gas. Chambers convicted on sniping and shelling, including attacks on civilians fetching water. The Karadžić judgment summary contains no finding on cutting utilities. The Galić dissent rejected obstruction of repairs. The deprivation of utilities as such was named by prosecutors and memorial researchers. No judgment in the sources checked made that finding.
AG-067.harm_found_later: Illness and deaths from lack of water, heat and power over three winters were not attributed to the cuts in the trial records checked. Only deaths from fire at water points reached judgment.

AG-068.summary: From 29 June 1993 residents of Kameido in Koto ward reported foul odors to local environmental health authorities, which traced them to the eight-story headquarters of the religious group Aum Shinrikyo. Officials asked to inspect the interior and were refused. They checked the surroundings and collected air samples. They also collected a gray-to-black oily fluid that had collected on the side of the building from mist leaving a rooftop cooling tower, and stored it refrigerated for later testing. Beyond the nuisance of the odor they found no readily apparent risk to human health. Intermittent misting continued until 2 July, when residents' demands led the group's founder, Shoko Asahara, to agree to stop using the rooftop device and vacate the building.
AG-068.records:
The local environmental health authority: registered five complaints on 29 June, 41 complaints on 30 June that the odors were causing appetite loss, nausea and vomiting, and 118 complaints on 1 July, all handled as an odor nuisance. Its fluid samples sat refrigerated without microbiological testing.
Japan's notifiable-disease system: four human anthrax cases nationwide in the whole of the 1990s. One of them was in an adjacent ward in August 1994, with no apparent association with this incident.
A 1999 retrospective survey by telephone of physicians: covered 39 medical facilities serving the roughly 7,000 residents of the mapped high-risk area. It found none who had seen a case of anthrax, an unexplained serious respiratory illness or hemorrhagic meningitis.
Press reports before March 1995: linked the group to a July 1993 emission of noxious fumes from buildings it owned in Tokyo. They did so without any agency classifying the event.
AG-068.gap: Three things kept the complaints below any threshold that would bring in the police or infectious-disease authorities: the recorder's category of odor nuisance, the refusal of access to the building, and the absence of human cases. An environmental health office held the fluid samples and had no reason to test them for pathogens. Nothing in the record pointed to hostile intent until a separate criminal investigation began.
AG-068.joining: Police investigating the Tokyo subway attack of 20 March 1995 obtained members' testimony about the group's intent, given in 1995. The nature of the Kameido incident reached the public at Asahara's arraignment on 23 May 1996. In November 1999, after long negotiation, the local environmental authorities agreed that the one remaining fluid sample could be tested for pathogens. It was transferred to Northern Arizona University. The testing done between 1999 and 2001 identified the organism and matched it to a veterinary vaccine strain used in Japan. The findings were published in 2004. The attacker was named through criminal proceedings. The group never publicized the act.
AG-068.harm_found_later: No human infections were found. The only recorded harm was the odor-related symptoms logged as complaints.

AG-069.summary: A chemical release in a residential district of Matsumoto on the night of 27 June 1994 killed seven people and sent 274 for treatment. The first routine analysis of on-site samples by the Nagano Forensic Science Laboratory found no toxic substances. Three days later the same laboratory and the Nagano Public Health Institute detected the agent in pond water. The National Research Institute of Police Science confirmed the finding, and the police announced it a week later. Police treated Yoshiyuki Kono, the resident who had made the first emergency call, as the perpetrator for about nine months, after finding the agent in his pond and chemicals in his house. In July 1994 inhabitants near an Aum Shinrikyo facility in Yamanashi Prefecture reported foul smells. A hydrolysis product of the same agent was detected in soils taken near the site and removed for forensic investigation.
AG-069.records:
Nagano police investigation headquarters and the Matsumoto police station: the crime-scene record.
Three laboratories: the Nagano Forensic Science Laboratory, the Nagano Public Health Institute and the National Research Institute of Police Science held the analytical record.
Hospitals: the casualty records, seven dead and 274 treated.
The Yamanashi complaints of July 1994 and the soil finding that followed them: these arose in another prefecture. The sources consulted do not name the authority that received them.
A rival religious group: publicly accused Aum of the Matsumoto attack, as the Christian Science Monitor reported on 21 March 1995. Aum sued it for defamation, according to the same report.
AG-069.gap: The Matsumoto record sat with Nagano prefectural police, which settled on a local resident. The Yamanashi record arose in another prefecture. By late 1994 the criminal investigators had traced purchases of raw chemicals by front companies and had come to suspect the group strongly. No case was brought and no search was carried out. The second attack, in the capital, supplied the occasion to act on what was already held.
AG-069.joining: In the OPCW account, the Tokyo subway attack of 20 March 1995 killed twelve passengers and station personnel and injured about 5,000. Two days later 2,500 police raided the group's facilities simultaneously, and almost all the perpetrators were arrested within two months.
