The Matsumoto attack was then attributed to Aum through the criminal process. Many newspapers publicly apologized to Kono. The Nagano police did not.

AG-070.summary: On 23 November 1995 a reporter for Russia's Independent Television found a 32-kilogram container holding cesium-137 in Moscow's Izmailovsky Park, acting on a tip from the Chechen commander Shamil Basayev. Earlier that month Basayev had claimed that several containers of radioactive material attached to explosives had been planted in Russia. The container was turned over to the FSB. A later update reported that it posed no public-health threat, and the CIA judged that it probably held only a small quantity of cesium. It was the first time Chechen fighters had threatened Moscow's population with radioactive material.
AG-070.records:
The television channel: the claim and the location.
FSB: took custody of the container, and reported measurements put its activity between 10 and more than 50 millicuries.
Officials: differing accounts of the source. An FSB officer said unofficially that it was part of a hospital X-ray machine, while Interior Minister Kulikov suggested that Basayev might have taken radioisotopes from the Budyonnovsk hospital.
AG-070.gap: At recognition there was no gap: the attacker announced the act and led a journalist to it.
AG-070.joining: The attacker supplied the link between the object and its author, so joining was immediate. The open questions concerned the origin of the material, on which Russian officials gave different accounts.

AG-071.summary: At about 2 a.m. on 20 October 1995 eight gunmen posing as soldiers struck the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation's bulk fuel installation at Kolonnawa and the nearby Orugodawatte storage complex on the edge of Colombo. They shot guards and set off explosives. Three large tanks were blown up at Kolonnawa, where at least 53,000 tonnes of fuel burned. Two tanks were on fire at Orugodawatte. The Deputy Defence Minister said only the Tamil Tigers had the capacity for such an attack. The government banned the sale of petrol and diesel, halted aviation fuel supplies to foreign airlines, imposed an indefinite curfew in Colombo and asked India for firefighting help. The losses were estimated at at least US$10 million in fuel and US$15 million in facilities.
AG-071.records:
Ceylon Petroleum Corporation: the record of tanks and fuel lost.
Defence Ministry and security forces: the attack and casualties among guards and attackers, recorded under defense-reporting censorship in force since late September.
Civil Defence Force: the firefighting, published later as a technical account in the Fire Engineers Journal (1997).
The government: the fuel-sale ban and the curfew, issued as orders.
AG-071.gap: Little gap opened. The attack hit one complex, at one moment, with visible fire over the capital. The government named the LTTE the same day on the basis of capacity alone. No claim of responsibility was reported in the source checked.
AG-071.joining: The government acted on the military, fuel and civil-defense records within hours and named the LTTE the same day. A single, spectacular target closed the aggregation gap.

AG-072.summary: Pirates and armed robbers in the Gulf of Guinea have attacked merchant ships and tankers. They have also, increasingly, kidnapped crew for ransom. The IMB reported that a record 130 crew members were kidnapped there in 22 incidents in 2020, over 95 percent of the 135 crew kidnapped worldwide. In 2025 ADF, a US Africa Command publication, linked the shift toward kidnapping for ransom to counterpiracy measures in the Bight of Biafra.
AG-072.records:
IMB Piracy Reporting Centre: compiles incidents reported to it. It encourages shipmasters and owners to report all actual, attempted and suspected attacks.
IMO: classifies incidents under the UNCLOS definition.
Decisions that draw on the IMB's figures: designating high-risk areas, insurance premiums and freight rates.
AG-072.gap: The categories do not translate. Until 2009 the IMB defined piracy by intent and capability regardless of location. The IMO applies the UNCLOS definition, which confines piracy to international waters and treats acts in internal waters and the territorial sea as armed robbery. Of 843 incidents the IMO recorded in West Africa between August 1995 and March 2014, 158 occurred in international waters, 296 in territorial waters and 389 in port areas. Anyiam notes that the IMB's statistics are not broken down by international and territorial waters.
AG-072.joining: In the sources checked no body joins the series into an authoritative count. Anyiam called the information on these acts 'distorted and unreliable with confusing statistics'.

AG-073.summary: On 20 July 1996 eight men were due to appear at Belmarsh Magistrates' Court charged with conspiracy to cause explosions on or before 15 July 1996. They included Donald (Donal) Gannon, Gerald (Gerard) Hanratty, John Crawley, Robert Morrow and Francis Rafferty. Five of them were later each imprisoned for 35 years for conspiring to plant 37 bombs at electricity substations around London to disrupt the capital's power supply. In January 1998 the Irish High Court granted warrants to transfer them to Portlaoise, with the agreement of both governments. In a 2019 BBC Spotlight series Crawley said, 'We were going to knock out the power supply of the southeast of England.'
AG-073.records:
Scotland Yard: announced the charges.
The trial court: the convictions for the 37-bomb conspiracy.
Irish High Court and the Minister for Justice: the transfer record.
A participant's broadcast interview 23 years later: the only public statement of the strategic aim.
AG-073.gap: The plot was stopped before any disruption occurred, so no operator or outage record exists. The event survives in police, court and prison-transfer files. Its intended scale was stated publicly only by a participant decades later.
AG-073.joining: Police joined the case before any attack. The courts convicted PIRA members as conspirators. Prevention removed the aggregation problem, since the disruption never reached the civilian recorders.

AG-074.summary: A Boeing 747 bound from New York to Paris exploded off Long Island shortly after takeoff on 17 July 1996. Because many witnesses described a streak of light, the FBI ran a criminal investigation alongside the NTSB accident investigation. The FBI closed its criminal investigation in November 1997. The NTSB concluded that an explosion of the center wing fuel tank, most likely ignited by an electrical short circuit, was the probable cause. In 2014 the NTSB denied in its entirety a 2013 petition by the TWA 800 Project to reconsider the case on the ground that a detonation or high-velocity explosion caused the crash.
AG-074.records:
FBI: the witness interviews, its documents covering 736 witnesses. It also held the criminal-forensic work on the wreckage.
NTSB: the reconstruction, fuel-tank, radar and probable-cause analysis. Explosive traces on three pieces of debris were recorded and attributed by the NTSB in part to the aircraft's earlier use in training police sniffer dogs.
NTSB witness group with ALPA, Boeing, the FAA, the IAM and TWA: sorted the FBI witness documents into 258 streak-of-light and 599 fireball witnesses. A missile visibility test at Eglin Air Force Base in April 2000 compared their descriptions with a missile launch.
AG-074.gap: Two institutions examined the same wreckage under different categories, a crime under the FBI's authority and an accident under the NTSB's. The NTSB witness group received the FBI's witness documents only in April 1998, after the criminal investigation had closed. The witness record and the technical record were joined about 21 months after the crash.
AG-074.joining: The NTSB joined the FBI's witness documents to its own analysis. It explained the streak as the crippled aircraft in flight and the fireball as its structural breakup, concluding that the witness reports were consistent with crippled flight and did not match a missile. It named no attacker. In denying the 2013 petition it stated that 'the petitioners did not show that the NTSB's conclusion or determination of probable cause were wrong'. It also stated that 'none of the physical evidence supports the theory that the streak of light observed by some witnesses was a missile.'

AG-075.summary: In spring 1997 the IRA warned of bombs on the M1, M5 and M6 on 3 April, and two small bombs were found. A hoax warning forced the abandonment of the Grand National at Aintree on 5 April. On 18 April the IRA combined two bombs with hoax warnings across motorways and railways, and on 21 April in central London.
AG-075.records:
Metropolitan Police and other forces: searches, arrests and devices found.
The courts: remand on conspiracy charges.
CAIN chronology: compiles the incidents without totals.
AG-075.gap: Each warning disrupted a different network. The mix of a few real devices with hoax warnings gave each call weight. The sources checked give no consolidated count of hoaxes, closures or costs. CAIN notes that the IRA showed its ability to disrupt ordinary life in Britain 'at minimum effort and risk'.
AG-075.joining: The IRA's warnings claimed authorship. No joined count of hoax disruption was located.

AG-076.summary: On 18 October 1998 ELN fighters bombed the Ocensa pipeline across the river from the village of Machuca. The crude and volatile gases flowed toward the village, ignited, and the fire swept it. In the days after, the ELN claimed responsibility for blowing the pipe. It accused the army of starting the fire as villagers scavenged fuel. The defense chiefs denied the allegation. In a video statement reported on 12 November 1998, ELN leader Nicolás Rodríguez ('Gabino') called the attack a 'grave error' and promised to punish those responsible.
AG-076.records:
ELN: the claim, then the admission.
Colombian defense command: its own account.
Reuters and the Colombian press: at least 70 dead by November 1998.
Later journalism: 84 dead and as much as 21,000 gallons of oil in the river (Harper's 2021).
Ocensa line: operated by a British, French and Canadian consortium. It carried crude from the Cusiana-Cupiagua field operated by BP.
AG-076.gap: The attacker's own statements settled attribution of the blast within four weeks. The open questions were the ignition, which Harper's describes as 'an unknown spark', and the number of dead.
AG-076.joining: The ELN's video admission closed attribution. No consolidated official count of the dead appears in the sources checked.
AG-076.harm_found_later: The death toll was not fixed in the sources checked: at least 70 in November 1998, 84 in a 2021 account. The river contamination is recorded only in passing.

AG-077.summary: Cancers among Italian soldiers who had served in the Balkans and on other missions raised the question whether depleted uranium munitions had harmed soldiers and civilians. UNEP's field mission of November 2000 visited 11 of the 112 sites in Kosovo identified as targeted with depleted uranium ordnance. It found no widespread ground contamination and judged the radiological and chemical risks insignificant. It also warned that remaining penetrators posed a risk of future contamination of groundwater and drinking water, and recommended their removal. An Italian parliamentary commission of inquiry reported in February 2018 that exposure had helped sow deaths and illnesses among soldiers, and accused military chiefs of denial. An expert whose report it cited, Giorgio Trenta, said he had never attributed the soldiers' tumors to depleted uranium. In 2016 a Rome appeals court had upheld a verdict against the defense ministry over the 1999 leukemia death of Corporal Salvatore Vacca, who had served in Bosnia, ordering more than €1.5 million in compensation.
AG-077.records:
UNEP: field samples from 11 of 112 targeted sites in Kosovo.
Italian courts: individual liability findings against the defense ministry.
The parliamentary commission: its own findings, drawn from court rulings and expert reports.
AG-077.gap: The bodies that assessed the exposure each worked from their own record and applied their own standard. For UNEP the record was field samples and the standard environmental risk. For the Italian courts it was individual service histories and liability. For the parliamentary commission it was rulings and expert reports and political responsibility.
AG-077.joining: UNEP joined targeting and sampling records for the environment and found low risk. The Italian courts and the parliamentary commission joined military records for compensation and accountability. Their findings differ from the scientific assessment. The commission chair, Gian Piero Scanu, cited repeated judicial rulings affirming a causal link.
AG-077.harm_found_later: Whether any cancers resulted from exposure could be judged only by later reconstruction. The institutions involved applied different causal thresholds to the same exposure.

AG-078.summary: In Concept 0140 of 30 January 2001 the energy regulator CREG answered a user's complaint about tariff increases caused by tower bombings and her proposal that the public treasury cover 70 percent of the cost. CREG stated that bombings had affected more than 600 transmission towers in the previous 18 months, that about 180 were still unavailable, and that these affected 10 percent of the transmission network, over 1,500 km of lines. The resulting restrictions forced the dispatch of more expensive 'security generation' to avoid rationing. CREG stated that transmission companies bear the cost of rebuilding towers. It stated that the extra generation cost from attack-caused restrictions is borne by all users of the national interconnected system and not only by users in the affected regions. It added that any budget funding was a matter for Congress and the Ministry of Finance.
AG-078.records:
Transmission companies: towers down and towers repaired.
The national dispatch: security generation.
CREG: tariff treatment.
The users: complaints of higher bills.
AG-078.gap: The regulator's rules treat restrictions caused by attacks as a separate cost category, spread across all users. They leave other local restrictions on the owners of the limited infrastructure. The category names no attacker. Because the cost is dispersed nationally through tariffs, no affected group holds a record large enough to press for attribution or compensation.
AG-078.joining: The regulator socialized the cost without attributing the attacks. The source checked shows no joining.
AG-078.harm_found_later: Every electricity user paid part of the campaign's cost through the tariff. The harm was recorded as a pricing component.

AG-079.summary: In summer 1999 birds and then people in and around New York City fell ill with an encephalitis. CDC announced it on 3 September as St. Louis encephalitis, a virus never before documented in the city. Animal-health laboratories concluded by mid-September that the bird disease was viral, and lacked the reagents to identify it. From 23 September an academic researcher at the University of California at Irvine and CDC came to the same conclusion that the agent was something else. By the week of 27 September CDC had confirmed a West Nile-like virus. Health officials confirmed 62 human cases, of whom 7 died. After an October 1999 media report suggested an unnatural origin, the Central Intelligence Agency examined the allegations and concluded that there was no indication of intentional causation.
AG-079.records:
A veterinarian at a Queens animal health clinic: had examined and treated birds with apparent nervous-system disorders by late June.
The wildlife pathologist at the New York State Department of Environmental Conservation: received dead birds from mid-August and could not identify a clear cause.
The Bronx Zoo's head pathologist: obtained the agreement of the US Army Medical Research Institute of Infectious Diseases to try to identify the virus in birds.
An infectious disease physician at a northern Queens hospital: reported two encephalitis patients to the New York City Department of Health on 23 August.
New York City Department of Health: then identified an initial cluster of six patients. The city began active surveillance on 30 August.
Westchester and Nassau county health departments: began active surveillance on 3 September.
USDA laboratory in Ames and the USGS National Wildlife Health Center in Madison: Samples went to both. The Madison center received almost 1,200 specimens.
CDC laboratory: not linked to the New York State network, so the state had to relay CDC results to local health departments.
CDC's account of 1 October 1999: bird tissues went to the USDA National Veterinary Services Laboratories on 10 September and virus isolates to CDC on 20 September. At CDC on 23 September polymerase chain reaction and DNA sequencing showed that the isolates were closely related to West Nile virus. As of 28 September the agencies recorded 17 confirmed and 20 probable human cases and four deaths.
AG-079.gap: Human and animal records belonged to separate systems with separate laboratories and reporting lines. Veterinary health officials were concerned that they were not always included in the daily conference calls. GAO found that some key public health officials were not aware of the similarities between the clinical symptoms in birds and in humans until days or weeks after the human outbreak began. According to GAO, those officials included the director of the city's Bureau of Communicable Disease. The earliest human infection, dated retrospectively to 2 August, was unreported and unknown until after the virus was identified in late September.
AG-079.joining: An animal-health recorder outside the public-health chain, the Bronx Zoo pathologist, pressed the joining, which CDC completed with an academic laboratory. The CIA's review of the bioterrorism allegation closed the hostile-act question. GAO's report of 11 September 2000, requested by Senators Moynihan and Schumer and eleven New York House members, set the chronology on the public record as a lesson for bioterrorism preparedness.

AG-080.summary: Gas transmission lines running from the Sui field in Balochistan have been blown up repeatedly since at least 2000, cutting supply to industry in Punjab and to towns in Balochistan. An attack on the Sui gas field on 11 January 2005 killed 15 people. Later blasts were claimed by Baloch armed groups such as the Baloch Republican Guards and the Baloch Raaji Aajoi Sangar, while others went unclaimed. The South Asia Terrorism Portal (SATP), a project of the Institute for Conflict Management, counted 254 attacks on gas and oil installations and tankers in Balochistan from March 2000 to 29 October 2023, with 36 deaths.
AG-080.records:
Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC): its own count of attacks on its 2,782 km transmission network, three in 2002, all in Balochistan, according to company sources. It raised its pipeline security force to 400, hired guards from local communities, and paid tribal leaders appointed as caretakers. Its sources said some had believed the blasts were internal explosions until the damage showed external charges, and that tribal feuds also drove attacks.
Sui Northern Gas Pipelines (SNGPL): supply stoppages, such as the cut to 700 large industries in Punjab and the NWFP in January 2003.
Local security commanders: descriptions of individual blasts, such as the March 2005 blast at Khamri Bridge, which was attributed to an unidentified group.
Armed groups: published claims for some attacks.
The Frontier Corps: guards the installations.
SATP's tally: the only cumulative series found. Its compilers describe their data as partial.
AG-080.gap: The company whose line was cut recorded each blast as a repair and a supply interruption. A local security officer recorded it as an incident. Those categories left open whether the cause was insurgency, a tribal dispute over guard contracts, or an internal failure. Payments to tribal caretakers surfaced only through company sources speaking anonymously. No published official series joined the companies' counts with the security forces' records. A non-governmental research portal assembled the cumulative picture. It describes its own data as partial.
AG-080.joining: In the sources checked no Pakistani authority published a joined count. At a Senate panel hearing on 28 January 2019 the Petroleum Division described a planned special force of about 50,000 for oil and gas security, without giving attack numbers. SATP joined reports into a running tally. Claims by armed groups narrowed the gap for single incidents.

AG-081.summary: Vitek Boden had been site supervisor for Hunter Watertech, the contractor that installed Maroochy Shire Council's radio-linked sewage control system. He resigned in December 1999 and was told in January 2000 that the council would not employ him. Between 28 February and 23 April 2000 he sent commands to pumping stations, on at least 46 occasions according to a MITRE case study. The pumps failed to run, alarms failed to reach the central computer, and the computer lost contact with pumping stations. About 800,000 liters of raw sewage spilled into parks, rivers and the grounds of a hotel. Police stopped his vehicle on the night of 23 April 2000 and found a laptop, a two-way radio and a PDS Compact 500 computer belonging to Hunter Watertech. On 31 October 2001 he was convicted and sentenced to two years.
AG-081.records:
Maroochy Shire Council and its water services: pump and alarm faults, and the spills.
Hunter Watertech: its employee Mr Yager was assigned to investigate the faults and recorded all radio traffic.
Queensland police: the vehicle stop and the seized equipment.
The courts: conviction on computer-misuse counts, one count of causing serious environmental harm and two theft counts, with compensation of $13,110.77 to the council. On appeal on 10 May 2002, six counts were set aside and the rest upheld.
AG-081.gap: The faults were first filed as installation problems ("At first it was easier to blame installation errors for the problems"). Each malfunction fitted a normal category for a newly commissioned system. Recognition required the installer's engineer to record radio traffic and to conclude that only human intervention could explain the pattern.
AG-081.joining: Mr Yager, the installer's engineer, joined the fault records by logging radio traffic and concluded that the malfunctions resulted from human intervention. Police tied them to one person through a vehicle stop. The trial court convicted, and the Queensland Court of Appeal upheld most counts. The attacker was named through prosecution.

AG-082.summary: On 21 September 2001, ten days after the September 11 attacks, a store of downgraded ammonium nitrate exploded at the Grande Paroisse (AZF) fertilizer plant in Toulouse, part of the TotalFinaElf group. The environment inspectorate counted 30 dead, 22 inside the plant and 8 outside, and about 2,500 injured. The blast raised fears of terrorism, and the attack hypothesis was argued again during the litigation. In September 2012 the Toulouse Court of Appeal overturned earlier acquittals and convicted the former plant director, Serge Biechlin, and Grande Paroisse of involuntary homicide through negligence. In January 2015 the Cour de cassation annulled that ruling because of a judge's link to a victims' association and sent the case to the Paris Court of Appeal.
AG-082.records:
Inspection générale de l'environnement, with technical support from INERIS: reported on 23 October 2001 that "it has not been possible to establish the precise cause of the accident".
The criminal courts: the judicial record and the expert findings.
Grande Paroisse, the operator: defended the case through four levels of proceedings.
AG-082.gap: A month after the blast the administrative inquiry reported without a cause, so classification passed to the criminal courts. In those courts an attack hypothesis remained in play for more than a decade alongside the negligence case.
AG-082.joining: The criminal courts acted as the classifiers. In 2012 the Toulouse Court of Appeal attributed the explosion to negligence by the director and the operator. The case then went to retrial in Paris. No attacker was named.

AG-083.summary: Letters mailed in September and October 2001 caused 22 recorded cases of anthrax, eleven inhalational and eleven cutaneous, with five deaths. Of the cases, twelve were mail handlers. The first cutaneous cases in New York and New Jersey went unrecognized until a laboratory identified the organism in a Florida patient in early October. At the Hamilton and Brentwood postal facilities, exposure went unrecognized until a letter was opened in the Hart Senate Office Building on 15 October, because prophylaxis had been recommended only for people who handled envelopes directly. The Justice Department closed the case in February 2010 by naming Bruce Ivins, an Army laboratory scientist who had died in July 2008.
AG-083.records:
Clinicians and clinical laboratories: individual cases.
City and state health departments: local investigations in Florida, New York City, New Jersey, the Washington area and Connecticut.
CDC: coordination of the local investigations.
US Postal Service: facility and workforce records. Its facilities were sampled only once exposure along the mail path was suspected.
FBI: the letters and powders and the criminal file. It withheld some information from health authorities for prosecution.
National Research Council: a later review of the forensic science, made at the FBI's request of September 2008.
GAO: a later review of the forensic science.
AG-083.gap: Each early cutaneous case was a single clinical encounter, below any outbreak threshold. The assumption that sealed envelopes posed no risk kept the postal workforce outside the exposure category until the Senate letter forced a re-examination. The criminal investigation's need for secrecy limited what health departments received.
AG-083.joining: CDC and the health departments joined the case record within weeks, prompted by one laboratory result and then by a letter opened at a single high-profile target. Attribution took far longer: the FBI publicly treated another scientist, Steven Hatfill, as a person of interest. The Justice Department settled his privacy suit for $5.8 million in June 2008. In February 2011 the National Research Council found that it is not possible to reach a definitive conclusion about the origins of the material on the scientific record alone. It said it had neither been asked for nor made findings on anyone's guilt or innocence. GAO reported on 19 December 2014 that the contractors' genetic tests were generally verified and validated and met the FBI's criteria. The same report stated that the FBI lacked a comprehensive approach to standardizing the testing process, and that its statistical approach could have been improved in three of six areas. GAO took no position on the conclusions the FBI reached in closing the case.
AG-083.harm_found_later: Mail handlers along the path of sealed envelopes, twelve of the 22 cases, stood outside the exposure category that guided prophylaxis until the Senate letter of 15 October. Their illness became attributable to the mailings only after the category was widened.

AG-084.summary: During the civil war the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) attacked power plants, telecommunications stations, health posts and village and district offices. On 30 March 2002 Maoists blew up the control room and switching station of the 12 MW Jhimruk hydropower plant, flooding its turbines and powerhouse. By then several small hydro plants and substations had been damaged and 37 telecommunications substations attacked, leaving phones dead in 12 districts for months. On 31 October 2004 insurgents attacking Gamgadhi, the Mugu district headquarters, destroyed its power station and telephone exchange. After the 2006 peace agreement the Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction estimated the cost of rebuilding destroyed structures at about Rs 50 billion.
AG-084.records:
Finance Secretary: said in April 2002 that there were 'estimates but no formal assessment of damage'.
Nepal Electricity Authority: had not assessed damage at Okhaldhunga.
Butwal Power Company, owner of Jhimruk: said it could not reach the site.
An unnamed official: put losses to public infrastructure since November 2001 at more than Rs 2 billion.
Not recorded: community-run micro-hydro plants, also destroyed, which no one counted.
Institute for Conflict Management: a 2004 analysis put infrastructure losses at Rs 18 billion without naming its source.
Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction: later used Rs 50 billion.
Republica: an editorial reported Rs 8.8 billion spent on 2,870 structures.
A parliamentary committee: found in 2016 that conflict-damaged health posts had not been rebuilt and that reconstructed offices were substandard.
AG-084.gap: Because the attacker was known, recognition was never in doubt. The damage, however, was recorded by owners who could not reach their sites, by a utility that had not assessed it and by officials offering estimates. The community-owned plants fell outside every register. Estimates moved from Rs 2 billion (2002) to Rs 18 billion (2004) to Rs 50 billion (after 2006) without a common method.
AG-084.joining: The Ministry of Peace and Reconstruction, created after the war, joined the damage into a reconstruction budget. In 2016 the parliamentary Social Justice and Human Rights Committee examined the results in Jumla, Rukum and Achham. It urged the Commission for Investigation of Abuse of Authority to investigate the substandard work. No body joined the infrastructure losses to the harm they caused.
AG-084.harm_found_later: The loss of electricity, telephones and health posts to rural districts for years is recorded only as structures to be rebuilt. The effects on health and livelihoods were never measured in the sources checked. The community-owned plants were never counted.

AG-085.summary: After armed men took more than 900 people hostage at the Dubrovka theater on 23 October 2002, security forces pumped a narcotic gas into the auditorium on 26 October and stormed the building. Official counts of hostage deaths varied, with 129 among the initial figures, because authorities counted differently and records were incomplete. The head of the rescue service, rescue workers and city health officials had not been told of the gas, the latter for reasons of secrecy. The FSB described it to investigators only as a special mixture based on fentanyl derivatives. On 20 December 2011 the European Court of Human Rights held in Finogenov and Others v. Russia that the decision to use force and gas did not violate the right to life. It held that the planning and conduct of the rescue and medical aid did violate that right, as did the investigation.
AG-085.records:
The FSB, which ran the crisis cell: the operational record and the identity of the agent. It withheld the identity even from investigators for national security reasons.
Ambulance services, bus drivers and hospitals: clinical and transport records without that information. One hospital official learned of the gas from the media.
The prosecutors' investigation: attributed the deaths to a combination of factors (stress, lack of oxygen, immobility, dehydration, sleep deprivation and the gas), and found that the multi-factor nature of the causes excluded a direct causal link with the gas. Its team included representatives of agencies involved in the operation.
European Court of Human Rights: found that documents were destroyed and that key witnesses, including crisis cell members and bus drivers, were not questioned.
AG-085.gap: The FSB, which used the agent, withheld its identity from the medical services treating its effects and from the investigators assessing the deaths. The investigation was not independent of the agencies involved.
AG-085.joining: Nine years after the event, the ECtHR joined the operational, medical and investigative records on application by survivors and relatives. It found the planning of the rescue and the investigation deficient. The domestic record continued to attribute deaths to multiple causes.
AG-085.harm_found_later: The deaths were recorded domestically as products of combined stress and deprivation, with the gas as an indirect cause. The Strasbourg court established the link between the deaths and the deficient medical preparation.

AG-086.summary: The New People's Army (NPA) repeatedly burned or bombed mobile-phone cell sites, relay stations and transmission towers of Globe Telecom. An NDF official on Negros confirmed that the NPA carried out the 4 January 2003 'punitive operations' against Globe cell sites. The official said the company's owners had refused to negotiate payment of 'revolutionary taxes'. Rappler reported that NPA members disabled a Globe tower in Ilocos Sur in December 2002, and that relay stations and a tower in Jamindan, Capiz were allegedly bombed in August 2008. Both attacks, according to Rappler, came after the company refused to pay, the second time a reported P80,000. In 2012 Globe's chief executive, Ernest Cu, said the company's refusal to pay appeared to have reduced attacks. Cu also said that the company worked closely with the armed forces and had suffered no attack that year.
AG-086.records:
NPA and NDF: held and publicized their own account of the attacks as punitive operations.
The military: described the January 2003 raids as 'terrorism' and 'extortion'.
Army and police officers: described individual raids locally, such as the August 2008 sequence of cell-site bombings in Albay and Sorsogon.
Globe's chief executive: gave a public account of attacks declining after the company refused to pay.
Not recorded publicly: whether any firm paid, in the sources checked.
AG-086.gap: Attacker publicity narrowed the question of who burned the towers. The question of who paid stayed open, because a payment to an insurgent appears in no published regulatory or company record. Each attack was also reported locally, by the officers of the province where it occurred. No national tally linking attacks, demands and payments was found.
AG-086.joining: In their own statements the insurgents joined the attacks into a campaign. Globe joined its experience into a public claim that refusal worked. In the sources checked, no government body published a joined record of tax demands and payments.

AG-087.summary: A cascading failure beginning in FirstEnergy's Ohio system blacked out large parts of the northeastern United States and Ontario on 14 August 2003. The outage came three days after the Blaster worm spread, and the timing prompted speculation that the worm had triggered or worsened it. Investigators traced the failure of FirstEnergy's control-room alarms to a race condition in its energy-management software. The race condition stopped the alarm function silently in the early afternoon. The operators, unaware of the loss, "made no alternate arrangements to monitor the system."
AG-087.records:
FirstEnergy: control-room and alarm records.
The reliability coordinators and NERC: records of their own.
U.S.–Canada Power System Outage Task Force: chaired by Spencer Abraham and Herb Dhaliwal (later John Efford). It had an Electric System Working Group, a Nuclear Working Group and a Security Working Group, made up of state and provincial representatives, federal employees and contractors.
AG-087.gap: In the first hours operators, reliability coordinators and governments held separate partial pictures. The failed alarm system left FirstEnergy's own record of the event incomplete.
AG-087.joining: The Task Force joined the records with binational authority. A computer-security contingent examined any cyber angle (Chapter 9 of the April 2004 final report). The final report placed the causes in FirstEnergy's failure to understand the deteriorating condition of its system, its failure to manage tree growth in transmission rights-of-way, and the reliability organizations' failure to provide real-time diagnostic support. None of these causes was hostile. In Kevin Poulsen's account of the report, the failure had nothing to do with viruses or cyber terrorists. The report recommended confirming NERC's ES-ISAC "as the central point for sharing security information and analysis" (Recommendation 42).

AG-088.summary: Human Rights Watch spent twenty-five days in and on the edges of West Darfur and interviewed refugees in Chad. In May 2004 it reported that food stores in all the villages visited had been systematically looted and burned. The report also recorded destroyed containers and implements for storing and preparing food. It described wells and pumps as looted or destroyed. In some villages, according to the report, Janjaweed forces had dug up and destroyed buried grain. HRW reported that cattle rustling was organized on an almost industrial scale, with stolen cattle gathered at collection points, sent to a government slaughterhouse in Nyala and exported by air. The UN International Commission of Inquiry on Darfur recorded the same pattern in its report of 25 January 2005.
AG-088.records:
Human Rights Watch: village-level findings and refugee testimony. HRW also recorded that the government restricted media access, and cited reports of government tampering with mass graves and other physical records.
Commission of Inquiry: set up at the request of Security Council resolution 1564 of 18 September 2004. From its own site visits, including the destroyed villages of Shataya and Masteri, it recorded that water pumps and wells had been destroyed and food-processing implements wrecked. It also recorded reports that wells had been poisoned with cattle carcasses.
The Sudanese foreign minister: said the death toll was "not more than 600 people at most".
AG-088.gap: The destruction was village by village, in a region where independent access was restricted. In most records it appeared under the categories of displacement and mortality. Livestock passed into a commercial export chain with its own paperwork.
AG-088.joining: In 2004 Human Rights Watch, a non-governmental organization, joined village findings and refugee testimony into a pattern. The Commission of Inquiry joined the wider record in January 2005. It found that government forces and militias had conducted widespread and systematic attacks that may amount to crimes against humanity. The Commission noted the resulting loss of livelihood and means of survival. Because genocidal intent appeared to be missing at least among the central authorities, it concluded that the government had not pursued a policy of genocide. It recommended referral to the International Criminal Court.
AG-088.harm_found_later: Deaths from the loss of food stores, wells and herds enter the record as famine or displacement mortality. The record does not attribute them to the destruction of those assets.

AG-089.summary: In 2003 political and religious leaders in Kano, Zamfara and Kaduna halted the oral polio vaccination campaign. They cited rumors that the vaccine contained anti-fertility agents, HIV and cancer-causing agents. Datti Ahmed, head of the Supreme Council for Sharia in Nigeria, said the vaccines had been 'deliberately adulterated.' Five northern states took part in the boycott, with Kano holding out longest, for about 11 months. The Supreme Council rejected the report of a federal technical committee set up on 29 October 2003. The impasse ended in July 2004, after state and religious representatives had observed vaccine testing abroad and a Kano team had endorsed an Indonesian manufacturer. The poliovirus spread to previously polio-free countries in West and Central Africa. In 2005 it reached Yemen, Saudi Arabia and Indonesia.
AG-089.records:
Federal technical committees (from 29 October 2003): laboratory tests of vaccine samples sent abroad.
Kano state government: its own assessment. Governor Ibrahim Shekarau stated that the federal test results were unsatisfactory.
Supreme Council for Sharia in Nigeria: public allegations, made against a background of distrust from Pfizer's 1996 Trovan trial in Kano.
Polio surveillance: cases in Nigeria and in the countries reinfected.
AG-089.gap: Authority over immunization was split: the states control primary health care, including immunization, while the federal government controls tertiary care. Kano could therefore stop a national campaign. Each test result was accepted or rejected according to who had appointed the testers. The Supreme Council rejected the first federal committee because it judged Muslims underrepresented. It then rejected a second committee's nominees. Political tension after the May 2003 presidential election, which the opposition challenged in the Supreme Court, compounded the dispute.
AG-089.joining: The joining that settled the matter was negotiated rather than technical. In February 2004 the federal government sent state and religious representatives to South Africa, Indonesia and India to observe testing. A Kano team endorsed the Indonesian manufacturer Biopharma. In July 2004 dialogue led by political and religious leaders, with WHO and UNICEF support, ended the impasse. No contamination was established in the sources checked. No one was named as an attacker.
AG-089.harm_found_later: Children paralyzed in the countries reinfected (over 1,500, according to a Lancet report cited by Jegede) are recorded as polio cases. The boycott's share appears only in later epidemiological reconstruction.

AG-090.summary: After the 2003 invasion insurgents repeatedly sabotaged oil pipelines in the north, electrical transmission lines and fuel lines and intimidated repair workers. At the same time a large share of refined fuel was diverted to the black market, and illegal connections drew power from the grid. Oil and electricity production consistently fell below US program goals. In 2006 peak electricity generation averaged 4,280 MW, against a goal of 6,000 MW.
AG-090.records:
US military: data counting enemy-initiated attacks, with a record 176 per day in October 2006.
Defense Intelligence Agency: later raised its April 2007 total from about 4,500 to about 4,900.
Ministry of Oil: production estimates, supplied without comprehensive metering.
World Bank and the ministry's Inspector General: estimates that millions of dollars of revenue were lost each year to smuggling.
State Department: reported that about 10 to 30 percent of refined fuels were diverted to the black market.
Institute for the Analysis of Global Security: a public 'Iraq Pipeline Watch' log of attacks on pipelines, oil facilities and oil workers, numbered to 469 entries by 27 March 2008. It described the log as updated only sporadically and possibly incomplete.
AG-090.gap: The categories did not translate. Military attack counts recorded enemy action, while the oil ministry recorded estimated output. The electricity losses mixed sabotage, theft, illegal connections and nonfunctioning meters. GAO found that State's production estimate 'may be overstated due to inadequate metering'. It also found that the protection forces had been 'underpaid, underequipped, and poorly led,' with the 'capability and loyalty' of some infrastructure battalions 'questionable'. Some tribes paid to protect transmission lines also sold materials from the downed lines. The guards were thus also an uncertain recorder. No record separated how much of the shortfall each cause produced.
AG-090.joining: GAO assembled the agencies' figures for Congress in May 2007 and stated their limits. The IAGS log joined incident reports into a public series and listed the UN among its sources. Attackers were named generically as insurgents and anti-coalition forces. In the sources checked, no body separated sabotage from theft and decay in the loss figures.

AG-091.summary: On 25 January 2003 the Slammer worm (the MS SQL Server 2000 worm) entered the network of a Davis-Besse consultant. It crossed a T1 line that bypassed the plant's firewall into FirstEnergy's corporate network and reached the plant network. The Safety Parameter Display System was unavailable for 4 hours 50 minutes, and the plant process computer for 6 hours 9 minutes. The analog backups were unaffected. The plant had been shut since February 2002 for an unrelated reactor-head defect.
AG-091.records:
FirstEnergy: an internal record, and an April 2003 filing by its employee Dale Wuokko describing the T1 connection as "a backdoor from the Internet to the Corporate internal network".
NRC: notification was required for an SPDS outage of eight hours or more, and this outage was shorter. The NRC declined to comment to the press.
Nuclear Network: a March 2003 industry advisory shared through it.
NERC: a June 2003 document recording that Slammer had also downed another utility's SCADA network through a remote computer and a VPN connection.
AG-091.gap: Because the outage fell under the NRC's eight-hour notification threshold, no event notification was required. The sector pattern, the worm reaching control networks at more than one utility, sat in an anonymized NERC document.
AG-091.joining: Kevin Poulsen, a journalist, joined the FirstEnergy filing, the industry advisory and the NERC material in a report of 20 August 2003. Nine days later the NRC issued Information Notice 2003-14 to licensees. The notice described the infection and stated that "the event was not deemed significant since the plant control and protection functions were not affected." No attacker was named. The worm was untargeted.

AG-092.summary: An explosive charge damaged the base of a Hydro-Québec transmission tower at Saint-Herménégilde, near Coaticook in the Eastern Townships close to the US border. The tower stood on a line carrying James Bay power to the Boston area. CBC later reported that the attack took place on the eve of President George W. Bush's 2004 visit. A group signing as IRI (Initiative de résistance internationaliste) sent a communiqué to La Presse, Le Journal de Montréal and the radio station CKAC. It presented the attack as a protest against the 'pillaging' of Quebec's resources by the United States. The IRI later claimed the firebombing of the car of a Canadian Petroleum Products Institute spokesperson. By then no arrests had been made for the tower bombing.
AG-092.records:
Hydro-Québec: the asset and damage record.
The police: attributed the damage to an explosive charge. They said they had never heard of the group.
Sûreté du Québec, Hydro-Québec and a federal counter-terrorism force: the investigation.
Three Montreal media outlets: received the communiqué, on which none of the agencies would comment.
Sûreté du Québec's anti-terrorism unit: later investigated the IRI's car-bomb claim.
AG-092.gap: The police identified an explosive charge, and the communiqué to the press supplied the political motive. The agencies declined to comment on the communiqué. The checked sources do not show when or how Hydro-Québec discovered the damage, or whether supply was interrupted.
AG-092.joining: The IRI's own claim joined the damage to a political motive. The provincial police, Hydro-Québec and the federal counter-terrorism force investigated together. No arrest for the tower bombing was reported by 2006. CTV later linked a claim signed 'Résistance internationaliste' for a bombing of a Canadian Forces recruitment center in Trois-Rivières to the same group's earlier acts.

AG-093.summary: At 21:38 and 21:39 on 4 November 2006, E.ON Netz switched off the two circuits of the 380 kV Conneforde-Diele line over the Ems so that the cruise ship Norwegian Pearl could pass. At 22:10:28 a cascade of line trips split the continental synchronous grid into three areas. More than 15 million European households lost supply. In the western area about 17,000 MW of consumption was cut by load shedding. The grid was fully resynchronized after 38 minutes. The operators' association, the regulators and the operator each investigated, and each attributed the event to operational causes in the E.ON Netz control area.
AG-093.records:
E.ON Netz: the switching log. On 15 November it said human error had caused the event, since its control center had not checked whether losing another line would overload the grid.
The neighboring TSOs: tie-line and protection records. The protection settings at the two ends of the Landesbergen-Wehrendorf line differed.
Each TSO: reported load shedding to UCTE and to its national regulator.
The UCTE investigation committee (set up 5 November, chaired by Gerard Maas of TenneT): joined the operator records.
ERGEG's ad hoc working group: part of a joint inquiry proposed by the Italian regulator, it joined the national regulators' reports.
AG-093.gap: For facts, the regulators depended on the operators. ERGEG stated that its members 'did not perform independent audits to check the validity of the information provided by the TSOs,' and noted that load-shedding figures sometimes differed between national reports and the UCTE interim report. It also found that a large amount of distribution-connected generation had tripped. Two joining bodies worked in parallel on the same operator records under different mandates (industry rule compliance and regulatory oversight).
AG-093.joining: ERGEG (interim report 20 December 2006) and UCTE (final report January 2007) joined the records within weeks. Both named the switching without an N-1 security check and insufficient inter-TSO coordination as causes. UCTE stated that the disturbance was 'not caused by some extraordinary climatic conditions or technical failures,' and ERGEG that it 'was not triggered by technical failures or external events.' No checked report discussed hostile action. Because the event struck more than twenty countries at once, one joined account was unavoidable.

AG-094.summary: Israeli air strikes on the fuel storage tanks of the Jiyeh power station during the July–August 2006 war released about 15,000 tons of fuel oil into the Mediterranean. The spill affected about 150 km of coastline in Lebanon and Syria. The General Assembly adopted resolutions 61/194, 62/188 and 63/211 on the 'oil slick on Lebanese shores,' asking Israel to 'assume responsibility for prompt and adequate compensation.'
AG-094.records:
Lebanon: notified the Regional Marine Pollution Emergency Response Centre for the Mediterranean (REMPEC) by letter of 21 July 2006.
Ministry of the Environment: put the clean-up cost at $150 million on a cost-per-ton model. On 5 August 2006 it asked UNEP for a post-conflict environmental assessment.
An Experts Working Group: estimated $137 to $205 million.
IMO and UNEP: convened an international meeting in Athens on 17 August 2006.
UNEP: put the release at 10,000 to 15,000 tonnes. Its fieldwork ran from 30 September to 21 October 2006.
AG-094.gap: On recognition the gap was narrow, with a single target and a known attacker. Damage estimates diverged across recorders. By June 2008 the assistance received came to around 10 percent of the average upper estimate.
AG-094.joining: The Secretary-General's reports joined the national, regional and UN assessments. The General Assembly assigned compensation responsibility to Israel without means of enforcement. Israel replied that 'it was not Israel which initiated the violence' and cited UNEP's finding of 'relatively limited long-term effects'. By August 2009 it had not paid compensation.

AG-095.summary: Alexander Litvinenko fell ill on 1 November 2006 after meeting Andrey Lugovoy and Dmitri Kovtun at the Millennium Hotel in London. He died at University College Hospital on 23 November. Doctors could not diagnose his condition, and samples sent to the Atomic Weapons Establishment at Aldermaston identified polonium-210 only several hours before he died. Sir Robert Owen pressed for a statutory public inquiry in place of the inquest so that sensitive government material could be considered. A judicial review overturned the Home Secretary's refusal. The inquiry was established on 31 July 2014. Its report of 21 January 2016 found that Lugovoy and Kovtun poisoned him, Lugovoy probably under FSB direction, in an operation probably approved by Mr. Patrushev and President Putin. It also found that the two had made an earlier attempt on 16 October 2006.
AG-095.records:
University College Hospital: the clinical record, which could not classify the illness.
Atomic Weapons Establishment: the analytical result.
The government: sensitive material that could be considered only by a statutory inquiry.
AG-095.gap: Routine hospital diagnostics had no category for the agent, so recognition depended on a weapons laboratory outside the health system. The government's sensitive material could not be considered at the inquest. The Home Secretary refused the statutory inquiry that would let one body consider it until a court overturned the refusal.
AG-095.joining: The statutory inquiry, established after judicial review, joined the clinical, forensic and closed government records and named the Russian state as the probable author. It found no evidence that a UK agency played a part in the death. Because of the Home Secretary's 'neither confirm nor deny' approach, it could not reach conclusions on whether Litvinenko had a relationship with the UK agencies. On 21 September 2021 the European Court of Human Rights (Carter v. Russia) found that Russia had violated the right to life in its substantive and procedural aspects. The Court cited a strong prima facie case that Lugovoy and Kovtun acted under the direction or control of Russian authorities.

AG-096.summary: In the early hours of 22 January 2006 explosions in North Ossetia damaged the main North Caucasus-South Caucasus gas pipeline and the Mozdok-Tbilisi line. The damage cut Russian gas to Georgia and Armenia during near-record cold. A later blast in Karachay-Cherkessia briefly cut power to part of Georgia. Russian officials first said the blasts appeared accidental. They then opened a criminal case, treating it as sabotage after investigators reported remains of improvised explosive devices, and suggested pro-Chechen insurgents. President Saakashvili accused Russia of 'serious sabotage' aimed at forcing Georgia to give up ownership of its gas pipeline network. Repairs were expected to take about three days on the main line and up to four weeks on the Mozdok-Tbilisi line.
AG-096.records:
Russian prosecutors: the criminal file. A spokesman for the deputy prosecutor said it was being treated as sabotage, a category distinct from terrorism.
A Gazprom official: said extra gas would be sent through Azerbaijan.
Russia's ambassador in Tbilisi: called the blasts 'a terror act, which was evidently planned beforehand'.
Georgia's Deputy Energy Minister: recorded the complete halt in gas imports.
Georgian authorities: set emergency priorities for hospitals, bakeries, homes and industry.
Russian Foreign Ministry: rejected Georgian claims as 'hysterical and confused'.
Putin: ordered the Interior Ministry and FSB to tighten control over Caucasus pipelines.
AG-096.gap: All physical traces lay in Russian territory and in a Russian criminal file. The harm fell in Georgia and Armenia. The Russian classification was sabotage by insurgents. The Georgian classification was state coercion, linked to the near doubling of the gas price from 1 January 2006 and to Russian interest in Georgia's pipelines. The two were built on different records and never met in a shared investigation.
AG-096.joining: In the sources checked, no joint or international investigation joined the records. Russia named regional insurgents without published findings. Georgia named the Russian state without offering proof. The attribution dispute remained open in the sources checked.

AG-097.summary: CBS's 60 Minutes reported on 8 November 2009 that hackers had caused a two-day blackout in Espírito Santo beginning 26 September 2007, which affected about three million people. The report made the same claim about a smaller blackout north of Rio de Janeiro in January 2005. It relied on six unnamed sources in intelligence, military and cybersecurity circles. Two days after the 2007 outage began, Furnas, the utility, had attributed it to soot and dust from field burning, deposited on insulators during eight months without rain. The national system operator ONS confirmed that a 345 kV line had failed because of polluted insulators. In January 2009 the regulator ANEEL concluded that Furnas had failed to maintain them and fined it $3.27 million. Two days after the broadcast, a blackout cut 40 percent of Brazil's power and shut down the Itaipu dam. Energy Minister Edison Lobão attributed it to rain and wind that short-circuited transformers on a key transmission line.
AG-097.records:
Furnas: the line-failure record.
ONS: the system-operation record.
ANEEL: the regulatory investigation and the fine.
Raphael Mandarino Jr.: as director of the Homeland Security Information and Communication Directorate, said he had investigated and found 'no evidence of hacker attacks'. He also said that Brazil's electric control systems were not directly connected to the internet.
Ministry of Mines and Energy and Itaipu: called 'some accident that affected one or more points in the transmission system' the most probable hypothesis for the 2009 outage.
The US sources: whatever unnamed intelligence fragments the broadcast relied on.
AG-097.gap: Before the foreign claim appeared, the Brazilian regulatory record had already classified the 2007 event as a maintenance failure. The anonymous intelligence fragments behind the claim were never placed where they could be compared with that record.
AG-097.joining: Marcelo Soares of Wired's Threat Level compared the Furnas, ONS and ANEEL records and found nothing supporting the hacking claim. Furnas said it had 'no knowledge of hackers acting in Furnas' power transmission system.' No attacker was named.

AG-098.summary: From late April 2007, during the dispute over relocating the Bronze Soldier memorial in Tallinn, distributed denial-of-service attacks hit Estonian government sites, banks and media. Many came through networks of compromised computers. RFE/RL reported that bank cards and mobile networks were temporarily frozen at the peak. Estonian officials blamed Russia, which denied involvement. In January 2008 a Tallinn court fined Dmitri Galushkevich, 20, 17,500 kroons for attacking the website of Prime Minister Andrus Ansip's Reform Party. In March 2009 State Duma deputy Sergei Markov reportedly said his assistant had carried out the attack and called it a reaction from civil society.
AG-098.records:
Banks, media outlets and ministries: their own outage records.
Estonian prosecutors: the criminal case. They requested legal cooperation from the Russian Public Prosecutor's Office, which refused.
The defense ministry: the government's assessment of a highly coordinated campaign beyond the capacity of one person.
AG-098.gap: Because the attacks were simultaneous and obvious, recognition was immediate. Attribution stalled at the border: the traffic ran through botnets, and Russia refused Estonia's request for legal cooperation. Estonian investigators were left with one domestic participant.
AG-098.joining: The only court finding concerned one participant. A Russian deputy's 2009 remark named an assistant without official confirmation. Estonian defense officials dismissed it as inconsistent with a coordinated campaign. No state attribution with an agreed record followed.

AG-099.summary: On 22 January 2007 the US Navy accidentally jammed GPS signals in downtown San Diego. A Coast Guard Navigation Center official later confirmed that Coast Guard vessels lost GPS service and that a paging company's service was shut down for about 30 minutes. The official also confirmed that two cell carriers lost GPS timing at downtown towers and switched to other methods without loss of service. Later accounts, by New Scientist in 2011 and an Exelis industry report in 2014, described failed Naval Medical Center pagers, a failed harbor traffic-management system, air traffic control on backup systems, lost cell signals and refused ATM withdrawals. Exelis said it took three days to find an explanation. A 2011 Voice of San Diego fact-check judged the New Scientist account misleading because it was exaggerated.
AG-099.records:
FAA: a report sent to the Coast Guard the day after the incident stated that 'there was no disruption to air traffic control'.
Coast Guard vessels: reported lost GPS service.
The cell carriers: lost GPS timing.
A paging company: recorded a shutdown of about 30 minutes.
Coast Guard Navigation Center: held these reports. A Coast Guard navigation official first made the episode public at a GPS conference later in 2007.
The port and the FAA: told a reporter in 2011 that they had no idea what he was referring to.
The Navy: said in 2011 that it was mystified.
AG-099.gap: Each user recorded the effect as a fault in its own system. The source was a military training activity whose emissions were unknown to the civilian users affected. Later retellings added effects that the Coast Guard official did not confirm.
AG-099.joining: The Coast Guard Navigation Center gathered the user reports. The outage was traced to the Navy's jamming and settled as unintentional. The joined record stayed with the Navigation Center and reached the public through a conference presentation. In 2011 Voice of San Diego checked the published account against the Coast Guard's information and found it exaggerated.
AG-099.harm_found_later: A paging outage of about 30 minutes may have affected Naval Medical Center pagers. The only way to establish any effect on patient care would be to link hospital and paging records to the outage window. No source reports such a link.

AG-100.summary: At least 11 km of the TVH cable linking Vietnam with Thailand and Hong Kong was taken from the seabed off Ca Mau on 25 March 2007 and reportedly sold as scrap. LIRNEasia describes the section as the Vietnamese portion of the SEA-ME-WE 3 link. With TVH out of service, Vietnam depended almost completely on a single remaining cable for international traffic. Officials estimated that repairs would take at least a month and cost over US$5.84 million. Vietnam Telecom International (VTI) put its lost revenue at US$4 million. After at least five cases since January, the Prime Minister ordered a crackdown.
AG-100.records:
VTI: hired a cable-repair vessel from Singapore, which returned because it did not carry enough cable for the repair.
Police: in Vung Tau they seized boats carrying 60 and 40 tons of undersea cable. They also broke up five rings that had sold about 500 tons of salvaged cable.
The border guards in Kien Giang: detected two fishing boats with 80 tonnes of cable.
Soc Trang: three boats with 80 tonnes were caught there.
Ministry of Defence: had contracted companies in August 2006 to salvage decommissioned pre-1975 copper cable.
Ba Ria–Vung Tau province: had allowed soldiers and fishermen to salvage old cable in 2006.
AG-100.gap: The salvage permits created a lawful category, recovery of abandoned cable. Under it, the removal of live fiber-optic cable entered police records as scrap trade. Seizures were logged by provincial police and border guards as cargo offenses, while the outage was an operator fault. VTI's deputy director said that the cable seized at Vung Tau did not match his company's cable. Ministry of Posts and Telematics officials doubted that the raids were anything but deliberate, because operational cables were buried one to two meters deep.
AG-100.joining: In mid-2007 the national government joined the operator's outage record with the seizures. The Prime Minister ordered a crackdown, and the province withdrew its salvage decision and banned salvaging. The Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Public Security and the Naval Command joined forces to pursue the thieves. Deputy minister Le Nam Thang warned that cable theft could be charged as destroying national communications. No foreign actor was involved or named.

AG-101.summary: At about 23:00 on 5 August 2008, shortly before the Russia-Georgia war, an explosion at valve 30 of the BTC crude pipeline near Refahiye started a fire that burned for several days. The explosion halted flows of about one million barrels a day and led the BTC partners to declare force majeure. The PKK's military wing claimed the blast on 7 August, while Turkish officials first described a technical malfunction. In December 2014 Bloomberg, citing four Western intelligence officials, reported that a cyber intrusion had suppressed alarms and raised pressure until the line exploded. The same report said US intelligence believed Russia was responsible. In 2015 Süddeutsche Zeitung reported, from an internal report, that explosives had been found at the site. The paper also reported that no security cameras or wireless network for the valve stations had existed through which such an intrusion could have run.
AG-101.records:
BTC officials: closed valves 29 and 31. BTC officials who visited the site told CNNTürk they had seen no sign of sabotage.
BOTAŞ: estimated the repair time.
The local authorities: ruled out sabotage and cited a system fault detected before the blast.
Energy Minister Hilmi Güler: said it was too early to say.
HPG: published its claim through the Firat News Agency.
BP: announced the force majeure declaration and the diversion of crude to Supsa.
US embassy cable from Baku, 28 August 2008: recorded BP's statement that it had 'never observed any deliberate actions by the Russians to target the Baku-Supsa or BTC pipelines'.
Western intelligence officials: held the material behind the 2014 cyber account.
The internal report: described explosives at the site.
AG-101.gap: The operator's records stayed with the operator and with the Turkish state, which is legally responsible for the pipeline's security and financially liable for losses from terrorist attacks. That position gave the state an incentive to prefer an accident finding. The intelligence material behind the cyber account was never published. The insurgent claim offered a ready explanation that matched neither the first official category (technical fault) nor the later cyber account. For six years each party's record supported a different category.
AG-101.joining: In December 2014 Bloomberg joined anonymous intelligence accounts into a Russian cyberattack attribution. Robert M. Lee, writing on the SANS ICS blog in June 2015, joined that account with the internal report described by Süddeutsche Zeitung and concluded that 'no real evidence was ever presented.' No government publicly named an attacker. Russian and Turkish officials declined to comment to Bloomberg.

AG-102.summary: On 30 January 2008 two cables were cut about five miles off Alexandria: one owned by FLAG Telecom and the SEA-ME-WE 4 cable. The cuts disrupted Internet use across the Middle East and parts of Asia. A FLAG cable in the Gulf, about 35 miles north of Dubai, was cut on 1 February. Qtel reported damage on 3 February to a cable linking Qatar with the UAE. Near the Gulf cut, a FLAG repair crew found an abandoned anchor of more than 5.5 tons. On 19 February Dubai authorities impounded two ships, MV Hounslow and MT Ann, one of which was released after its owner agreed to pay US$60,000 in damages to FLAG.
AG-102.records:
FLAG Telecom and the SEA-ME-WE 4 consortium of 16 companies: the faults and repair findings.
Egypt's transport ministry: reviewed onshore footage covering 12 hours before and after the Alexandria cuts. It found that no vessels had sailed in the area and noted that the area was marked on maps as a no-go zone.
Egypt's telecommunications ministry: said no ships were registered near the cut.
Reliance Globalcom, FLAG's parent: studied satellite images of ship movements.
Dubai Port Trust, the Dubai Police CID and the coast guard: handled the anchoring case.
Qtel: recorded its own fault.
AG-102.gap: Four faults in different seas within five days invited a single explanation, although each fault was recorded by a different owner and coastal state. Bloggers speculated about sabotage, on which FLAG and government authorities declined to comment. Egypt answered the anchor hypothesis with a negative finding based on its own footage. In the sources checked, no operator or authority published a cause for the Alexandria cuts. FLAG did not say how the anchor in the Gulf had cut the cable or which vessel it came from.
AG-102.joining: Reliance Globalcom joined its fault position with satellite imagery of ship movements and passed the result to the Dubai authorities. Dubai Port Trust officials said the ships had improperly dropped anchor. One ship was released after its owner paid compensation. Two sailors from the other were to be referred to the Dubai Public Prosecution. The sources checked show no public joining of the Alexandria records. No hostile actor was named.

AG-103.summary: Distributed denial-of-service attacks on Georgian internet infrastructure began as early as July 20, 2008, including an attack on the president's website. Many of the most serious attacks began as Russian forces moved on August 7–8: the parliament's website was defaced and government sites were hit. In Gori, official and local news sites were shut down before Russian aircraft arrived. In August 2009 the US Cyber Consequences Unit reported that the attacks disrupted government email and communications and that the National Bank of Georgia was offline for ten days. The Unit found that the first wave used botnets apparently controlled by Russian organized crime and that the second recruited civilian sympathizers through social networks and hacker forums.
AG-103.records:
Georgian site operators: outage records.
US Cyber Consequences Unit, a private research institute: a technical analysis.
A US defense intelligence analyst: published a case study.
Russian forums: the attack tools posted for volunteers.
AG-103.gap: Simultaneity with an invasion removed any recognition gap. Attribution stayed open because the attacks ran through civilian volunteers, criminal botnets and forums that gave the state distance.
AG-103.joining: The US-CCU reported in 2009 that it found no direct link between the attacks and the Russian government or military, although the attackers' timing showed advance knowledge of military plans. A 2011 case study by a US defense intelligence analyst described the operations as closely synchronized with land, air and sea operations but called them alleged. Moscow officially denied involvement.

AG-104.summary: From 11 October 2008 to 4 July 2009, six explosions near Dawson Creek damaged EnCana sour-gas and natural gas pipelines, a wellhead, a metering shed and a gas facility. Two of the three blasts that followed the first threatening letter caused sour-gas leaks. The fourth went off 250 meters from the nearest home. Anonymous letters to local media demanded a stop to oil and gas operations in the area. The RCMP called the attacks domestic terrorism and had 250 investigators on the case by July 2009. EnCana raised its reward from C$500,000 to C$1 million. Wiebo Ludwig, convicted in April 2000 of bombing a Suncor well site in Alberta, was arrested in January 2010 and released without charge. No one was charged.
AG-104.records:
A hunter: found the first crater on 11 October 2008.
EnCana: operational records of each damaged asset. EnCana also offered the reward.
Dawson Creek Daily News: received four anonymous letters, three handwritten and one typed (April 2010).
RCMP: led the bombing investigation from its Vancouver headquarters and called in its Integrated National Security Enforcement Team. It had interviewed 450 people by July 2009.
The Dawson Creek detachment of the RCMP: handled the April 2010 letter as a separate file.
British Columbia Crown counsel: had not approved charges after the January 2010 arrest.
AG-104.gap: The craters left by the devices and the intent announced in the letters made recognition immediate. On attribution the records stayed apart: the RCMP kept the letter and bombing investigations separate ('I want to make sure that we're not associating one with the other'). One handwritten letter was found to be a hoax. In the sources checked, DNA on the typed 2010 letter produced no charge.
AG-104.joining: In 2008-2009 the RCMP joined the six blasts into one domestic-terrorism investigation and brought in its national security unit. No court named an attacker. Around 2013 the RCMP said only that the investigation had not concluded.

AG-105.summary: Sanlu, which had received complaints about sick infants from early 2008, detected melamine in its infant formula in its own tests on 1 August 2008. On 3 August the company alerted city authorities and the local health office. Fonterra, a New Zealand shareholder, learned of the contamination on 2 August and sought the New Zealand government's help. Prime Minister Helen Clark bypassed the local authorities to inform Beijing directly. A recall began only in mid-September, when two infant deaths and almost 600 sick children were reported. By early December the Ministry of Health counted 294,000 infants sickened and 51,900 hospitalized.
AG-105.records:
Individual hospitals: the kidney cases.
Gansu provincial health authorities: reported to the central health bureau in July 2008 that sick babies with kidney problems had drunk only Sanlu powder.
Sanlu: the complaint log and its laboratory results.
The city authorities and the local health office: received the company's report in August.
Fonterra: the information it passed to the New Zealand government.
Ministry of Health: ran 22.38 million examinations and revised the count from 53,000 to 294,000.
Propaganda controls: in place on food-safety news in the two years before the Beijing Olympics.
AG-105.gap: Kidney stones in infants arrived at hospitals one at a time and in different provinces, each case below any threshold that would generate an alert. The categories in use were clinical. Sanlu held the record that joined the cases and passed it only to local authorities, under controls on food-safety reporting during the Olympic period. Some six weeks passed between the company's detection of melamine and the exposure of the cover-up. The route that worked ran through a foreign shareholder and a foreign prime minister.
AG-105.joining: Fonterra, a foreign corporate shareholder, and the New Zealand government went around the local administrative chain in September 2008. The Ministry of Health then joined the clinical cases nationally through mass screening. The act was adulteration for profit, with no hostile intent toward the service. Its institutional mechanics are nonetheless those the volume describes.
AG-105.harm_found_later: The count of sickened children rose from almost 600 in mid-September to 294,000 by early December. The rise shows how much of the harm existed only in unjoined clinical records until national screening.

AG-106.summary: A 14-year-old in Łódź adapted a television remote control into an infrared device that could move the points of the city's tram network. According to police, he testified that he had switched points three times, once causing a tram to jump the tracks. The Daily Telegraph reported four derailments, and RMF FM reported twelve passengers injured. He was to face a juvenile court on charges of endangering public safety. On 15 January 2008 RMF FM reported that points without safeguards in Łódź still worked on infrared.
AG-106.records:
MPK Łódź, the municipal tram operator: was checking whether the tram driver had contributed to the derailment.
Łódź police (spokesman Mirosław Micor): the interrogation and the device found at the boy's home. The police also held his school exercise book listing the best junctions and the signals to change.
The juvenile court: received the case.
A tram driver: told The Telegraph that he had steered right and the tram swerved left.
The press: reported the injuries.
AG-106.gap: Derailments at points enter an operator's record as technical or driver faults. MPK Łódź's review was still examining its own driver after the police had a suspect. The checked sources do not show how the derailments were joined into one deliberate series or how the boy was identified.
AG-106.joining: Łódź police joined the incidents through the boy's statement and the search of his home, and named him as the cause. The press then reported that the infrared control remained unprotected.

AG-107.summary: In late 2009 engineers at Newark noticed that satellite-positioning receivers for a new airport navigation aid lost signal at certain times of day. An Exelis report says that the FAA investigated for about two months before tracing the cause to a truck driver's inexpensive jammer, used to prevent his employer from tracking his movements. On 3 August 2012 the FAA complained to the FCC that the Port Authority had been experiencing interference during pre-deployment testing of the airport's ground-based augmentation system (GBAS). The next day an FCC agent used direction finding to locate a pickup truck at an airport gate. Its driver admitted operating a jammer to block the GPS tracking system his employer had installed. On 2 August 2013 the FCC proposed a forfeiture of US$31,875.
AG-107.records:
Engineers: recorded the receiver outages from late 2009.
FAA: investigated (Exelis) and filed the complaint with the FCC.
Port Authority, operator of the GBAS: experienced the interference during testing.
The FCC Enforcement Bureau's New York office: located the emitter.
Port Authority police and security personnel: stopped the vehicle.
AG-107.gap: The outages were intermittent, occurred at certain times of day and came from a moving vehicle, in a system still under test. To connect them to the emitter, direction-finding measurements were needed.
AG-107.joining: The FAA and the FCC joined the airport's interference reports with direction-finding measurements. The FCC issued a Notice of Apparent Liability against Gary P. Bojczak, adopted on 1 August and released on 2 August 2013. The disruption was settled as a private, non-hostile act.

AG-108.summary: Nigeria's crude exports fell below 1 million barrels per day in August 2022 for the first time since at least 1990. In early October 2022 NNPC chief executive Mele Kyari told a parliamentary committee of an illegal 4-kilometer line from the Forcados export terminal, operated by Shell's SPDC, into the sea. Kyari said the line had gone unnoticed for nine years and had been found during a six-week clampdown on theft. Menas Associates gave a different account, tying the nine-year 4-kilometer line to the Trans Escravos pipeline, announced by the former militant leader Tompolo on 9 October. Menas also reported a separate line on the Forcados Export Trunk Line on 16 October, less than a kilometer from a military post. In August 2023 NEITI put losses that 'is from theft and sabotage' at over 619.7 million barrels, worth $46.16 billion, for 2009–2020.
AG-108.records:
NNPC: export figures. NNPC is also a joint-venture partner.
SPDC: operator of the terminal.
The military: its post lay less than a kilometer from the Forcados connection (Menas).
Tantita Security Services: holder of a ₦48 billion a year contract to halt crude theft.
Tompolo: claimed to have found as many as 58 illicit connection points in Delta and Bayelsa states.
The National Assembly committee: received Kyari's testimony.
