NEITI: industry reports covering production and losses, approved by government, company and civil-society stakeholders under the EITI Standard.
AG-108.gap: Theft through a concealed connection produces no incident record of its own. In the sources checked, it surfaced only as an aggregate national loss attributed to 'theft and sabotage'. Tompolo claimed that security forces 'are actually heavily implicated in the industrial scale theft of crude oil'. One connection sat beside a military post. Menas noted that it was 'unclear why their use has significantly increased since the beginning of the year'.
AG-108.joining: An anti-theft clampdown, during which the former militant leader Tompolo publicized illicit lines, brought the connections to light. NNPC disclosed the Forcados line to parliament. NEITI aggregated losses nationally without naming perpetrators. No operator of the Forcados line was named in the sources checked.

AG-109.summary: In the final months of the war against the LTTE, government forces shelled on a large scale in three consecutive No Fire Zones where civilians had been encouraged to gather. In the war zone, all hospitals were hit by mortars and artillery, some repeatedly, although their locations were well known to the government. UN staff compiled casualty figures, and UN satellite imagery showed heavy artillery fire while the war was under way. The Secretary-General's Panel of Experts (April 2011) found that 'the Government systematically shelled hospitals on the frontlines,' and an internal review led by Charles Petrie (November 2012) found that senior UN officials had worked to soften statements and remove casualty figures. The review also found that they had dismissed their own staff's death tolls as unverified.
AG-109.records:
UN staff: death tolls compiled with what the internal review called a 'rigorous methodology.'
UN satellite imagery: heavy artillery shelling and more civilians in the war zone than the government claimed. The top UN official in Sri Lanka downplayed it in a letter to the government.
Hospital staff: strikes on hospitals.
Government of Sri Lanka: a 'humanitarian rescue operation' with a policy of 'zero civilian casualties.'
The Panel of Experts: later used UN documents, reports by NGOs and individuals, satellite images (16 of them in the report, showing hospitals repeatedly hit), photographs and video. The government did not permit it to visit the country.
AG-109.gap: Inside the UN, the records had been joined while the shelling continued. The gap came from a decision not to publish or attribute them. According to the internal review, UN officials feared that criticism would lead the government to restrict humanitarian access. The review also records that UN aid workers had been barred from the northern war zone in late 2008. It notes that member states held no formal meeting on the conflict's final months in the Security Council, Human Rights Council or General Assembly.
AG-109.joining: The Panel of Experts, established by the Secretary-General in May 2010, joined the records two years after the event and found that most civilian casualties in the final phases were caused by government shelling. The government rejected the report as 'illegal' and 'biased, baseless and unilateral.' The internal review then examined the UN's own conduct, calling its failure to protect civilians a 'grave failure'. The draft, which AP obtained, contained an executive summary that was deleted from the published version.
AG-109.harm_found_later: A UN report released in 2011 said up to 40,000 Tamil civilians may have been killed in the final months. The hospital deaths within that number were reconstructed only after the war, from records the UN had held at the time.

AG-110.summary: Malware in the control systems of the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant, a declared uranium enrichment facility under IAEA safeguards, was designed to change the speed of IR-1 centrifuges while the control room received signals that the plant was operating normally. In late 2009 or early 2010 Iran decommissioned and replaced about 1,000 IR-1 centrifuges. The Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) judged that this level of breakage exceeded expectations. The code became public in summer 2010 through a programming error. ISIS tied it publicly to the losses only in December 2010.
AG-110.records:
Plant operators: failure and replacement records, which are not public. The New York Times (2012) quoted participants as saying the attack sent the control room signals that 'everything downstairs was operating normally.'
IAEA safeguards inspectors: counted installed and operating cascades. The IAEA report of 18 February 2010 showed centrifuges in 11 of the 18 cascades of module A26 disconnected.
Symantec's W32.Stuxnet Dossier: an attack sequence, as summarized by ISIS, that raised centrifuge frequency as high as 1,410 Hz and, after about 27 days, lowered it toward 2 Hz.
Ali Akbar Salehi, head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran: said on 23 November 2010 that the virus had been discovered before it could cause harm.
President Ahmadinejad: said a software attack had caused 'problems for a limited number of our centrifuges.'
AG-110.gap: The operators' category was equipment failure. The attackers anticipated it: participants told the New York Times that they expected 'the Iranians would blame bad parts, or bad engineering, or just incompetence,' and that no two attacks were exactly alike. Inspectors counted machines for safeguards purposes and recorded no causes. Code analysts knew what the malware commanded and had no plant data to confirm which plant it served. Each holder answered its own question. The operators' own display was falsified, so the first record was compromised at its source.
AG-110.joining: ISIS (David Albright, Paul Brannan, Christina Walrond), a private Washington research institute, joined the public IAEA counts with Symantec's code analysis on 22 December 2010. It concluded that 'Stuxnet is a reasonable explanation for the apparent damage to module A26,' while listing open questions. These included that Iran had not admitted a Stuxnet attack on Natanz and that ordinary explanations such as manufacturing flaws had not been ruled out. The attackers were named only through press reporting: on 1 June 2012 the New York Times, citing participants, reported that the worm had been developed by the United States and Israel.

AG-111.summary: Shortly after midnight on 28 July 2010 an explosion damaged the tanker M. Star in Omani waters in the Strait of Hormuz. The Marshall Islands-flagged ship, operated by Mitsui O.S.K. Lines, was carrying 270,000 tons of oil from Das Island in the UAE to Chiba. A crew member saw a flash of light before the blast. A lifeboat was blown off, and a crew member was cut by broken glass. The ship reached Fujairah under its own power.
AG-111.records:
Mitsui O.S.K. Lines: the crew's account. Its spokeswoman said an attack was 'highly likely'.
The Fujairah port director, quoted by the UAE news agency WAM: said the tanker had been hit by a large wave caused by a tremor.
An unnamed official source quoted by WAM: ruled out an attack.
An Iranian shipping official quoted by Mehr: said an earthquake was the likely cause.
The US Geological Survey: had no reports of recent earthquakes in the area.
The US Navy's Fifth Fleet: said it was investigating and did not know the cause.
Japan's transport ministry: did not immediately suspect an attack and said the possibility could not be ruled out.
AG-111.gap: On the first day each institution reported within its own category (port casualty, seismic event, naval incident, owner's damage report). Before the hull was examined, coastal-state explanations were issued. The flag state, the coastal state where the blast occurred, the port state and the operator's state were four different states.
AG-111.joining: On 6 August 2010 WAM reported an unnamed UAE official as saying that investigators had found traces of homemade explosives on the hull, which bore a square dent. The same official said investigators believed that a small boat carrying explosives had approached the tanker, indicating a terror attack. The al-Qaeda-linked Abdullah Azzam Brigades posted an online claim of responsibility. Japan's transport minister asked the UAE to verify the findings.

AG-112.summary: Cholera appeared in Haiti in October 2010, nine months after the January earthquake. By late 2016 it had sickened nearly 800,000 people and killed nearly 9,000. A French–Haitian investigation (Piarroux et al., July 2011) traced the start of the epidemic to Meille, near Mirebalais, where newly arrived Nepalese MINUSTAH troops had come on 9, 12 and 16 October. It concluded that contamination of the Artibonite and one of its tributaries 'downstream from a military camp triggered the epidemic.' In May 2011 the UN's Independent Panel of Experts reported that the strain most closely matched strains previously confined to South Asia and that camp sanitation was not sufficient to prevent contamination. Yet the panel called the outbreak the result of a 'confluence of circumstances' and 'not the fault of, or deliberate action of, a group or individual.'
AG-112.records:
Haiti's Ministry of Public Health and Population: established a National Cholera Surveillance System within days of detection. It reported 604,634 cases and 7,436 deaths through 20 October 2012.
Health facilities: reported cases by commune to departmental health directorates. Only the first cases in each department received bacteriological confirmation.
Cuban medical brigades and MSF: their own case surveys, which the French–Haitian team used as a check.
The UN panel, led by Alejandro Cravioto: its own field and strain findings.
AG-112.gap: Haiti's surveillance system counted cases by place and date and was not designed to identify a source. The French–Haitian team wrote that an epidemiological study cannot establish the exact contaminating event and that identifying the source and responsibilities falls to legal authorities. The UN's own panel joined comparable records and declined to assign fault.
AG-112.joining: The French–Haitian team was sent at the request of Haitian authorities to the French Embassy and worked in November 2010. It joined surveillance data, field investigation and timing and pointed to the camp. The UN panel joined field and laboratory findings and named no responsible party. On 1 December 2016 Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon told the General Assembly that 'we simply did not do enough with regard to the cholera outbreak and its spread in Haiti,' without stating that peacekeepers brought the disease. He proposed $400 million for the cholera response and assistance to victims.
AG-112.harm_found_later: Deaths were recorded as cholera deaths in the national surveillance system. Their link to the camp rests on outside reconstruction, and the 2016 apology did not state it.

AG-113.summary: Jammers in North Korea disrupted GPS reception across South Korea's northwest in repeated waves. Data reported by the Central Radio Management Office counted 181 cell towers, 15 aircraft and one naval vessel affected in August 2010 (jammer at Kaesong). For March 2011 the same data counted 145 towers, 106 aircraft and 10 ships (Kaesong and Mount Kumgang). For April–May 2012 they counted 1,016 aircraft and 254 ships. During drills in spring 2016 about 962 aircraft and 700 fishing boats reported GPS problems. The legislator Jun Hyeon-hee counted 2,143 jamming attacks from North Korea since 2010. From 29 May to 3 June 2024 pilots filed about 500 reports of GPS anomalies and ground-proximity warnings in the Incheon FIR. On 8–9 November 2024 the Joint Chiefs of Staff warned ships and aircraft in the West Sea of North Korean jamming from Haeju and Kaesong.
AG-113.records:
The Central Radio Management Office: kept cross-sector counts.
A government-funded jammer-location project (2010–2015): developed direction-finding from receiving stations.
Pilots: reported anomalies through aviation channels.
The ships and fishing boats: reported position loss.
The cell towers: counted among affected systems.
The JCS: issued warnings.
The ICAO Council: expressed serious concern about North Korea's jamming on 5 July 2012.
ITU and ICAO: planned a joint study.
ICAO: sent Pyongyang a warning letter in 2016. After Seoul complained in 2024, ICAO warned North Korea to stop.
South Korea's July 2024 working paper to the APANPIRG CNS Sub-group: counts the incidents without naming their source.
AG-113.gap: Because interference was simultaneous over a wide area and the radio regulator kept counts across sectors, the gap narrowed. The fragments still sit in separate categories: a pilot's terrain warning, a fishing boat's lost fix and a cell tower's fault fall to different authorities. South Korea's 2024 paper to a regional ICAO technical body recorded the incidents without a named source. The ICAO Council itself had addressed North Korea by name.
AG-113.joining: From 2010 the radio regulator joined counts across aviation, maritime and mobile records. The government and the JCS named North Korea at home. ICAO received the matter and warned Pyongyang. No North Korean acknowledgment appeared in the sources checked.

AG-114.summary: Between 2011 and 2020 four explosions hit Bulgarian ammunition sites, beginning with an EMCO warehouse near Lovnidol on 12 November 2011. Two blasts struck VMZ Sopot facilities near Iganovo in 2015 and also destroyed EMCO-owned ammunition. In 2020 an explosion hit a depot near Maglizh holding fuses from the Arsenal plant. No one was hurt, and prosecutors identified no clear cause for any blast. In late April 2015 EMCO's owner, Emilian Gebrev, his son and the company's production director were poisoned with a nerve agent. On 28 April 2021 Bulgarian prosecutors announced that they had joined the four blast cases and assumed a link to the poisoning. The announcement came eleven days after the Czech government linked the 2014 Vrbětice depot explosions to Russian military intelligence.
AG-114.records:
The prosecution service: investigated the Lovnidol blast and found an explosive device. It suspended the probe in 2013 because it could tie no perpetrator to the blast.
The Iganovo and Maglizh blasts: recorded without an identified cause. A fire later in 2015, which investigators believe was arson, destroyed evidence in the Iganovo case.
The poisoning case: a separate criminal case in which Bulgaria charged three Russians in 2019.
The shells destroyed at Lovnidol: more than 3,000 152 mm rounds. They had been stored at Vrbětice in the Czech Republic and shipped to Lovnidol between 4 October and 4 November 2011.
AG-114.gap: The blasts were spread over nine years and three owners, injured no one and had no established cause. The Lovnidol probe was suspended even though a device had been found. The link depended on records held abroad: the Czech findings on Vrbětice, where the Lovnidol shells had been stored, and later the travel data on Unit 29155 officers compiled by open-source investigators. EMCO itself disputed several facts on which prosecutors relied in 2021, including that a fire preceded the Lovnidol blast and that the stock there was destined for Georgia.
AG-114.joining: The prosecution service and the State Agency for National Security (DANS) assumed a link between the blasts, the poisoning and the Czech explosions. The joined cases went to the Specialized Prosecution Office, and prosecutors announced cooperation with Czech authorities. The Prosecutor General's spokesperson, Siika Mileva, said the investigation indicated that Russians had sought to disrupt military supplies to Georgia and Ukraine. Open-source investigators supplied much of the linkage: in November 2019 Bellingcat, Der Spiegel and The Insider tied the Gebrev poisoning to GRU Unit 29155. In October 2023 The Insider and Bellingcat tied the Lovnidol blast to the same unit through travel data. The sources checked report charges only in the poisoning case.

AG-115.summary: Several organizations counted attacks on health care in Syria, each with its own method and threshold. Between March 2011 and July 2019, Physicians for Human Rights corroborated 578 attacks on at least 350 facilities and the killing of 890 medical personnel. The Syrian American Medical Society recorded 200 attacks in four northern governorates in 2016. The Turkey-based health cluster logged 402 incidents between early November 2015 and December 2016. When researchers matched the SAMS and PHR records for 2016, only part of them overlapped.
AG-115.records:
PHR: corroboration under what it calls a conservative methodology, with attribution to parties. It attributed 521 of the 578 attacks to Syrian government and allied forces, including 297 by Syrian government forces and 224 by forces identified as either Russian or Syrian government.
SAMS: field data collectors using a mobile questionnaire or text messages in Aleppo, Idleb, Hama and Homs.
Health cluster for northern Syria, based in Turkey: alerts from cluster partners via WhatsApp and an anonymized online data-entry tool, covering mainly areas with a substantial presence of armed opposition groups. An attack counted as verified only if reported by at least one cluster partner and one external partner with most key data points matching.
WHO Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care: WHO states that it "does not collect nor verify information on perpetrators."
AG-115.gap: PHR, SAMS, the health cluster and WHO each used its own definitions, verification rule and geographic reach. As a result, the same strike could be counted, excluded or attributed differently. Haar and colleagues found that of 90 incidents at health facilities verified by PHR and 177 recorded by SAMS in 2016, only 60 could be matched to each other. WHO, the body with the widest UN mandate, excludes perpetrators by design.
AG-115.joining: Academics working with PHR and SAMS (Haar et al., PLOS Medicine, April 2018) matched two of the datasets and concluded that there may have been significantly more attacks than any single method captured. No official body joined the datasets. Attribution to the Syrian government and Russia came from PHR, whose data the UN Secretary-General has shared with the Security Council. WHO names no perpetrator.

AG-116.summary: The cause of each oil spill in Nigeria is recorded through a joint investigation visit (JIV). A spill recorded as caused by sabotage or theft entitles the affected community to no compensation. Amnesty International and the Centre for Environment, Human Rights and Development (CEHRD) reported in Bad Information that 'the companies themselves are the primary investigators'. The report also stated that there was 'no legitimate basis' for the companies' claim that most spills came from sabotage and theft. In March 2018 Amnesty's Decode Oil Spills project identified at least 89 spills (46 Shell, 43 Eni) with 'reasonable doubts surrounding the cause'. The project, which worked with 3,545 volunteers from 142 countries, had its findings verified by the pipeline expert Accufacts. Shell called the allegations 'false, without merit', and Eni said Amnesty's statements were 'not correct and, in some cases, not acceptable'.
AG-116.records:
Operating companies (Shell's SPDC and Eni's Nigerian Agip): lead the JIVs.
Shell: has posted its JIV reports online since 2011.
NOSDRA, the spill regulator: publishes spill data on its online monitor under cause categories (oil theft and sabotage, corrosion, equipment failure, operational or maintenance error, unspecified). For January–August 2023 the data attributed 5,167 of 5,575 spilled barrels (reported as 92.73%) to theft and sabotage.
Regulations: require a site visit within 24 hours of a report. Shell met that deadline 26% of the time and Eni 76%.
Communities and their lawyers: their own accounts. In the Bodo case Shell 'massively understated' the volume spilled and, after legal action, paid £55 million in compensation.
AG-116.gap: Each spill produces its own form, and the classification is made by the party whose liability depends on it. Amnesty and CEHRD found that 'regulatory certification of companies' oil spill processes is not credible'. The merged category 'oil theft and sabotage' joins criminal tapping with deliberate damage, so the hostile category is never tested on its own terms. Doubtful classifications appear only when forms and photographs are pooled across spills, companies and years.
AG-116.joining: Outside parties without legal authority did the joining: Amnesty and CEHRD in Bad Information, and Amnesty's crowdsourced Decode Oil Spills project in 2018. The Decode Oil Spills project asked the Nigerian government to reopen investigations into the 89 spills and to give NOSDRA the tools to hold companies to account. The companies rejected the findings. This joining was aimed at the attack classification itself and named no attacker.
AG-116.harm_found_later: When an operational spill is recorded as sabotage, harm to farms and fisheries becomes uncompensable. Only retrospective review of photographs and forms can reassign the record, as the Decoders project attempted.

AG-117.summary: In 2011 the CIA used a hepatitis B vaccination drive run by a Pakistani doctor, Shakil Afridi, in Abbottabad in an attempt to obtain DNA confirming that Osama bin Laden's family lived in the compound. The Guardian and The New York Times reported the operation in July 2011. The Pakistani Taliban, whose campaign against vaccination predated the disclosure, issued fatwas accusing health workers of spying. For more than a decade, attacks continued on polio vaccination teams and their police escorts. In May 2014 Lisa Monaco, the President's homeland security adviser, wrote to the deans of 13 US schools of public health that 'the CIA will make no operational use of vaccination programs,' a policy CIA Director John Brennan had instituted in August 2013.
AG-117.records:
Pakistan's Social and Living Standards Measurement survey: children's vaccinations by household.
A report cited by Dawn in January 2024: 109 killed and 162 injured in polio-related attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since 2012, most of them police and health workers. The article does not name the body that compiled the report.
The press: reported the CIA's operation.
The CIA: the operation, in the agency's own files.
AG-117.gap: The cause sat in an intelligence operation, while the effects appeared years later in household surveys and in counts of attacks. The institutions that kept those records had no access to the cause and no category for it. In the sources checked, no official body linked the operation to the decline in immunization.
AG-117.joining: Economists Monica Martinez-Bravo and Andreas Stegmann joined household vaccination data with 2008 district vote shares for the Islamist coalition Muttahida Majlis-e-Amal. Their study appeared in the Journal of the European Economic Association and was summarized as Cato Research Brief No. 276 (November 2021). A one-standard-deviation increase in Islamist support was associated with a 9 to 13 percent larger decline in first-dose vaccination after the disclosure. Neither changes in vaccination drives nor changes in facility availability explained the result. A CIA spokesperson said the agency changed its practice after concerns from the public health community. The sources checked record no official account of the harm.
AG-117.harm_found_later: Children left unvaccinated after 2011 appear in surveys without any link to the operation. The link exists only as a statistical reconstruction a decade later.

AG-118.summary: After a pump burned out at the Curran-Gardner Public Water District near Springfield, Illinois, a contract repairman reviewed the SCADA logs on 8 November 2011. He found a June login from a Russian IP address under the system integrator's username, which the district passed to the EPA. On 10 November the Illinois Statewide Terrorism and Intelligence Center issued a report titled 'Public Water District Cyber Intrusion,' which stated that a Russian intruder had turned the SCADA system on and off. The report also stated that the intruder had burned out the pump. DHS's ICS-CERT and the FBI then found 'no malicious traffic from Russia or any foreign entities'. The integrator, Jim Mimlitz, had logged in at the district's request while on vacation in Russia. DHS found that the pump had failed for an electrical-mechanical reason.
AG-118.records:
District operators and a contract repairman: the SCADA logs and the failure record.
The EPA: received the district's report.
The fusion center: produced and distributed the intrusion report, which also stated that usernames and passwords had been stolen.
Illinois State Police: said several agencies, DHS among them, contributed and the center only distributed the report.
DHS: said the report was an Illinois product and so did not undergo DHS review.
The integrator: the explanation of the login.
The Water ISAC, the DHS daily report and ICS-CERT: had not circulated the claim to utilities, according to the consultant Joe Weiss.
ICS-CERT and the FBI: the forensic review.
AG-118.gap: Five months separated the two fragments that the fusion center joined, a foreign login and a mechanical failure. The center did not call the one recorder who could explain the login. Each of the two bodies that might have reviewed the product treated it as the other's, so no review took place. The report then left its intended circle through an emergency-management mailing list and reached Weiss and the press. Some commentators called it the first real attack on US critical infrastructure.
AG-118.joining: ICS-CERT and the FBI interviewed Mimlitz and reviewed the logs. By 23 November 2011 ICS-CERT had told a working group that 'there is no evidence to support claims made in the initial Fusion Center report,' which rested on 'raw, unconfirmed data'. Mimlitz said the logs showed no on/off commands. No attacker existed to name. In October 2012 the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations listed the case ('Russian "Cyberattack" in Illinois') in its staff report on fusion centers. It appeared under the heading 'Fusion Centers May Have Hindered, Not Aided, Federal Counterterrorism Efforts.' The fusion center's own review concerned how the report leaked.

AG-119.summary: On 4 and 5 September 2012, roughly two dozen fires were set at mobile-phone masts in cities across northern Nigeria. In an email on 6 September, the Boko Haram spokesman Abul Qaqa said the group had attacked the masts 'as a result of the assistance they offer security agents'. He said that assistance helped the security forces arrest the group's members. The operators' association ALTON said at least 25 of its members' base stations, many of them hubs, had been destroyed in Borno, Yobe, Bauchi, Gombe and Kano. Its members threatened to suspend service in the North. The police chief ordered round-the-clock surveillance of telecommunications installations.
AG-119.records:
Operators: site losses and costs. An ALTON spokesman put the cost of a base station at N500 million to N1 billion.
The police chief: ordered protective surveillance.
Boko Haram: its own claim and motive.
This Day: reported that cell-phone communication in the affected states had been disrupted.
AG-119.gap: Within a day, the attacker's claim joined fires in several states into one campaign and stated its purpose.
AG-119.joining: Boko Haram joined the incidents itself by claiming them. ALTON, the operators' association, joined its members' losses into a single count. Attacker publicity removed the aggregation gap.

AG-120.summary: A company insider with privileged access unleashed the wiper malware that infected more than 30,000 Saudi Aramco computers on 15 August 2012. The infected computers had to be replaced. A group calling itself the Cutting Sword of Justice claimed the attack as 'an act of retaliation against the Al-Saud regime.' Aramco said oil production and exploration were unaffected because they ran on isolated networks. Aramco restored its main internal network services by the end of August.
AG-120.records:
Aramco: recorded and disclosed the damage.
Symantec: reported on 16 August that the malware (W32.Disttrack) was used 'in specific targeted attacks against at least one organization in the energy sector' and overwrote the master boot record.
Kaspersky's analysis of the same day: judged it 'more likely' a copycat inspired by the April 2012 Wiper story and rejected a technical link to Wiper. It found two sightings in its telemetry, both apparently from security researchers in China.
US intelligence officials: considered Iran responsible without making their basis public.
AG-120.gap: Narrow: one company, simultaneous and visible destruction, and a public claim. The remaining questions concerned attribution behind the claimant.
AG-120.joining: Saudi Aramco joined its own record within days. The claimant publicized the act. The attribution to Iran came from anonymous US intelligence officials quoted in the New York Times (Nicole Perlroth, 23 October 2012). A 2016 Shamoon variant against Saudi organizations was reportedly launched from Iran.

AG-121.summary: In the UNCLOS arbitration brought by the Philippines, the tribunal found on 12 July 2016 that Chinese fishermen had harvested endangered sea turtles, coral and giant clams on a substantial scale, using methods that inflict severe damage on the coral reef environment. Chinese authorities, it found, were aware of the harvesting and had not fulfilled their due-diligence obligations to stop the fishermen. The tribunal also found that China's land reclamation and construction at seven Spratly features had caused severe harm to the coral reef environment, in breach of Articles 192 and 194 of UNCLOS. It also found that the construction had permanently destroyed evidence of the natural condition of the features. China did not participate.
AG-121.records:
Philippine government: reports in the record before the tribunal, among them a Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources report of 28 May 2012.
Professor Kent Carpenter and others: expert reports in the same record.
China's State Oceanic Administration: reports that also formed part of the record.
The tribunal: appointed three independent experts on coral reef biology (Sebastian Ferse, Peter Mumby and Selina Ward), an expert hydrographer to assist in evaluating the Philippines' technical evidence, and an independent expert on navigational safety.
China: its position entered the record through its December 2014 Position Paper and letters to members of the tribunal from the Chinese Ambassador to the Netherlands.
AG-121.gap: Damage to reefs appeared in the records of one claimant's agencies and of scientists. The fishing fleets were nominally private, so their conduct reached a state only through toleration. No domestic institution had authority over both the conduct and the place.
AG-121.joining: An international tribunal joined the ecological records, using experts of its own choosing, and found China in breach of Articles 192 and 194 of UNCLOS.
AG-121.harm_found_later: China's construction, the tribunal found, permanently destroyed evidence of the natural condition of the features in dispute.

AG-122.summary: In April 2012 destructive malware, which became known as Wiper, shut down computer systems at businesses across Iran. There were also reports of data-loss incidents at Iran's Oil Ministry. The International Telecommunication Union, a UN specialized agency, asked Kaspersky Lab to investigate. Kaspersky never recovered the Wiper program itself. Its search turned up Flame, an espionage platform in the wild as early as February–March 2010, which Kaspersky announced on 28 May 2012.
AG-122.records:
Affected Iranian organizations: the wiped systems.
Kaspersky: obtained 'several hard drive images that were attacked by Wiper' and recovered from one of them a registry hive with deleted entries. The entries showed a service created and deleted on 22 April 2012, just before the system went down, which let it state 'with certainty that the incidents took place.'
Hungary's CrySyS Lab and Iran's MAHER CERT: described the same espionage malware separately, as sKyWIper and Flamer.
Kaspersky's telemetry: placed Flame in several countries of the region, among them Iran, Lebanon, Syria and Israel. Wiper incidents were reported only in Iran.
AG-122.gap: The wiper destroyed the traces needed to analyze it. Kaspersky wrote that 'once it was activated, no data survived,' and that the absence of samples was 'causing many to doubt the accuracy of these reports.' The victims' records were therefore of damage without a cause. The investigation was commissioned by an international technical agency and run by a foreign private firm, which found a different and older intrusion.
AG-122.joining: After the ITU, a UN specialized agency without attribution or enforcement functions, commissioned the investigation, Kaspersky joined Iranian hard-drive images with its global telemetry. It concluded that 'Wiper was a separate strain of malware that was not Flame,' that 'there is no information in the code or otherwise that can tie Flame to any specific nation state,' and that a state most likely sponsored it. The Washington Post (19 June 2012), citing unnamed Western officials, reported that the United States and Israel had jointly developed Flame. The paper also reported that the April attacks on the Oil Ministry were carried out by the Israeli side without the knowledge of the US side.

AG-123.summary: Internet service in Egypt had been slowed since 22 March 2013. Seacom announced that at 06:20 GMT on 27 March the SEA-ME-WE 4 cable system suffered a cut off the coast of Egypt. On Wednesday 27 March Egyptian naval forces captured three scuba divers on a fishing boat off Alexandria. The military spokesman, Col. Ahmed Mohammed Ali, said on Facebook that they had been caught cutting an undersea cable of Telecom Egypt. Telecom Egypt's executive manager said the damage behind the slowdown had been caused by a ship.
AG-123.records:
Seacom: recorded and published the 27 March fault.
The navy: recorded the interception and arrests, which the military spokesman announced.
Telecom Egypt: owned the cable the divers were said to be cutting. It attributed the slowdown to a ship damaging another cable.
Egyptian authorities: interrogated the men, who were not named.
AG-123.gap: Two records gave different causes for the same week of disruption: the arrest tied the divers to an attempted cut at a single site, but the operator attributed the service damage to a ship. The sources checked give no motive, sponsor or prosecution, and none of them links the divers to the 27 March fault.
AG-123.joining: The armed forces tied the divers to an attempted cut by arresting them on the spot. No public account joined the arrest with the operators' fault records, and no group or state was named.

AG-124.summary: On 20 March 2013 malware shut down about 32,000 computers at three banks, among them NongHyup and Shinhan, as well as at the broadcasters KBS, MBC and YTN. On 21 March investigators said the malicious code traced to a Chinese IP address. On 22 March the Korea Communications Commission said the address belonged to a NongHyup computer used only on the bank's internal network that happened to match a public Chinese address. On 10 April 2013 the government said North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau had masterminded the attack.
AG-124.records:
Each broadcaster and bank: its own damage records.
The KCC and a joint response team of government, military and civilian organizations: the forensic analysis.
The Ministry of Science, ICT and Future Planning: cited more than 30 of 76 code samples identical to earlier attacks and 22 of 49 IP addresses previously used in North Korean attacks since 2009. It also cited at least six computers inside North Korea that had accessed the financial institutions' systems 1,590 times since 28 June 2012.
AG-124.gap: Simultaneous damage at several prominent institutions made the attack obvious at once, although the attackers had been inside the systems for up to eight months. The error lay in joining: an internal address was taken for a Chinese one and announced before it was checked.
AG-124.joining: Within three weeks a government investigation had joined the records and named North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau. Lee Seung-won, a KCC official, said of the earlier error: 'We were careless in our efforts to double-check and triple-check.'

AG-125.summary: Shortly after midnight on 16 April 2013, attackers cut AT&T fiber-optic lines in an underground vault. They fired more than 100 rounds of .30-caliber rifle ammunition over 19 minutes into PG&E's Metcalf substation south of San Jose. The shots struck 17 transformers, whose radiators leaked oil until the equipment overheated. PG&E rerouted power and no customers lost electricity, although the cable cuts knocked out 911 service in the area. The damage was estimated at about $15 million. No one has been identified or charged.
AG-125.records:
Santa Clara County Sheriff: the criminal case. Sheriff Laurie Smith said the objective appeared to be "shutting down the system".
PG&E: the equipment damage, then a $100 million, three-year security program.
AT&T: the cut fiber-optic lines.
FBI: did not consider the attack terrorism, since no group claimed it and no political or social agenda was identified.
FERC: a staff study of critical substations commissioned before the attack.
DHS's Office of Infrastructure Protection: also held part of the record.
AG-125.gap: Because the attack hit one site in one night and caused no outage, the fragments were joined into one deliberate act quickly. The gap lay in classification: the investigating agency applied a terrorism category that required a group or an agenda and declined it. The event drew national attention only ten months later, through press reports. Separately, the DOE Inspector General concluded in April 2014 that a FERC presentation on the critical-substation study "should have been classified and protected from release."
AG-125.joining: Jon Wellinghoff, by then the former head of FERC, told the Wall Street Journal in February 2014 that the attack was "the most significant incident of domestic terrorism involving the grid that has ever occurred". The FBI held that a terrorist organization was not responsible. FERC ordered NERC on 7 March 2014 to propose physical-security standards and approved CIP-014-1 on 20 November 2014. In October 2015 DHS Assistant Secretary Caitlin Durkovich said, "While we have not yet identified the shooter, there's some indication it was an insider." The classification and the attacker remain open.

AG-126.summary: Syria's government asked for a UN investigation of an alleged attack at Khan al-Assal in March 2013. On 26 March 2013 Ban Ki-moon appointed Ake Sellstrom to lead the fact-finding mission, whose role did not include identifying perpetrators. The mission reported clear findings of sarin use at Ghouta on 21 August 2013 without naming a user. The OPCW Fact-Finding Mission likewise determines use or likely use without attribution. Security Council resolution 2235 (2015) established the OPCW-UN Joint Investigative Mechanism to identify perpetrators. The Mechanism attributed the Khan Shaykhun attack of 4 April 2017, which killed around 100 people, to Syria, and the Umm Hawsh attack of September 2016 to ISIL. It lapsed in November 2017 after Russia vetoed a one-year extension. The OPCW Conference of the States Parties then gave the Technical Secretariat the mandate to identify perpetrators (decision C-SS-4/DEC.3, June 2018). On 27 January 2023 its Investigation and Identification Team found reasonable grounds to believe that the Syrian Arab Air Forces carried out the Douma attack of 7 April 2018, which killed 43 named people.
AG-126.records:
Hospitals, opposition medical networks and the Syrian government: casualty records, under rival claims.
The UN mission: samples and interviews for Ghouta. It could not compare the samples with Syrian official stores, so it could not determine the agent's origin.
Ake Sellstrom, head of the UN mission: said in March 2014, 'We do not have the evidence to say who did what.'
Syria: delayed the team's entry, first over the scope of the investigations and then over Ghouta.
The Fact-Finding Mission: determinations of use or likely use. These are the threshold the Investigation and Identification Team requires before it will investigate an incident.
The Joint Investigative Mechanism: the attribution record from 2015 to 2017. Its head, Edmond Mulet, briefed the Security Council.
The Investigation and Identification Team: the attribution record since 2018, under a standard of reasonable grounds to believe.
AG-126.gap: Authority to find and authority to name were placed in different bodies with different sponsors. The first mission was confined by its mandate to the question of use and delayed in its access by the inviting government. When a body with authority to name produced names, a permanent member of the Security Council ended its mandate. The naming resumed only after a treaty body, by vote, gave its own secretariat the power, without Security Council endorsement.
AG-126.joining: The UN mission and the Fact-Finding Mission joined incident records promptly. The naming was done from 2015 to 2017 by the Joint Investigative Mechanism, then by the Investigation and Identification Team, whose authority Russia and Syria reject. No court has adjudicated these attributions. The sources consulted record no formal attribution of the Ghouta attack of 2013 by any UN or OPCW body.

AG-127.summary: On 4 August 2020 ammonium nitrate unloaded from the ship Rhosus in 2014 and stored in hangar 12 of the Port of Beirut exploded, killing 218 people and wounding 7,000. For six years the hazard had been recorded and passed on among customs, the port authority, the transport ministry, the courts, the army, State Security and the highest offices of state. Three days after the blast President Michel Aoun said the investigation would examine negligence or accident and 'the possibility of external interference through a rocket or bomb or other act'. Hezbollah and Israeli officials quickly ruled out Israeli involvement.
AG-127.records:
Human Rights Watch: the source for every record below except the FBI report.
A customs official: alerted colleagues to the cargo's danger on 21 February 2014.
The captain's lawyers: wrote to the Ministry of Public Works and Transport on 7 April 2014.
The Ministry of Public Works and Transport: passed on only part of the information.
The harbor master: sent two warning letters in 2014.
A judge of urgent matters: ordered the cargo offloaded and stored 'in an appropriate place' on 27 June 2014, on incomplete ministry information.
The Port Authority: assigned hangar 12 in October 2014.
The head of the port's Manifest Department: recommended handing the material to the army or re-exporting it.
Army Command: reportedly said it had no need for the material.
Military Intelligence: took no apparent steps to secure the material.
General Security and the Interior Minister: acknowledged knowing of the cargo and said it lay outside their jurisdiction.
State Security: a report of 20 July 2020 that found port officials negligent.
The President and Prime Minister: did not act in a timely way once informed.
The FBI: a report, cited by caretaker Prime Minister Hassan Diab, that put the quantity that exploded at 500 tons.
AG-127.gap: Within its own remit, each office recorded the hazard and forwarded it as a procedural matter. The ministry passed on partial information to the court, security agencies disclaimed jurisdiction, and the army declined the material. State Security's findings reached senior officials after what HRW calls 'an unconscionable delay.' Each holder treated removal as another's responsibility.
AG-127.joining: In August 2021 Human Rights Watch joined more than 100 documents, obtained through open-source research, Al-Jadeed's investigative unit, the Samir Kassir Foundation and six confidential sources. It reported that officials had failed to supervise repair work on hangar 12 that may have triggered the blast and asked the UN Human Rights Council to mandate an independent investigative mission. The domestic investigation stalled. Judge Fadi Sawan charged 37 people, mostly mid- and low-level officials, and was removed by the Court of Cassation in February 2021. His successor, Tarek Bitar, faced parliamentary and other immunities. The sources checked name no hostile actor.

AG-128.summary: The Donetsk Filter Station, on the contact line near Avdiivka and Yasynuvata, officially supplied water to 345,309 people on both sides of the line (Voda Donbasa, December 2016 figure). UNICEF estimated that its shutdown could affect up to 1.1 million. The station was repeatedly shelled or lost power: on 22 July 2017 fighting cut its electricity and left hundreds of thousands without water for 48 hours. On 22 December 2017 staff stopped the chlorine supply to avoid a gas release and took shelter during the third shelling in 24 hours. On 17 May 2018 shelling damaged switchgear and transformers and the station suspended operation.
AG-128.records:
Voda Donbasa: the operator, based in the non-government-controlled area. It reported each incident.
The WASH Cluster (UN humanitarian coordination): numbered incident reports recording shelling, chlorine risk and population served. It raised them with the OSCE.
The OSCE Special Monitoring Mission: recorded weapons use near the station, including multiple-launch rocket systems. Its statements did not name the firing party.
UNICEF: published population and risk figures.
Ukrainian ministries: recorded Avdiivka's water reserves and the risk to chlorine storage.
The separatist authorities: blamed the Ukrainian Armed Forces for the July 2017 damage.
The Ukrainian side: denied that charge.
AG-128.gap: The incident records were detailed and frequent, but each recorder worked under a mandate that stopped short of attribution. The operator reported damage, the humanitarian cluster service impact, and the monitoring mission weapons and impacts without naming a side. The question of whether the station was being targeted, or hit as a by-product of positions built around it, belonged to no recorder.
AG-128.joining: The WASH Cluster joined operator reports into a running incident series and passed them to the OSCE, which used them to call for a ceasefire around the station. In July 2017 the open-source analysts of the Atlantic Council's DFRLab joined OSCE posts, UNICEF figures and satellite imagery. The imagery showed new trenches and at least four likely separatist positions around the station. The analysts argued that blaming Ukrainian forces overlooked separatist encroachment, without determining who caused the July 2017 outage. No official institution named a responsible party.
AG-128.harm_found_later: In the records checked, the health effects of repeated water and chlorination interruptions for several hundred thousand people were not linked to particular strikes.

AG-129.summary: In December 2014 a Twitter account calling itself the 'president of anti-nuclear reactor group' posted KHNP documents and blueprints. It threatened further leaks unless specific reactors at Gori and Wolseong were shut down by Christmas. KHNP said reactor safety was not compromised and that the material contained no core technology information. On 17 March 2015 a special investigation team said, as an interim result, that the malicious code resembled that usually used by North Korean hackers and that several IP addresses traced to North Korea. The team counted 94 compromised items, mostly for training and education.
AG-129.records:
KHNP: its network and personnel records. The personal information of 10,000 employees leaked.
A joint government team: monitored KHNP systems through the end of 2014.
A joint investigation led by the Seoul Central District Prosecutors' Office: conducted the inquiry.
The attacker: its own postings formed a public record.
AG-129.gap: Because the attacker announced the intrusion, recognition was immediate. The joining that remained linked the leaks to emails and online communities used by current and former KHNP officials, including, according to 38 North, the hijacked accounts of retired employees. 38 North notes a lack of cyber incident reporting requirements in South Korea.
AG-129.joining: In March 2015 the prosecutor-led team named North Korean hackers, and North Korea denied involvement.

AG-130.summary: Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 was destroyed over eastern Ukraine on July 17, 2014, killing all 298 people aboard. On October 13, 2015 the Dutch Safety Board concluded that a 9M314M warhead carried on a Buk-type missile detonated outside the aircraft, without stating who launched it. On May 24, 2018 the Joint Investigation Team found that the Buk launcher came from Russia's 53rd Anti-Aircraft Missile Brigade in Kursk. The District Court of The Hague sentenced three men to life imprisonment and acquitted one on November 17, 2022. On February 8, 2023 the JIT reported strong indications that the Russian president decided on supplying the Buk to the DPR separatists.
AG-130.records:
The Dutch Safety Board: the technical safety record, held under rules that bar it from apportioning blame.
The JIT (Netherlands, Australia, Belgium, Malaysia, Ukraine): the criminal record.
Bellingcat, an open-source group: identified some of the people involved.
The District Court of The Hague: the trial record.
AG-130.gap: A single, obvious target made the event recognizable at once. The gap lay between institutions whose mandates divided cause from author. Russia, which rejected the JIT's results and was not a member, did not supply the records that could establish the chain of command.
AG-130.joining: The JIT and the Dutch court joined the records into findings of individual guilt. On May 25, 2018 the Netherlands and Australia held Russia responsible for its part in the downing. Bellingcat, an unexpected party, contributed identifications of people involved.

AG-131.summary: The Mosul Dam has been grouted continuously since it opened in the early 1980s. A 2006 US Army Corps of Engineers report called it 'the most dangerous dam in the world.' ISIS captured the dam in 2014 and held it briefly (for several weeks, according to the AP) before Iraqi and Kurdish forces retook it in August 2014. No grouting took place for six weeks after the capture. The grouting did not return to full levels, partly because militants controlled the factory that produced the cement. In late February 2016 the US Embassy in Baghdad warned of 'a serious and unprecedented risk of catastrophic failure with little warning'. It estimated that 500,000 to 1.47 million Iraqis probably would not survive a breach, while Iraq's water resources minister called the danger 'far off.'
AG-131.records:
The Iraqi Ministry of Water Resources and the dam operator: the grouting and monitoring records.
The US Army Corps of Engineers: risk assessments, in 2006 and in a report dated 30 January 2016 that found a 'significantly higher risk of failure than originally understood'. That report emerged in an Iraqi parliamentary report made public in early 2016.
The US Embassy in Baghdad: a public fact sheet with casualty estimates.
Nasrat Adamo, a former chief engineer of Iraq's irrigation ministry: cited a 1984 Iraqi government flood study.
The Iraqi Dams Company and the Italian firm Trevi: the repair contract.
AG-131.gap: The occupation itself was visible and attributed. The harm pathway was cumulative and technical: missed grouting, workers who refused to carry out repairs and the loss of cement supply raised the probability of failure without any single event. The ministry and the US assessors held the same engineering data under opposed judgments of risk. The Iraqi government sought to downplay the warning while advising Tigris valley residents to move away from the river.
AG-131.joining: USACE joined the monitoring data into a higher-risk finding dated 30 January 2016, which reached the public through an Iraqi parliamentary report and the US Embassy. In early March 2016 Iraq signed an 18-month contract worth about $296 million with Trevi for emergency repairs. ISIS was named as the occupier. No authority attributed a failure risk to ISIS as an act of sabotage.

AG-132.summary: Between March and August 2014 intruders compromised several servers of Seoul Metro, which runs four subway lines carrying several million passengers a day, and nearly 60 employee computers. The intrusion became public on 5 October 2015, when Ha Tae-kyung, a legislator of the ruling party, said National Intelligence Service analysis had found the malicious code resembled code used in earlier North Korean attacks. A Seoul Metro spokesman said there were data and information leaks but none related to direct operations. He added: 'We still don't know who was behind the attack.'
AG-132.records:
Seoul Metro: its internal records.
The National Intelligence Service: analyzed the malicious code.
A member of the National Assembly: disclosed the intelligence findings.
AG-132.gap: For more than a year the intrusion stayed inside the operator and the intelligence service. The operator and the legislator citing the service gave different accounts of authorship.
AG-132.joining: The NIS linked the code to earlier North Korean attacks in analysis that reached the public through a legislator. The sources consulted contain no formal government attribution.

AG-133.summary: Shortly after Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, Ukrainian authorities used a dam in Kherson region to shut the North Crimean Canal, which had supplied about 85 percent of Crimea's drinking and irrigation water. By early 2017 Crimea's agriculture minister said that irrigated land had fallen almost thirtyfold. Crimean authorities banned water-intensive crops such as rice and soy. On 26 February 2022 the Crimean official Sergey Aksyonov told Sputnik that the dam had been destroyed by the Russian military.
AG-133.records:
Ukrainian water authorities: the works and the flow.
Vasily Stashuk, Ukraine's top irrigation official at the time: warned of a humanitarian catastrophe.
Mikhail Romashchenko, another Ukrainian official: called Crimea a region with a catastrophically low water supply.
Andrey Ryumshin, agriculture minister on the Crimean side: reported the fall in irrigated land.
Valery Lyashevsky of the State Committee on Water, also on the Crimean side: said that agriculture had been "cancelled".
Russian-installed officials: said they could not afford to divert water from mainland Russia.
AG-133.gap: The cause was a single, open act of water administration. The disputed question therefore concerned its classification: control of a national water resource, or a measure directed at a civilian population. The agricultural figures came from administrations that did not recognize each other's authority.
AG-133.joining: Neither side's records were joined to the other's by any institution, and none classified the shutdown. Russian forces removed the dam in February 2022, which ended the dispute without any institution classifying the preceding eight years.

AG-134.summary: On 16 October 2014 an explosion destroyed a depot in the Vrbětice military area, leased from the Czech army by the private arms trader Imex Group, killing two Imex employees. A second depot exploded on 3 December 2014 and about 400 local residents were evacuated. In 2014 the Interior Ministry cited "inappropriate storage" of munitions, and the case was treated as a possible accident or malpractice. On 17 April 2021 Prime Minister Andrej Babiš said there was "unequivocal evidence" that Russian military intelligence (GRU) was behind the blasts. On 29 April 2024 the National Centre Against Organized Crime (NCOZ) closed the case. It stated that members of GRU Unit 29155 had acted to prevent the delivery of weapons and ammunition to areas where the Russian army was operating.
AG-134.records:
Imex Group: the lease, the stock records and its contacts with prospective buyers.
The Czech army: owned the site.
The Interior Ministry: cited improper storage in 2014.
The security service BIS and NCOZ: the intelligence and criminal files.
Two men posing as would-be arms buyers from the People's Guard of Tajikistan: had asked Imex for access to the depot from 13 to 17 October 2014.
The travel and telephone records: placed the unit's commander, Andrey Averyanov, in Austria from 13 October until hours after the first blast.
AG-134.gap: The physical record was destroyed with the depots, whose contaminated site was not cleared until autumn 2020. An analyst quoted by Euronews states that the case was closed in 2015 for lack of material. The improper-storage frame and a public dispute between the then finance minister, Babiš, and Imex kept the inquiry within an accident-or-negligence category. The fragments that mattered lay outside the Czech case: the true identities of the two GRU officers, Anatoliy Chepiga and Alexander Mishkin, emerged from the 2018 Salisbury poisoning investigation. The records could be joined only once those identities were matched against the names used at Vrbětice.
AG-134.joining: Czech police and intelligence joined the records after the site clearance and the Salisbury identifications. Babiš announced GRU involvement on 17 April 2021, and the Czech Republic expelled dozens of Russian diplomats. Bellingcat, with The Insider, Der Spiegel and Respekt, published travel and phone data that corroborated the official account. NCOZ worked in a joint investigation team with British police and in close cooperation with Ukrainian and US police authorities. After Russia refused legal assistance, it closed the case under Section 159a(5) of the Criminal Procedure Code. It named GRU Unit 29155, and no prosecution followed.
AG-134.harm_found_later: Two Imex employees died and damage exceeded CZK 1 billion. For six years their deaths sat in an accident-or-negligence file, and the 2021 attribution produced no prosecution.

AG-135.summary: By the Yemen Data Project's count, the Saudi- and UAE-led coalition carried out 25,054 air raids in Yemen between March 2015 and April 2022. Strikes hit agricultural sites, fishing boats, a site near a water-drilling rig and a water-bottling factory, among other targets tied to food and water. The coalition's own review body examined incidents one at a time and absolved coalition members in most of them. An academic study that combined several datasets found the destruction of food production 'systematic in nature and coverage.'
AG-135.records:
The coalition's Joint Incidents Assessment Team (JIAT, set up in 2016): announced findings one incident at a time without a transparent methodology.
JIAT: called the 10 September 2016 strike near a water-drilling rig at Beit Sahdan, Arhab, an 'unintended mistake'. It said the 30 August 2015 strike on a water-bottling factory in Hajjah missed its target 'due to weather conditions.'
OHCHR: counted at least 31 civilians killed in the Beit Sahdan strike.
Human Rights Watch: identified 75 JIAT reports by July 2018.
The Yemen Data Project: compiled raids from open sources and coded each target by its original use. Incidents without target information were left uncategorized.
Extension workers of the Sanaa Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation: recorded targets from March 2015 to early August 2016.
The Sanaa Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation: issued separate damage assessments.
The Ministry of Fish Wealth: recorded 146 fishermen killed and 220 boats destroyed through December 2017.
AG-135.gap: JIAT's unit of analysis was the single incident. Its question was whether each strike was lawful, so a pattern across agricultural sites, water sites and fisheries could not appear in its findings. The records that would show the pattern sat with bodies on opposite sides of the war or outside it: Sanaa ministries, an independent open-source project and NGOs. FAO and other international agencies halted support to the Sanaa ministries when Western embassies closed in February 2015, which cut those ministries off from the international system.
AG-135.joining: In a paper distributed by the World Peace Foundation in October 2018, Martha Mundy combined Yemen Data Project raids with Ministry of Agriculture and Irrigation target records. The combination also included Ministry of Fish Wealth data and a 2017 survey of farmers in wadis Zabid and Siham. She concluded that there was 'strong evidence that Coalition strategy has aimed to destroy food production and distribution' in areas controlled by Sanaa. She added that deliberate destruction of family farming and artisanal fishing is a war crime under Article 54 of Additional Protocol I. She held no investigative authority. Human Rights Watch (August 2018) set JIAT findings beside its own investigations and found that JIAT had absolved coalition members of legal responsibility in the vast majority of attacks. The coalition was named throughout. The dispute concerned pattern and intent.
AG-135.harm_found_later: The harm passes through livelihoods and markets: the 2017 farmer survey cited by Mundy found yields down 42 percent in Wadi Zabid and 46 percent in Wadi Siham, mainly from irrigation water shortages. Mundy also cites other research that found fish catches and sales down by at least half, losses that incident investigations do not count.

AG-136.summary: On December 23, 2015 attackers who had gained footholds through BlackEnergy spear-phishing took substations of three Ukrainian regional distribution companies offline, including those of Kyivoblenergo and Prykarpattyaoblenergo. About 225,000 customers lost power for several hours. The attackers ran a modified KillDisk to erase operator systems and flooded a customer call center with thousands of calls so that customers could not report outages. Operators restored power by switching to manual mode. The SBU blamed Russia, and the Sandworm group is the suspected actor.
AG-136.records:
The three companies: outage and restoration records.
Kyivoblenergo: first reported the outages.
DHS ICS-CERT: issued its report on February 25, 2016. The initial estimate of about 80,000 affected customers rose to about 225,000 in the DHS report.
The SBU: the criminal file.
SANS ICS: confirmed a coordinated attack on January 9, 2016.
SANS and the E-ISAC: published a joint analysis on March 18, 2016, which did not address attribution.
AG-136.gap: Near-simultaneous outages at three companies left little doubt that an attack had occurred. The telephone flood was aimed at the outage record itself, delaying the companies' picture of who had lost power.
AG-136.joining: SANS, a private training and research organization, confirmed a coordinated attack 17 days later. DHS ICS-CERT reported two months later, and the SBU blamed Russia. The SANS and E-ISAC analysis set attribution aside.

AG-137.summary: From at least December 2015, a group that Symantec tracked as Dragonfly used malicious emails, watering-hole attacks and trojanized software to install backdoors at energy-sector organizations. There were strong indications of activity in the United States, Turkey and Switzerland, and a marked increase in 2017. Symantec found screen captures whose file names combined machine descriptions with organization names. Many contained "cntrl", "possibly indicating that these machines have access to operational systems." DHS and the FBI later reported that the actors had accessed files on industrial control systems. They also reported that DHS had reconstructed screenshot fragments of a human-machine interface the actors had viewed.
AG-137.records:
Victim companies: each recorded a credential-theft or backdoor incident on business networks.
Symantec: telemetry across customers and countries. Its report of 20 October 2017 did not name a state.
DHS and FBI: alert TA18-074A, 15 March 2018, covering activity since at least March 2016 in the energy, nuclear, commercial facilities, water, aviation and critical manufacturing sectors.
US prosecutors: an indictment returned 26 August 2021 and unsealed 24 March 2022. It covered intrusions from 2012 to 2017, including the business network of Wolf Creek Nuclear Operating Corporation.
AG-137.gap: Each victim saw a routine phishing or backdoor incident on its business network. The campaign's reach toward operational systems was visible only to a vendor with telemetry across many firms and to federal agencies. Symantec itself described the operational access as a possibility.
AG-137.joining: Symantec joined the incidents in 2017 and said it could not definitively determine the group's origins. DHS and the FBI then characterized the activity as "a multi-stage intrusion campaign by Russian government cyber actors," and in 2022 the Justice Department named three officers of the FSB's Center 16 as defendants for the 2012–2017 intrusions. The three were Pavel Akulov, Mikhail Gavrilov and Marat Tyukov. Recognition came in stages over several years.

AG-138.summary: A US airstrike hit the MSF trauma center in Kunduz in the early hours of 3 October 2015, killing at least 42 people (24 patients, 14 staff and 4 caretakers). MSF's internal review of 5 November 2015 found 'no armed combatants or fighting within or from the hospital grounds'. The review stated that the attack continued for more than 30 minutes after MSF first informed Resolute Support and US military officials in Kabul and Washington. Gen. Joseph Votel presented the US military investigation at the Pentagon on 29 April 2016. It attributed the strike to 'a combination of human errors, compounded by process and equipment failures' and disciplined 16 personnel without criminal charges.
AG-138.records:
MSF: the coordinates it had given the US Department of Defense, the Afghan Ministries of Interior and Defense and the US Army in Kabul (most recently on 29 September 2015). It also held its record of calls during the attack and its casualty list.
The US military: the no-strike list, which included the hospital, and the operational record of the mission. The aircrew could not access the list because of a radio system problem.
MSF: asked the United States to consent to an inquiry by the International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission, created under Article 90 of Additional Protocol I.
AG-138.gap: Little aggregation gap arose: a single, well-known facility was hit, and the attacking force was identified at once. The gap concerned authority to investigate, since only the attacking military had access to the operational record. The treaty body that MSF asked for could also act only with the consent of the states concerned.
AG-138.joining: The US military joined its own records and concluded that the strike was a mistake, stating that the label 'war crimes' is typically reserved for intentional acts. MSF's president, Meinie Nicolai, said it was 'incomprehensible that, under the circumstances described by the US, the attack was not called off,' and MSF maintained its request for an independent investigation. In the sources checked, that investigation did not take place.

AG-139.summary: Just before midnight on 24 January 2015 saboteurs blew up transmission towers near Notal in Naseerabad district, Balochistan. The Water and Power Secretary, Younus Dagha, said the damage sent a backward surge into the Guddu power plant and set off a cascade. By his account, the cascade cut power to more than 80 percent of the country, including Islamabad and Karachi, for several hours. The ministry blamed terrorism, joining the blast to two earlier sabotage incidents in the area: three towers of the Guddu–Sibi line on 13 January and an OGDCL gas supply line on 23 January. The Express Tribune reported that Baloch separatists attacked the lines, and no group claim was reported in the sources checked. The same day's reporting described dangerously low furnace oil stocks and gas diversions that had made about a third of generation unavailable. The ministry denied a shortage, and Dagha rejected low production as a cause.
AG-139.records:
The Ministry of Water and Power: recorded three sabotage incidents.
Minister Khawaja Asif: reported the incidents as the cause, in place of any fault in the transmission system, to Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, who had ordered a report on the shutdown.
Dagha: spoke of 220 kV lines between Sibi and Quetta (Express Tribune) and of towers 75 and 76 of the Uch–Sibi line (Dawn). Accounts of the damaged line differ.
Sharbat Umrani, head of the local police station: confirmed that a tower near Notal had been blown up.
Dagha: said restoration could have come two hours earlier if the National Transmission and Dispatch Company (NTDC) had supplied the 10 MW needed to restart the Bin Qasim plant.
K-Electric: said Karachi's supply was fully restored by 6:30 a.m.
Press reports on the state oil importer PSO: recorded near-empty furnace oil stocks and unpaid letters of credit, which the ministry disputed.
AG-139.gap: Both earlier attacks were recorded as local damage on lines already under repair. Dagha said that because the Sibi–Guddu line had been under repair for about ten days, the system could not be protected from going offline. The earlier attacks stayed below national notice until the third attack coincided with a weak grid and produced a national cascade. The fuel-supply records that bore on the state of the grid belonged to other institutions and were not joined to the sabotage account in any inquiry found.
AG-139.joining: Within a day, under the Prime Minister's instruction to report, the ministry joined the three incidents into a sabotage account. It named terrorism and no group. The national cascade narrowed the gap by making the attack visible, while the joined account also served a ministry whose grid capacity and fuel management were under question.

AG-140.summary: On 22 June 2015 an attack on the Transandino pipeline, which the government attributed to the FARC, spilled about 410,000 gallons of crude into four water sources, including the Mira River. Tumaco's municipal water supply was suspended for 180,000 people. In later years Ecopetrol reported two separate series on its pipelines. One counted attacks: 18 on the Transandino by September 2019 and 13 on the Transandino in the first eight months of 2020. Most of the network's attacks in 2019 were attributed to the ELN. The other counted illicit valves for theft, for which Ecopetrol named no perpetrator: 469 on the Transandino by September 2019 and 706 in the first eight months of 2020. Ecopetrol reported that armed groups used only 38% of the stolen product and that the rest was discarded onto soil and into rivers. On the Caño Limón–Coveñas line, illicit valves forced the closure of the Tibú aqueduct intake.
AG-140.records:
Ecopetrol: reported 'atentados' and illicit valves as separate counts. It also reported the soil and water areas contaminated and the barrels spilled.
The Ministry of Housing: recorded the 2015 Tumaco water emergency.
The Navy: delivered water, as did Ecopetrol tanker trucks and 30 trucks supplied through the national disaster-management unit (UNGRD).
Ecopetrol: said it worked with the armed forces, police and regional authorities against the theft.
AG-140.gap: The theft series is far larger than the attack series and carries no attribution, although Ecopetrol said armed groups used part of the stolen product. A valve recorded as theft does not enter the count of attacks. It causes water and environmental harm that other institutions record as an emergency or as contamination.
AG-140.joining: Ecopetrol joins both series in its own reporting and works with the security forces against them. The government named the FARC for the 2015 attack, and most 2019 attacks were attributed to the ELN. In the sources checked, no institution joins the theft series with the water-supply and environmental records into one account of harm, or attributes the valves to particular groups.
AG-140.harm_found_later: Contamination of rivers and water intakes from illicit valves harms downstream communities through a long causal route. That harm is recorded as water emergencies and contamination and is not attributed to the conflict.

AG-141.summary: During a government offensive, the Ain al-Fijeh spring in Wadi Barada, the main water source for Damascus, was damaged on or after 23 December 2016. Water was cut to an estimated 5.5 million people in and around the capital (Bellingcat gave over four million). The Damascus Water Authority cut supply after the water was alleged to be contaminated with diesel. The government maintained that armed groups had contaminated or demolished the supply. In March 2017 the UN Commission of Inquiry found that the Syrian air force struck the spring in 'at least two air raids' and reported 'no evidence of deliberate contamination' of the water supply.
AG-141.records:
Damascus Water Authority: the alleged diesel contamination. It cut the supply.
Syrian government: the statement that rebels had poisoned the spring.
A rebel: a post on 23 December saying that regime bombing had caused the contamination. A video posted by the same rebel on 25 December said a water tunnel was being mined.
Videos posted online: damage near the spring on 23 December with the structure still intact, a bomb landing close to it and a second appearing to strike it.
Commercial satellite imagery: damage and a crater near the outflow on 29 December, compared with imagery of 25 October.
AG-141.gap: The utility's record of diesel in the water was accurate about the water and silent about cause, so each side attached it to its own account of an attack. The record of cause had to be assembled from videos of uncertain upload date and from satellite images.
AG-141.joining: Bellingcat (Nick Waters, 4 January 2017) geolocated the videos and compared them with satellite imagery. It concluded that 'the most likely scenario is that the regime was responsible for the damage to the spring structure,' with bombing the most likely route by which diesel entered the water. The Commission of Inquiry named the Syrian air force. It said the attack 'amounts to the war crime of attacking objects indispensable for the survival of the civilian population,' and rejected the government's claim that armed groups had contaminated or demolished the supply.

AG-142.summary: The transmission lines carrying imported electricity to Kabul were repeatedly cut by explosions at pylons north of the capital. From late January 2016 the destruction of towers in Baghlan, which the government blamed on the Taliban and the Taliban denied, left Kabul, a city of about five million, with weeks of blackouts. In September 2019 the destruction of three pylons in Baghlan carrying power imported from Uzbekistan cut supply to 11 of 34 provinces, with no claim of responsibility. In 2021 the utility, Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat (DABS), reported 23 pylons destroyed or damaged in about one month (June) and more than 30 blown up in three months (July), and blamed 'enemies of light'.
AG-142.records:
DABS: each damaged pylon, the outage it caused and the repair, with running counts published in 2021 that named the attackers only as 'enemies' or 'enemies of light'. Its spokesman spoke of 'unknown attackers' in June 2021.
Security forces: mine clearance before repair crews could work, including two of four mines planted under one Parwan pylon in July 2021.
Baghlan officials and the central government: named the Taliban in 2016.
Taliban: denied destroying the pylons.
Baghlan tribal elders: planned in 2016 to meet Taliban commanders to secure safe passage for repair crews.
A local activist: casualty counts for the fighting in Baghlan in 2016.
AG-142.gap: Because restoring supply was the utility's purpose, each incident entered its records as a damaged pylon and an outage, with a generic enemy in the perpetrator field. No group claimed the 2019 or 2021 attacks, and the main insurgent denied the 2016 attacks. No institution with investigative authority joined the utility's counts to an attribution. Repair depended on mine clearance and local negotiation, which produced no record of who held the ground.
AG-142.joining: DABS joined its own incidents into public counts over one-month and three-month periods in 2021. The government named the Taliban in 2016 without a published investigation. In the sources checked, no body established responsibility before the Taliban took power in August 2021, after which the question lapsed.
AG-142.harm_found_later: In Kabul, weeks-long blackouts pushed households to coal and fell hardest on poor households without generators, a harm recorded only as outage duration.

AG-143.summary: On 29 December 2016 DHS and the FBI published a joint analysis report on the Russian operation they called Grizzly Steppe. After DHS alerted US utilities to the associated malware, Burlington Electric scanned its systems and found the code on one laptop. On 30 December the Washington Post, citing unnamed US officials, reported that Russian hackers had penetrated the US electricity grid through a Vermont utility. Governor Peter Shumlin and Senator Patrick Leahy issued statements about Russian attempts on the grid. The utility stated the same day that it had found the malware on a single laptop "not connected to our organization's grid systems," and the Post changed its headline and added an editor's note.
AG-143.records:
DHS and the FBI: the indicator list and the alert they sent.
Burlington Electric: the scan result and the isolated laptop, which it reported to federal officials. In a follow-up statement on 31 December it said federal officials had told it that similar internet traffic had been seen elsewhere in the country.
US officials (unnamed): an account given to the Post.
Governor Shumlin and Senator Leahy: acted on the press report.
AG-143.gap: An indicator list sent to every utility produced a match at one small utility. An account from the federal side reached the press before the utility's own. The Post, according to The Intercept, did not contact the utility before publishing.
AG-143.joining: Burlington Electric supplied its own account within hours. The Post revised its headline to one about risk to grid security. No attacker was established, and the claim that the grid had been entered was withdrawn.

AG-144.summary: Jessica Reznicek and Ruby Montoya began in November 2016 by setting fire to construction equipment at a Dakota Access pipeline worksite in Buena Vista County, Iowa. Until May 2017 they burned equipment and damaged valves along the route in Iowa and South Dakota. Their tools were oxyacetylene torches, tires and gasoline-soaked rags. In July 2017 they described their actions at a press conference.
AG-144.records:
Energy Transfer: damage to equipment and valves, and restitution of $3,198,512.70.
FBI: the investigation.
US federal prosecutors: the September 2019 indictment on nine counts. Both defendants pleaded guilty to conspiracy to damage an energy facility.
US federal court: the sentence of 30 June 2021.
AG-144.gap: The incidents fell at sites in the Southern and Northern Districts of Iowa and in the District of South Dakota. The sites included locations in Mahaska, Boone and Wapello counties. The sources reviewed do not show investigators linking them before the perpetrators' public claim.
