AG-144.joining: Reznicek and Montoya joined the incidents themselves by public claim in July 2017. In 2019 prosecutors indicted both. Judge Rebecca Goodgame Ebinger sentenced Reznicek to eight years, applying a terrorism enhancement. Acting US Attorney Richard D. Westphal said, "This was a federal crime of terrorism."

AG-145.summary: Two and a half weeks after the South China Sea award, flight-information screens at Noi Bai displayed messages attacking Vietnam's and the Philippines' South China Sea claims. At Tan Son Nhat the screens showed the same messages, and the public-address system broadcast them for about four minutes before it was shut off. Vietnam Airlines' website was defaced, and data on about 400,000 frequent-flyer members appeared online. Airlines switched to manual check-in at many of Vietnam's airports, which press reports linked to more than 100 delayed flights. The group calling itself China 1937CN Team claimed the attack. Deputy Transport Minister Nguyen Nhat said flight control and security had not been affected and that authorities had stopped the attacks by about 18:00.
AG-145.records:
The airports and Vietnam Airlines: the operational timeline.
Vietnam Airlines: confirmation of the website defacement, and the statement that it had isolated the affected systems by 17:45 and restored the site by 18:30. It would not say whether the customer data had leaked.
Ministry of Transport: the public statements.
Ministry of Public Security: an investigation through its A85 and A68 units, with the Northern and Southern Airports Authorities.
Information Security Authority, Vietnam's CERT, FPT and Viettel: assistance to Vietnam Airlines.
The attackers: their own screen messages, which formed a public record.
AG-145.gap: Attacker publicity and simultaneous, visible effects left no aggregation problem; the open question was state sponsorship.
AG-145.joining: The attackers claimed the act. The government referred it to the police and, in the sources consulted, named no state. The group's founder, Liu Yongfa, told the Global Times that 1937CN was a non-government organization and did not want to be a victim of politics.

AG-146.summary: From November 2016 US personnel at the embassy in Havana reported symptoms, and similar reports followed at other posts. In December 2020 a State Department-sponsored National Academies committee chaired by David Relman reported that directed, pulsed radiofrequency energy appeared to be the most plausible mechanism for these cases, especially those with distinct early symptoms. The committee could not rule out other mechanisms. Intelligence community assessments of 1 March 2023 and 10 January 2025 judged foreign-actor responsibility very unlikely. In 2025, however, two components judged at low confidence that a foreign actor likely had, or had a roughly even chance of having, a relevant capability. In June 2026 the Director of National Intelligence rescinded both assessments without issuing a new finding.
AG-146.records:
CIA: its own officers' reports from Havana in late 2016 and early 2017, which it did not share with the State Department.
State Department: the diplomats' records.
The State Department's Accountability Review Board, chaired by Ambassador Peter Bodde: a June 2018 report. It reported that the lack of a designated official at the Under Secretary level was the single most significant deficiency in the department's response and that no task force was formed.
National Academies committee: named its lack of access to specific health or personal information on the affected individuals as one of its challenges.
January 2025 assessment (ICA 2025-00008-B): five components at 'very unlikely', one at 'unlikely' and one abstaining. It stated that collection and investigation had linked no foreign actor to any reported incident.
AG-146.gap: Each agency held its own employees' cases under its own rules. During the first months the CIA withheld its cases from the State Department. The medical committee had no access to personal health records. The intelligence assessments relied on the absence of collection linking any actor to any incident.
AG-146.joining: Several authorities (an Accountability Review Board, a National Academies committee, NIH, the National Intelligence Council) attempted the joining repeatedly and produced different classifications. No attacker was named. The DNI's June 2026 memo recalled the earlier assessments without a new finding, saying they had selectively excluded relevant intelligence, suppressed alternative analysis and relied on an ethically flawed medical study.
AG-146.harm_found_later: Biden-era officials said they did not doubt that the injuries were real and deserving of government compensation. The cause remained unassigned.

AG-147.summary: Overnight on 17-18 December 2016 the Pivnichna (North) substation of Ukrenergo near Kyiv lost power for just over an hour, cutting an estimated one fifth of the city's consumption. Ukrenergo's head, Vsevolod Kovalchuk, first said that 'an equipment malfunction or a cyber attack' could be the cause. On 19 January 2017 the company said that workstations and SCADA servers had been disrupted by 'external influences'. On 12-13 June 2017 ESET (Industroyer) and Dragos (CrashOverride) published the malware. A later Dragos reassessment by Joe Slowik concluded that the attackers had tried to put Siemens SIPROTEC protection relays into a denial-of-service state and had failed because of coding errors. It also concluded that, after restoration, that state would have exposed transmission equipment to damage and a longer outage.
AG-147.records:
Ukrenergo: the operational and SCADA record. It first left the cause open between equipment malfunction and cyberattack.
ISSP (a Ukrainian firm investigating for Ukrenergo): linked the outage to the December 2015 attack. It also linked it to the December 2016 intrusions at the national railway, several government ministries and a national pension fund.
ESET and Dragos: the malware samples, and the technical analyses they published.
The investigators: reported only generically.
AG-147.gap: The single target narrowed recognition of an attack to about a month, but the mechanism stayed with private vendors for six months. Dragos reconstructed the intended physical harm (relay disablement) only later. The December 2016 intrusions in transport, government and pensions were recorded by separate institutions and joined by a private consultancy.
AG-147.joining: Ukrenergo confirmed external interference in January 2017. ISSP joined the outage to the wider December 2016 campaign. Dragos joined its samples to ELECTRUM, a group it associates with Sandworm. ESET linked Industroyer to the TeleBots group. Neither vendor named a state in the sources checked. The attacker did not claim the act.
AG-147.harm_found_later: The relay attack's potential damage to transmission equipment, and a far longer outage, were invisible in the outage record and appeared only in Dragos's later reassessment.

AG-148.summary: At the end of September 2016 Amnesty International reported that it had found 30 likely chemical attacks by Sudanese government forces in Jebel Marra since January 2016, with estimates of up to 250 deaths. The OPCW said that it was not possible at that stage to draw any conclusions from the report. Sudan's foreign minister, Ibrahim Ghandour, called the findings fabricated and unfounded. The UN peacekeeping chief, Hervé Ladsous, told the Security Council that he had not come across "any evidence of chemical weapons in Darfur", noting that the UN had no presence in Jebel Marra. Amnesty asked member states at the OPCW Executive Council meeting of 11–14 October 2016 to seek clarification from Sudan under Article IX of the Chemical Weapons Convention and, failing that, to request a challenge inspection.
AG-148.records:
Amnesty International: its research record of the alleged attacks.
UN mission in Darfur (UNAMID): could not verify reports of fighting in Jebel Marra because the government restricted its access.
OPCW: the treaty authority to seek clarification or conduct a challenge inspection at a state party's request. On the basis of the report alone, it said it could draw no conclusions.
AG-148.gap: Jebel Marra was closed to the recorders with authority, and the treaty body could act only on a state party's request.
AG-148.joining: Amnesty International, a human-rights organization, joined the available records into an attack claim naming the government. Neither the UN nor the OPCW adopted it in the sources checked. Ladsous said the UN should cooperate fully with any future OPCW investigation. On 22 October 2016 President al-Bashir called the claims empty lies.

AG-149.summary: The Indore–Rajendra Nagar (Patna) Express derailed at Pukhrayan near Kanpur on 20 November 2016, killing 152 people. On 21 January 2017 the Hirakhand Express derailed near Kuneru in Andhra Pradesh, killing about 40. Moti Paswan, arrested by Bihar police in January 2017 over a pressure-cooker bomb at Ghorasahan, later claimed he had planted a bomb at Kanpur. Bihar police said Pakistan's ISI was behind the Kanpur accidents. Railway Minister Suresh Prabhu alleged sabotage in both derailments and asked the Home Minister for an NIA probe. On 23 February 2017, at a rally in Gonda, Prime Minister Modi said that 'police found out that it was a conspiracy from across the border'. An NIA preliminary team found 'no trace of explosives, wires or timers' at Kanpur. In January 2018 a team of IIT experts reported that no explosive device caused the derailment. The NIA filed no chargesheet. In December 2020 the Commissioner of Railway Safety attributed Kuneru to a fractured tongue rail.
AG-149.records:
Bihar police: the arrested men's claims from a separate bomb case. They tied the Kanpur accidents to the ISI.
Uttar Pradesh police (DGP Javeed Ahmed): called the claims of the three men in custody (Moti Paswan, Uma Shankar and Mukesh Yadav) 'off the mark'. They said their own investigation had found no trace of explosives on the tracks.
Railway Board chairman, A. K. Mital: the statement 'We never said sabotage caused accidents in Kanpur. Someone else said it.'
NIA preliminary team: reported 'no trace of explosives, wires or timers' at Kanpur and considered the accident a classic rail fracture (Indian Express, 25 Jan 2017, as cited by Alt News).
Forensic Science Laboratory in Hyderabad: found no explosive traces at Kuneru.
A team of IIT experts engaged by the investigators: reported in January 2018 that no explosive device caused the Kanpur derailment.
Moti Paswan: told the NIA that his claim had been boasting.
Commissioner of Railway Safety (South Central Circle), Ram Kripal: attributed Kuneru to a 'fracture of tongue rail' and could not determine whether the fracture came from material failure or from the rail outliving its codal life. He found the East Coast Railway's civil engineering department 'blameworthy' and named no individual as responsible. He did not mention the NIA FIR, which had listed Maoist sabotage as a possibility.
AG-149.gap: Here the records were joined too early and in the wrong order. A claim recorded by one state's police in an unrelated bomb case was attached to an accident in another state before the railway and forensic records were complete. The railway minister extended the sabotage claim to an accident in a third state. The head of government repeated the attachment at an election rally. The safety inquiry and the criminal inquiry ran under separate authorities. The safety report on Kuneru did not refer to the criminal file.
AG-149.joining: The NIA took over both cases and combined the forensic and expert findings. In January 2018 an official said it would submit a final report after the IIT findings. It filed no chargesheet (Tribune, December 2020, on Kuneru; Kharge, June 2023, on Kanpur). In Parliament, Home Minister Rajnath Singh said the Prime Minister 'did not directly mention the ISI'. In December 2020 the Commissioner of Railway Safety closed Kuneru as an equipment failure.
AG-149.harm_found_later: At Pukhrayan, the deaths were investigated within a terrorism inquiry that produced no chargesheet. The Kuneru report assigned blame to a department and named no responsible person. In the records checked, the maintenance failure behind the deaths was therefore charged to no one.

AG-150.summary: Suspected al-Shabaab militants repeatedly destroyed telecommunications masts in northeastern Kenya from 2016. In December 2016 the Kulan Post reported the fourth mast dismantled in ten days. A confidential Kenyan security report cited by the Daily Nation in September 2019 said more than eight masts had been destroyed that year, with Safaricom the hardest hit. That report alleged that an unnamed Somali telecommunications company paid al-Shabaab up to US$3 million for the attacks and other support, to secure a monopoly along the border. Hormuud, Somalia's largest operator, denied aiding the militants. In November 2019 the UN Panel of Experts on Somalia reported that it had received reports of attacks on 12 Hormuud towers between 2017 and 2019, almost all in Gedo region, attributed to the Kenya Defence Forces (KDF). The panel had independently corroborated five of them, which killed two civilians. The KDF denied any involvement.
AG-150.records:
Local administrators: individual mast attacks, recorded as security incidents. In December 2016 the Tarbaj deputy county commissioner confirmed two deaths at a Safaricom site in Dagaxkut.
Mandera's governor, Ali Roba: tied the mast attacks to a militant plan to cut the county off before an ambush.
A confidential Kenyan security report, cited by the Daily Nation on 8 September 2019: destroyed masts at Welmerer, Amuma, Yumbis, Hulugho, Jabibar and Galmagala. It joined them into a claim against an unnamed Somali telco.
Hormuud: the attacks on its own towers in Somalia (at least 12) and their damage.
The UN Panel of Experts, which monitors the Somalia sanctions regime: corroborated five of the attacks on Hormuud towers, including a July 2018 shelling of a Hormuud station that killed a security guard and his relative. It noted that the attacks might prevent al-Shabaab from triggering improvised explosive devices while carrying humanitarian costs from lost coverage.
AG-150.gap: Each mast attack was a small, remote incident recorded locally on one side of the border. A foreign operator counted the matching attacks on the other side. The two parties with the fullest counts were a Kenyan security service and a Somali company, and each count supported an accusation against the other side. No authority covered both jurisdictions. Under its sanctions mandate, the UN panel examined only the attacks in Somalia.
AG-150.joining: Three parties joined records for different purposes. A confidential Kenyan security report, disclosed through the press, named a Somali telco as sponsor of al-Shabaab's attacks, an allegation that remained unproven in the sources checked. Hormuud joined its own losses into a claim against the Kenyan military. The UN Panel of Experts corroborated five of those attacks in its 2019 report. Hormuud and the KDF each denied the accusation against it, the KDF in a meeting with the UN experts.
AG-150.harm_found_later: The Kenyan report said the attacks left communities and security personnel without communication. The UN panel noted humanitarian costs from lost coverage in Somalia. None of the records checked measures that harm.

AG-151.summary: Pemex recorded 6,873 fuel theft incidents in 2016 and 9,509 in 2017. In 2016 thieves took more than 2.2 billion liters of fuel. On 27 December 2018 President López Obrador announced a plan against fuel theft, saying 'there are networks that were created to steal gasoline'. He deployed soldiers to strategic facilities and moved fuel by guarded truck and train in place of pipelines, a change that caused fuel shortages. At about 7 p.m. on 18 January 2019 a rudimentary illegal tap on the Tuxpan–Tula pipeline at Tlahuelilpan, Hidalgo exploded while about 800 people were collecting fuel. The official figures give 137 dead (69 at the scene and 68 of 81 people hospitalized).
AG-151.records:
Pemex: theft incidents and stolen volumes. Its former head of security, Eduardo León Trauwitz, was under investigation.
Milenio: a 2017 account from a source that Pemex officials tipped off thieves about pipeline schedules and supplied extraction equipment.
The army and police officers at Tlahuelilpan: the theft took place in their view after they had responded to a report. They did not stop the residents.
Security minister Alfonso Durazo: said the military 'detected the leak about four hours before Pemex closed the valve', because Pemex did not at first consider it an 'important' leak.
Health minister Jorge Alcocer: gave 85 dead on 20 January.
AG-151.gap: Tap counts measured incidents and volume figures measured losses, but neither recorded the insiders who made theft possible. A leak at an illegal tap fell below the operator's threshold for an important leak.
AG-151.joining: In December 2018 the new government joined the theft records with claims of networks inside the fuel system and in response changed the logistics of the national fuel system. No organizer of the Tlahuelilpan tap was named in the sources checked. In 2026 the exact cause of ignition was still reported as unknown.

AG-152.summary: From 28 September 2016 to 12 March 2018 Yemen's national cholera surveillance system reported 1,103,683 suspected cases and 2,385 deaths, in what its analysts called the largest documented cholera epidemic of modern times. In the same war, Saudi-led coalition air raids hit medical facilities and water infrastructure. The case counts and the strike counts were kept by different bodies. Only outside researchers and NGOs joined them.
AG-152.records:
Yemen's health authorities: the national surveillance system, which recorded suspected cases presenting at health facilities and confirmed them by culture. Their published analysis, funded with WHO and Médecins Sans Frontières, associated rainfall with the second wave.
Yemen Data Project: 86 air raids on medical facilities and 107 on water tanks, trucks, drills and dams between 26 March 2015 and 30 June 2020.
Civilian Impact Monitoring Project: 115 incidents involving medical or water infrastructure between January 2018 and July 2020.
PHR and Mwatana: 120 attacks on health facilities and personnel between March 2015 and December 2018, including 35 coalition air attacks on 32 facilities.
UNICEF and WHO: said in June 2017 that Yemen was facing "the worst cholera outbreak in the world" without saying that either side was more responsible.
AG-152.gap: The epidemiological record is organized by governorate, onset date and rainfall. The strike records are organized by target type and attacker. The two share no category. No institution with authority over both public health and the conduct of hostilities received both. The causal route from a strike on a water system to an infection weeks later is long and probabilistic.
AG-152.joining: Kennedy, Harmer and McCoy, in a letter in The Lancet Global Health in August 2017, combined WHO case data with a dataset of territorial control. They found that 77.7 percent of cases and 80.7 percent of deaths occurred in Houthi-controlled areas. They argued that the coalition "played a key role in the collapse of health, water, and sanitation systems in rebel-controlled areas". In August 2020 Oxfam joined the Yemen Data Project and CIMP counts. Neither had authority to attribute legally. No UN finding linking the strikes to the epidemic was found in the sources checked.
AG-152.harm_found_later: Cholera deaths were recorded as disease deaths. Only a later reconstruction, which no official body undertook, could estimate any share caused by strikes on water and sanitation.

AG-153.summary: On 15 August 2016 a coalition airstrike hit the MSF-supported Abs hospital in Hajjah governorate. MSF counted 19 dead, including one of its staff, and 24 injured. The coalition's Joint Incidents Assessment Team (JIAT) was created in 2016 from 14 people seconded by coalition members. It classified the strike as an 'unintended error' made while targeting a vehicle it considered a legitimate military target, and cited seven fatalities. MSF rejected the finding and stated that it had shared the hospital's coordinates with the coalition at least every three months since July 2015, most recently five days before the strike.
AG-153.records:
MSF: the coordinates shared with the coalition, the casualty count and the roof logo marking the hospital. It also recorded the sequence in which a car carrying at least one injured patient parked at the emergency entrance for several minutes before it was struck.
JIAT: its own reconstruction, with a lower casualty figure and a targeting rationale.
Mwatana: 35 coalition aerial attacks on 32 health facilities, March 2015 to December 2018.
UN Panel of Experts: findings on other attacks, including one on al-Thawra Hospital in 2018 that it could not attribute.
AG-153.gap: Because each strike hit one identifiable facility and the attacker's air force was not in doubt, recognition was immediate. The disagreement concerned facts and classification: the attacking coalition's own body produced the official finding. Its casualty count and sequence of events differed from the operator's records.
AG-153.joining: JIAT joined coalition records and attributed the strike to error. In March 2020 PHR and Mwatana set MSF's findings against JIAT's conclusions. They recorded that HRW and the UN Group of Eminent Experts had condemned JIAT as ineffectual. MSF called for independent investigation of potential violations. In the sources checked, no independent body with authority to compel coalition records reviewed the case.

AG-154.summary: The master of a ship near Novorossiysk reported on 22 June 2017 to the US Coast Guard Navigation Center that his GPS placed the vessel inland near Gelendzhik airport while it was more than 25 nautical miles away. He also reported that more than 20 ships in the area had the same problem. The US Maritime Administration issued a safety alert stating that the incident had not been confirmed. In March 2019 the nonprofit C4ADS published 'Above Us Only Stars', which identified 9,883 suspected spoofing instances at ten locations since February 2016 affecting 1,311 civilian vessel navigation systems.
AG-154.records:
Ship masters: logs and reports.
US Coast Guard Navigation Center: found no anomalies in GPS signals. It replied that accuracy in the area should be three meters and advised a software check.
MARAD: its advisory system.
AIS aggregators such as MarineTraffic: tracks showing ships in the area periodically shifting inland.
International Space Station: a scientific receiver on board.
Russian procurement: records of purchases.
AG-154.gap: Each master reported to an authority whose category was signal performance, so reports were handled as receiver faults. MARAD could issue only an unconfirmed advisory. Spoofing appeared in AIS archives as positional errors spread across thousands of tracks. No authority with jurisdiction over the coast where the transmitters stood collected them.
AG-154.joining: C4ADS joined AIS archives, the space-station receiver data and procurement records in a year-long study ending in November 2018. It found a close correlation between spoofing and the movements of the Russian head of state. The study attributed mobile systems to the Federal Protective Service (FSO). By line-of-sight analysis it placed a Black Sea transmitter at a coastal palace. It located a Syrian source in the northwestern quadrant of Khmeimim airbase. No state authority adopted these findings in the sources checked.

AG-155.summary: WHO and Insecurity Insight's Security in Numbers Database both compiled attacks on health care worldwide from public sources in 2017. Researchers compared their 2017 records event by event and found that only 33 (12.9 percent) of 254 distinct events in a combined comparable dataset appeared in both. In 22 of 31 countries the two datasets had no event in common. A capture-recapture estimate suggested at least 637 publicly reported events in those countries, so that each dataset captured only about 45 percent.
AG-155.records:
WHO, 2017: a dataset built mainly from daily automated English-language Google Alerts and other sources. ACLED supplied half of its events.
WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (launched in December 2017): now collects data through partners and country offices and 'does not collect nor verify information on perpetrators.'
Insecurity Insight, 2017: manual searches of English-language news, humanitarian and newsletter sources plus reports from NGO partners, without ACLED.
Both 2017 datasets: the perpetrator, where available. According to the study, both rely on 'hidden curation of events.'
AG-155.gap: WHO and Insecurity Insight each used their own sources, search methods and definitions, so the same year produced two largely separate records. The authors conclude that 'source variation appears to best explain the lack of overlap'. They also conclude that 'the underreporting of attacks is greater than we feared.'
AG-155.joining: Academics and practitioners joined the two datasets for one year. The study, by Parada, Fast, Briody and colleagues, appeared in Conflict and Health in 2023. In the sources checked, no institution reconciles them on a continuing basis. WHO states that it lacks the mandate to address who carries out attacks.

AG-156.summary: From 2018 a rising number of the wells feeding Libya's Great Man-Made River were sabotaged. The UN counted 96 of 366 wells out of service in May 2019. In July 2019 Abdullah El-Sunni, head of the Tripoli-based water authority, told Reuters that 101 of 479 wells on the western system had been dismantled. Late on 19 May 2019, during the Libyan National Army's offensive on Tripoli, an armed group stormed the Jabal al-Hasawna control station. The group, according to the project's statement, forced workers to close all flow control valves, cutting water to Tripoli and other cities in western and central Libya. The UN Humanitarian Coordinator, Maria Ribeiro, said such attacks 'may be considered war crimes'. The Tripoli government blamed a group under Khalifa Ehnaish, which it said belonged to Haftar's forces and had cut the water in 2017. The LNA denied involvement. In April 2020 an armed group took over the Shwerif water control station, halted pumping and cut water to more than two million people in Tripoli and nearby towns. The UN humanitarian coordinator for Libya, Yacoub El Hillo, called the cutoff 'particularly reprehensible.'
AG-156.records:
Man-Made River project: a statement on the May 2019 seizure.
Tripoli water authority: the condition of the wells. It blamed the fall in western flows, from 1.2 million to about 800,000 cubic meters a day, on 'sabotage and lack of funding and maintenance'.
UNICEF: a draft report listing kidnappings of water workers and looting of equipment.
UN Humanitarian Coordinator: the wells out of service and the population relying on the system (about 1.5 million people, some 600,000 of them children).
The head of the National Centre for Disease Control: the statement that all water was contaminated.
The central monitoring room of the western pipeline system: hit around early May 2019, so engineers could no longer gauge pressure and flow.
AG-156.gap: The same damage arose from several motives that the records did not separate: people dismantling well heads to sell copper, tribesmen in the south closing or destroying pipes to press demands on Tripoli, and armed groups using the water supply as a lever. Each well loss was small. The UN and the authority counted differently defined sets of wells (the UN 96 of 366, the authority 101 of 479). The damage to the monitoring room removed the operator's own means of observing the network as a whole.
AG-156.joining: The UN humanitarian system joined the well counts into a public warning and described attacks of the May 2019 kind as possible war crimes without naming a perpetrator. The Tripoli government named Ehnaish and tied him to the LNA, which denied it. Reuters joined the authority's figures with UNICEF's unfinalized draft. The May cut-off was a single, visible act, whereas the well sabotage remained a dispersed series with no attribution in the sources checked.
AG-156.harm_found_later: A UNICEF spokesman estimated that about four million people would lose safe water without action. He listed cholera, hepatitis A and diarrhea as likely outcomes. The health authorities would record any resulting illness without a link to the well sabotage.

AG-157.summary: Kim Jong-nam, half-brother of North Korea's leader, had liquid smeared on his face at a low-cost terminal of Kuala Lumpur's airport on 13 February 2017 and was pronounced dead on the way to a hospital. On 24 February Malaysian officials announced that he had been killed with VX nerve agent. Malaysian police detained a Vietnamese and an Indonesian woman. Four of seven North Korean suspects were believed to have left the country. Malaysia released the body to North Korea on 30 March 2017 under a deal that returned nine Malaysians held in Pyongyang. In August 2018 the High Court found enough evidence to infer a well-planned conspiracy between the two women and the four missing North Koreans. But prosecutors dropped the murder charge against the Indonesian on 11 March 2019. On 1 April 2019 the Vietnamese defendant pleaded guilty to a reduced charge of causing injury with a dangerous weapon.
AG-157.records:
Malaysian police and officials: the criminal record. They announced the cause of death.
Malaysian High Court: the trial record.
US State Department: a determination, made on 22 February 2018 and announced on 6 March 2018, that North Korea had used VX, under the Chemical and Biological Weapons Control and Warfare Elimination Act of 1991.
AG-157.gap: A single person was attacked in a public place, and the agent was identified within eleven days. Recognition was therefore immediate. The open element was naming: the North Korean suspects were beyond reach. By releasing the body to North Korea, Malaysia ended a standoff in which nine of its citizens were held in Pyongyang.
AG-157.joining: Malaysian police joined the record quickly and sought Interpol's help for the North Korean suspects. Naming the state was left to a foreign government, the US State Department, acting under its own sanctions statute. The Malaysian proceedings ended without a judgment on the principals.

AG-158.summary: On June 27–28, 2017 destructive malware spread through a centralized update of the M.E.Doc tax accounting software used by many Ukrainian businesses. Ukrainian public and private entities accounted for 80% of affected systems. The radiation monitoring system at the Chornobyl nuclear power plant went offline. On February 15, 2018 the UK government judged that the Russian military was responsible, citing the NCSC's assessment that it was almost certainly responsible. It named Ukrainian financial, energy and government sectors as the primary targets and said the attack masqueraded as a criminal enterprise. Ukraine and the United States also attributed it to Russia, which denied the allegations.
AG-158.records:
Each victim organization: its own infection record.
Chornobyl plant: the loss of its radiation monitoring system.
UK NCSC and allied agencies: intelligence assessments.
AG-158.gap: Simultaneous infection through one software vendor made the event obvious at once. The malware presented itself as ransomware, a criminal category, and governments settled authorship about eight months later.
AG-158.joining: Ukraine, the United States and the United Kingdom made official attributions naming Russia. On February 15, 2018 the UK attributed the attack to the Russian military.

AG-159.summary: In June 2017 a cyber-attack crippled Merck's in-house manufacturing of active ingredients, its formulation and packaging systems and its research operations, most of which were restored within six months. Merck's third-quarter 2017 results stated that sales were reduced by about $240 million because of a borrowing of Gardasil 9 from the CDC Pediatric Vaccine Stockpile. According to the results, the borrowing was driven in part by the temporary production shutdown resulting from the cyber-attack and by higher demand than planned. On 15 February 2018 the White House stated that the Russian military launched the attack known as NotPetya.
AG-159.records:
Merck's SEC filings: 'the cyber-attack,' without naming the malware or the attacker. They recorded about $135 million in lost third-quarter sales in certain markets and the stockpile borrowing as a reduction in sales.
Fierce Pharma, summarizing Merck's annual report: a $260 million effect on 2017 sales and $125 million in lost Gardasil 9 sales.
CDC: the stockpile from which the doses were borrowed.
US government: attribution of NotPetya to the Russian military, naming no company and no health effect.
AG-159.gap: The health consequence of the attack appeared as a reduction in a national vaccine reserve. The manufacturer recorded it as a sales effect and CDC as a stockpile loan. Neither category describes a harm to public health. Merck's filings do not name the malware or the attacker. The attribution statement names no company and no health effect.
AG-159.joining: In the sources checked, the vaccine-supply effect was not joined to the attribution in an official record. The White House issued the attribution about eight months after the attack. US and UK investigations named the Russian military without reference to the stockpile.
AG-159.harm_found_later: Whether any vaccination was delayed or forgone because of the drawdown cannot be determined from the records that exist.

AG-160.summary: Spearphishing against South Korean targets, which began in December 2017, ended in a destructive attack shortly before the opening ceremony of the PyeongChang Winter Olympics on 9 February 2018. The attack took down the official Olympics website and stadium Wi-Fi, affected broadcasts and kept spectators from printing tickets. Code features pointed to North Korea's Lazarus Group. In March 2018 Kaspersky found that the Rich header had been forged to match Lazarus and called the fingerprints 'a skillful imitation'. It found indicators pointing to Sofacy (APT28) that it said could also be false. On 19 October 2020 the US Justice Department announced the indictment, returned on 15 October in Pittsburgh, of six officers of GRU Unit 74455. It alleged that two of them (Yuriy Andrienko and Petr Pliskin) developed components of Olympic Destroyer.
AG-160.records:
The organizers: the outage record.
Security vendors: the samples, and the competing attributions they published.
Intezer: reported links to Chinese groups.
Recorded Future: noted similarities to Lazarus loaders.
Cisco Talos: noted similarities to NotPetya and BadRabbit.
Microsoft: made and then retracted a claim about an exploit.
The Washington Post: reported, citing anonymous officials, that Russian military spies were responsible.
A federal grand jury in Pittsburgh: the investigative record behind the 2020 indictment. It was assembled with help from the governments of South Korea and New Zealand, Ukrainian and Georgian authorities, UK intelligence services, Google, Cisco, Facebook and Twitter.
AG-160.gap: Planted indicators made the joining of technical records produce a wrong attacker. Vendor reports, each built from the samples it held, disagreed. In the sources consulted, no South Korean body issued a formal attribution. A naming backed by a grand jury indictment came more than two and a half years later.
AG-160.joining: Private vendors joined samples first and diverged. In March 2018 Kaspersky identified the false flag and declined to name an actor, advising 'don't rush with attribution'. In October 2020 a US grand jury and the Justice Department named the GRU unit.

AG-161.summary: On 23 September 2017 eight Mapuche community members, among them Héctor Llaitul, were detained in La Araucanía, Biobío and Los Ríos. They were held in pretrial detention for an alleged 'asociación ilícita terrorista' behind a series of arson attacks. These included the burning of 28 Sotraser trucks in San José de la Mariquina on 28 August 2017. The case rested on chat messages that the Carabineros intelligence unit UIOE said it had intercepted with tools called 'Antorcha' and 'Tubicación'. CIPER later reported that these tools did not exist. On 19 October 2017 the Second Chamber of the Supreme Court unanimously granted amparo and ordered their release. A PDI examination then found a message file created on a seized phone after its seizure. The phones had sat for 32 days in a UIOE room to which one officer held the only key. Generals Bruno Villalobos and Gonzalo Blu of the Carabineros resigned in 2018.
AG-161.records:
Carabineros' UIOE in Temuco and the intelligence directorate Dipolcar: General Gonzalo Blu's 'Informe 130', presented to prosecutor Luis Arroyo on 20 September 2017.
The Carabineros crime laboratory (Labocar): its officers told the prosecutor that only Captain Leonardo Osses held the key to the room where the phones were kept. They also said that a modem used to connect Llaitul's phone was his.
The Fiscalía in Temuco and the PDI: the forensic examination, which the PDI carried out.
Sotraser and the other owners of burned vehicles: their own record of the arson attacks.
The courts: the Supreme Court and the Temuco guarantee court.
AG-161.gap: Intelligence produced under secrecy passed into a terrorism prosecution as finished product. The phones stayed in the custody of the unit that produced the attribution. The arson attacks themselves were real, and their victims recorded them. What joined the attacks to named persons was a record manufactured inside one institution and accepted by a second.
AG-161.joining: The Fiscalía's own review dismantled the attribution through the PDI's forensic examination. Prosecutor Luis Arroyo filed a criminal complaint on 25 January 2018, alleging that the chats were false and that the case was a 'montaje'. When the PDI tried to search the UIOE on 26 January, Carabineros surrounded the building with an armed contingent. In March 2018 the investigative outlet CIPER published the confessions and technical traces. Among them was the acknowledgment by Álex Smith, the civilian intelligence official who built the tools, of how the material was falsified.

AG-162.summary: During the Syrian Democratic Forces' advance on Raqqa, a United States B-52 struck towers attached to the Tabqa Dam on 26 March 2017. The B-52 used three 2,000-pound bombs, one of them a bunker-buster that failed to explode. The dam stopped generating electricity. In Raqqa, news that it was about to collapse caused panic. An agreement between the SDF and the Islamic State on 27 March let repair teams reach the dam. On 20 January 2022 The New York Times reported, citing former US officials, that the dam had been on a no-strike list. The paper attributed the strike to Task Force 9, a US special operations unit.
AG-162.records:
OCHA's situation report of 8 April 2017: recorded that hostilities reportedly damaged the control room on 26 March. It also recorded that an airstrike reportedly hit the dam on 28 March as technicians tried to reach the control rooms, killing the acting director, a technician and a Syrian Arab Red Crescent member. It recorded that a repair team opened a floodgate on 29 March and that the resulting canal flooding drove 3,000 people to elevated ground. It further recorded that Turkish authorities reduced the flow into Syria and that the SDF press center's statement of 5 April on opened floodgates could not be confirmed independently.
The US military: the strike records and the no-strike list.
Lieutenant General Stephen Townsend: said at the time that the dam was "not a coalition target".
CENTCOM: in 2022 confirmed three 2,000-pound bombs and said they targeted the attached towers.
AG-162.gap: OCHA recorded consequences and named no party, writing that damage was reportedly caused by hostilities. The strike records and the no-strike designation sat with the force that had struck, whose commander had publicly denied that the dam was a target. The humanitarian record and the targeting record never met. The dam's protected status became public only through journalism in 2022.
AG-162.joining: In January 2022, almost five years later, The New York Times joined the targeting record to the damage. It drew on former officials and on an internal military report that warned flooding could put tens of thousands of civilians at risk. CENTCOM confirmed the bombs and denied targeting the dam. No official inquiry into the strike was found in the sources checked.
AG-162.harm_found_later: OCHA recorded the deaths of the three dam workers without attribution. The loss of electricity and water treatment entered the record as outages, the displacement as flight. Both remained without an author until the press reconstruction.

AG-163.summary: Intruders reached the Triconex safety instrumented system of the Petro Rabigh refining and petrochemical complex. While reprogramming safety controllers, they caused faults that tripped part of the plant offline in June 2017 and again on 4 August 2017. The first trip was treated as an equipment problem. After the second, investigators found a malware framework built to move from an engineering workstation into Tricon 3008 controllers through a zero-day vulnerability.
AG-163.records:
The plant's control room: logged process-safety trips. On 4 August control room engineers on the weekend shift 'spotted nothing out of the ordinary' (E&E News).
Schneider Electric, the Triconex vendor: called to the June trip, it ran tests on site, took the controller to its lab and 'found nothing terribly unusual'. After August it ran a parallel investigation.
Saudi Aramco: a 37.5 percent shareholder without responsibility for the plant's security, it sent a team after August.
FireEye's Mandiant unit: incident response.
DHS: later analyzed the malware, which it named HatMan.
Dragos: later analyzed the malware.
MIT Technology Review (2019): described the owner's identity as kept secret.
AG-163.gap: Each trip was a working safety system doing its job, so it entered the record as a process-safety event. The vendor's inspection was scoped to a device fault. MIT Technology Review reports that the first outage was 'mistakenly attributed to a mechanical glitch' and that the owners called in investigators after the second shutdown. Aramco's specialists were unable to tally the infections. FireEye identified the victim only as a 'critical infrastructure organization'. For fear of discouraging other victims from sharing information privately, experts declined to name the company.
AG-163.joining: After the second trip the plant's owners joined the record through contracted responders and the vendor. FireEye's October 2018 report pointed to the Central Scientific Research Institute of Chemistry and Mechanics (TsNIIKhM) in Moscow. The report acknowledged that FireEye had found no specific proof that the institute developed the tool. In March 2022 the US Department of Justice unsealed an indictment returned in June 2021. It charged Evgeny Gladkikh, a TsNIIKhM programmer, with conspiring to hack 'a foreign refinery' between May and September 2017, where the malware caused two automatic emergency shutdowns. The owner, whose identity was kept secret, made no public attribution in the sources checked.

AG-164.summary: The WannaCry ransomware spread on 12 May 2017 and disrupted NHS trusts and general practices in England. On 27 October 2017 the National Audit Office found that at least 81 of 236 trusts were affected. It also found that the Department of Health did not know the full extent of the disruption. On 19 December 2017 the Foreign Office minister Lord Ahmad stated that the National Cyber Security Centre judged it "highly likely" that the North Korean Lazarus Group was responsible.
AG-164.records:
NHS England: initially identified 45 organizations, including 37 trusts, as infected. It identified 6,912 cancelled appointments and estimated that more than 19,000 were cancelled in total, figures that do not cover all appointment types.
The NAO: counted at least 81 trusts affected and 603 primary care and other organizations infected, including 595 GP practices.
The Department of Health: before 12 May it had no formal mechanism to check whether local organizations had acted on NHS Digital's alerts.
NHS Digital: told the NAO it believed no patient data were compromised.
The Foreign Office: its statement referred to 48 NHS trusts.
Hospital Episode Statistics: admissions and A&E attendances.
AG-164.gap: Because the ransom note announced the attack, recognition was immediate. The open question was the extent of the disruption, which each trust and practice recorded for itself. The Department did not know how many organizations lost access to records because they shared systems with an infected trust. Three official figures for trusts circulated: 37 infected in NHS England's initial count, 48 in the Foreign Office statement and at least 81 affected according to the NAO.
AG-164.joining: The NAO joined the central records in October 2017 under its audit authority and did not address attribution. The NCSC assessment, announced by the Foreign Office on 19 December 2017, named the Lazarus Group. Imperial College researchers (Ghafur et al., 2019) linked Hospital Episode Statistics to infection status. They found about 6 percent fewer admissions per infected hospital per day, 5.9 million pounds in lost activity and no difference in mortality.
AG-164.harm_found_later: Patient harm could be estimated only by later linkage of national hospital statistics to infection status. The authors called mortality "a crude measure of patient harm." In five areas some patients had to travel to other A&E departments. The NAO record contains no count of clinical harm.

AG-165.summary: From the summer of 2018 ships near the port of Shanghai had their AIS positions spoofed into rings on the east bank of the Huangpu River. On the day in July 2019 when the US container ship Manukai reported problems, nearly 300 vessels were affected. The Manukai lost the signal on both GPS units, its AIS transponder failed and a backup distress system could not get a fix. On 5 June 2019 the Run 5678 struck the New Glory on the Huangpu. AIS data show that the New Glory had been spoofed at least five times in the preceding six months. It is not certain that spoofing occurred during the collision. As of November 2019 nobody had identified who was behind the spoofing.
AG-165.records:
The Manukai's captain: a report to the US Coast Guard Navigation Center, which collects GPS outage reports.
Commercial AIS data: the spoofed positions, including at least 394 spoofings of one Huangpu Maritime Safety Administration (MSA) patrol boat in nine months.
Strava's heat map: the same circles on land.
Police and the MSA: dealt with sand smugglers who cloned other ships' AIS identities. In June 2019 a tanker with a cloned AIS identity, which police believed was smuggling oil, rammed an MSA patrol boat.
AG-165.gap: AIS identity cloning by sand and oil smugglers was going on at the same time as the spoofing, so false positions fell into an existing category of transponder crime. The US report went to a US outage-reporting center without jurisdiction in China.
AG-165.joining: C4ADS bought AIS data from a commercial provider, found the ring pattern and shared its findings with Todd Humphreys of the University of Texas at Austin. MIT Technology Review published the analysis in November 2019. No institution identified the perpetrator. Hypotheses ranged from sand thieves or other environmental criminals to state testing of an experimental capability. Humphreys thought state testing possible and said he did not think a rogue actor was responsible.

AG-166.summary: The Ebola outbreak in North Kivu and Ituri was the second-largest on record, with more than 3,300 cases and 2,200 deaths by late November 2019. It occurred in an area where multiple rebel groups operate. Response workers and facilities were attacked repeatedly. Two treatment centers were razed in late February 2019. In late November 2019 attacks on a response workers' camp at Biakato Mines and a coordination office in Mangina killed three response workers and a policeman. These attacks led WHO and its partners to withdraw staff. By then Mike Ryan, executive director of WHO's emergencies program, counted 386 attacks on response workers, with at least seven deaths and 77 injuries.
AG-166.records:
WHO and the response coordination: attacks on response workers and facilities.
National surveillance and WHO: Ebola incidence by area.
Researchers: a timeline of conflict events and an ethnographic analysis of local conditions.
AG-166.gap: Attacks were recorded as security incidents and cases as epidemiological events. Neither record carried the other's consequences. Response teams were often caught in crossfire among rebel groups, government forces and UN peacekeepers, which left motive and actor unclear.
AG-166.joining: Wells and colleagues (PNAS, November 2019) joined a timeline of conflict events and an ethnographic analysis with incidence data. They found that the speed of case isolation and the effectiveness of vaccination varied with unrest. They also found that 'conflict events were found to reverse an otherwise declining phase of the epidemic trajectory.' WHO reported counts and condemned the attacks, without naming the attackers in the sources checked.
AG-166.harm_found_later: Infections and deaths that followed interrupted isolation and vaccination were recorded as Ebola cases. Their link to specific attacks exists only in model-based reconstruction.

AG-167.summary: Reported drone sightings halted flights at Gatwick from 19 to 21 December 2018. The airport closed for about 30 hours, and about 1,000 flights and more than 140,000 passengers were disrupted. At Gatwick, military and private-sector counter-drone equipment was installed. Police arrested a local couple, who were not charged. Sussex Police later paid them £200,000 to settle a wrongful-arrest claim. On 27 September 2019 Sussex Police drew a line under the investigation and reported no further lines of inquiry. Its report gave 129 sightings, 109 of them from credible witnesses, and at least two drones on six occasions. In 2021 Brendan Schulman, DJI's departing vice president, said freedom-of-information material showed the event "did not actually involve a drone."
AG-167.records:
The airport: the closure record.
Sussex Police: witness statements and the sighting log.
Military and private-sector teams: the counter-drone deployment.
Ian Hudson, an independent analyst: later obtained and summarized freedom-of-information material on the incident.
AG-167.gap: The record consisted of witness sightings, with no perpetrator identified. The police classification therefore rested on the sightings alone and could be disputed by anyone who examined the same material.
AG-167.joining: Sussex Police joined the sightings and called the event "a serious and deliberate criminal act designed to endanger airport operations," not terror-related. It then closed the case without charging anyone. An industry executive and an analyst using FOI releases, both outside parties, disputed whether a drone had flown at all.

AG-168.summary: Chunghwa Telecom data showed that the two cables linking the Matsu Islands to Taiwan had been cut 27 times in five years. On 2 February 2023 a Chinese fishing vessel was suspected of cutting the first cable about 50 km offshore. On 8 February a Chinese cargo ship cut the second. Matsu's 14,000 residents were left on an intermittent microwave link, because no cable-laying ship could arrive before 20 April. On 25 February 2025 a cable between Taiwan and Penghu was severed. The coast guard detained the Togo-registered Hong Tai 58 and its Chinese crew. As reported in June 2025, a district court in southern Taiwan sentenced the captain to three years in prison under the Telecommunications Management Act.
AG-168.records:
Chunghwa Telecom: recorded each break. Its figures did not show which country the vessels came from. The Washington Post reported that the company had found nothing to show that the 2023 cables were severed intentionally.
The National Communications Commission (NCC): matched the two 2023 breaks to Chinese vessels with AIS data. It said an improved microwave backup was still under construction.
The coast guard: chased the fishing vessel until it returned to Chinese waters. In 2025 it detained the Hong Tai 58 and reported that the ship had dragged its anchor in a straight line over the cable.
The prosecutors and the court: the prosecutors charged the captain, and the court convicted him.
AG-168.gap: Each break entered the operator's record as a repair. The government stopped short of calling the 2023 cuts a deliberate act by Beijing. The Lienchiang County head said compensation would require hard proof of who was responsible. Analysts and local officials described the breaks as purposeful harassment. That judgment rested on the frequency of the breaks, and no institution adopted it as a finding.
AG-168.joining: The NCC joined AIS tracks to the two 2023 breaks and identified the ships as Chinese. The government named no state. In 2025 the coast guard's detention and the criminal proceedings joined a specific vessel to a specific break. DatacenterDynamics reports that the court found the damage deliberate. The sources checked report no formal Taiwanese attribution of the breaks to the Chinese state.
AG-168.harm_found_later: Half a dozen Matsu hotel and restaurant owners reported business down at least 50 percent during the 2023 outage. Their compensation depended on proof of who cut the cables, which no record supplied.

AG-169.summary: In March 2018 Sergei and Yulia Skripal were found unconscious in Salisbury. They had been poisoned with a Novichok nerve agent, which scientists of the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory analyzed. At the end of June 2018 Dawn Sturgess and Charlie Rowley were found unconscious in Amesbury. Wiltshire Police first treated the case as drug-related. Sturgess died about four months after the Salisbury attack, after spraying herself from a discarded bottle she took for perfume. The public inquiry into her death was announced in November 2021 and chaired by the former senior judge Lord Hughes of Ombersley. On 4 December 2025 it reported that the attack must have been authorized at the highest level, by President Putin, and that he bears moral responsibility for her death. The two men who brought the bottle to Salisbury are known as Alexander Petrov and Ruslan Boshirov and are thought to be GRU officers. UK police had named Anatoliy Chepiga and Alexander Mishkin as the suspects in September 2018.
AG-169.records:
Scientists of the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory: the analytical record. They linked the batches used in the two poisonings.
Wiltshire Police, in Amesbury: the first classification. Its officers thought the pair might have taken a contaminated batch of heroin or crack cocaine, partly because Rowley was a known intravenous opiate user, and its warning aimed at local drug users drew criticism from the inquiry.
Paramedics, one of whom had attended the Salisbury incident: suspected organophosphate poisoning. They gave Rowley antidotes for both opiate and organophosphate poisoning, probably saving his life.
The inquiry: criticized the lack of information sharing between emergency services about the overlapping symptoms and the mixed public messaging.
AG-169.gap: The second poisoning entered the record under a routine category, because nothing at the scene connected two local residents with a counter-intelligence case three months old. One recorder, the paramedics, had an alternative classification. It did not travel to the agency that controlled the response.
AG-169.joining: On 4 July 2018 police said that further testing was under way to establish the substance and that they were keeping an open mind. They also said it was not yet clear whether a crime had been committed. Laboratory analysis then linked the Amesbury cases to the agent used in March. The inquest was converted into a statutory inquiry able to receive closed intelligence. Seven years after the death, the inquiry named the Russian state at the level of its president.
AG-169.harm_found_later: Sturgess had no connection to the target. Her death became attributable to the operation through the laboratory link to the March case and, finally, through the inquiry's finding.

AG-170.summary: Between 27 June and 4 July 2018 attackers copied the personal particulars of about 1.5 million SingHealth patients and the outpatient dispensed-medicine records of about 160,000. They 'specifically and repeatedly targeted' the Prime Minister's records. IHiS, the public-health IT agency, detected unusual database activity on 4 July. MOH, SingHealth and the Cyber Security Agency (CSA) were informed on 10 July, when investigations confirmed a cyberattack. The government announced the attack on 20 July. The minister convened a Committee of Inquiry (COI), which found that the attack bore the characteristics of an Advanced Persistent Threat group. On 15 January 2019 the minister told Parliament 'we know the identity of the attacker' but would not comment further 'for national security reasons'. On 6 March 2019 Symantec named a group it called Whitefly as behind the breach, without naming a state.
AG-170.records:
IHiS: the workstation and database logs. In an earlier incident (in January, according to testimony to the COI), several workstations sent suspicious queries to the SingHealth database. The incident was not reported, because the IHiS procedure allowed reporting only for 'an actual breach or instance where (critical information infrastructure) was successfully compromised', as senior manager Ernest Tan told the COI. No investigation located the workstations or checked them for malware.
The CSA: informed on 10 July.
The COI: heard 37 witnesses over 22 days of hearings. It found that SingHealth had no management line of sight over cybersecurity risk and was wholly dependent on IHiS.
The Personal Data Protection Commission: imposed penalties of S$750,000 on IHiS and S$250,000 on SingHealth.
Symantec: reported that Whitefly had attacked organizations, mostly in Singapore, in healthcare, media, telecommunications and engineering. It reported that the group had been active since at least 2017.
AG-170.gap: Under the operator's reporting rule the threshold was a confirmed compromise. Earlier signs of the intrusion therefore stayed in IHiS records and never reached the national agency. The hospital group itself held no part of the security record, because its monitoring had been delegated. After the records were joined, the government withheld the attacker's identity for national security reasons.
AG-170.joining: Over five months the COI, convened by the minister, joined the IHiS, CSA and witness records, with 37 witnesses and 26 written representations. The government stated that it knew the attacker and declined to name it. A private security firm, Symantec, named a group, linked it to other attacks on organizations in Singapore and named no state.

AG-171.summary: Vastaamo, a private psychotherapy provider that also worked as a subcontractor for Finland's public health system, was hacked in 2018 and again in 2019. Its database of some 33,000 clients was taken. In October 2020 the attacker demanded bitcoin from the company. When the company refused, the attacker demanded payments from individual patients under threat of publishing their therapy notes. About 24,000 people filed criminal complaints, a record number in Finland. French police arrested Aleksanteri Kivimäki near Paris in February 2023. On 30 April 2024 the Länsi-Uusimaa District Court convicted him of an aggravated data breach, nearly 21,000 aggravated blackmail attempts and more than 9,200 aggravated disseminations of information infringing private life. It sentenced him to six years and three months.
AG-171.records:
Vastaamo: its system records. The company was later suspected of lax protection of client data and declared bankruptcy in 2021.
Each patient who received an extortion message: one fragment, which the patient could report to police. About 24,000 people filed complaints according to AP.
The police: about 22,000 victims of personal extortion attempts, according to KrebsOnSecurity.
Lawyers for groups of victims: information on harm. Jenni Raiskio, representing about 1,500 clients, told Helsingin Sanomat in March 2024 that at least a few victims had died by suicide.
AG-171.gap: The intrusions of 2018 and 2019 entered no public record until the extortion began in October 2020. Once the attacker contacted victims directly, the gap narrowed because thousands of victims reported at once.
AG-171.joining: Finnish police joined the complaints into one case. A district court convicted a named individual. The company's former chief executive, Ville Tapio, was dismissed and prosecuted. He received a suspended three-month sentence in April 2023, according to KrebsOnSecurity. The case led Finland to fast-track a law allowing citizens to change their personal identity codes after gross data breaches.
AG-171.harm_found_later: Psychological harm and any deaths among victims are recorded only in victims' own accounts and lawyers' statements. No official count links them to the breach.

AG-172.summary: Drones and cruise missiles struck the Abqaiq oil processing facility and the Khurais oil field on 14 September 2019. Houthi forces claimed the attack. The United States, France, Germany and the United Kingdom accused Iran, which denied involvement. The UN Panel of Experts on Yemen reported that 'despite their claims to the contrary, the Houthi forces did not launch the attacks,' and the UN Secretariat later assessed that the cruise missiles used in this and three other 2019 attacks on Saudi Arabia were of Iranian origin.
AG-172.records:
The Yemen sanctions Panel of Experts: examined range and approach in its report submitted to the Security Council's Yemen sanctions committee on 27 December 2019. It reported that the sites 'were approached respectively from a north/northwestern and north/northeastern direction, rather than from the south,' and its investigators doubted that the weapons had sufficient range to have been launched from Houthi-held territory.
The UN Secretariat: reporting in June 2020 on resolution 2231, it assessed that 'the cruise missiles and/or parts thereof used in the four attacks are of Iranian origin'. It also assessed that the drones used in the May and September attacks were entirely or partially from Iran.
Saudi Foreign Minister Adel al-Jubeir: said in September 2019 that Riyadh would await the UN investigation before deciding its response.
AG-172.gap: Detection posed no problem, because the attack was simultaneous, visible and claimed. Attribution was divided among UN bodies with different tasks: the Yemen Panel said who had not launched the weapons, and the 2231 report said where the weapons came from. As described in the sources checked, neither report named who launched them.
AG-172.joining: The United States and three European states named Iran on their own authority. In the sources checked, no international body joined the findings into an attribution. The Houthi claim, which gave the attack a ready author inside an existing war, did not hold up before the Panel.

AG-173.summary: On Sunday 16 June 2019 a collapse of Argentina's interconnected system (SADI) cut power across Argentina and Uruguay and parts of neighboring countries. Bloomberg reported that Argentine officials had not excluded hacking while President Mauricio Macri said the outage was being investigated. A preliminary memo by the wholesale market administrator Cammesa described a short circuit that disconnected the Colonia Elía–Belgrano 500 kV line. It also described an automated disconnection of the Mercedes–Colonia Elía line, whose cause remained under investigation. By July the regulator ENRE planned to sanction the transmission company Transener and the distributors after the final report.
AG-173.records:
Cammesa: dispatch, the preliminary memo and penalties for the 69 of 74 distributors and large users that failed to cut the demand they had committed to.
Transener: operator of the SADI.
ENRE: the regulator, with the sanctions.
Edenor and Edesur: cut demand by 38% when they needed to cut 52%.
The Secretariat of Energy under Gustavo Lopetegui: a report to the Senate naming five generators that disconnected early, and the statement 'fue una falla en el sistema mayorista'.
AG-173.gap: The cyber hypothesis was raised before any technical record existed and was carried by press reports of what officials had not excluded.
AG-173.joining: Within weeks Cammesa, ENRE and the Secretariat of Energy produced the technical and liability account under their regulatory roles. They spread responsibility among the transmitter, distributors and generators. No attacker was named.

AG-174.summary: Fires at Santiago Metro stations accompanied the October 2019 unrest in Chile. President Piñera's government raised indications of foreign intervention shortly after 18 October. In late December 2019 the government gave the prosecutor's office a 112-page social-media report. Interior Minister Gonzalo Blumel called it 'extraordinarily sophisticated' information obtained through big-data technology. La Tercera reported that the report covered almost five million accounts and about 60 million comments and found that 19.3% of the accounts originated abroad. La Tercera also reported that it sorted them into five groups, including foreign supporters of the protests (TeleSur and RT among them) and K-pop fans. National Prosecutor Jorge Abbott said within hours that it was open-source information and not intelligence. In October 2020 the head of the Fiscalía Oriente, Manuel Guerra, called it 'pure smoke'. He said the data on foreign intervention never reached the prosecutors.
AG-174.records:
The Public Prosecutor's Office: investigated the Metro fires as crimes.
The government: first presented the social-media report as the work of the National Intelligence Agency (ANI).
La Tercera: reported in January 2020 that the report came from the Spanish firm Alto Data Analytics.
Interferencia: reported in January 2020 that the Luksic family's Quiñenco group had connected Alto with the ANI.
Interior Minister Gonzalo Blumel: acknowledged in January 2020 that Quiñenco had served as a bridge, while denying that the government had commissioned or paid for the report.
Alto Data Analytics: on 13 February 2020 published a study that found the protests rooted in preexisting conditions. The study reported concentrated posting, a group of anomalous accounts active in both Chile and Colombia (58% of those disclosing a location placed in Venezuela) and protest events organized from abroad.
The Comptroller General: ruled in September 2020 that Alto had supplied the report free as a sample, so procurement law did not apply. It also ruled that the Lobby Law did not apply because the report passed between public bodies.
AG-174.gap: A private analytics firm, which no agency had a duty to test, held the social-media data. The prosecutors held the criminal record of the fires. They received nothing from the executive on foreign intervention, according to Guerra, so the two records were never joined.
AG-174.joining: The executive joined commercial social-media analysis into a foreign-influence narrative and passed it to prosecutors. The national prosecutor, the press and the Comptroller examined the narrative and rejected or narrowed it. Guerra said the investigations of the Metro fires suffered from scarce records and from violence by people who had no coordination among themselves. No foreign actor was named in any legal proceeding in the sources checked.

AG-175.summary: During the 2019 harvest, fires burned wheat and barley fields across central and northern Iraq. On 26 May one fire south of Tuz Khurmato covered about 220 square kilometers. Iraqi authorities first denied any ISIS link and attributed the fires to farmers burning fields to fertilize the soil. A day later they said they would investigate and prosecute those responsible. ISIS's al-Naba newsletter urged and claimed the burning of farms. An open-source analysis concluded that 'ISIS insurgents are likely responsible for the bulk of the fires.'
AG-175.records:
The Iraqi fire service: 236 fires destroying 5,183 hectares of farmland in one month (AFP, 7 June 2019).
The Nineveh agricultural department: 119 fires in a few weeks (same AFP report).
The government: statements on cause.
ISIS's al-Naba: articles on 23 and 30 May, the second titled 'Burn the land of the Apostates and avoid the properties of Muslims'. They claimed fires in Salahaddin, Hawija and Diyala and attacks on firefighters, generators and tractors, and claimed 'hundreds of hectares' in Kirkuk, Nineveh, Salahaddin and Diyala.
al-Amaq: claimed fires around Makhmour, Hawija, Khanaqin and Salahaddin.
NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire data, with Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8 imagery: the burns, recorded from space.
AG-175.gap: Every fire had an ordinary explanation ready: residue burning, cigarettes, sparks, sunlight focused through glass, a heatwave, air-strike side effects, local extortion, land disputes, or revenge by militias, as in earlier years. Fire services and provincial agricultural departments counted fires and hectares. That count records damage and leaves cause open. The government's first public category was agricultural practice. The security analyst Hisham al-Hashemi told AFP that ISIS had claimed dozens of fires while the rest were 'certainly the product of land disputes.' The pattern appeared only when satellite fire data were set beside field reports and the attacker's claims.
AG-175.joining: Wim Zwijnenburg (PAX), writing for Bellingcat on 3 June 2019, used NASA fire detections together with Sentinel-2 and Landsat imagery. He joined these with media reports, ISIS claims and military activity. He counted roughly 150 burn-scar sites covering at least 1,000 square kilometers (his conclusion gives 'at least 50 sites'). He attributed most fires to ISIS while cautioning that burned areas could not always be linked to specific attacks. The attacker's own partial claims narrowed the gap. The sources checked contain no results of the government's investigation.
AG-175.harm_found_later: Lost harvests and the extortion of farmers fall on livelihoods and food supply. That harm appears in no casualty count. Kirkuk officials told AFP the 2019 harvest had been expected to be double the previous year's.

AG-176.summary: From 20 May 2019, fires burned wheat and barley fields across Syria. They burned most extensively in the areas held by the Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria. By 14 June the Administration's agriculture and economy body put the loss at about 450,000 dunums and 18 billion Syrian pounds. Syria Direct reported more than 40,000 hectares and about 19 billion. ISIS claimed crop burnings in al-Hasakah and other provinces in its al-Naba newsletter, while residents and rumors blamed pro-government militias extorting farmers, government forces, Turkey or the SDF. A 2022 satellite study joined burned-area data with incident reports. It found a strong correlation between ISIS-related incidents and burned farmland across governorates in 2019.
AG-176.records:
The Autonomous Administration's Economic and Agricultural Authority: recorded burned area and losses for compensation, with committees formed with internal security forces to assess damage. Its co-head was Suleiman Barudo (also spelled Baroudu).
The Autonomous Administration: detained 12 suspects.
The Raqqa Civic Council: estimated that about 15 percent of Raqqa's wheat farmland had burned and called the fires likely arson.
Qamishli: allocated 90 firefighting units.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights: counted six civilian deaths in al-Hasakah governorate by 15 June.
ISIS's al-Naba: carried claims.
Syrians for Truth and Justice: collected field reports from six governorates.
MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat 8 and Sentinel-2 imagery: recorded the burn scars.
AG-176.gap: The fires fell under different authorities on each side of the front lines, so no single authority recorded the whole pattern. Each field fire also had several ordinary or local explanations (harvest accidents, extortion by militias, shelling, private disputes). The Autonomous Administration documented losses for compensation. The press reports checked cite no official finding on cause or perpetrators. The Syria Justice and Accountability Centre called for impartial investigations. ISIS's claims were general and could not be matched to particular fires.
AG-176.joining: Partial joining came from NGOs within weeks (Syrians for Truth and Justice, 22 June 2019) and from academics three years later. Jaafar, Sujud and Woertz (Regional Environmental Change, October 2022) joined MODIS, Landsat, Sentinel-2 and VIIRS data with 75 located farmland fires attributed to ISIS. The attribution of those fires came from press reports and an anonymous international observer. The study found r = 0.83 across governorates between ISIS-related incidents and percent burned farmland in 2019. It also noted that burning had risen since 2014. No authority named the authors of particular fires.
AG-176.harm_found_later: The deaths and losses were recorded as fire damage, without a responsible party. Lost harvests and household income fell on farmers in al-Hasakah, a major wheat region.

AG-177.summary: On 5 March 2019 an external party exploited a known vulnerability in Cisco firewalls. The exploit caused internet-facing firewalls at a low-impact control center and multiple remote generation sites to reboot over about ten hours. Each firewall was down for less than five minutes, and communications between field devices, sites and the control center were briefly lost. NERC recorded that the outages "had no impact to generation." The operator was the renewable-energy company sPower.
AG-177.records:
The registered entity: firewall logs and monitoring tools ("Seeing several of these outages at different sites raised suspicion").
DOE: Form OE-417 emergency alert of 7 March, update of 8 March and final report of 9 March 2019.
NERC and WECC: a Lessons Learned document of 4 September 2019 that names neither the entity nor the firewall manufacturer.
E&E News: a May 2019 report of a denial-of-service attack on a western utility.
The National Security Archive: FOIA release of the DOE documents, October 2019.
AG-177.gap: In its public record the regulator anonymized the entity and the vendor and filed the event as a lesson on patching. The operator's identity entered the public record only through a journalist's reporting and FOIA requests to DOE.
AG-177.joining: NERC turned the event into an anonymized industry lesson. E&E News reporter Blake Sobczak and the National Security Archive filed FOIA requests. The DOE documents released in October 2019 identified sPower, a company owned by AES and AIMCo. No attacker was named.

AG-178.summary: For about two months in mid-2019 GPS signals around Ben Gurion Airport were disrupted, apparently by spoofing. During the disruption, pilots landed using an alternative method. On 5 August 2019 the Israel Airports Authority announced that the disruption had ended and said it had caused no safety issues.
AG-178.records:
The Israel Airports Authority: the disruption and the alternative landing method.
Israeli officials: pointed to Russian forces in Syria, and unnamed defense officials said the interference originated in Syria.
The IDF: refused to comment publicly on the source.
The Russian embassy: dismissed the allegations as 'fake news'.
AG-178.gap: For the airport authority, the interference was an operational matter without safety consequences. The authority did not say how the interference was stopped or whether the security establishment had been involved. The IDF kept its assessment of the source out of public view.
AG-178.joining: Todd Humphreys of the University of Texas and his team traced the signal to the Russian air base at Khmeimim in Syria. They used satellite data and sensors on the International Space Station. He said he was 90 to 95 percent sure that Moscow was behind the interference. He described Israel as collateral damage of Russian efforts to protect its troops from drone attacks. In March 2019 C4ADS had placed the most likely location of a Russian spoofing system in the northwestern quadrant of Khmeimim airbase.

AG-179.summary: During the 2019 Syrian government offensive in northwest Syria, health facilities whose coordinates had been shared through the UN humanitarian deconfliction mechanism were struck. On 1 August 2019 the UN Secretary-General set up a three-member Board of Inquiry, chaired by a retired Nigerian lieutenant general, Obiakor. The Secretary-General released a summary of its report to the Security Council on 6 April 2020. On 13 October 2019 The New York Times reported that Russian aircraft had bombed four hospitals on the deconfliction list on 5 and 6 May 2019. Its report drew on radio intercepts, spotter logs and witness accounts.
AG-179.records:
OCHA: the coordinates of notified facilities. The Syria Justice and Accountability Centre reported that OCHA passed them to the Russian government and the US-led coalition and not directly to the Syrian government or armed groups.
The Syrian American Medical Society: at least 14 of its facilities hit after their coordinates were shared through OCHA, as Physicians for Human Rights told the Security Council on 30 July 2019.
A network of observers: logged aircraft movements and recorded Russian Air Force radio traffic.
The Board of Inquiry: investigated incidents at six locations among those the Secretary-General referred to it. It excluded As-Suqaylabiyah National Hospital (26 May 2019) because it was neither on the deconfliction list nor UN-supported.
AG-179.gap: The Board's mandate excluded legal findings and questions of responsibility. Because the Syrian government did not answer its requests, it could not visit any site. Its findings were graded as probabilities: highly probable that government forces struck Rakaya, plausible or highly probable that "the Government of Syria and/or its allies" were responsible for three others, and probable that armed opposition groups or Hayat Tahrir al-Sham struck Nayrab. It did not name Russia. The flight logs and radio recordings that could identify the aircraft sat with private observers outside any official procedure.
AG-179.joining: The UN Board of Inquiry joined the UN's own notification records with incident reports and declined to name Russia. SJAC criticized the Board for failing to identify the UN's role in sharing coordinates. The New York Times joined spotter logs, radio recordings and witness accounts and named the Russian Air Force for four strikes.
