The Russian Foreign Ministry did not answer the specific questions and pointed to earlier statements that its aircraft struck "accurately researched targets."

AG-180.summary: Turkey and Turkish-backed forces took control of the Alouk water station during the October 2019 offensive in northeast Syria. The station served about 460,000 people in al-Hasakah governorate, including al-Hasakah city, Tal Tamer and the al-Hol and Areesha camps. Its pumping was interrupted several times in early 2020 as COVID-19 spread, most recently on 29 March. Turkey said the authorities controlling the al-Mabroukeh electricity station and Tishreen Dam had failed to supply power; local officials called the stoppages a pressure tactic.
AG-180.records:
UNICEF's representative in Syria, Fran Equiza: recorded on 23 March 2020 that the supply had 'yet again' been interrupted. The statement gave no cause and named no party.
Turkish authorities: described the interruptions as a failure of electricity supply from areas held by the Kurdish-led administration.
Local officials: described them as 'a pressure tactic to force Kurdish-led authorities to supply electricity' to areas held by Turkish-backed factions.
Human Rights Watch: received reports of the interruptions from aid organizations. HRW also heard from humanitarian workers that al-Mabroukeh does not serve the pumping station and that enough electricity remained to run it.
AG-180.gap: Because the station's operation depended on electricity from territory held by the other side, each stoppage could be entered as a power failure or as deliberate denial. The two authorities kept incompatible accounts. UNICEF, the UN agency that recorded the interruptions, declined to state a cause. In the sources checked, no body with access determined the cause of each stoppage.
AG-180.joining: On 31 March 2020 Human Rights Watch joined aid-agency reports with the parties' statements. It called on Turkish authorities to 'do everything they can to resume supplying water' through the station. It reminded all parties of their obligation to protect 'objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population,' without settling the question of intent. UNICEF asked that water facilities not be used 'for military or political gains.'

AG-181.summary: On 5 August 2019, when the government revoked Jammu and Kashmir's special status, it cut mobile, internet, SMS and landline services across the region. It later restored some services but kept mobile internet limited to 2G into 2021. On 10 January 2020 the Supreme Court, in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, held that the freedom of speech could not be restricted without stated reasons and duration. The court gave the government one week to review the ban, required restoration for essential services such as hospitals and educational institutions, and ordered the government to publish its orders. Harm to business was estimated by the Kashmir Chamber of Commerce and Industry. Rights groups and health researchers estimated the harm to health care and education. The government cited national security and fear of loss of life.
AG-181.records:
The government: the suspension orders, which the Kashmir Times editor alleged in October 2019 had been suppressed.
Kashmir Chamber of Commerce and Industry: estimates of business losses, cited by the Internet Freedom Foundation at more than Rs 40,000 crore, and of job losses of more than half a million.
Health and Human Rights Journal: a report (April 2020) recording that 2G speeds kept health workers from COVID-19 guidance.
Forum for Human Rights in Jammu and Kashmir: harm to students and teachers.
Internet Freedom Foundation: the duration and form of the restrictions.
#KeepItOn coalition: a call for restoration of 4G.
AG-181.gap: Because the state ordered the disruption and its author was never in doubt, the gap lay in the record of harm. The orders that would date and bound the disruption were allegedly suppressed until a court required their publication. A chamber of commerce, rights groups and health researchers each estimated the harm separately, in its own unit. No public authority measured the effect on patients.
AG-181.joining: The Supreme Court ruled on legality and required the orders to be published, but the sources checked report no assessment of harm by the court. In the same sources, no public body joined the estimates of economic, health and educational harm.
AG-181.harm_found_later: Effects on patients, including lost access to telemedicine and to COVID-19 guidance during 2020, appear only in advocacy and journal reports. They could be established only by later reconstruction from health records.

AG-182.summary: A computer on the internet-connected administrative network of the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant was infected with malware resembling DTrack, spyware that a Kaspersky report attributes to the Lazarus Group. An antivirus company tipped off CERT-In, which informed NPCIL on 4 September 2019. An inter-agency team from CERT-In and NCIIPC was sent for clean-up in mid-September. When reports based on data uploaded to VirusTotal spread from 28 October, the plant's information officer R. Ramdoss called them 'baseless' and 'false propaganda'. On 30 October NPCIL confirmed the infection and said 'the plant systems are not affected'.
AG-182.records:
An antivirus company: the first observation.
Pukhraj Singh (researcher): told of the intrusion by a third party, he alerted the National Cyber Security Coordinator in early September (reported as 3 or 4 September).
CERT-In: the notice to NPCIL and, with NCIIPC, the clean-up.
Department of Atomic Energy: specialists who investigated.
VirusTotal, a public malware repository: the data dump linked to the plant.
The plant: attributed a unit stoppage on 19 October to a low steam-generator level and mechanical issues.
AG-182.gap: The plant's denial addressed its stand-alone control systems ('Any cyberattack on the Nuclear Power Plant Control System is not possible'), while the infection sat on the administrative network. The security agencies' records were not published, and the public learned of the intrusion through a third-party repository.
AG-182.joining: A researcher and a public malware repository brought the fragments to public notice. NPCIL confirmed the infection one day after the plant's denial. The government named no attacker: the Lazarus link rests on Kaspersky's analysis of DTrack.

AG-183.summary: Four oil tankers were attacked near Fujairah on 12 May 2019. On 13 June the Marshall Islands-flagged, Norwegian-owned Front Altair and the Panama-flagged, Japanese-owned Kokuka Courageous, which was carrying methanol, were damaged in the Gulf of Oman. Iran's mission to the United Nations categorically denied responsibility for the June attacks.
AG-183.records:
Emirati-led investigation of the May attacks: concluded that a sophisticated state actor was responsible.
Yutaka Katada, president of the Kokuka Courageous's operator Kokuka Sangyo: said after the June attacks that the crew reported being hit by a flying object that they had seen with their own eyes.
US Central Command: released video that it said showed the crew of an IRGC patrol boat removing an unexploded limpet mine from the Kokuka Courageous.
Norwegian Maritime Authority: reported that the Front Altair was hit by three explosions.
AG-183.gap: Each ship involved a flag state, an owner's state and a coastal state, and a fourth party, the US Navy, recovered the physical material. The operator's account (a flying object) differed from the naval record (a limpet mine). The US Secretary of State blamed Iran without offering proof, and Japan's government asked the United States for 'concrete evidence'.
AG-183.joining: US Secretary of State Mike Pompeo blamed Iran within hours of the 13 June attacks. On 14 June the UK Foreign Office stated that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps almost certainly attacked the two tankers and that no other state or non-state actor could plausibly have been responsible. The same statement said the UK was confident Iran bore responsibility for the May attack. Japan's government sought further proof from the United States, and Iran denied any involvement.

AG-184.summary: On April 19, 2019 equipment failed at Belarus's Mozyr refinery, whose managers suspected crude carrying dichloroethane at dozens of times industry norms. On April 20 transport of Russian export oil through Druzhba practically stopped. Transneft head Nikolai Tokarev told President Putin the contamination was sabotage by a private company in Samara Oblast, and Forbes noted rumors of a sabotage scenario. The Investigative Committee opened a case for making a trunk pipeline unfit for use, organizing a criminal group and theft. It alleged that a group stole oil and poured contaminated oil into the private Nikolayevka reception node to hide the theft. On May 7 a Samara court ordered four suspects held for two months pending trial.
AG-184.records:
Mozyr refinery: the equipment failure and the contamination.
Transneft: operated the trunk system into which private reception nodes such as Nikolayevka fed oil.
Investigative Committee: the criminal file.
Energy Minister Alexander Novak: announced on May 7 that a group of companies had transferred oil with excess organochlorine compounds and that four people were detained.
AG-184.gap: Quality control was split between private reception nodes and Transneft. The former node owner Roman Trushev said Transneft's regulations required checks only every ten days, regulations that Meduza could not examine. Dichloroethane had been banned in Russian oil extraction in 2001, after an equipment failure similar to Mozyr's. The ban on organochlorides in oil production was canceled in May 2012. Transneft issued no official statement until the eleventh day of the crisis.
AG-184.joining: The Investigative Committee joined the record within about three weeks and classified the event as theft and concealment by a criminal group, a classification that set sabotage aside. Transneft's sabotage account and the criminal case both named private actors. No state actor was named.

AG-185.summary: Nicko Silar was born on 17 July 2019 at Springhill Medical Center in Mobile while the hospital was under a ransomware attack. She died in 2020, aged nine months, after months of intensive care at another hospital. Her mother, Teiranni Kidd, sued the hospital and the delivering physician. The suit alleged that device failures caused by the attack prevented proper monitoring during delivery and that the hospital did not reveal the severity of the attack publicly or to her. The day before the birth, the hospital had stated publicly that its staff 'has continued to safely care for our patients.'
AG-185.records:
Springhill Medical Center: its IT outage records and the clinical record of the delivery. The hospital's public statements described care as safe.
The delivering physician: according to the hospital, 'fully aware of the inaccessibility of the relevant systems'.
The receiving hospital: the record of the infant's care and death.
The lawsuit, filed in Mobile County in 2019: brought these records into one procedure.
AG-185.gap: The outage, the delivery and the death were recorded by different units and institutions. The hospital argued that under Alabama law it had no duty to give the patient details of the attack. No reporting rule required a hospital to link a cyber outage to a clinical outcome.
AG-185.joining: A private plaintiff joined the records through civil litigation, in a suit that The Wall Street Journal first reported on 30 September 2021. The hospital denied wrongdoing, asked the court to dismiss the conspiracy claim and placed responsibility on the physician, who denied causing the injuries. The sources checked name no attacker.
AG-185.harm_found_later: The possible contribution of the attack to the infant's death became public only through a malpractice suit two years later, and only because a family sued.

AG-186.summary: At about 4:56 p.m. on 7 March 2019 a fire near the Malena substation in Bolívar took out 765 kV lines carrying power from the Guri hydroelectric plant. Guri's protections tripped its turbines, and most of Venezuela was without power for more than 80 hours. Energy minister Luis Motta Domínguez spoke of 'sabotaje' minutes after the failure. The government blamed Juan Guaidó and US Senator Marco Rubio and described a US cyberattack on the Guri control room. On 12 March Attorney General Tarek William Saab opened an investigation of Guaidó for 'presunta implicación en el sabotaje realizado al Sistema Eléctrico Nacional'. Engineers outside the government attributed the failure to vegetation fires under the lines. At least 43 deaths in hospitals and among dialysis patients were counted by networks of doctors and patients. The health minister called these reports 'absolutamente falso'.
AG-186.records:
Corpoelec: the operational record, though no technical report from the operator appeared in the sources checked. Corpoelec and the communications ministry did not answer press requests for comment.
Winston Cabas, president of the electrical engineers' association AVEEMA: said a fire near Malena affected 'dos de las tres líneas de 765 kV' and overloaded the third.
Miguel Lara, a former manager of the dispatch center OPSIS: said March and early April bring the most vegetation fires along the 765 kV line.
Faculty of Engineering of the Universidad Central de Venezuela: a report describing 'un efecto dominó' from Guri to the Macagua and Caruachi plants and the loss of 85–90% of national supply.
Attorney General's office: the criminal investigation.
Médicos por la Salud, which monitors 40 major public hospitals: counted 24 deaths from 8 to 11 March from patient records and death certificates passed on by hospital staff (15 at the Manuel Núñez Tovar hospital in Maturín and four premature babies in Caracas). Its earlier survey (19 November 2018–9 February 2019) had recorded 79 deaths from power failures.
Codevida: 19 deaths of dialysis patients.
Opposition deputy José Manuel Olivares: put hospital deaths at 26.
Diosdado Cabello, president of the Constituent Assembly: acknowledged two deaths from the blackout's 'impacto directo'.
AG-186.gap: Corpoelec, the one institution with the operational record, kept it closed (engineer José Aguilar said of the cause 'Eso es secreto de Estado'). The attack claim came from ministers and passed directly into a criminal investigation of the opposition leader. Independent engineers held partial technical accounts without the operator's data. The doctors who held the death records had no access to grid data.
AG-186.joining: The government joined the outage to a political narrative and named the United States, Rubio and Guaidó. No official body published a joined technical account. Engineers, a university faculty and journalists reconstructed the cascade and attributed it to vegetation fires under the lines. Aguilar said 'no es ataque cibernético'. No attacker was substantiated.
AG-186.harm_found_later: Hospital and dialysis deaths were counted only by non-governmental networks, at least 43 by 12 March. The government issued no count, and the health minister called the reports 'absolutamente falso'. Cabello acknowledged two deaths. The state that claimed an attack disowned most of the harm.

AG-187.summary: On 23 April 2020 the Israel National Cyber Directorate (INCD) issued an alert about attempts to attack SCADA systems of wastewater treatment plants, water pumping stations and sewerage networks. It told operators to change passwords on internet-connected systems. Attacks on 24–25 April affecting several organizations were reported in the media. In July the Water Authority confirmed two further attacks on small agricultural drainage installations. On 9 May the computer system managing traffic at Iran's Shahid Rajaee port terminal crashed, and the port was out of service for a few days. The Washington Post linked the outage to Israel.
AG-187.records:
Utilities and agricultural operators: the intrusion records.
INCD and the Israeli CERT: warnings. At the time there were no official reports of confirmed intrusions.
Water Authority: warnings, and a description of the summer targets as 'specific, small drainage installations in the agriculture sector,' repaired locally with no damage to the water system.
Israel: later confirmed the attempted April attack.
An unnamed Western official: told the Financial Times that the April attack 'was close to successful.'
Iranian port operators at Shahid Rajaee: the record of the outage.
AG-187.gap: On recognition the gap was narrow: although many small operators held internet-exposed controllers, a national cyber authority issued a single national alert covering water, wastewater and sewerage systems. The Water Authority reported the later incidents. On public attribution the gap was wide: neither Israel nor Iran officially acknowledged targeting the other's civilian infrastructure. Iran's response 'largely consisted of denial of the origin, nature and extent of these attacks' (Baram, Ram and Ben Israel).
AG-187.joining: In its national alert, the INCD treated the April attempts as one campaign. Attribution to Iran, which an Iranian regime insider dismissed, came from media reports and anonymous officials. The Washington Post attributed the port outage to Israel (18–19 May 2020), citing US and foreign sources. Israel 'did not assume formal responsibility,' though IDF Chief of Staff Aviv Kochavi said on 19 May that Israel would act with 'unique methods of combat' (Al-Monitor). Anonymous Israeli officials later described the port operation as small, 'like a knock on the door.'

AG-188.summary: Prime Minister Scott Morrison announced on 19 June 2020 that Australian organizations had been targeted by a 'sophisticated state-based cyber actor'. The targets spanned all levels of government, industry, political organizations, education, health, essential services and critical infrastructure. He said the attacks had been increasing 'over many months'. The same day the Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) published Advisory 2020-008, 'copy-paste compromises'. It described exploitation of unpatched Telerik UI, Microsoft IIS, SharePoint, Citrix and Exchange systems, and spearphishing when exploits failed. Morrison declined to name the state, saying Australia 'doesn't engage lightly in public attribution'. Reuters reported, citing three sources, that the government regarded China as the main suspect, which Beijing denied.
AG-188.records:
Each targeted organization: the record of its own intrusion.
ACSC: the findings of its investigations of compromised networks, published as a set of techniques with no victim list and no actor name. It found no sign that the actor intended disruptive or destructive activity.
Morrison: said investigations had found no large-scale personal data breaches and that many attacks had been thwarted.
Australian intelligence: noted similarities, according to Reuters sources, with the March 2019 intrusion into Parliament and the three largest political parties, which Australia had never attributed publicly.
AG-188.gap: The intrusions came through different products into victims in different sectors, and none disrupted a service. Each therefore stayed below the level at which an organization would announce it. Only the national agency that investigated many of the incidents could see one actor behind them. The decision to name a state lay with the government, which kept it apart from the technical finding.
AG-188.joining: The ACSC joined the incidents through its incident response and published the joined record as an advisory, issued with the Department of Home Affairs. After discussing the campaign with allies, including the British Prime Minister, the Prime Minister made it public while withholding the name of the state. He did so to raise awareness and, according to a government source, to alert potential targets. Anonymous officials named China to Reuters, and China's Foreign Ministry denied involvement.

AG-189.summary: On 4 May 2020 CPC Corporation, Taiwan's state-owned oil company, first described a disruption of its systems as a crash and then acknowledged a ransomware attack. At CPC gas stations customers lost electronic payment, while energy production was unaffected. Over the same days other critical-infrastructure firms were hit, and Chunghwa Telecom disclosed a breach and published indicators of compromise on 6 May. On 15 May the Ministry of Justice Investigation Bureau (MJIB) reported more than ten victims of an organized 'ColdLock' ransomware attack. The MJIB, according to press reports of its statement, pointed to the Winnti group or a group 'closely related' to it on the basis of a configuration file and a domain name left behind. The incident-response firm CyCraft concluded that the ransomware was a 'smokescreen', because the malware carried no payment details, contact address or key for decryption.
AG-189.records:
CPC: its own outage, recorded first as a system crash and then as ransomware.
Chunghwa Telecom: its own outage, recorded as a breach for which it published indicators of compromise.
MJIB: a threat report joining more than ten critical-infrastructure victims, including a large multinational semiconductor vendor.
CyCraft: combined its own customer's case with the MJIB report and the Chunghwa indicators. It judged the aim to be 'political deterrence', citing the timing one week before the presidential inauguration.
CFR Cyber Operations Tracker: later classified the incident as sabotage with China as suspected sponsor.
CyberScoop: could not independently confirm the Winnti link.
AG-189.gap: Each victim first recorded an IT failure and then extortion, a criminal category that implies a profit motive and treats each company as a separate case. The attackers staged the ransomware before the 1–3 May Labor Day holiday weekend. They spread it across energy, telecommunications and technology firms, so each regulator held only a part of the record.
AG-189.joining: Within eleven days the MJIB joined the cases and pointed to a group that researchers have linked to the Chinese government. CyCraft, a private incident-response firm, added the reasoning that the ransomware was a cover. The criminal disguise delayed the joining by days and did not prevent it.

AG-190.summary: DoppelPaymer ransomware, spotted on 10 September 2020, corrupted about 30 servers at Düsseldorf University Hospital. On 11 September a woman with an aortic aneurysm was redirected to Helios University Hospital in Wuppertal, 32 km away, and died shortly after arriving. After her death, prosecutors opened a negligent-homicide investigation against the unknown attackers. In November 2020 Markus Hartmann, chief public prosecutor in Cologne, said that 'the medical condition was the sole cause of the death' and that 'the delay was of no relevance to the final outcome.'
AG-190.records:
Düsseldorf University Hospital: its IT records.
A compromised server: the ransom note, addressed to the affiliated Heinrich Heine University and not to the hospital.
The police: told the attackers they had hit a hospital. The attackers then withdrew the demand and supplied a decryption key.
The ambulance service and the Wuppertal hospital: the patient's transport and treatment records.
Cologne public prosecutor's office: joined the medical and technical records in the homicide inquiry.
AG-190.gap: Little aggregation gap existed at the stage of recognition. The early public claim of a death caused by ransomware joined two facts, the outage and the death, before the clinical records had been examined. The clinical review then broke the link.
AG-190.joining: The Cologne public prosecutor's office joined the records with criminal-law authority and, after about two months, settled causation in the negative. The prosecutor indicated that the choice of ransomware linked the attack to Russian groups, but gave no detail. The attackers remain unknown.
AG-190.harm_found_later: The case shows the reverse of a hidden harm. The legal standard of individual causation did not sustain a harm that had been publicly attributed to the attack. As for other patients, any diffuse effect on them went uncounted.

AG-191.summary: From 2020 online discussion of attacks on the power grid increased. A 14-page document circulating on a Telegram channel favored by accelerationist groups offered a white-supremacist guide to low-tech attacks, including attacks on power grids with guns. A DHS bulletin of October 2021 assessed that a four-rotor drone found on 16 July 2020 on the roof of a Pennsylvania power station was meant to hover over live high-voltage wires and short out the station. Three people claiming to be Boogaloo adherents were charged with conspiring to attack an electrical substation in Las Vegas. In 2022 three men pleaded guilty to conspiring to provide material support to terrorists over plans to attack substations nationwide. On 30 November 2022 DHS renewed its national bulletin, listing "US critical infrastructure" among potential targets.
AG-191.records:
Utilities and investigators: site incidents such as the drone on the roof.
FBI and federal prosecutors: criminal cases in Nevada and the 2022 material-support case against Christopher Brenner Cook, Jonathan Allen Frost and Jackson Matthew Sawall.
DHS: intelligence bulletins, including October 2021, and the national bulletin of 30 November 2022.
The planners: their own online material.
AG-191.gap: Single incidents were recorded as local security events. Their place in a pattern was set out in restricted intelligence bulletins, which reached the public mostly through press reporting.
AG-191.joining: DHS and the FBI joined site incidents and online material into threat bulletins without attributing the scattered incidents to one organization. CNN reported a DHS bulletin on the heightened threat from domestic violent extremists days before the Moore County attack. It published the October 2021 drone assessment two days after that attack.

AG-192.summary: On 12 May 2020 three gunmen attacked the MSF-run maternity ward of Barchi National Hospital in Dasht-e-Barchi, a majority Shiite neighborhood of Kabul. They killed at least 24 people, including mothers, newborns and nurses. MSF said the attackers went straight to the maternity ward, ignoring closer medical units. Its head of programs in Afghanistan, Frederic Bonnot, said 'they came to kill the mothers.' No group claimed the attack. The Taliban denied involvement and accused President Ashraf Ghani of blaming them. On 15 May US envoy Zalmay Khalilzad stated that the Islamic State affiliate (ISIS-K) carried it out.
AG-192.records:
MSF: patient census (26 mothers in care, 11 killed, 5 wounded, 10 sheltered in safe rooms) and the attackers' route through the compound.
Afghan security forces: the clearance operation in which the three attackers were killed.
US government: an assessment linking the attack to ISIS-K and to a same-day attack on a funeral in Nangarhar. That attack killed 34 people, and ISIS-K did claim it.
Taliban: a public denial.
AG-192.gap: The absence of a claim left attribution to inference. The two governments that named a perpetrator did so while the US–Taliban agreement of 29 February 2020 was being implemented, so the identity of the attacker carried political weight. The Taliban accused Ghani of trying to scuttle the deal.
AG-192.joining: The US government joined the attack with the same-day claimed attack in Nangarhar and named ISIS-K. Khalilzad said the group 'has demonstrated a pattern for favoring these types of heinous attacks against civilians.' MSF described the attackers' conduct, suspended its operations in Dasht-e-Barchi and, in the sources checked, did not attribute the attack. No judicial or independent finding was located.

AG-193.summary: In January 2020, according to HumAngle, the Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN) reported that Boko Haram had cut Maiduguri off from the national grid by damaging facilities between Damaturu and Maiduguri. In late January 2021 ISWAP militants, according to AFP, sabotaged the Damaturu–Maiduguri line, leaving the city of about three million without grid power for almost two months. On 27 February an ISWAP improvised explosive device injured five electricity workers. Power returned on 24 March 2021, and after a new outage on 27 March TCN announced that 'again, two towers along Maiduguri-Damaturu line have been vandalized.'
AG-193.records:
TCN: announced outages and damage. It named Boko Haram in January 2020, according to HumAngle, and described the March 2021 damage as vandalism without naming a group.
AFP: attributed the January 2021 sabotage to ISWAP.
VOA: reported that no group had claimed the March attack.
HumAngle: reported a security advisory calling for a special security team supported by the government, the electricity company and security agencies.
Residents: turned to generators and solar systems during the outage.
AG-193.gap: Each attack hit the single line that fed a state capital, so each one produced an immediate, citywide outage that no one could overlook. What stayed unsettled was authorship: the operator's wording moved between naming an insurgent group and reporting 'vandalized' towers. The attacks were rarely claimed, and in the sources checked the security agencies did not publish incident records.
AG-193.joining: In the press, AFP, VOA and HumAngle joined the TCN outage notices to the insurgency and named ISWAP for the 2021 sabotage. TCN had named Boko Haram for the January 2020 cut. TCN's engineering response was a temporary bypass, and a Damboa–Maiduguri line was planned as a second source of supply.

AG-194.summary: On 12 October 2020 a sequence of faults cut all four lines feeding Mumbai. One of the four high-voltage lines into Mumbai was already out after a conductor snapped on 10 October. An insulator trip, a hydro-station fault, an overload and a final manual trip followed. The islanding scheme could not carry the load, and the city went dark. On 28 February 2021 Recorded Future reported that a China-linked group it called RedEcho had targeted ten Indian power-sector organizations and two seaports. The organizations included four of the five Regional Load Despatch Centres. The New York Times cited the report to suggest the blackout 'may have been caused by a cyberattack from China'. Maharashtra's energy minister Nitin Raut said 'There is truth in the claims made by NYT'. Union Power Minister R.K. Singh said two teams had investigated: one attributed the outage to human error, the other found cyberattacks that were not linked to the failure. Singh added that 'we don't have evidence' of a Chinese or Pakistani role.
AG-194.records:
Grid operators: the trip and dispatch record.
CERT-In: emailed the Power Ministry on 19 November 2020 about ShadowPad malware at some POSOCO control centers.
NCIIPC: a mail of 12 February 2021 warning that RedEcho was targeting the Regional Load Despatch Centres.
Power Ministry: said POSOCO operations were unaffected.
Recorded Future: external network observations. It notified Indian government departments before publication.
Maharashtra Cyber, commissioned by state power officials: a report delivered to the state government in March 2021, stating that at least 14 trojans had been implanted in the IT and OT environments of the state's grid control systems.
Home Minister Anil Deshmukh: said the preliminary report indicated malware on state utility servers. He named no country.
Telangana officials: a central alert about suspected Chinese malware at 40 substations.
The Chinese embassy and Foreign Ministry: rejected the accusations.
US DOE CyOTE program (Idaho National Laboratory): later reconstructed the outage as 'a series of reliability failures' that exposed a separate malware intrusion.
AG-194.gap: The parties held different objects: grid operators held the outage sequence, a foreign private firm the intrusion telemetry and a state police cyber unit the host forensics. The alerts came from CERT-In, NCIIPC and a central authority, whose alert went to Telangana. The state and central governments drew opposite conclusions from different fragments. No body with authority over both the grid record and the forensic record published a joint account.
AG-194.joining: The New York Times joined the outage to Recorded Future's telemetry into an attack hypothesis. Maharashtra's energy minister endorsed it, but the state's home minister named no country. The Union Power Ministry rejected the hypothesis. Recorded Future described RedEcho as China-linked without firmly tying it to a known group, and the central government named no state. The CyOTE study treats the intrusion as real and the outage as non-hostile.

AG-195.summary: Alexei Navalny collapsed into a coma on 20 August 2020, about 30 minutes into a flight from Tomsk to Moscow. The pilot diverted to Omsk, where local doctors and specialists flown in from Moscow said he showed no signs of severe poisoning. He was evacuated to the Charite in Berlin. Germany requested technical assistance from the OPCW under subparagraph 38(e) of Article VIII of the Chemical Weapons Convention. In the biomedical samples, OPCW-designated laboratories found a cholinesterase inhibitor whose biomarkers have structural characteristics similar to the toxic chemicals added to Schedules 1.A.14 and 1.A.15 in November 2019. The inhibitor is not itself listed in the Convention's Annex on Chemicals. The OPCW issued its report on 6 October 2020 and named no perpetrator. Russia officially declined to open a formal investigation. On 14 December 2020 Bellingcat and The Insider, with Der Spiegel and CNN, identified a clandestine FSB sub-unit of about 15 operatives that had shadowed Navalny since at least 16 January 2017.
AG-195.records:
The Omsk hospital: the first clinical record, which reported no poisoning. It initially refused to release him for evacuation before reversing that decision.
The Charite: the Berlin record.
OPCW-designated laboratories: the analytical record, with the OPCW acting on Germany's request for technical assistance.
Telecom, travel and passport data: call logs and cell-tower geolocation, flight and train bookings, a leaked travel database and passport files. These held the record of the FSB team's 37 trips to destinations Navalny reached by plane or train between 2017 and 2020.
AG-195.gap: Within the jurisdiction of the state suspected of the act, the first recorder classified the collapse as non-toxic. Only after the patient left that jurisdiction could the act be recognized. The OPCW procedure confirmed the substance and had no mandate to name. At the time no law enforcement agency in any country was investigating.
AG-195.joining: Laboratories joined the clinical record within weeks. A consortium of journalists and open-source investigators named the individual officers by joining leaked commercial and state data sets. They identified at least fifteen operatives, with a core team of seven reporting to Colonel Stanislav Makshakov.

AG-196.summary: On 1 September 2021 the FBI issued a Private Industry Notification on ransomware against the food and agriculture sector. Among other cases it listed a US farm that lost about 9 million dollars in January 2021 and a global meat processor whose US plants shut for several days in May 2021. It also listed a bakery shut for about a week in July 2021 through its IT managed service provider. A second notification, on 20 April 2022, reported six grain cooperatives attacked between 15 September and 6 October 2021, as well as two incidents in early 2022 that could affect the planting season. It stated that ransomware actors may be more likely to attack agricultural cooperatives during critical planting and harvest seasons.
AG-196.records:
Each victim firm: its own incident record.
FBI: assembled reported incidents into the two notifications and coordinated with CISA (and, for the 2022 notice, with the Department of Agriculture). It asked recipients for boundary logs, Bitcoin wallet information, decryptor files and benign samples of encrypted files.
Open-source reports: the May 2021 shutdown reduced cattle and hog slaughter and drove wholesale meat prices up as much as 25 percent.
The 2022 notice: the ransomware families used against the cooperatives (Conti, BlackMatter, Suncrypt, Sodinokibi and BlackByte) and a LockBit 2.0 attack on a multi-state grain company in March 2022. It also recorded two intrusions at a feed-milling company in February 2022 that were stopped before encryption, and secondary infections at several cooperatives after a July 2021 attack on a business software provider.
AG-196.gap: The recorders are numerous, private and small: individual cooperatives, each below the threshold at which any agricultural or food-safety authority would take notice. They report voluntarily to a law enforcement agency that aggregates for warning. One incident is a business interruption; six in three weeks during harvest form a pattern that only the aggregator can see.
AG-196.joining: The FBI joined the incidents in the two notifications and related their timing to the agricultural calendar without naming a sponsor. The actors are identified by ransomware family, and the sector-level harm appears nowhere as a single figure.
AG-196.harm_found_later: Losses to growers whose deliveries or inputs were delayed appear, if at all, as ordinary commercial losses. They are not recorded anywhere as consequences of the intrusions.

AG-197.summary: From late June to late July 2020, explosions and fires struck the Khojir missile facility east of Tehran (25–26 June), the Sina Athar clinic in Tehran (30 June, 19 killed) and the centrifuge assembly building at Natanz (2 July). The same series struck power stations in Shiraz, Ahvaz and Isfahan, petrochemical plants at Mahshahr and wooden ships at the port of Bushehr (15 July), among other sites. Separate authorities gave separate ordinary causes. Iran confirmed in September that Natanz had been sabotaged. In the sources checked, the other incidents were not officially linked to it or to each other.
AG-197.records:
USIP Iran Primer: compiled the following accounts, from the Shiraz fire marshal to the Isfahan power company.
Shiraz fire marshal: said an explosion caused the fire, which state authorities later blamed on a 'transformer malfunction'.
Ministry of Defense: blamed leaking gas tanks at Parchin, though satellite imagery placed the blast at Khojir.
Tehran officials: attributed the Sina Athar blast to a gas leak and to 'gas canisters in the clinic's basement'.
AEOI spokesman Behrouz Kamalvandi: first called Natanz an accident with minimal damage.
Ahvaz fire chief: cited a 'transformer explosion' at the Zargan power station. An electricity industry spokesperson later cited a 'faulty connection'.
IRNA: attributed the Karoun petrochemical chlorine leak to a ruptured pipe.
A local official: blamed a Baqershahr blast on 'human error'.
Bushehr port crisis management director: said the cause of the ship fires was unknown.
Isfahan power company: blamed a 'worn-out transformer.'
Keivan Khosravi, spokesman of the Supreme National Security Council: said on 4 July that expert teams had determined the cause of the Natanz incident. He added that details would be released 'at the appropriate time' 'due to security considerations.'
AG-197.gap: Each incident fell to a different recorder with an accident category ready to hand: fire services, power companies, the Defense Ministry, the atomic energy agency, provincial officials. The incidents were spread across provinces and sectors. The one body that determined a cause withheld it. Foreign Ministry spokesman Abbas Mousavi denied that the incidents were caused by cyberattacks. Analysts argued that admitting sabotage would have made the security institutions look weak, so recognition and public acknowledgment were kept apart.
AG-197.joining: Journalists and analysts compiled the incidents into lists (USIP Iran Primer, from 10 July 2020) and used commercial satellite imagery to relocate the Khojir blast. An unnamed Middle Eastern intelligence official told the New York Times that Israel was responsible for Natanz. The Times reported that Iranian investigators quickly judged a planted bomb the most likely cause. On 6 September 2020 Iran confirmed that Natanz had been sabotaged. Israeli Defense Minister Benny Gantz said 'not every incident that unfolds in Iran is connected to us.' The joining of the full series remains journalistic and unofficial. Some of the joined incidents may be ordinary accidents.

AG-198.summary: After war began in Tigray in November 2020, MSF teams visited 106 health facilities between mid-December 2020 and early March 2021. They found that nearly 70 percent had been looted, more than 30 percent damaged and only 13 percent functioning normally. Every fifth facility visited had been occupied by soldiers: Eritrean soldiers were using the facility in Mugulat as a base, and Ethiopian forces had occupied Abiy Addi hospital until early March. On 3 November 2021 the Ethiopian Human Rights Commission and the UN Human Rights Office released a joint report covering the first nine months of the conflict. Human Rights Watch stated that it 'glosses over the deliberate and extensive destruction and pillaging of health infrastructure.'
AG-198.records:
MSF: facility-by-facility observations. These included deliberately smashed equipment at Adwa hospital, some 20 ambulances taken from facilities around Adigrat, and seized ambulances later seen in use by soldiers near the Eritrean border.
OCHA and partners: an assessment that about 70 percent of assessed hospitals and health centers were partly or fully damaged (as cited by Sahle and Woldegiorgis).
Pre-war counts cited by the same authors: 47 hospitals, 224 health centers, 712 health posts and 269 functional ambulances.
EHRC and OHCHR: a joint investigation of abuses in the first nine months.
AG-198.gap: Field records came from an operator that could reach some facilities and not others. From June 2021 the Ethiopian authorities blocked access to lifesaving assistance and services in Tigray. The one joint investigation with a UN partner was co-led by the national human rights commission of a party to the conflict. The investigation, according to HRW, gave the destruction of health infrastructure little attention.
AG-198.joining: In March 2021 MSF joined its own visits into a public finding of a deliberate and widespread attack on health care. It named Eritrean and Ethiopian forces as occupiers of specific facilities. Sahle and Woldegiorgis combined the MSF and OCHA findings with pre-war counts in a commentary published on 3 November 2021. HRW noted that the UN High Commissioner and the Ethiopian commissioner themselves described the joint report as far from a full account of the devastation.
AG-198.harm_found_later: In the sources checked, maternal, child and vaccine-preventable deaths after the collapse of a system that had vaccinated more than 96 percent of children are not recorded as effects of the attacks. MSF reported hearing of women who died in childbirth because they could not reach a hospital.

AG-199.summary: The Tigray war began on 4 November 2020. For more than two years Ethiopian and allied forces blocked almost all supplies of cash, fuel and electricity into Tigray. The IPC analysis issued in June 2021 reported that armed groups had vandalized farms and pillaged food stocks. It also reported that about 90 percent of the 2020 harvest was lost and that in parts of the Western and Central zones 80 to 90 percent of cattle were looted. It placed about 353,000 people in Phase 5, Catastrophe, with about 401,000 projected for July to September. The report states on its face that it was not endorsed by the Government of Ethiopia, and Ethiopia's UN ambassador rejected its methodology.
AG-199.records:
The IPC analysis: drew mainly on remote phone surveys and a face-to-face survey of newly arrived displaced people. It recorded that mobile network constraints limited sampling and that experts from Tigray could take only limited part because of poor telephone and internet connectivity.
The IPC: stopped providing Tigray data after its famine warning because the region was inaccessible.
UN relief chief Mark Lowcock: said "There is famine now in Tigray".
The head of Ethiopia's National Disaster Prevention and Preparedness Committee: said "We don't have any food shortage."
Yale Lowenstein Clinic: worked from hundreds of reports by the Ethiopian government, UN agencies, rights and humanitarian groups and journalists. It also drew on interviews with relief workers, health professionals and former officials of the interim administration.
Researchers at Ghent University: combined IPC figures, a Somalia mortality study and village fieldwork in Dogu'a Tembien into civilian death estimates. They had no data for areas without access, such as Irob and zones under Amhara or Eritrean control.
AG-199.gap: The shutdown of electricity and telecommunications cut the recording system at its base, so the body with authority to classify famine had to work from phone surveys and interviews with the newly displaced. It then stopped reporting on Tigray. Crop and livestock destruction entered the record as reports of looting, a category that does not by itself produce a food security classification. The government that controlled access was also the party whose endorsement the classification needed. It withheld that endorsement and disputed the method.
AG-199.joining: The IPC joined what it could reach in June 2021 and published without government endorsement. In June 2023 the Yale Lowenstein Clinic concluded that Ethiopia and its allies had violated the prohibition on starving civilians as a method of combat. After concluding that IPC-based figures overestimate hunger mortality, the Ghent researchers revised their estimate in 2023. The new figure was 162,000 to 378,000 civilian deaths from violence, famine and lack of health care, down from about 300,000 to 600,000.
AG-199.harm_found_later: Deaths from starvation and loss of medical care could be estimated only by later academic reconstruction. The Ghent figures put famine deaths at 96,000 to 218,000 by December 2022, deaths from lack of health care at 30,000 to 100,000 and direct killings at 36,000 to 60,000. The figures moved by roughly half in a single revision.

AG-200.summary: After the military coup of 1 February 2021, security forces occupied hospitals and arrested and charged health workers. They also attacked clinics and medics. On 5 May 2021 the UN Country Team, drawing on WHO's surveillance system, reported at least 158 attacks on health care, with at least 11 deaths and 51 injuries. It counted 51 health facilities occupied by security forces, of which at least 31 were still occupied. Its count also included at least 139 doctors in the civil disobedience movement, reportedly charged under Section 505(a) of the Penal Code. A coalition brought together Physicians for Human Rights (PHR), Insecurity Insight and the Johns Hopkins Center for Public Health and Human Rights. From 1 February 2021 to 10 January 2022 it counted 415 attacks and threats, including 286 health workers arrested or detained, 128 facilities attacked and 30 health workers killed. It attributed the violence mainly to the military.
AG-200.records:
WHO's Surveillance System for Attacks on Health Care (SSA): incidents verified by triangulation, each with a published 'level of certainty'. As WHO Myanmar stated on 1 May 2021, the system 'does not aim at identifying perpetrators'.
PHR coalition: open-source records compiled under a method informed by the Berkeley Protocol. It attributed incidents mainly to the military and also to other armed actors, and stated that its incidents were 'neither a complete nor a representative list of all incidents'.
The military authorities: recorded the same health workers as criminal defendants charged under the Penal Code.
Mandalay Medical Cover, a volunteer group: gave testimony to the UN Human Rights Council on arrests of health workers and obstruction of care.
AG-200.gap: Because the attacks were open and their author was not in doubt, the gap here concerns the harm and the naming. By design, the UN system's record counts incidents and leaves the perpetrator field empty. The NGO record names the perpetrator and disclaims completeness, while the military's record converts the same events into prosecutions. None of these records counts the patients who lost care when facilities were occupied and staff were arrested.
AG-200.joining: An NGO and academic coalition joined open-source reports into a running count and named the military. The UN Country Team publicized WHO's counts without naming a perpetrator. In the sources checked, no body with authority over the military joined these records into a finding of responsibility.
AG-200.harm_found_later: Harm to patients appears only as a reported drop in people seeking care at occupied facilities and as testimony of deaths from obstructed care. No record checked counts it. It could be established only by reconstruction from health-system data that the coup disrupted.

AG-201.summary: Ransomware attributed by the FBI to the DarkSide group hit Colonial Pipeline on or about 7 May 2021. The intruders had entered in April using the password of a disused VPN account that lacked multi-factor authentication. Colonial shut down part of the pipeline because, according to Deputy National Security Adviser Anne Neuberger, it feared that the ransomware could spread from its business systems to operational networks. Several days of panic buying of gasoline followed. The company paid about 75 bitcoin, of which the Justice Department seized 63.7 bitcoin in June 2021.
AG-201.records:
Colonial Pipeline: incident response and the decision to shut down.
FireEye/Mandiant: forensic analysis of the entry point.
FBI: attribution to DarkSide and tracing of the ransom.
CISA: brought in by the FBI after Colonial reported to law enforcement.
Justice Department: the seizure, announced 7 June 2021.
AG-201.gap: The gap was minimal. The ransom demand announced the act, and the shutdown of a major fuel pipeline was visible at once. Only the reporting channel was dispersed. CISA's acting director, Brandon Wales, testified on 11 May 2021 that Colonial had not contacted CISA directly and that CISA had received its information from the FBI.
AG-201.joining: The FBI named DarkSide within days. A month later the Justice Department traced and seized most of the ransom and thanked Colonial "for quickly notifying the FBI."

AG-202.summary: On 3 April 2021 the data feed from the Lofoten–Vesterålen (LoVe) ocean observatory went dead. The observatory is a seabed sensor network run by the Institute of Marine Research (IMR) and partly funded by Equinor. Surveys with remotely operated vehicles found a sensor node dragged from its location with its cable severed and about 4.2 to 4.3 km of cable, weighing roughly 9.5 to 10 tons, missing. A September mission found a second node moved and damaged. The loss became public through NRK in November 2021. Later that month the research vessel G.O. Sars found about 3 km of the cable up to 11 km from its original position.
AG-202.records:
IMR: the outage record and the survey results. It tried to identify vessels active in the area in April and noted that some were likely underway without transponders.
Norwegian Defence Research Establishment (FFI): received and filtered the observatory's data before IMR researchers saw it, because of the sensitivity of some of the data. The network can collect data about passing submarines.
The police: followed up the case together with IMR.
The military and the Police Security Service: investigating, according to The Drive.
AG-202.gap: Seven months passed between the outage and public disclosure. An IMR scientist said that the crew of a vessel that had snagged the cable should have noticed and would likely have reported it, but the sources record no such report. The network's dual civil and defense role placed the incident between a research institute, a defense laboratory and the police. The AIS record was incomplete.
AG-202.joining: IMR and the police followed up together. After the cable was found, Geir Pedersen, quoted by Ingeniøren, said the most likely explanation was that a vessel had dragged it, with a large bottom trawler as the leading hypothesis. No vessel or state was named in the sources checked, and no finding was published.

AG-203.summary: Two explosive drone attacks on the tanker Mercer Street off the coast of Oman failed on the evening of 29 July 2021. A third, on 30 July, blew a hole about six feet across in the topside of the pilot house. It killed the ship's master, a Romanian citizen, and a British member of the security detail. Western diplomats described the tanker as owned by a Japanese company.
AG-203.records:
The crew: reported the first two attacks by distress call.
The explosive investigative team from USS Ronald Reagan: boarded the ship, interviewed surviving crew and recovered pieces of the third drone, including a vertical stabilizer and internal components nearly identical to previously collected Iranian drone parts. RDX was identified in chemical tests.
Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain: received the material before it went to a US national laboratory.
UK explosive experts: reviewed the material at Fifth Fleet headquarters.
Israeli experts: reviewed it virtually.
AG-203.gap: A single target, the deaths of two third-country nationals and the recovered drone fragments brought the record under one investigation within a week. Japan, the owner's state, was reportedly reluctant to attribute the attack and agreed only after several days of consultations.
AG-203.joining: US Central Command announced on 6 August 2021 that US experts had concluded the drone was produced in Iran and that UK and Israeli experts concurred. The same day G7 foreign ministers called it 'a deliberate and targeted attack' and said that 'All available evidence clearly points to Iran.' The UN Security Council discussed the attack in closed session.

AG-204.summary: During years of rolling load-shedding, Eskom recorded incidents at its coal-fired stations that its own investigators classified as sabotage. On 16 and 17 May 2022 technicians found a cable supplying a steam valve and a pipe supplying control air cut at Tutuka Unit 5. Eskom said on 19 May 2022 that Tutuka was 'the fifth incident of sabotage since March 2021'. In November 2022 a maintenance company worker removed an oil drain plug from a bearing at Camden Unit 4, damaging the bearing and tripping the unit. Chief executive André de Ruyter facilitated a private intelligence investigation by George Fivaz Forensic & Risk, funded with R18 million by Business Leadership South Africa. In an e.tv interview in early 2023 de Ruyter described criminal cartels operating inside the utility.
AG-204.records:
Eskom's internal forensic report: given to management in June 2022, it concluded that the Tutuka cable and pipe had been cut deliberately, which 'amounts to acts of sabotage', by someone who 'knows the plant very well'. It could not identify the perpetrator because there was no CCTV in the area and poor access control made gate records unreliable.
Eskom: 270 active internal investigation cases on 1 July 2022.
Police stations: a case docket for each incident at the local station. Standerton held the Tutuka docket, later transferred to the Hawks, and Ermelo held the Camden docket (CAS 107/11/2022, opened 10 November 2022).
SAPS and the Hawks: at Scopa on 19 October 2022, SAPS held 131 Eskom-related cases and the Hawks 83, 18 of them in court.
Prosecutors: decided case by case. On 24 January 2023 de Ruyter told MPs that an Ermelo prosecutor 'refused to deal with' a coal-truck bribery case after an arrest and confession.
George Fivaz Forensic & Risk: the intelligence reports. Eskom told the SIU on 5 May 2023 that it was 'not in possession of the report'.
SIU: examined contracts at Kusile, Medupi, Tutuka, Duvha and Grootvlei.
Parliament's Scopa: took testimony.
AG-204.gap: Eskom recognized sabotage in its own records: the Tutuka report recommended involving the State Security Agency because sabotage at a national key point threatens national security. Yet the incidents traveled as separate local dockets. SAPS confirmed meetings with de Ruyter on 4 June and 5 July 2022 but said they conveyed 'no specific information containing elements that would enable the SAPS to open criminal investigations'. The Hawks said they learned of the private probe from media reports and from a report that de Ruyter's attorneys submitted on 25 April 2023. The private reports sat outside every body with authority to act on them.
AG-204.joining: Chief executive André de Ruyter, who had no investigative authority, joined the incidents through a privately funded probe. In September 2023 SIU head Andy Mothibi told Scopa that the probe had not been approved by the Eskom board. He said that de Ruyter had informed neither the board, the SIU, the Hawks nor SAPS, and that this amounted to maladministration. He also said the reports described 'a clear, organised nature of crime and corruption being committed at Eskom' and 'cannot be ignored'. Hawks head Godfrey Lebeya said the reports provided no evidence on their own and that the Hawks were working to corroborate allegations, including against 10 'groupings' in Mpumalanga. Police minister Bheki Cele said de Ruyter had provided no report stating that an individual politician was involved. No court finding naming a sabotage network was found.
AG-204.harm_found_later: The contribution of sabotage to load-shedding rests on de Ruyter's statement that sabotage and corruption in the coal supply chain caused at least 1,000 MW of unavailable capacity. No official reconstruction apportioning lost generation to sabotage was found.

AG-205.summary: Just before midnight on 18 June 2021 AIS data showed the British destroyer HMS Defender and the Dutch frigate HNLMS Evertsen leaving Odesa and coming within two nautical miles of the entrance to Sevastopol harbor. At the same time, live webcams showed both ships moored in Odesa. Earlier in 2021, AIS data had placed Swedish naval vessels in Russian waters off Kaliningrad. A few days later Russia's Defence Ministry said it had fired warning shots to deter HMS Defender off Crimea, a claim the UK Ministry of Defence denied.
AG-205.records:
AIS receiving station at Chornomorsk near Odesa: passed the false positions to MarineTraffic.
MarineTraffic and other aggregators: displayed the false positions.
Webcam feeds: the YouTube broadcasts of Odessa Online and archived Windy.com screenshots recorded the ships in port.
Marineschepen.nl, a Dutch naval news site: confirmed that the tracks were false.
NATO: did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Sweden's armed forces: said in March 2021 that errors in publicly available information could affect confidence in the authority.
AG-205.gap: AIS aggregators publish the positions their receivers ingest. USNI News reported that it was unclear how the false data entered the feed. The falsification was exposed because the ships lay in a harbor watched by public webcams.
AG-205.joining: H I Sutton of USNI News joined the AIS feed with the webcam footage on 21 June 2021. In July 2021 Wired reported an analysis by SkyTruth and Global Fishing Watch. The analysis found that over 100 warships from at least 14 European countries, Russia and the United States appeared to have had their locations faked since August 2020. Bjorn Bergman of Global Fishing Watch said a track can be entirely simulated and imputed into the data stream from a terrestrial AIS receiver. No party was named as responsible.

AG-206.summary: On 26 October 2021 a cyberattack disabled the subsidized-fuel card system at gas stations across Iran. The card users received the message 'cyberattack 64411,' the number of a hotline run through the Supreme Leader's office. In Isfahan, videos showed billboards displaying 'Khamenei! Where is our gas?' After 'cyberattacks,' Khuzestan Steel halted production 'due to technical problems' on 27 June 2022. A group calling itself Predatory Sparrow claimed the attack with a video. It said Mobarakeh and Hormozgan steel, also state-owned, were targeted as well. In December 2023 the same group claimed an attack that disrupted about 70 percent of Iran's gas stations.
AG-206.records:
ISNA (semiofficial): first called the 2021 fuel outage a cyberattack and then removed its reports, saying it too had been hacked.
Iranian state television: quoted an unnamed official of the National Security Council acknowledging the attack in 2021. No group immediately claimed it.
Check Point: attributed a July 2021 attack on Iran's railways, in which the number 64411 had also appeared, to a group calling itself Indra.
Khuzestan Steel: in 2022 reported a halt after cyberattacks and did not blame any group.
National Iranian Oil Products Distribution Company: in December 2023 announced restoration of the card system without naming an attacker.
Passive Defense Organization: said in December 2023 that it was preparing a response.
Petroleum Minister Javad Owji: accused Israel and the United States in December 2023.
AG-206.gap: The gap in recognition was minimal. The attackers designed effects that consumers and the public would see. They displayed messages addressed to the Supreme Leader and claimed responsibility publicly in 2022 and 2023. The gap that remained concerned attribution to a state, which most Iranian bodies left unstated. In 2023 one minister assigned it to Israel and the United States.
AG-206.joining: Attacker publicity joined the incidents: Predatory Sparrow's claims tied the steel and 2023 fuel attacks to a series. CSO Online, citing Check Point Research, listed earlier attacks on Iran's railways, steel industry, offshore oil company and roads ministry. No claim of responsibility for the October 2021 fuel attack appears in the sources checked.

AG-207.summary: At about 01:00 on 14 May 2021 the attacker executed Conti ransomware within Ireland's Health Service Executive (HSE), disrupting health services nationally. The post-incident review by PwC, commissioned by the HSE Board and dated 3 December 2021, found that the intrusion began when a user opened a malicious Excel file attached to a phishing email sent on 16 March 2021. The attacker, it found, was present for about eight weeks. During that time security tools and staff at several hospitals recorded signs of the intrusion that never led to an HSE incident investigation.
AG-207.records:
The antivirus product on the first infected workstation: detected Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz on 31 March 2021 but was set to monitor mode and did not block them. Its signatures had not been updated for over a year.
HSE servers: first compromised by the attacker on 7 May. Six voluntary hospitals and one statutory hospital followed between 8 and 12 May.
Hospital C: on 10 May identified malicious activity on a domain controller. Its antivirus detected Cobalt Strike on two systems without quarantining the files.
The security provider of Hospital C: told it the risk was low because the antivirus had remediated the threat.
Hospital A: on 12 May communicated alerts of malicious activity to the HSE's Office of the Chief Information Officer.
The antivirus provider: on 13 May emailed the HSE security operations team about unhandled threat events dating back to 7 May on at least 16 systems.
Hospital A and the Department of Health: on 13 May prevented attacks on their own networks.
HSE: had no chief information security officer and no security operations center.
AG-207.gap: Each alert stayed with a local hospital, a vendor console or a server team. None was treated as grounds for opening an incident. With no central security function, nobody had both the duty and the means to place the hospital alerts and the vendor report side by side before the ransomware ran.
AG-207.joining: PwC joined the logs and alerts in its review dated 3 December 2021, about seven months after the attack. It found that earlier detections "did not result in a cybersecurity incident and investigation initiated by the HSE" and that "opportunities to prevent the successful detonation of the ransomware were missed." The review did not concern state attribution. The attacker announced itself through the ransomware and its demand.

AG-208.summary: After former president Jacob Zuma began serving a prison sentence for contempt of court, violence and looting began in KwaZulu-Natal on 8–9 July 2021 and spread to parts of Gauteng within about a day. Trucks were burned at Mooi River Plaza on the N3, which closed, and shopping malls were looted. The expert panel appointed by the president put the dead at about 354 and the loss to the economy at about R50 billion. The panel (Sandy Africa, chair, with Silumko Sokupa and Mojankunyane Gumbi) reported on 29 November 2021 that 'there was a failure by the intelligence structures to anticipate and respond adequately to the violence'.
AG-208.records:
State Security Agency: issued an orange alert to the Ministry of State Security on 30 June 2021.
A document drafted on the eve of the unrest: stated that no information had been identified about gatherings in a specific area. The panel found its basis and sender unclear.
SAPS Crime Intelligence: at least six of its senior leaders had been suspended before the violence.
National Security Council: does not seem to have received any clear, direct intelligence about the violence.
The police minister: had received no intelligence briefing from the national commissioner from at least December 2020.
The KwaZulu-Natal premier: had received no regular intelligence briefings.
Sector bodies: damage, recorded in their own terms.
ICASA, the communications regulator: reports of 113 vandalized network towers.
Transnet: force majeure on the Natcor rail line between Gauteng and the Durban and Richards Bay ports, declared on 14 July.
AG-208.gap: Warning fragments sat in two intelligence services, one with suspended leadership, and pointed in different directions. The council with authority to act had not been meeting regularly and met only after the violence began (14, 16, 19 and 21 July). In KwaZulu-Natal SAPS initially excluded the SANDF from intelligence briefings. Damage to network towers entered the regulator's records as vandalism, and damage to freight rail entered the operator's as force majeure. These categories carry no question of organization.
AG-208.joining: Four months later the presidential expert panel, with access to ministers and agencies, joined the intelligence and coordination records. It reported that submissions identified 'elements of organisation behind the looting of the malls' and, in the findings checked, named no organizer.

AG-209.summary: Insurgents attacked Palma, the town next to the Afungi LNG site, from three directions on 24 March 2021, and cellular service was quickly cut. On 26 March about 180 of the roughly 200 people sheltering at the Amarula hotel left in a convoy that was ambushed. Pinnacle News estimated that two-thirds of the town's buildings had been burned. The Defense Ministry estimated on 28 March that 'tens of defenseless people' had been killed. The government soon claimed to have retaken Palma, but journalists flown to Afungi contradicted the claim the next day by reporting fighting just outside the LNG project. The Islamic State claimed the attack on 29 March. Total reversed its plan to restart construction at the LNG project.
AG-209.records:
Defense Ministry: brief statements and casualty estimates.
The military: said seven people died in the convoy, against other estimates near 50.
OCHA: the population of Palma district, about 110,000 civilians, including 43,600 displaced people.
DAG, a private contractor: its helicopters evacuated civilians.
Reports: differed on whether insurgents destroyed the cellular infrastructure or government forces blocked communications.
Total: suspended work because Palma lay within its security perimeter. The government had agreed to maintain a 25-km security cordon around the project.
The Islamic State: published its own claim and casualty figure (55).
AG-209.gap: Official counts ran below other estimates. The cut in cellular service limited reporting from the town during the attack. Insurgent publicity closed the question of whether an attack had occurred. The dispersed and contested part of the record concerned the toll and the cause of the communications cut.
AG-209.joining: Cabo Ligado, a monitoring project of ACLED and the Mozambican outlet Zitamar News, joined official statements, OCHA figures, news reports and social-media posts into a weekly incident list, flagging where sources conflicted. The Islamic State claimed the attack.

AG-210.summary: A ransomware attack on the evening of 1 May 2021 encrypted the electronic health record, imaging and telemedicine systems of Scripps Health. Scripps Health is a San Diego County system whose hospitals accounted for about a quarter of regional acute inpatient discharges. Physicians at UC San Diego Health, which was not attacked, compared the records of its two emergency departments for four-week periods before, during and after the attack. During the attack and recovery period they found a higher daily census (218 to 251), more EMS arrivals (1,741 to 2,354) and more patients leaving without being seen (158 to 360). They also found longer waiting times, more stroke code activations (59 to 102 in the abstract) and more confirmed strokes (22 to 47).
AG-210.records:
Scripps Health: its own outage and financial records. According to Fierce Healthcare, it reported a cost of $112.7 million, mostly lost revenue, and about 150,000 patient records were compromised.
San Diego County EMS system: ambulance diversion. Its median daily total rose from 27 to 47 hours during the attack period.
The unaffected emergency departments: higher volumes and slower throughput, recorded in their routine operational data.
AG-210.gap: The harm from the attack was recorded mainly by hospitals that were not attacked, as ordinary changes in census, waiting times and stroke volume. No reporting obligation or incident category connects a neighbor's surge to another organization's cyber incident. The regional effect therefore stayed outside the attacked system's incident records. NPR reported that liability concerns, privacy law, fear of reputational damage and technical obstacles keep data on such attacks scarce.
AG-210.joining: Clinician-researchers at the neighboring system (Dameff, Tully, Longhurst and colleagues, JAMA Network Open, May 2023) joined their own emergency department records with county diversion data two years after the attack. The paper does not name the attacked organization, which NPR and the trade press identified as Scripps. The authors concluded that targeted hospital cyberattacks 'should be considered a regional disaster.' No public body joined the regional records, and no attacker was named in the sources checked.
AG-210.harm_found_later: A hospital that was not attacked carried an added load, including a doubling of confirmed strokes. That load became visible only when the hospital compared its own records across periods two years later. The study found no significant change in door-to-CT or acute stroke treatment times, so the record documents strain without measured clinical harm.

AG-211.summary: Microsoft reported on 24 May 2023 that Volt Typhoon, a state-sponsored actor based in China and active since mid-2021, had targeted critical-infrastructure organizations in Guam and elsewhere in the United States. Its report named sectors including communications, utilities, transportation and maritime. It described the use of valid accounts and living-off-the-land techniques, with traffic routed through compromised small-office and home-office network equipment. The National Security Agency published an advisory the same day. On 31 January 2024 the Justice Department confirmed a court-authorized operation that removed the group's KV Botnet malware from infected routers. In April and July 2024 China's National Computer Virus Emergency Response Center (CVERC), with the Global Times, published reports calling Volt Typhoon an invention of Western intelligence agencies. The reports attributed the activity to the Dark Power ransomware gang.
AG-211.records:
Microsoft: detection data. It notified targeted or compromised customers.
NSA: an advisory with a hunting guide.
FBI: obtained a court order in December 2023 and removed the botnet malware from end-of-life routers, mostly Cisco and NetGear models.
Each victim organization: its own logs.
CVERC: reports citing ThreatMon and Trellix.
ThreatMon and Trellix: both firms rejected CVERC's use of their work.
AG-211.gap: Living-off-the-land activity resembles routine administration, so each victim's logs show little that crosses an alert threshold. Because traffic is routed through other people's routers, part of the record lies outside the victims' networks. Many targets are small operators.
AG-211.joining: Microsoft and US government agencies joined the victims into one campaign and named China. CVERC answered with reports contesting the naming.

AG-212.summary: On 19 October 2025 China's Ministry of State Security alleged, and CNCERT published a technical report stating, that the US National Security Agency had exploited a flaw in a foreign-brand phone's messaging service from March 2022 to monitor more than ten staff of the National Time Service Center. In 2023 and 2024, by their account, the NSA took control of office computers and attacked the internal network, an internet authentication server and a firewall with 42 weapons, modules and malicious files. They also described an attempt to attack the high-precision ground-based timing system. The report attributes the activity to the NSA by similarity to the DanderSpritz framework and to Equation Group persistence methods. It lists 58 command-and-control IP addresses as a partial list. Neither the report nor press coverage describes an outage of timing services. The US Embassy did not immediately comment.
AG-212.records:
CNCERT: the forensic findings, tool analyses and server lists.
Ministry of State Security: made the disclosure and said it had guided the center in removing the risks.
National Time Service Center: generates China's standard time and provides timing services to the communications, finance, power, transport and defense sectors.
AG-212.gap: Over more than two years before it was joined, the intrusion moved from staff phones to office computers to core network devices. Outside parties have no access to the underlying records, so the joining cannot be checked.
AG-212.joining: Chinese state security authorities joined the records and named the NSA. The sources consulted report no independent verification and no US response.

AG-213.summary: On April 25, 2022 explosions hit the Ministry of State Security building in Tiraspol, and preliminary information indicated a hand-held anti-tank grenade launcher. On April 26 two blasts at Maiac in Grigoriopol district knocked out two Soviet-era radio antennas that broadcast Russian radio. The Transnistrian interior ministry then reported that drones launched from Ukraine had flown over Cobasna, site of a large Russian ammunition depot, and that shots were fired. No one claimed responsibility.
AG-213.records:
The de facto Transnistrian authorities: recorded the incidents.
Transnistrian interior ministry: issued the drone claim, which was not independently verified.
Moldova's president: convened the Supreme Security Council and ordered security checks of critical infrastructure.
Ukraine's presidential office, the Kremlin, the OSCE and the US Defense Secretary: each commented.
AG-213.gap: The incidents took place in a territory outside Moldova's effective jurisdiction. They were recorded by unrecognized authorities whose claims no one could verify. Each government framed them to fit its own account of the war.
AG-213.joining: Transnistrian leader Vadim Krasnoselsky blamed Ukraine. Moldovan President Maia Sandu called the incidents an attempt to escalate tensions and blamed pro-war factions within the region. Ukrainian presidential adviser Mykhailo Podolyak accused Russia of staging the blasts. The Kremlin expressed concern without naming anyone. US Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin said the US was still analyzing the cause. Nobody joined the records with authority.

AG-214.summary: From February 26, 2022, two days after the invasion began, saboteurs attacked signaling cabinets and railway computer systems used to move Russian forces. They were Belarusian railway workers and their supporters, the security-force defectors' group BYPOL and the exiled IT group Cyber Partisans. The Cyber Partisans said they had disrupted the railway's scheduling and document systems on January 24, 2022. Ukraine's railway chief Alexander Kamyshin publicly called the saboteurs brave and honest people. Belarus's Interior Ministry declared damage to railway infrastructure an act of terrorism and reported more than 80 sabotage incidents by early April. In early April security police shot three alleged saboteurs in the knees near Bobruisk, and state TV said they had resisted arrest. On May 18, 2022 Lukashenko signed amendments making attempted terrorist acts punishable by death. The amendments bear on the terrorism charges in the rail cases.
AG-214.records:
Belarusian Railways: attributed its ticketing outage after the January hack to technical reasons. It did not comment on the sabotage.
Interior Ministry: counted incidents and brought terrorism cases.
Viasna, a rights group: counted at least 11 people charged with terrorism over rail incidents by mid-June 2022.
The opposition groups: published their own claims.
A RUSI analyst: judged the sabotage's effect on Russian logistics hard to separate from poor Russian planning.
AG-214.gap: There was little gap in recognition. The saboteurs publicized the acts and Ukrainian officials praised them. The record gap concerns effect: without independent media in Belarus, no institution could separate the sabotage's contribution from other causes of Russian supply failure.
AG-214.joining: Belarusian authorities named the campaign terrorism and prosecuted participants. The saboteurs and Ukrainian officials publicized it themselves.

AG-215.summary: The Black Sea Grain Initiative of July 2022 created a Joint Coordination Centre in Istanbul, inaugurated on 27 July 2022. In it, Ukraine, Russia, Türkiye and the United Nations monitored commercial vessels carrying Ukrainian grain. Russia withdrew from the initiative on 17 July 2023, after twelve months in which, according to the President of the General Assembly, it had facilitated the export of over 32 million metric tons of grain and foodstuffs. A drone attack on the Danube port of Izmail on 23 August 2023 destroyed 13,000 metric tons of grain bound for Egypt and Romania. Ukraine's deputy prime minister Oleksandr Kubrakov said that 270,000 tons had been destroyed since Russia left the deal.
AG-215.records:
Joint Coordination Centre: hosted by Türkiye with representatives of all four parties. It monitored vessel movements and cargo and reported on shipments.
UN: published the vessel movement series.
