Ukrainian authorities: the tonnage destroyed in port attacks.
AG-215.gap: The gap was very narrow. Until the withdrawal, a standing international body had held the shipping records with which to measure the interruption. The strikes hit large, identifiable facilities and were reported at once.
AG-215.joining: While it operated, the Joint Coordination Centre joined the shipping records. It worked under an agreement that placed the attacking and defending states in the same recording body. After Russia's withdrawal, only Ukraine reported the tonnage destroyed.

AG-216.summary: The CPC terminal at Novorossiysk handles about 80 percent of Kazakhstan's oil exports, according to RFE/RL. In late March 2022 storm damage to two of its three mooring buoys interrupted its operation. From 20 June operation was interrupted by planned intermittent shutdowns to search the seabed for unexploded ordnance near the subsea pipeline. The shutdowns were reported days after President Tokayev said at the St. Petersburg economic forum that Kazakhstan could not recognize the Donetsk and Luhansk entities. A Novorossiysk court order of 6 July suspended operations for 30 days over oil-spill documentation. On appeal on 11 July the Krasnodar Regional Court replaced the suspension with a fine of 200,000 rubles. In 2025 Ukrainian forces struck the line: on 17 February drones damaged the Kropotkinskaya pumping station, and on 29 November a naval drone disabled the SPM-2 mooring. After the November strike, Kazakhstan's foreign ministry told Ukraine to stop attacking what it called civilian infrastructure.
AG-216.records:
Inspections ordered by Deputy Prime Minister Viktoria Abramchenko: found incomplete oil-spill response documentation.
Novorossiysk office of the transport regulator Rostransnadzor: drew up the administrative-offense protocol and sought the closure.
Novorossiysk court: ordered the suspension to prevent environmental damage.
Krasnodar Regional Court: reduced the suspension to a fine.
Russian officials and the port: recorded the ordnance search, with dozens of possible items found near the terminal (Kommersant, via Maritime Executive).
CPC: the storm damage and, in 2025, the damage to its pumping station and mooring.
Ukraine's General Staff: confirmed the February 2025 strike.
Kazakhstan's foreign ministry: recorded the November 2025 strike as an attack on civilian infrastructure.
AG-216.gap: In 2022 each interruption entered a technical or legal category (weather damage, ordnance safety, spill-response documentation) held by a different Russian authority, so no record on its own carried a coercive purpose. Treating them as one pattern of pressure on Kazakhstan required setting their timing against political events, which only the press did.
AG-216.joining: Maritime Executive set the June ordnance shutdown against Tokayev's statement. No Kazakh or Russian authority joined the 2022 interruptions or named a coercive purpose. The coercion hypothesis remains press speculation. The 2025 strikes were joined and named at once: Ukraine's General Staff confirmed the February strike, and Ukraine answered Kazakhstan's November protest by saying that its operations targeted Russian aggression.

AG-217.summary: As Russian forces took the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone, the automated radiation monitoring network run by the SSE Ecocentre showed gamma dose rates above control levels at many observation points. At 08:05 on February 25, 2022 the website of Ukraine's nuclear regulator (SNRIU) said the reasons could not be established because of the occupation and fighting. At 09:00 it relayed Ecocentre experts' explanation that heavy military vehicles had disturbed the topsoil, an explanation that passed to international media and the IAEA. A 2023 paper in the Journal of Radiological Protection reportedly found no contamination change and called the resuspension explanation barely plausible. The paper was based on a survey led by SNRIU and its technical support organization and funded by Norway's DSA. A security researcher presented a fabrication hypothesis at Black Hat USA 2023 and later argued that the values were plausibly injected into the monitoring network at 13 timestamps.
AG-217.records:
SSE Ecocentre: the network's data.
SNRIU: public statements.
IAEA: received the resuspension explanation.
SNRIU and its technical support organization: the later survey results.
An independent researcher: an analysis of the published time series.
GammaTRACER probes: an internal memory that holds up to 12,800 records and is cyclically overwritten.
AG-217.gap: While the zone was occupied and inaccessible, the Ecocentre and SNRIU accepted the first plausible physical explanation. The later survey found no contamination without explaining why the high values appeared. No institution in the sources checked held a mandate to examine whether the monitoring data chain had been tampered with. The probe memory has likely been overwritten.
AG-217.joining: Two sources joined the records in part: the regulator's own survey (published 2023) and an independent researcher (2023–2024). No institution has determined whether the values were artifacts, manipulation or cyber interference, and nobody has been named.

AG-218.summary: In the night of 26-27 April 2022, between about 3 and 5 a.m., long-distance fiber cables on the Paris-Lyon, Paris-Strasbourg and Paris-Lille routes were cut at several sites. These included Meaux, Souppes-sur-Loing, La Chapelle-la-Reine, Le Coudray-Montceaux and Fresnes-en-Woëvre. Free and SFR customers lost service in several cities, and Bourgogne-Franche-Comté was reportedly offline for a few hours. The Paris prosecutor opened a preliminary investigation for damage liable to harm the fundamental interests of the Nation, obstruction of an automated data system and criminal association. The DGSI and the DCPJ handled the investigation. On the night of 17-18 October 2022 a telecom chamber at Aix-en-Provence was opened and fiber bundles serving the Marseille-Lyon, Marseille-Milan and Marseille-Barcelona routes were cut. No perpetrator of either event was identified in the sources checked.
AG-218.records:
Each operator: the cuts on its own network.
SFR, which manages the cables: reported vandalism around Paris and Lyon.
Free: reported 'multiple malicious acts'.
Bouygues Telecom: said it did not use the affected links.
Orange: reported no incident.
Netalis, an ISP: recorded three major outages a few dozen minutes apart.
Down Detector: logged more than 2,200 user reports.
The Paris prosecutor, the DGSI and the DCPJ: the criminal file, with the operators as civil parties.
Economy Ministry: acknowledged that the cuts could be vandalism.
Zscaler, a cloud-security firm: described the October cut publicly and adjusted its routing.
The police: secured the Aix-en-Provence site before repairs.
AG-218.gap: The gap narrowed within hours. The April cuts were near-simultaneous, struck the core links of two national operators and were visible to customers across the country. The categories still diverged. SFR and the Economy Ministry spoke of vandalism, but an official source called the cuts a coordinated malicious act. The prosecutor filed them under offenses against the fundamental interests of the Nation. The October cut entered the public record through a foreign security vendor's account.
AG-218.joining: The Paris prosecutor joined the April cuts into one investigation by 27 April, under national-interest offenses. No authority was found to have publicly joined the April and October events, and no attacker was named. The press (Siècle Digital) drew the parallel between them.

AG-219.summary: After the full-scale invasion, three main recorders counted attacks on Ukraine's health system, each with its own unit and attribution rule. WHO, which named no perpetrator, documented at least 2,881 attacks on health care from 24 February 2022 to February 2026, with 233 health workers and patients killed and 930 injured. Ukraine's Ministry of Health counted facilities: as of early December 2024, 1,878 damaged and 289 destroyed. A coalition of six organizations, including PHR, Insecurity Insight, eyeWitness to Atrocities and the Ukrainian Healthcare Center, counted 2,000 attacks, including 285 health workers killed, on a map updated to April 2025 and attributed them to Russia.
AG-219.records:
WHO: attacks on health workers, facilities, ambulances and medical warehouses, published without naming a perpetrator. It separately described the 'cascading effects of strikes on civilian infrastructure,' including thermal power plants, on health services.
Ministry of Health: damaged and destroyed facilities and ambulances (235 damaged, 264 destroyed, 125 seized). It stated that comprehensive information on occupied territories cannot be obtained.
NGO coalition: incidents defined by WHO's definitions as used by the Safeguarding Health in Conflict Coalition, mapped online, with attribution to Russian forces. Its members are eyeWitness to Atrocities, Insecurity Insight, the Media Initiative for Human Rights, PHR, Truth Hounds and the Ukrainian Healthcare Center.
AG-219.gap: Because the attacker was not in doubt, recognition was immediate. The counts diverge because one counts attacks, another counts damaged buildings, and the ministry cannot see occupied territory. The 'attack on health care' category excludes altogether the strikes on energy infrastructure that disable hospitals.
AG-219.joining: In the sources checked, no single body reconciled the counts. The NGO coalition aligned its definitions with WHO's to make counts comparable and added attribution. WHO publishes without naming the attacker. The Ministry of Health attributes damage to Russian aggression but counts in a different unit.
AG-219.harm_found_later: Patients harmed by loss of heat, power and water after strikes on energy infrastructure fall outside the 'attack on health care' category of all three counts. WHO's February 2026 release described these 'cascading effects' separately from its count.

AG-220.summary: The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU) reported on September 19, 2024 that nine waves of Russian attacks between March 22 and August 31, 2024 hit electricity infrastructure in 20 of the 24 regions under Ukrainian control. By its account the attacks destroyed around 9 GW of generation, killed at least 18 civilians and injured at least 84 near the strikes. The mission said they also disrupted water, sanitation, heating and public health services. In a written response of March 6, 2026, the Kyiv city administration said that no deaths linked to cold from heating or power outages appeared in the reporting data of services and health authorities. Two widely reported deaths of elderly residents were attributed by forensic examinations to chronic cardiovascular disease, city and regional authorities said. Al Jazeera counted at least 10 hypothermia deaths reported by emergency and health officials in Ternopil and Rivne regions in early 2026. It also counted at least 18 carbon monoxide deaths from indoor burning of wood and coal.
AG-220.records:
HRMMU: casualties near strike sites.
Kyiv city administration: the reporting data of services and health authorities.
Forensic examiners: the clinical cause of death.
State Emergency Service: reports of individual hypothermia deaths.
Officials: national hypothermia statistics, compiled only after the winter.
AG-220.gap: Cause-of-death records name the clinical cause (cardiovascular disease, carbon monoxide poisoning) and leave out the outage that preceded it. The Kyiv administration recorded outdoor hypothermia deaths, mainly among homeless people, as unconnected to heating or power outages. Michele Heisler, medical director of Physicians for Human Rights, said that cold raises cardiovascular and respiratory mortality without being recorded as hypothermia. The risk lasts up to about 23 days after exposure, according to Heisler.
AG-220.joining: HRMMU counts only casualties near the strikes. No institution in the sources checked has published an excess-mortality reconstruction.
AG-220.harm_found_later: This harm is central to the case: indirect deaths from an acknowledged campaign against power and heat disappear into clinical cause-of-death categories. As a result, only linked mortality and outage records could count them.

AG-221.summary: On 8 October 2022 cables of the GSM-R digital train radio network were cut at Berlin-Hohenschönhausen and near Herne in the Ruhr. For about three hours rail traffic across northern Germany stopped. Transport Minister Volker Wissing called the cuts deliberate destruction. The Federal Public Prosecutor General took over the whole investigation on suspicion of anti-constitutional sabotage and assigned the police work to the Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA). The opened sources report no finding on the perpetrators and name no state or group.
AG-221.records:
Deutsche Bahn: the outage, from about 6:30 to 9:30 a.m., and the cut cables. Its documents, reported in July 2023, counted more than 1,500 sabotage actions on rail infrastructure in 2022 against about 1,200 in 2021, with 310 in Berlin alone.
The North Rhine-Westphalia interior ministry: told the state parliament's interior committee that the outage resulted from deliberate damage by unknown persons. It also said, citing Deutsche Bahn, that the Herne cables had been laid according to recognized technical rules.
The Federal Public Prosecutor General and the BKA: the investigation. The federal prosecutors warned that discussing findings in state parliamentary committees could jeopardize it.
AG-221.gap: Two cuts within hours, at sites several hundred kilometers apart, suggested coordination and put the case on the federal state-protection track. The operator's count of sabotage actions gave no base rate for distinguishing a state operation from other causes. The secrecy around the federal investigation left the state parliament without information.
AG-221.joining: The Federal Public Prosecutor General joined the two sites into one investigation. After the transfer, the North Rhine-Westphalia government declined to give its parliament further details. The opened sources report no conclusion and name no attacker.

AG-222.summary: In September 2022, amid protests against a government plan to cut fuel subsidies, gangs dug trenches and placed shipping containers at the entrances to the Varreux terminal, Port-au-Prince's main fuel terminal. UNICEF, citing WHO data, said 'three-quarters of the major hospitals in Haiti are affected by the lack of fuel'. Digicel's chairman, Maarten Boute, said about 30 percent of its antennas were out of fuel. On 21 October 2022 the UN Security Council unanimously adopted a sanctions regime. It imposed an asset freeze and travel ban on Jimmy Chérizier, leader of the G9 Family and Allies alliance. The resolution said his confederation played a leading role in the blockade. It also called for an arms embargo on non-state actors.
AG-222.records:
WHO and UNICEF: hospital fuel data.
Bernard Mevs, Fondation Saint-Luc and other hospitals: staff and service cuts, and closure warnings.
Digicel: antennas without fuel.
UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator Ulrika Richardson: said 'lives are being lost in Haiti because hospitals are unable to access fuel'.
WFP: about $6 million in relief supplies lost by UN agencies and non-profits.
The UN Security Council: the sanctions resolution.
AG-222.gap: A single site was seized openly, and within weeks the Security Council named the leader of the gang alliance responsible, so no gap arose.
AG-222.joining: Recognition and naming were immediate. The Security Council's resolution named Chérizier and the G9's role in the blockade.
AG-222.harm_found_later: Deaths from hospital service cuts were reported in general terms: the UN coordinator said lives were being lost. The sources checked give no count.

AG-223.summary: Since 2022 aircraft around the Baltic Sea have reported GNSS jamming and, increasingly, spoofing. In April 2024 two Finnair flights to Tartu had to return to Helsinki because GPS interference prevented landing. Finnair suspended the route from 29 April to 31 May because Tartu's approach procedures required GPS. Estonia's foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, called the incident a Russian 'hybrid attack'. In June 2025 Lithuania's air navigation service provider registered a record 1,022 pilot reports. The national regulator counted 302 reports from January to early March 2026.
AG-223.records:
Pilots: report to the air navigation service provider of the airspace they are in, which in Lithuania is Oro Navigacija.
The Communications Regulatory Authority of Lithuania: compiles the counts and notes that only pilot-reported incidents are recorded.
ADS-B aggregations such as GPSJam.org: maps of affected areas.
University of Texas and Stanford researchers: analyzed sources.
The spectrum administrations of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, and later Finland: brought cases to the ITU.
AG-223.gap: Each report is a single pilot's observation of degraded navigation, logged by the provider of whatever airspace the aircraft was in. The Lithuanian regulator notes that jamming systems in Kaliningrad reach more than 400 km, so many disruptions occur over Latvia or Poland before aircraft enter Lithuanian airspace. Counts depend on pilots filing. Oro Navigacija stresses that aircraft can rely on ground-based navigation aids. Lithuanian authorities estimated that more than 30 jamming sources may have operated in Kaliningrad and the Baltic Sea during 2025.
AG-223.joining: A University of Texas researcher placed a circle-spoofing source somewhere in western Russia from the points where aircraft lost and regained authentic GPS. In March 2025 the ITU Radio Regulations Board considered a submission by Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. It stated that measurements had geolocated the source within the territory of the Russian Federation and urged Russia to cease. In November 2025 the Board again urged Russia to cease interference to receivers in Estonia, Finland, Latvia and Lithuania from a source on its territory. Moscow reportedly denied conducting widespread jamming.

AG-224.summary: From the spring of 2022 grain was taken from occupied Ukrainian territory, moved through Crimean ports and sold as Russian. By May 2022 Ukraine's Defense Ministry estimated that at least 400,000 tons had been taken out of the country. The bulk carrier Matros Pozynich left the Crimean coast on 27 April 2022 with its transponder off. Ukrainian officials said it carried nearly 30,000 tons of Ukrainian wheat. After warnings that the grain was stolen, it was turned away at Alexandria and Beirut. It appeared in imagery at Latakia.
AG-224.records:
Ukraine's Defense Ministry: the loss estimate.
Ukrainian officials: warnings to the authorities in Egypt and Lebanon.
TankerTrackers and Maxar Technologies: the imagery that CNN joined to the ship's track.
RFE/RL's Schemes unit: hacked documents of the Kherson occupation administration, leaked Russian customs data and Import Genius trade records. From these it documented nearly 35,000 tons of wheat, barley, corn and peas sold in 2023 from Kherson and Crimea, exported at discounted Russian customs rates or duty-free, with named consignees in Spain, Turkey, Azerbaijan, Iran and Syria.
NASA Harvest: satellite estimates that put the 2023 wheat harvest in Crimea and the occupied parts of four other regions at at least 6.4 million tons.
AG-224.gap: Buyers relied on origin declarations from their suppliers: a Spanish buyer said its suppliers had confirmed the Russian origin of the cargo. Each consignment had been documented as a Russian export and recorded by a customs service that treated it as Russian produce. No institution held both the field-level provenance and the export documentation.
AG-224.joining: Journalists and open-source analysts joined the records over more than two years, using customs data, hacked administrative files, ship tracking and satellite imagery. In 2022 a Ukrainian Foreign Ministry sanctions envoy named Agro-Fregat and seven other Russian firms as exporters of stolen grain. The sources checked contain no court judgment joining the record.
AG-224.harm_found_later: The loss falls on farmers in occupied territory whose harvest left the country as someone else's export. No record attributes a specific loss to a specific farm.

AG-225.summary: ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants over missile strikes on Ukrainian electric infrastructure from at least October 10, 2022 until at least March 9, 2023. The warrants for Lt. Gen. Sergei Kobylash, commander of Long-Range Aviation, and Adm. Viktor Sokolov, commander of the Black Sea Fleet, were announced on March 5, 2024. Those for Sergei Shoigu and Valery Gerasimov were issued on June 24, 2024. The charges are the war crimes of directing attacks at civilian objects and of causing excessive incidental harm, together with the crime against humanity of inhumane acts. The Chamber described the strikes as a course of conduct involving the multiple commission of acts against a civilian population, carried out pursuant to a state policy. In June 2024 Reuters reported that ICC prosecutors were also examining Russian cyberattacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure as possible war crimes. According to Reuters, these included at least four major attacks on energy infrastructure.
AG-225.records:
The damage records: the strikes hit 20 regions and left millions without electricity, water and heating.
The UN Commission of Inquiry: found the attacks on energy infrastructure disproportionate, widespread and systematic.
The ICC Prosecutor: assembled the warrant applications, which are confidential.
AG-225.gap: Each strike was public and its author known, so recognition was immediate. The open task was legal: joining damage records from some 20 regions into one course of conduct and tying it to individual commanders. As Marchuk notes, this required linkage material beyond records of the strikes' effects. She suggests the Prosecutor relied heavily on intelligence.
AG-225.joining: Under the Rome Statute, the ICC Prosecutor and Pre-Trial Chamber joined the records about 17 to 20 months after the campaign began and named four individuals.
AG-225.harm_found_later: Marchuk links the crime against humanity charge to the strikes' effect on civilians, millions of whom lost electricity, water and heating for long periods in freezing temperatures. This indirect harm is not attributed in casualty counts (see the entry on deaths from power and heat loss).

AG-226.summary: From 30 November 2022, about two months after nationwide protests began, hundreds of poisoning incidents were reported at schools in 28 provinces across Iran, most of them girls' schools. Officials at times blamed poison, but the government concluded that most incidents were caused by girls' anxiety or hysteria. In July 2023 a member of the UN Fact-Finding Mission on Iran said that reports suggested the poisonings may have been orchestrated to punish girls. A Stanford open-source investigation (November 2025) concluded that the girls' symptoms were real and likely physical in cause and that officials had failed to investigate properly.
AG-226.records:
Iranian officials: acknowledged some incidents, conducted the government's investigation and limited the spread of information.
The students and others posting on social media: videos and claims, which the Stanford team checked.
The UN Fact-Finding Mission: investigated from outside the country. Its requests to visit Iran went unanswered.
AG-226.gap: Hundreds of incidents were reported locally across 28 provinces, but the authority to join them lay with a government that downplayed the girls' symptoms and limited information.
AG-226.joining: The government joined the reports into a largely non-hostile classification. Outside joining came from a UN fact-finding mission without access to the country and from academic open-source investigators. In the sources checked, no perpetrator was named.

AG-227.summary: During the January 2022 unrest, which began over energy prices, mobile internet in Kazakhstan was disrupted on 4 January. A nationwide shutdown began at about 11:00 UTC on 5 January and lasted to 10 January, with brief partial restorations each day. The outage affected banks and mobile payment systems. Many government websites, including the president's, were unavailable. Officials did not say who ordered the shutdown. Forbes Kazakhstan's sources said operators were instructed to block all traffic. A source at Kcell said the National Security Committee (KNB) carried out the blocking itself. Top10VPN, using the NetBlocks Cost of Shutdown Tool, estimated the cost at $410.3 million for 144 hours of outages affecting about 16 million users.
AG-227.records:
Operators: traffic and outage records.
Kazakhtelecom: announced a 50 percent discount for January after the shutdown.
The KNB and the State Technical Service: the blocking arrangements. The State Technical Service did not answer Eurasianet's questions.
External measurement platforms: CAIDA IODA, Cloudflare Radar, Google Transparency Report and RIPE Atlas recorded the outage from outside.
Top10VPN: cost estimates, above $429 million in January 2022 and $410.3 million in its 2022 annual review. No official loss figures were found.
AG-227.gap: Because the state was the disruptor, the security service kept the records that would show the order and its scope. The measurable record of the outage and its cost was produced abroad by network-measurement firms and researchers without access to the orders.
AG-227.joining: External measurement platforms and civil-society groups joined the outage record and cost estimates within days. The government cited a terrorist threat and did not publish the order. No hostile third party was involved.
AG-227.harm_found_later: Harm to payments, commerce and access to services appears only in an outside cost model. No official record attributing losses to the shutdown was found.

AG-228.summary: On December 12, 2022 several dozen Azerbaijanis, presented by pro-government media as environmental activists, blocked the Lachin corridor, the only road linking Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenia, protesting alleged illegal mining. Eurasianet reported that a protester said the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources had supplied their tents. It also reported that another protester wore the jacket of AzerSu, the state water company. On February 22, 2023 the International Court of Justice indicated a provisional measure to ensure unimpeded movement of persons, vehicles and cargo along the corridor. On April 23, 2023 Azerbaijan installed a checkpoint, saying it would stop transfers of weapons and soldiers from Armenia. Armenia and Russia denied the claim.
AG-228.records:
Russian peacekeepers: guarded the road and clashed with protesters and journalists.
The Red Cross and the peacekeepers: essential supplies passed with them.
The region: faced shortages of food and fuel.
Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry: blamed the peacekeepers for blocking a visit to a disputed mine.
Journalists: documented links between protesters and state bodies.
The ICJ: indicated provisional measures in the case Armenia brought under the Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination.
AG-228.gap: The blockade was public; coercion requires notice. Its authorship was disguised: a civilian protest about mining gave the state room to deny responsibility until it replaced the protest with a checkpoint.
AG-228.joining: Journalists linked the protesters to state bodies on the first day. About ten weeks later the ICJ indicated free passage in the CERD case. Azerbaijan acknowledged control openly when it set up the checkpoint, four months after the protest began.
AG-228.harm_found_later: Food and fuel shortages during the blockade were reported. In the sources checked, no judicial finding tied them to a named actor.

AG-229.summary: An airstrike hit the Mariupol Maternity House and Children's Hospital on 9 March 2022. The Russian embassy in London, quoting Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, posted that the hospital had long been out of operation and was used by Ukrainian armed forces and 'radicals'. Twitter removed the post under its rules on denying violent events. The OSCE Moscow Mechanism report, published on 13 April 2022, concluded that the attack was Russian and that no effective warning had been given. It further concluded that, 'based upon Russian explanations, the attack must have been deliberate.'
AG-229.records:
Hospital staff, journalists on site and Ukrainian authorities: the strike and casualties.
The Russian Foreign Ministry and embassies: a counter-account of military use.
Human rights groups and open-source analysts: compiled imagery and accounts.
The OSCE experts: appointed after a group of participating states including the United States, Germany, Britain and France invoked the Moscow Mechanism. They did not travel to Ukraine and worked from open-source material and the accounts of human rights and nonprofit groups.
AG-229.gap: A single, well-documented target narrowed the recognition gap at once. The dispute was over classification: whether the hospital was a military objective. The attacking state supplied its own account through diplomatic channels.
AG-229.joining: Within five weeks the OSCE Moscow Mechanism mission joined open-source and NGO records remotely. It named Russia and classified the attack as a war crime. The US ambassador to the OSCE, Michael Carpenter, said the mission 'categorically dismissed' the claim of military use. The platform Twitter acted on the Russian embassy's post after the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport reported it.

AG-230.summary: From October 2022 Gazprom cut gas supplies to Moldova by 30%. Transnistrian authorities then cut by 73% the deliveries from the Cuciurgan (MGRES) plant, which had supplied about 70% of Moldova's electricity. After Russia began striking Ukraine's grid on October 10, Ukraine suspended electricity exports to Moldova. Russian strikes on Ukraine in mid-November and early December also cut power in Moldova. Moldova's imports from Romania ran over a single 400 kV line from Isaccea that passes through Transnistria.
AG-230.records:
Gazprom: set the reduced gas deliveries.
The Transnistrian authorities: controlled Cuciurgan.
The grid operator: Moldelectrica's real-time map showed the outages on November 15, 2022.
Deputy Prime Minister Andrei Spinu: said the Isaccea line had not been damaged and had switched off automatically for safety reasons after frequency problems.
AG-230.gap: Coercion needs notice; the gas cut was public. The November 15 blackout entered the Moldovan record as an automatic protective disconnection of an undamaged line, set off by strikes on another state's grid. The gas cut passed through a contract and through a power plant controlled by a breakaway authority.
AG-230.joining: Analysts at the Atlantic Council described the gas cut as an attempt to pressure Moldova's pro-EU government. In the sources checked, no institution formally classified it as a hostile act.

AG-231.summary: On the night of 3 December 2022 gunfire damaged two Duke Energy substations in Moore County, North Carolina. About 45,000 customers lost power. The county declared a state of emergency, set a curfew and closed schools. No arrests had been made by August 2023. A federal law-enforcement memo obtained by NewsNation stated that power stations in Oregon and Washington had reported "physical attacks on substations using handtools, arson, firearms and metal chains," possibly in response to an online call for attacks on critical infrastructure.
AG-231.records:
Duke Energy: the outage and restoration.
The Moore County Sheriff's Office: the criminal investigation, for which it called in the FBI. The sheriff described the attack as "intentional vandalism" and said it "wasn't random".
DOE: monitoring, according to a department adviser.
A federal law-enforcement memo: grouped incidents reported by power stations in Oregon and Washington.
DHS's national bulletin, renewed on 30 November 2022: listed "US critical infrastructure" among potential targets.
North Carolina's Office of the Chief Medical Examiner: the autopsy of Karin Zoanelli, 87.
AG-231.gap: The single large outage in Moore County drew national attention at once. The Oregon and Washington incidents had been reported station by station, with no public count. The memo that grouped them by method circulated in law-enforcement channels and reached the public through the press. FERC's physical-protection rules do not apply to state-regulated distribution substations. An unnamed official said the two Moore County substations were likely outside the federally regulated system.
AG-231.joining: Federal law enforcement grouped the incidents by method without naming an attacker. The Moore County investigation produced no arrest. The attack on one county narrowed the gap for that event. The wider series remained a list of similar methods.
AG-231.harm_found_later: The medical examiner found that the failure of Karin Zoanelli's oxygen concentrator during the outage "precipitated her demise". The examiner wrote that "the manner of death is best classified as Homicide". The finding became public on 30 August 2023, nine months after the attack.

AG-232.summary: The 73 km pipeline carrying Dnipro water from Kherson oblast to Mykolaiv was damaged on April 12, 2022. After about a month without piped water, the city built a new intake from the Southern Bug. The river's water is hard and salty and fails drinking standards. It was supplied only as technical water for washing, and drinking water was distributed free. Mayor Oleksandr Senkevych said the occupiers had fired on the pipe. A BBC investigation in October 2022 drew on satellite images and open-source photos reviewed by military experts. It concluded that Russian forces had destroyed the pipeline deliberately, most likely with placed explosives.
AG-232.records:
The city: recorded the loss of supply and switched to river water.
The mayor: made public statements.
The damaged section: lay where repairs were impossible because Russian troops were close.
The BBC: investigated the cause.
AG-232.gap: Mykolaiv's outage was obvious at once. The damaged section could not be reached, so the city's record held the loss of supply without a cause established on site.
AG-232.joining: Mayor Oleksandr Senkevych attributed the damage to occupying forces. BBC journalists later reconstructed the cause from imagery. UN experts told the BBC the act was certainly a violation of international humanitarian law.
AG-232.harm_found_later: The sources checked contain no assessment of the health or infrastructure effects of months of salty tap water in a large city.

AG-233.summary: On 23 November 2022 attackers compromised servers of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in New Delhi, encrypting about 1.3 TB of data on five servers. The attack halted outpatient and inpatient digital services, including the smart laboratory, billing, report generation and appointments. By 13 December online services had only partly resumed. On 25 November Delhi Police's Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (IFSO) unit registered a case of extortion and cyber terrorism. On 14 December unnamed official sources said the attack was suspected to have originated from a location in China and a location in Hong Kong. On 16 December the Minister of State for IT, Rajeev Chandrasekhar, told the Rajya Sabha in a written reply that the servers had been compromised by 'unknown threat actors' because of improper network segmentation.
AG-233.records:
AIIMS: the disruption of its services. It reported the incident to CERT-In.
CERT-In: analyzed the incident and advised remedial measures.
The IFSO unit: a criminal file for extortion and cyber terrorism.
Delhi Police: asked the CBI to seek information from companies in China and Hong Kong through Interpol.
The Delhi Police cybercrime special cell and the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre: also investigating.
The Intelligence Bureau and the NIA: also investigating.
The anonymous official sources: made the geographic attribution public.
The Minister of State for IT: a written reply to Parliament that named no actor and no country.
AG-233.gap: At least seven agencies held parts of the record under different mandates: incident response, extortion, terrorism, intelligence and international police cooperation. None was charged with a public finding on the actor. The location of servers used in an attack was released informally and stood in for attribution. The formal record kept the actor unknown.
AG-233.joining: The government's formal account to Parliament joined the technical cause (improper segmentation) and the damage (five servers, 1.3 TB) and left the actor unnamed. In the sources checked, no agency published a joined finding.
AG-233.harm_found_later: Harm to patients from about three weeks of disrupted digital services at India's leading public hospital was not measured in any record checked.

AG-234.summary: Since February 2022 Russian courts have tried growing numbers of people, many of them minors, for setting fire to railway relay cabinets and other infrastructure. Investigative Committee chair Alexander Bastrykin has accused Ukrainian intelligence of trying to recruit teenagers for sabotage. By June 2026 Mediazona counted at least 240 people under 18 detained in terrorism and sabotage cases, mostly for attacks on infrastructure, mainly railways. Using Supreme Court Judicial Department data, OVD-Info found that sabotage convictions (Art. 281) rose from 12 in 2023 to 69 in 2024. Vyorstka counted at least 158 minors convicted of terrorism or sabotage between the invasion and mid-2025.
AG-234.records:
Goszheldornadzor, the rail safety regulator: classifies derailment causes. For the first four months of 2022 it attributed them to track condition (55.3%), shunting by the carrier (29.6%) and rolling-stock repair and maintenance (2.6%).
The FSB and Investigative Committee: bring terrorism and sabotage cases.
The courts and the Supreme Court's Judicial Department: publish partial conviction statistics.
AG-234.gap: For early 2022 the safety regulator published technical causes (track, shunting, maintenance). Deliberate damage enters the record when a criminal case is opened under terrorism or sabotage articles, which are counted separately. OVD-Info notes that the data on these cases are incomplete. The sources checked contain no official consolidated count of sabotage on the rail network.
AG-234.joining: Independent outlets and NGOs (Mediazona, OVD-Info, Vyorstka) combined court files, Judicial Department data and media reports into running counts. In public statements the Investigative Committee named Ukrainian intelligence as recruiter. Mediazona noted that some videos of arson by minors appeared on social media accounts linked to Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR).

AG-235.summary: After the full-scale invasion of February 2022, Russia alleged that US-supported biological laboratories in Ukraine were engaged in military biological activity. It requested a formal consultative meeting of BWC states parties under Article V. The meeting, held in Geneva in September 2022, was only the second such meeting in the convention's history. Russia failed to persuade the states parties. It then lodged a complaint under Article VI with the Security Council. In November 2022 the Council rejected Russia's draft resolution to create a commission of all fifteen Council members to investigate (2 in favor, 3 against, 10 abstentions).
AG-235.records:
Russia: submitted its allegations to the consultative meeting and to the Security Council.
Ukraine and the United States: answered the allegations at the consultative meeting. The United States said they had rebutted every claim.
The states parties and the Security Council: received the competing submissions.
AG-235.gap: The treaty's procedures could receive the claim, hear the replies and vote. The convention's states had no body of their own to investigate. Russia's draft would have created one for the occasion, but the Council declined to do so.
AG-235.joining: Russia used both formal complaint procedures of the convention to join its claims into an allegation of attack preparation. Neither the states parties nor the Security Council accepted it. Russia and China voted for the draft, China citing unanswered questions from the consultative meeting. The United States called the draft based on disinformation. The United Kingdom said the allegations had no credible basis in fact and cited Russia's long-standing disinformation efforts. France called them lies and unfounded.

AG-236.summary: On 20 October 2022 the SHEFA-2 cable, already damaged halfway between Faroe and Shetland, was hit again just east of the Shetland mainland. The second hit cut most mobile and internet services in Shetland. A large section of the national media favored a Russian sabotage explanation, while the Shetland Fishermen's Association said it was 'purely speculation' that a trawler had caused the damage.
AG-236.records:
HM Coastguard staff: believed by 4 a.m. on 20 October that the 'subsea cable has been severed by a fishing vessel'.
The Maritime and Coastguard Agency: confirmed to the Scottish Government that the vessel had been identified as a UK-registered fishing vessel.
The UK Government: by the afternoon of 20 October it was 'confident that it was an accident'.
Scottish Government emergency planners: held the same information.
Faroese Telecom, the owner: consistently said a fishing vessel was the likely cause. AIS tracking was understood to be one factor behind that view.
AG-236.gap: Within hours the agencies had joined the facts, but the joined record stayed inside government. A statement planned for the next day to 'quell any rumours re sabotage' was never issued. A week later no one had published supporting records for either explanation. The MCA said it 'does not comment in individual referrals or investigations' while it investigated under the Merchant Shipping Act.
AG-236.joining: In January 2023 the record became public through emails released under freedom of information legislation. The Scottish Government's answer to a parliamentary question from Shetland MSP Beatrice Wishart confirmed that it had known the cause from the start. The vessel's identity was redacted in the released documents. The disruption was settled as an accident with no attacker named.

AG-237.summary: Sandworm, a group serving Russia's GRU, executed code through an end-of-life MicroSCADA system at an unnamed Ukrainian critical infrastructure organization on October 10, 2022, and caused an unscheduled power outage. On October 12 it deployed a CaddyWiper variant in the victim's IT environment. Mandiant reported that the attack coincided with the start of a multi-day set of coordinated Russian missile strikes on critical infrastructure in several cities, including the victim's. Mandiant responded in late 2022 and published on November 9, 2023. In April 2024 CERT-UA reported that Sandworm had infected energy, water and heating suppliers in ten regions in March 2024 through at least three compromised supply chains.
AG-237.records:
The victim: an unscheduled outage on a day of mass missile strikes on infrastructure across Ukraine. Its IT environment held the wiper damage of October 12.
Mandiant: the forensic artifacts. It could not fully recover them because the attacker had removed artifacts from the SCADA system.
CERT-UA: intrusion records for 2024 across suppliers in ten regions.
The Record: put the number of targeted facilities at nearly 20.
AG-237.gap: That week the cyber-induced outage was one outage among many caused by strikes. Anti-forensics removed part of the trace. The victim was not named. Mandiant, the incident-response firm, published about thirteen months after the event. It said it could not assess a possible link to the missile strikes and noted only that the timing overlapped with Russian kinetic operations.
AG-237.joining: Mandiant, a private incident-response firm, joined the forensic record and named Sandworm in November 2023, about thirteen months after the event. It declined to assert coordination with the missile strikes. CERT-UA, a state body, joined the 2024 intrusions into one campaign and named Sandworm within weeks. The Record reported that the operation was possibly meant to amplify the impact of missile and drone strikes. The attacker made no claim.
AG-237.harm_found_later: Any harm from the cyber-induced outage is inseparable in routine records from harm caused by missile strikes on the same days and in the same city.

AG-238.summary: From 17 February 2022 armed groups affiliated with JNIM surrounded Djibo. By October 2022 over 89,000 community members and at least 285,000 internally displaced people lived there. An OCHA briefing note of 19 October 2022 reported that the groups had 'sabotaged many facilities', making access to water particularly difficult. The note also reported that they had destroyed telephone installations and bridges to isolate the town and planted improvised explosive devices along strategic roads. It added that food and medicine shortages followed. On 26 September 2022 a resupply convoy was ambushed near Gaskindé, within 25 km of Djibo. Bellingcat used satellite imagery to verify JNIM's own video and counted 95 destroyed vehicles along more than five kilometers of road.
AG-238.records:
OCHA briefing note: population, water, telephone and road sabotage, shortages and IED deaths.
UN agencies and MSF: warnings of food and medicine shortages, according to Bellingcat.
Africanews, cited by Bellingcat: convoy casualties of at least 27 soldiers and 10 civilians.
JNIM: claimed the ambush and posted video.
Bellingcat: Sentinel-2 and Planet imagery.
AG-238.gap: Because the siege was conducted openly, recognition was immediate. The record gap lay in counting destruction and casualties in a town cut off by the attacker. The attacker's own video was one of the main sources of the convoy record.
AG-238.joining: Bellingcat, an open-source group, joined satellite imagery with JNIM footage to count the destroyed convoy. The humanitarian agencies compiled the service losses. JNIM was named as the besieger from the outset.
AG-238.harm_found_later: Deaths from hunger and from the loss of water facilities were not counted in the sources checked. The OCHA note reports food insecurity and civilian deaths from IEDs without totals.

AG-239.summary: On 6 April 2022 Recorded Future's Insikt Group reported that TAG-38, a likely Chinese state-sponsored group, had targeted at least seven State Load Despatch Centres in northern India near the disputed border in Ladakh. Insikt Group also reported that the group had targeted a national emergency response system and the Indian subsidiary of a multinational logistics company. The group used the ShadowPad backdoor and likely controlled it through compromised internet-facing DVR and IP-camera devices. The firm judged that the targeting offered limited economic espionage or traditional intelligence-gathering opportunities. It judged the targeting likely aimed at information gathering on critical infrastructure or at pre-positioning for future activity. One of the centres had also been targeted in the earlier RedEcho activity.
AG-239.records:
The targeted centres: the victims. They run real-time grid control and dispatch for their states.
Recorded Future: external network telemetry. It notified the appropriate Indian government departments before publication.
Power Minister R.K. Singh: dismissed the report, saying, 'We have a very robust security system'.
The Ministry of Electronics and IT: did not return a call for comment.
Zhao Lijian, China's foreign ministry spokesman: said China opposed all cyberattacks and told the firm not to 'throw mud at China.'
AG-239.gap: The victims were separate state-level operators. The command channels ran through third-party cameras outside their networks. Because the government's only public response was the minister's reassurance, the only joined record in public view was a foreign private firm's.
AG-239.joining: Recorded Future, a private intelligence firm, joined intrusions at seven state-level centres and other targets into one activity cluster. It attributed the cluster to a likely Chinese state-sponsored group. The Indian government gave no public account of its own.

AG-240.summary: In September 2022 Equinor reported drones of unknown origin near some of its offshore installations. The newspaper Stavanger Aftenbladet counted sightings at no fewer than six, including Johan Sverdrup, Kristin, Gullfaks C, Snorre A and Gina Krog. It reported that at Heidrun a drone came within about 50 meters, inside the 500-meter safety zone. On 26 September the Petroleum Safety Authority urged operators to be more vigilant. It warned that drones could endanger helicopters, become an ignition source in explosion-hazard areas or be used for deliberate attacks. On 27 September, as the Nord Stream leaks were being reported, Energy Minister Terje Aasland announced heightened preparedness for onshore and offshore installations. The announcement followed close contact between the government, the police, the armed forces and operators.
AG-240.records:
Equinor: recorded the sightings and reported them to the Petroleum Safety Authority and the police.
The Southwest police district: opened an investigation and notified the Police Security Service (PST).
The Petroleum Safety Authority: framed the matter as a safety risk in a letter to operators.
The government and armed forces: handled preparedness.
Stavanger Aftenbladet, a regional newspaper: compiled the sightings across installations.
AG-240.gap: Each sighting was a safety observation at one installation, filed with a safety regulator and a police district. Equinor declined to give details. The first cross-installation count came from a newspaper. The sources show no recorder able to establish where the drones came from.
AG-240.joining: The government joined the reports into a preparedness decision without naming an actor. The sources checked report no public attribution from the police investigation.

AG-241.summary: From about 03:02 UTC on February 24, 2022, high volumes of malicious traffic came from KA-SAT modems in Ukraine. From about 04:15 UTC, larger numbers of modems across much of Europe dropped off the network over about 45 minutes. Viasat's forensics found that attackers had used a misconfigured VPN appliance to reach the management network and had then sent management commands that overwrote modem flash memory. SentinelLabs identified the AcidRain wiper. Tens of thousands of modems failed, including a majority of the active ones in Ukraine, with customers also affected in Poland, Germany, the United Kingdom, France and the Czech Republic. Enercon lost remote monitoring and control of 5,800 wind turbines (11 GW). On May 10, 2022 the Council of the EU, the UK National Cyber Security Centre and the US State Department attributed the attack to Russia.
AG-241.records:
Viasat and Skylogic (the Eutelsat subsidiary operating the consumer partition): the network record. They worked with Mandiant, law enforcement and government agencies.
Enercon: reported a 'massive disruption' of satellite connections whose 'exact cause' was not yet known. It informed the BSI.
BSI: recorded a satellite operator's malfunction that restricted maintenance of some turbines. It expected no effect on grid stability and left the cause to the company's investigation.
Ukraine's SSSCIP: Victor Zhora said the attack was organized by Russian hackers. The attack disabled modems used by Ukrainian military and government agencies.
ENISA: counted at least 27,000 affected devices.
AG-241.gap: A turbine maker lost a supplier's link, the BSI saw a satellite operator's malfunction with no expected effect on grid stability, and Ukrainian users lost communications amid an invasion. Each downstream victim saw only its own outage. German critical-infrastructure rules covered generation plants only above a capacity threshold, which an amendment lowered from 420 MW to 104 MW in January 2022. The gap narrowed quickly because one provider held the network record: Viasat described a targeted denial-of-service attack from modems in Ukraine and, through its forensic work with Mandiant, established the management-network intrusion.
AG-241.joining: Viasat joined the network record and published its account on March 30, 2022 without naming an attacker. SentinelLabs, an independent research team, published its AcidRain analysis on March 31. The EU, UK and US attributed the attack to Russia on May 10, about eleven weeks after it. Enercon's statement noted that the services failed almost simultaneously with the start of the invasion.

AG-242.summary: Russian forces have held military control of the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant since early March 2022. IAEA experts have been stationed there since September 2022. On 7 April 2024 drones struck several buildings at the plant, including a direct hit on the dome of reactor unit 6, the first direct targeting of the plant since November 2022. Russia and Ukraine accused each other. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi declined to assign blame, saying attribution required indisputable proof and that on the front line a drone may be operated by one side and belong to the other. In February 2025 a drone struck the protective structure over the destroyed fourth reactor at Chornobyl. Ukraine named Russia, which Moscow denied. In December 2025 the IAEA reported that the structure had lost its primary safety functions, including confinement, without attributing the strike.
AG-242.records:
IAEA team at Zaporizhzhia: impacts, damage and the status of power lines (on 4 April 2024 the plant lost its only backup power line). The team reported to the IAEA Board of Governors and the UN Security Council.
Russia and Ukraine: requested an emergency Board meeting on the April 2024 strikes. Each named the other.
Russia's ambassador, Mikhail Ulyanov: said the agency was afraid to name Ukraine.
Ukraine's UN ambassador, Sergiy Kyslytsya: called the strike a Russian false-flag operation.
AG-242.gap: The IAEA, the only recorder with a continuous neutral presence and technical authority, treats attribution as beyond what it can prove. The records of the two parties each name the other. Grossi cited the varied trajectories of drones, their ability to hover and circle, and the plant's front-line position as obstacles to the proof the agency requires.
AG-242.joining: Through public updates and reports, the IAEA joins site observations and declines to name the attacker. Grossi told the Board on 11 April 2024 that the strikes were an ominous indication of a readiness to continue. On 15 April he told the Security Council that they set a very dangerous precedent of successful targeting of reactor containment. The United States told the Board that it condemned such actions regardless of who the culprit was. In the sources checked, no international body named the attacker.

AG-243.summary: At 6:59 p.m. on 17 October 2023 a munition exploded on the grounds of al-Ahli Arab Hospital in Gaza City. The Gaza Ministry of Health attributed the explosion to Israel and reported 471 killed and 342 injured. The Israeli military attributed it to a misfired Palestinian Islamic Jihad rocket. In late October, US intelligence officials told The Washington Post that they had 'high confidence' that Israel was not responsible and only 'low confidence' that Palestinian fighters were. They kept an estimate of 100 to 300 deaths. Human Rights Watch concluded on 26 November 2023 that an apparent rocket-propelled munition, of a type commonly used by Palestinian armed groups, hit the grounds, and called for further investigation to determine who launched it.
AG-243.records:
Gaza Ministry of Health: casualty count and attribution to Israel. HRW could not corroborate the count and noted an unusually high ratio of killed to injured.
Al-Shifa Hospital's director: a toll 'closer to 250.'
Gaza Explosive Ordnance Department and Ministry of Interior: munition remnants taken from the site and not shown publicly more than a month later.
Israeli military: its account of a misfired rocket.
US intelligence: videos geolocated from four locations, a damage assessment, and intercepted communications provided by Israel, judged reliable and authentic but insufficient for firm attribution.
Al Jazeera livestream: explosions near the hospital in the minutes before and after the blast.
HRW: photogrammetry of the crater, five witnesses and analysis of trajectories in videos.
AG-243.gap: Parties to the conflict joined the records publicly before the physical records (remnants, crater, casualty lists) had been examined. The remnants that could settle the munition's origin stayed with the Gaza authorities, and the intercepts with Israeli and US intelligence. Each joining party held a different part of the record and assigned it a different confidence.
AG-243.joining: Four sets of joiners reached partly divergent conclusions: the Gaza Ministry of Health (Israel responsible), the Israeli military (misfired Islamic Jihad rocket), the US intelligence community (high confidence that Israel was not responsible, low confidence on the launching group) and HRW (apparent rocket-propelled munition, launching party undetermined). HRW stated that an independent investigation could be conducted by the UN Commission of Inquiry and asked Gaza authorities and Israel to release what they held. In the sources checked, no body with access to all records had published a finding.

AG-244.summary: From October 2023 Israeli military operations struck and raided hospitals across Gaza, including two operations at al-Shifa Medical Complex (November 2023 and March 2024). WHO counted attacks on health care, and the Palestinian Ministry of Health counted casualties among medical staff. Israel alleged that hospitals were misused by Palestinian armed groups. The UN Human Rights Office documented at least 136 strikes on at least 27 hospitals and 12 other medical facilities between 12 October 2023 and 30 June 2024.
AG-244.records:
WHO: 187 attacks on health care in Gaza by 24 November 2023, damaging 24 hospitals (data shared with HRW). WHO's surveillance system 'does not collect nor verify information on perpetrators.'
Palestinian Ministry of Health: more than 500 medical professionals killed by the end of June 2024 and 77,704 people injured by the end of April 2024.
Israeli military: allegations of military use of hospitals.
OHCHR: verified incidents, including shootings inside hospitals, and reports of mass graves at al-Shifa after the March 2024 raid.
AG-244.gap: The attacks were recognized immediately and the attacking force was generally known, so the dispute concerned classification. The attacking party held the record that would decide whether a hospital had lost its protection (military use). OHCHR found its allegations 'vague and broad' and in some cases 'contradicted by publicly available information.' WHO's count, the largest in coverage, omits perpetrators.
AG-244.joining: In its thematic report of 31 December 2024, the UN Human Rights Office joined incident records, casualty counts and Israel's public allegations. It stated that 'insufficient information has so far been made available to substantiate' the military-use allegations and described the strikes as a pattern of Israeli attacks. For the apparent targeting of people inside hospitals, it found attribution difficult to determine in most cases.
AG-244.harm_found_later: OHCHR received reports that injured people died while waiting for admission or treatment and that newborns died because their mothers could not reach care. These deaths are recorded, if at all, as deaths from their underlying conditions. The attacks do not appear as their cause.

AG-245.summary: On 8 January 2023 supporters of Jair Bolsonaro invaded the buildings of Brazil's three branches of government in Brasília. In the days after, transmission towers were knocked down or damaged in several states, among them a Furnas tower in Medianeira (Paraná) and an Evoltz tower on the Madeira bipole line near Porto Velho (Rondônia). On 16 January the regulator Aneel counted seven episodes and stated that none had interrupted transmission. By 24 January it counted 11 episodes, with 4 towers knocked down and 16 damaged. The Federal Police opened three inquiries on 11 January. On 17 October 2023 the joint congressional inquiry (CPMI) on the 8 January events issued its final report. The report described the tower attacks, together with blockades of refineries and fuel distribution bases, as a movement 'articulado e coordenado em nível nacional' aimed at producing 'o caos social'.
AG-245.records:
Furnas and Eletronorte (Eletrobras subsidiaries), Evoltz, Taesa and ISA CTEEP: each transmission company held the record of its own towers.
Aneel: recorded the episodes as 'atos de vandalismo' and distinguished towers knocked down from towers damaged. It stated that 'é de responsabilidade das transmissoras a avaliação técnica sobre a origem e causa dos eventos'. It named the Federal Police, the Federal Highway Police and Abin as partners in its security work.
ONS, the system operator: kept a list of tower attacks running back to 2020.
Federal Police: opened one inquiry for each of three towers. It sent forensic teams to Paraná (sabotage carries up to five years in prison).
Federal Highway Police: found soil dug out from under the base of a Chesf tower in Pernambuco in January 2023.
Ministry of Mines and Energy: asked the governments of São Paulo, Rondônia and Paraná to take preventive measures and investigate.
AG-245.gap: Every episode fell on a different company's line in a different state. None crossed the threshold that matters most to the electricity regulator, an interruption of supply. The line's owner was the institution responsible for assessing cause, the regulator's category was vandalism, and the police opened inquiries tower by tower. Spread over two weeks and at least four states, the episodes did not appear as a campaign in any one record.
AG-245.joining: Operational joining came quickly: on 10 January the Ministry of Mines and Energy, Aneel and ONS formed a crisis cabinet to monitor tower falls. By 16 January the energy minister had met the justice minister and the Federal Police director general to reinforce patrols. Attributive joining came nine months later from the CPMI, a congressional commission whose conclusions pass to prosecutors as recommendations. The CPMI combined the ONS list with an intelligence report that found signs of sabotage and with the wider 8 January investigation. It recommended indicting 61 people for the coup-related acts. No charge or court finding specific to the towers was found. The timing next to a public political event narrowed the gap.

AG-246.summary: At Bahanaga Bazar station in Balasore district, Odisha, the Coromandel Express entered a loop line on 2 June 2023 and struck a parked freight train. The derailed coaches hit a passing express on the adjacent line. At least 275 people were killed. Railway Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw attributed the crash to "a change in electronic interlocking," and Railway Board member Jaya Varma Sinha listed someone digging near the system's cables among possible causes. On 4 June Vaishnaw announced that the Railway Board had recommended a Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) probe. The CBI arrested three railway employees on 7 July 2023 and in early September 2023 charged them with culpable homicide and destruction of evidence.
AG-246.records:
Commissioner of Railway Safety: the statutory accident inquiry. The Commissioner visited the site the day after the crash.
Railway Board officials: public accounts of the interlocking system and possible causes.
CBI: the criminal file. The accused were a senior section engineer (signals), a section engineer and a technician posted in Balasore district.
AG-246.gap: After railway officials had listed outside interference among possible causes, a criminal agency was brought in beside the statutory safety inquiry. The event therefore ran under two categories at once: a safety failure and a possible crime.
AG-246.joining: The CBI's charges fell on the railway's own signaling staff. No outside saboteur was named.

AG-247.summary: In the small hours of 8 October 2023 a pressure drop was detected in the Balticconnector gas pipeline between Finland and Estonia. The offshore valves were closed. Several telecom cables were damaged in the same incident. Finnish investigators recovered the 6-ton anchor of the Hong Kong-registered container ship Newnew Polar Bear from the seabed near the pipeline and reported a drag trail. The pipeline reopened for commercial operations in April 2024 after repairs costing about US$38 million.
AG-247.records:
Gasgrid Finland and Estonia's Elering: investigated the pressure drop.
Finland's Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment: monitored supply.
Finland's National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and Estonian investigators: a joint criminal investigation. They held the recovered anchor.
Chinese authorities: the ship and its crew.
AG-247.gap: The ship left the Baltic with its flag and owner under Chinese jurisdiction. China did not invite Estonian criminal investigators to take part in its inquiry. The NBI said the cause could be technical failure, negligence or a deliberate act and that final conclusions could be made only after all necessary investigative measures had been completed.
AG-247.joining: Finland's NBI joined the pipeline and cable damage with the anchor and said there were 'sufficient reasons to suspect' that the Newnew Polar Bear was linked to the damage. About ten months after the incident, China notified Finland and Estonia that the damage was an accident caused by a storm. Markku Mylly, a former director of the European Maritime Safety Agency, said there had been no storms in the Gulf of Finland at the time. Estonia's prosecutor's office said China's statement could not be used as evidence in a criminal investigation. In May 2025 the ship's captain appeared in a Hong Kong court on a criminal charge over the damage and was held pending trial. The charges reportedly surprised Finnish and Estonian authorities.

AG-248.summary: At 8:30 a.m. on 15 August 2023 an incorrect actuation of the protection system shut the 500 kV Quixadá–Fortaleza II line in Ceará, owned by Eletrobras Chesf. About 600 milliseconds later, loss-of-synchronism protections split the national grid into three areas, cutting about 19,000 MW, some 27% of load. Energy minister Alexandre Silveira said the ONS could not yet determine whether the cause was technical, human failure 'ou até dolo'. He asked the Ministry of Justice for investigations by the Federal Police and Abin. On 22 August the Federal Police opened a confidential inquiry into 'sabotagem e atentado contra a segurança de serviço de utilidade pública'. The ONS disturbance analysis report (RAP), released on 26 September, attributed the event mainly to voltage-control equipment at wind and solar parks near the line, whose performance was 'muito aquém dos modelos matemáticos fornecidos pelos agentes'.
AG-248.records:
Chesf: owner of the line.
ONS: the preliminary finding of incorrect actuation of the line's protection system, and the disturbance analysis report.
The generating agents: mathematical models of their plants, submitted to ONS.
Ministry of Mines and Energy: its own part of the record.
Federal Police: the criminal inquiry.
Abin: the requested investigation.
AG-248.gap: Here the joining apparatus worked. The gap lay between the models submitted by the agents and their behavior in the field. The ONS said this kept it from identifying the risks of the pre-disturbance operating scenario. The minister's suspicion of intent came before the technical analysis.
AG-248.joining: Under its statutory role, the ONS joined operator and generator data and named a technical cause within six weeks. The criminal inquiry ran on a separate track, opened at ministerial request. No attacker was named.

AG-249.summary: Beginning May 11, 2023, attackers exploited a critical Zyxel firewall vulnerability (CVE-2023-28771, announced April 25) at companies operating parts of Danish energy infrastructure. Of the 16 companies targeted on May 11, 11 were compromised. A second wave began May 22. In all, 22 companies were compromised. Several went into island mode, and one stayed in island operation for six days.
AG-249.records:
Individual companies: firewall and network records. Each company decided whether to island.
SektorCERT: a non-profit owned and funded by Danish critical-infrastructure companies. It held data from about 270 sensors across Danish critical infrastructure.
The police's National Center for Cybercrime (NC3) and the Center for Cyber Security: contacted by SektorCERT on 25 May.
AG-249.gap: The targets, often small utilities, each saw one compromised firewall. Only a sensor network spanning many companies showed that the attacks were simultaneous and selected ("The attackers knew in advance who they wanted to hit"). The body that saw the pattern is owned by its members and placed consideration of state actors outside its area of responsibility.
AG-249.joining: SektorCERT joined the records through its cross-company sensors and published a TLP:CLEAR report in November 2023. It recorded traffic from the first wave to an IP address that had been linked to Sandworm. SektorCERT wrote that "Whether Sandworm was involved in the attack cannot be said with certainty," and said it was inclined to believe that two different groups carried out the two waves. In January 2024 the security firm Forescout reported that the address had belonged to a botnet since dismantled and was later used by a Mirai variant. Forescout also reported that the second wave was part of opportunistic mass exploitation and that Sandworm likely had no role. No attacker was named.

AG-250.summary: When two dams above Derna gave way during Storm Daniel on the night of 10–11 September 2023, the flood destroyed much of the city. Death tolls diverge widely: the UN put the toll at nearly 4,000 and eastern officials at about 3,800 on the basis of bodies buried. Earlier figures ran to 6,000 across eastern Libya. Derna's deputy mayor said the dams 'had not been maintained since 2002.' No attack was suspected. The prosecutors treated the failure as mismanagement and negligence.
AG-250.records:
Libyan audit bureau: a 2021 report that criticized delays in resuming repair work on the two dams.
Abdel Wanis Ashour, engineer and academic: a study of November 2022 warning that a 'catastrophe' threatened Derna without maintenance.
A Turkish company: began repairs in 2010 and stopped when the 2011 revolution broke out.
Prosecutor General: said the dams had been cracked since 1998.
Libyan national ministries: split between 'two rival governments, one in the west and one in the east.'
AG-250.gap: Warnings sat with an audit bureau, an academic study, a municipality, a foreign contractor and ministries divided between two governments. The repair contract lapsed with the 2011 revolution. No holder of the warnings acted on them before the storm.
AG-250.joining: On 25 September 2023 Prosecutor General Al-Seddik al-Sur ordered the arrest of eight officials, seven of them from offices responsible for water resources and dam management, on suspicion of 'bad management' and negligence. Derna's mayor was among the detainees, on separate suspicions concerning city development funds. In late July 2024, 12 civil servants received prison sentences of nine to 27 years. Al-Monitor reported in September 2024 that high-ranking officials, among them the mayor, were not investigated, which conflicts with the 2023 arrest report.

AG-251.summary: The Russian-held Kakhovka dam and hydropower plant collapsed early on June 6, 2023, flooding the lower Dnipro and draining the reservoir. NORSAR registered signals at 02:35 and 02:54 local time on regional stations in Romania and Ukraine. It found them consistent with an explosion and unlike a dam collapse. The New York Times, citing a US official, reported that satellites with infrared sensors detected a heat signature of an explosion just before the collapse. US intelligence agencies made no formal attribution. On June 15, 2023 the Mobile Justice Team of the Atrocity Crimes Advisory Group, with Global Rights Compliance lawyers, concluded that it was highly likely Russian forces deliberately destroyed the dam with pre-emplaced explosives.
AG-251.records:
NORSAR: seismic records.
US intelligence: infrared satellite records.
Ukraine's Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food: recorded that the reservoir had supplied irrigation water to 584,000 hectares, including 94% of irrigation systems in Kherson oblast, 74% in Zaporizhzhia and 30% in Dnipropetrovsk.
Mobile Justice Team: its own assessment.
AG-251.gap: A single, catastrophic target made recognition immediate. The dispute concerned cause and author: each technical record fit an explosion without naming who set it. The structure lay in Russian-held territory.
AG-251.joining: Nine days after the collapse, the Mobile Justice Team named Russian forces as highly likely responsible. The team was funded by the US State Department, the EU and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. NORSAR did not attribute responsibility and said it could not determine the type of device. On June 6 White House spokesman John Kirby said the US could not say conclusively what happened. US intelligence analysts reportedly leaned toward Russia without a formal attribution. The Kremlin said Ukraine had sabotaged the dam.
AG-251.harm_found_later: The agricultural loss is cumulative: the ministry said irrigated farming in southern Ukraine would not be possible in the near future without restoring the water source. That harm appears only in later harvest records.

AG-252.summary: After the Gaza war began in October 2023, aircraft over the eastern Mediterranean and the Levant reported spoofed satellite positions. GPS placed planes and ships at Beirut's airport, ground proximity warnings were disrupted, and pilots began turning off satellite-based systems. Israel acknowledged blocking GPS for defensive purposes but did not comment publicly on more advanced interference. The OPSGROUP working group reported in September 2024 that about 1,500 flights a day were being spoofed, up from about 300 in the first half of that year.
AG-252.records:
Flight crews: reports to their operators and to national authorities.
OPSGROUP: almost 2,000 crew survey responses.
University of Texas radionavigation laboratory: data from receivers in low Earth orbit.
The spectrum administrations of Jordan and Egypt: complaints filed with the ITU.
Israel: acknowledged only defensive GPS blocking.
AG-252.gap: Spoofing gives no warning on the flight deck, so detection depended on crews noticing anomalies and on each operator's reporting threshold. Affected states could record interference arriving from beyond their borders, Jordan from sources west of its borders, but they had no authority over its source. The emitting state's military did not publish its activity.
AG-252.joining: OPSGROUP, a private membership group of pilots and dispatchers, led a working group of 950 participants and published its final report on 6 September 2024. IFALPA and other industry bodies contributed. Eurocontrol, NASA (Langley) and the University of Texas were among those providing support. University of Texas researchers traced the false signals to an air base run by the Israeli military. In November 2024 the ITU Radio Regulations Board invited Israel to cease interference that Jordan reported from sources west of its borders. In March 2025 the Board noted that Israel had found no source on its territory matching the complaints, and urged it to cease. After meetings with Jordan and Egypt in July 2025, Israel committed to limit such transmissions to imminent and verifiable threats to human life or critical national infrastructure. It also committed to keep them to no more than 15 minutes. In November 2025 the Board recorded that no further complaints had been reported and that the cases had been resolved.

AG-253.summary: From the seizure of the Galaxy Leader on 19 November 2023 the Houthis attacked merchant ships around the Red Sea. They had declared Israeli commercial ships fair game until Israel ended its campaign in Gaza. The attacks stopped after the Gaza ceasefire that began on 10 October 2025, by which time AP counted at least nine mariners killed and four ships sunk. The most recent attack had hit the Dutch-flagged Minervagracht on 29 September 2025. The IMF said the attacks reduced Egypt's foreign-exchange inflows from the Suez Canal by US$6 billion in 2024.
AG-253.records:
The Houthis: announced attacks and named targets.
The ship owners: issued their own statements. Vroon did so for the Shorthorn Express.
MarineTraffic and other AIS sources: ship movements.
IMF: an estimate of the loss to Egypt's Suez Canal inflows.
AG-253.gap: For confirmed attacks, the attacker's publicity settled attribution. The recording problem moved to the other side: claims outran records. Raydan and Nadimi found that ships the Houthis claimed to have attacked in the Mediterranean in May 2024 appeared in AIS data to be operating normally. They found that the owner of the Shorthorn Express, claimed as attacked en route to Haifa in June 2024, said 'no signs of an attack were noticed'. They also found that the prolonged suspension of traffic at Haifa that serious attacks would have caused did not occur.
AG-253.joining: Analysts at the Washington Institute joined Houthi claims with AIS data and owners' statements. They judged the Mediterranean and Haifa claims to be 'part of the Houthi propaganda campaign for now'. The Houthis gave no formal acknowledgment that the campaign had ended. An undated letter from their military chief of staff, Maj. Gen. Yusuf Hassan al-Madani, to Hamas's Qassam Brigades warned that operations would resume if attacks on Gaza resumed.

AG-254.summary: The Sudan Research Group at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, led by Maysoon Dahab, estimated more than 61,000 deaths from all causes in Khartoum State in the first 14 months of the war (April 2023 to June 2024). About 26,000 of them were violent. The deaths recorded on the three lists it combined made up about 5% of the estimated total and 7% of the intentional-injury deaths. The violent-death estimate for one state exceeded the 20,178 killings that ACLED had recorded for the whole country. The health ministry's war-related tally stood at 5,565.
AG-254.records:
ACLED: conflict events and reported fatalities (20,178 killings nationwide for the period).
Sudan's health ministry: a war-related death tally (5,565). The ministry said it had observed far fewer deaths than the study estimated.
UN: a figure for the whole country. The study's Khartoum violent-death estimate also exceeded it.
