Three informal lists outside these institutions: decedent records from a public survey shared on social media, a private survey distributed through community 'study ambassadors', and social-media obituary pages posted by first responders. They held 6,715 records in all.
Hundreds of graves in greater Khartoum: they appeared beside homes, outside cemetery records.
AG-254.gap: Many deaths went unregistered in Sudan even before the war. Then the fighting cut people off from hospitals, morgues and cemeteries, while repeated internet and telecommunications disruptions left millions unable to contact the outside world. Each recorder counted under its own rules: ACLED counted killings reported in the sources it monitors. The study found deaths from disease and starvation to be the leading cause across most of the country. These deaths fall outside counts of violent events.
AG-254.joining: An academic group with no official mandate joined three non-official lists by capture-recapture analysis and released the result as a preprint before peer review. Its funding came from the US government (CDC, USAID) and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office. The study did not attribute deaths to a belligerent. The army's spokesman referred questions to the health ministry and blamed the RSF. The RSF did not dispute the estimates and blamed air strikes, artillery and drone strikes, which it said only the army could carry out.
AG-254.harm_found_later: According to the study, more than 90% of all-cause and violent deaths in Khartoum State went unrecorded. Most of the war's mortality therefore became visible only through this reconstruction. None of the routine records links the deaths from disease and starvation to the conduct of hostilities.

AG-255.summary: On December 12, 2023 Kyivstar, Ukraine's largest mobile operator with nearly 24 million subscribers, lost mobile and internet service for millions of users. The outage disrupted air raid sirens in some areas and some banks, ATMs and point-of-sale terminals. Kyivstar restored its basic services on December 20. The SBU's cyber chief, Illia Vitiuk, said the attackers had been in the network since at least May 2023 and probably had full access from November. He said they wiped almost everything, including thousands of virtual servers and computers. A group calling itself Solntsepek claimed the attack. Ukraine's security services identified it as a front for Sandworm, a unit of Russia's GRU.
AG-255.records:
Kyivstar: recorded the outage and said its IT infrastructure was partly destroyed.
SBU: opened criminal proceedings. It traced the breach to a compromised employee account.
Solntsepek's own channels: the group's claim.
AG-255.gap: Little gap opened for the outage itself. One large target and a public claim made the attack obvious. The months-long intrusion before it stayed invisible to the operator.
AG-255.joining: Within about three weeks the SBU joined the record and named Sandworm. In April 2024 Vitiuk said the files would go to the ICC once suspicion notices were issued and argued that cyberattacks on civilian infrastructure should be treated as war crimes. Reuters reported in June 2024 that the SBU had given details of the incident to ICC investigators, who were examining such cyberattacks as possible war crimes.

AG-256.summary: Nigerian operators reported thousands of fibre cuts a year: MTN Nigeria counted more than 6,000 cuts to its optic cable in 2023. Airtel Nigeria's chief executive, Carl Cruz, cited an average of 1,000 a month in early 2024. President Tinubu signed the Designation and Protection of Critical National Information Infrastructure Order in June 2024. The Communications Minister, Bosun Tijani, announced its gazette in August 2024. The Order designates towers, fibre and submarine cables, data centers and related assets as critical national information infrastructure. It makes wilful damage an offence punishable by up to ten years in prison. It assigns enforcement to the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) and the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC). The Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC) later counted 19,384 fibre cuts, 3,241 equipment thefts and more than 19,000 denials of site access between January and August 2025. In June 2025 the operators' association chairman said that the industry had been 'too slow' to put the Order into operation.
AG-256.records:
Each operator (MTN, Airtel, Globacom): its own cuts and repair costs.
NCC: publishes major outages on its Uptime monitoring site by cause (fibre cut, power failure, equipment vandalism) and compiles national counts. Causes are mixed in the same counts: road contractors, equipment theft, vandalism and denial of site access. In one road-contractor case, a China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation crew cut a Globacom line running through Kebbi, Niger and Sokoto states on 8 May 2025.
AG-256.gap: Many recorders apply their own categories. On its own, a cut is a repair job below any security threshold. The NCC's cause categories record the kind of damage, so a 'fibre cut' by a road contractor and a deliberate cut enter the same count.
AG-256.joining: The NCC aggregates counts nationally. The Order assigns protection to the national security apparatus (ONSA, NSCDC), creating a channel from operator records to authorities that can treat them as security incidents. ONSA has worked with the NCC against theft cartels. In the sources checked, no hostile actor has been named. The counts are treated as crime and negligence.

AG-257.summary: Callers posing as bank staff, police or FSB officers defrauded mostly elderly Russians. The callers then pressed them to set fire to enlistment offices, bank branches, cars and, during the March 2024 presidential election, at least 47 polling stations in 30 regions. Mediazona counted 187 scam-organized arsons since the invasion, most in 2024, within 280 attacks by anti-war or scam-induced arsonists. Of 132 cases with known charges, 79 were brought for property damage, 21 for hooliganism and 28 under terrorism articles. The courts rejected coercion defenses. At least four scam victims died. Russia's Prosecutor General claimed the scams were funded by organizations linked to Kyiv. A Sberbank deputy chairman reportedly said about 40% of stolen money reached Ukraine's armed forces. Mediazona reported both claims without confirmation.
AG-257.records:
Local police, the Investigative Committee and the FSB: each opened cases under different articles (Art. 167 property damage, Art. 213 hooliganism, Art. 205 terrorism).
The courts: issued verdicts.
The banks: the fraud record.
Prosecutor General: issued attribution claims.
Mediazona: found that charging depended less on the act than on the investigating body. Ten of the 28 terrorism cases came from the FSB directorate for St. Petersburg and Leningrad Oblast.
AG-257.gap: Each incident entered the record as a local fraud plus a local arson, under categories that varied by agency. No national count was published. The people prosecuted were the coerced victims, so the organizers never appeared in the case files.
AG-257.joining: In January 2025 Mediazona, an independent outlet, analyzed 45 first-instance arson verdicts, 21 published election-case verdicts and media reports. It could not establish who runs the calls. The Russian state named Kyiv without public support. Ukrainian authorities distanced themselves.
AG-257.harm_found_later: Harm falls on defrauded and coerced victims who lost savings and were then convicted as offenders. The routine court records classify them as perpetrators.

AG-258.summary: Over the night of 25-26 August 2023 unauthorized 'Radio-Stop' emergency signals halted more than 20 trains near Szczecin. On 27 August further signals stopped trains in Podlaskie. On 29 August, 13 signals halted 25 trains in four provinces. Some transmissions carried the Russian anthem and part of a Putin speech. On 27 August police detained two Polish men aged 24 and 29 in Białystok and charged them with causing imminent danger to land traffic. One of them was a police officer. Polish media cited official counts of more than 700 false Radio-Stop activations in 2019, about 500 in each of 2020 and 2021, and about 480 in 2022.
AG-258.records:
PKP PLK (the rail infrastructure manager): recorded the stops and notified the ABW, the police, railway security and carriers. It stated that passengers were not endangered.
Police and prosecutors: the criminal file. Podlaskie Police suspended the arrested officer.
Stanisław Żaryn, the government's security-services spokesman: said officials were considering sabotage and that Russia and Belarus had tried to destabilize the Polish state.
A deputy interior minister: spoke of pre-election destabilization.
A routine statistic: it counted hundreds of false Radio-Stop activations a year and existed before the August cluster.
AG-258.gap: Because the unencrypted signal was already producing hundreds of false stops a year, a hostile campaign had to rise above a high background rate before it registered as more than nuisance. The operator itself notified the ABW. The anthem broadcasts gave the incidents a political meaning that the stop signals alone did not carry.
AG-258.joining: Police detained two suspects within hours of the 27 August Podlaskie signals. The sources checked do not tie the Szczecin or 29 August stoppages to them. Government officials raised Russian involvement and pre-election destabilization, but no foreign link was established in public. The public record treats the Białystok case as domestic criminal conduct and leaves the question of foreign direction open.

AG-259.summary: In March 2023 the Internal Security Agency (ABW) detained the first members of a network of foreign nationals, most of them Ukrainian, who were paid by Russian services to monitor rail routes carrying weapons and aid to Ukraine. The group had installed cameras recording rail traffic, mainly in Podkarpackie and near the Rzeszów-Jasionka airport. It also watched the Rzeszów train station, the naval port of Gdynia and border crossings with Ukraine. Its leader drew up plans to derail a train carrying military equipment to Ukraine. On 19 December 2023 the district court in Lublin sentenced 14 members to between one and six years. In December 2025 prosecutors charged a Russian national outside Poland, Mikhail Mirgorodsky, with leading an organized criminal group of a terrorist nature. The ABW said the group was formed with the direct support and at the request of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). Mirgorodsky was also charged with inciting an attempted train derailment.
AG-259.records:
ABW: the counterintelligence file. It found the cameras.
The prosecutors and the Lublin court: the criminal case.
The group: its leader coordinated it over Telegram from outside Poland. Its members were paid per task in cryptocurrency, from 300 to 400 dollars for mounting a camera to up to 10,000 dollars for the planned derailment.
AG-259.gap: The operation was built for concealment: its cameras on public land produced no incident in any rail operator's record. Its recruits were paid helpers with no visible link to a state. Detection depended on counterintelligence work outside the view of every civilian recorder.
AG-259.joining: ABW, together with prosecutors, joined the cameras, payments and communications into an espionage and organized-crime case. In March 2023 the interior minister, Mariusz Kamiński, said that the group was paid on an ongoing basis by the Russian services. The court convicted 14 people in December 2023. The December 2025 charges named the FSB as the sponsor of the network.

AG-260.summary: On 25 April 2023, ten days into the war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a WHO representative, Nima Saeed Abid, stated that armed fighters had occupied the National Public Health Laboratory in Khartoum. He said they had 'kicked out all the technicians,' leaving polio, measles and cholera isolates without power or staff, a 'huge biological risk'. He would not say which group held it. On 29 October 2025, after the RSF took El Fasher, WHO reported that more than 460 patients and companions had reportedly been killed at the Saudi Maternity Hospital. NPR reported that six health workers were abducted on 28 October.
AG-260.records:
WHO: verified attacks on health care, 14 of them by 25 April 2023. Before the El Fasher killings its figures stood at 1,204 deaths among health workers and patients, with the number of verified attacks reported as 185 by NPR and 285 by UN News.
Sudan Doctors Network, whose spokesperson is a doctor based in Manchester: reports on the El Fasher killings and abductions.
Videos: believed to have been filmed by RSF fighters.
Laboratory staff: knowledge of the samples held.
AG-260.gap: WHO verifies attacks and states that it does not collect or verify information on perpetrators. Its most authoritative statements, including the warning about the laboratory, therefore left the responsible party unnamed. Loss of access delayed verification of what happened inside the laboratory.
AG-260.joining: Attribution of the El Fasher atrocities to the RSF came from the UN Human Rights Office, which reported summary executions by the RSF in the city, and from videos believed to have been filmed by RSF fighters. RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo pledged to investigate. WHO joined field reports into verified counts and named no party. In the sources checked, no public body determined who held the laboratory or what happened to its isolates.
AG-260.harm_found_later: The biosafety consequences of the laboratory's occupation, and deaths from the collapse of laboratory and hospital services, have no record linking them to the seizure.

AG-261.summary: From at least 22 November 2023, actors using the CyberAv3ngers persona logged into internet-exposed Unitronics Vision Series controllers that still used default passwords. They replaced the screens with the message "You have been hacked, down with Israel. Every equipment 'made in Israel' is CyberAv3ngers legal target." On 25 November the Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa, Pennsylvania (more than 6,600 customers), found a controller disabled at a booster station serving Raccoon and Potter Townships. The station raised an alarm and operators switched to manual control. In December 2023 a private group water scheme in the Erris area of County Mayo, Ireland, lost supply to about 160 households for two days after the same device type was compromised.
AG-261.records:
Aliquippa authority: a station alarm and a switch to manual operation. The incident was investigated by federal authorities.
CISA: an alert on the device on 28 November.
FBI, CISA, NSA, EPA and the Israel National Cyber Directorate: joint advisory AA23-335A (1 December, updated 14 December). It stated that "The victims span multiple U.S. states" without listing them, and noted that the same controllers are used in energy, food and beverage manufacturing, and health care.
Ireland: the Department of the Environment, Climate and Communications, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and An Garda Síochána. The department said there was "no suggestion that services in Ireland were specifically targeted".
US Treasury: sanctions of 2 February 2024 on the head of the IRGC Cyber-Electronic Command and five other officials.
AG-261.gap: Unitronics controllers sit in many small and private systems (a municipal authority, a 160-household group scheme) that report through different national channels. No list of victims was published. The gap stayed narrow because the attackers wrote their claim onto every screen they reached, so each local outage arrived already labeled as part of one campaign.
AG-261.joining: The defacement message joined the incidents at the local level. Within a week of Aliquippa, US agencies joined the American cases into a multi-state advisory and attributed them to IRGC-affiliated actors. Ireland's NCSC "identified all of the equipment in Ireland vulnerable to this attack, and notified the owners". Treasury named IRGC-CEC officials in February 2024 and stated that the operation "did not disrupt any critical services." Attacker publicity narrowed the gap.

AG-262.summary: On the night of 3 January 2026 an attack damaged five high-voltage cables on a bridge near a gas power station in Berlin-Lichterfelde, cutting power to about 45,000 households and some 2,000 businesses. The outage lasted about 100 hours, the longest in Berlin since the Second World War. A group calling itself the Vulkangruppe (Volcano Group) claimed the attack in a note that German antiterrorism authorities considered credible. The authorities describe the group as left-extremist and terrorist. The group had also been linked to a March 2024 fire at a high-voltage pylon that halted production at the Tesla plant in Grünheide, which federal prosecutors are investigating as suspected terrorism. In September 2025 a separate arson on two pylons in Berlin-Johannisthal had cut power to about 50,000 households and businesses for about 60 hours.
AG-262.records:
The grid operator: the outage and the restoration, which reached 7,000 households and 150 businesses by the next morning.
The transport system: traffic lights failed and outer sections of the S-Bahn ran replacement buses.
The fire brigade, churches and the German Red Cross: the emergency centers they ran.
The antiterrorism authorities: the criminal case and their assessment of the claim note.
The earlier outage of September 2025: emergency numbers, public transport and nursing homes had also been affected.
The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution: names left-wing extremists as the relevant perpetrators of attacks on the power supply.
AG-262.gap: The target was a single, evident point of failure, the outage was immediate and large, and the attackers claimed the act, so the gap scarcely opened. The remaining question was whether the claim was what it appeared to be.
AG-262.joining: Antiterrorism authorities joined the outage to the claim within a day and treated the group as left-extremist. The sources checked name no state.

AG-263.summary: In the early hours of 26 July 2024, the day of the Paris Olympics opening ceremony, arsonists cut and set fire to conduits carrying fiber-optic cables that relay safety information. The damage affected three of France's four main high-speed lines, in the west, north and east; an attempt on the fourth axis was foiled. About 800,000 passengers were expected to be affected over the weekend before normal service resumed on 29 July. That day police also reported that fiber-optic networks of several telecom operators had been sabotaged in six areas of France. The Paris prosecutor opened a separate investigation, run jointly by counterterrorism investigators and the national gendarmerie.
AG-263.records:
SNCF: the damage and the disruption.
The night maintenance workers in central France: a sighting of intruders, who fled when the workers called police.
The Paris prosecutor, Laure Beccuau: an investigation for undermining the fundamental interests of the nation, organized-gang damage and attacks on an automated data processing system.
The police: the detention on 28 July of an ultra-left activist at an SNCF site in Oissel. He had keys to SNCF technical premises.
The telecom operators: the fiber cuts.
AG-263.gap: Because the rail attacks were simultaneous and aimed at a symbolic date, recognition was immediate. Attribution stayed open: the interior minister called the attacks intentional and precise, pointed to methods traditional on the ultra-left and asked whether the perpetrators had been manipulated. The telecom cuts three days later went to a separate investigation, with no public statement linking them to the rail attacks in the sources checked. No claim of responsibility was reported in the first days.
AG-263.joining: SNCF, the government and prosecutors joined the rail records at once and recognized an attack. Attribution was left open, with no state named in the sources checked.

AG-264.summary: On or about 12 June 2024 attackers killed six soldiers near the village of Salkam in Dosso region. AFP reported this as the first attack of its kind on the nearly 2,000-km pipeline that carries crude from the Agadem fields to Benin's coast. The army called the attackers 'armed bandits'. About a week later the Patriotic Liberation Front (FPL), which demands the release of the deposed president Mohamed Bazoum, said it was behind an attack on the pipeline. It threatened oil installations and called on the Chinese companies running the pipeline to end their support for the junta. State television showed damage in Zinder region and an oil spill. The public prosecutor, Ousmane Baydo, said the authorities knew which group was the author of the act and had claimed it.
AG-264.records:
The army: an announcement of the Salkam attack that gave no date, described the attackers as 'armed bandits' and reported no claim.
The FPL: its own claim.
State media: the Zinder damage, with a statement that the 'malicious individuals' responsible would be prosecuted.
The public prosecutor: the naming of the claimant group as the author.
The operator, the Chinese company Wapco: no statement in the sources checked.
The background: the episode occurred during a border and export dispute with Benin.
AG-264.gap: By calling the Salkam attackers 'bandits', the army placed the attack with ordinary banditry. The rebel claim concerned the separate sabotage in Zinder, which the authorities confirmed within days.
AG-264.joining: The attacker's public claim joined the Zinder sabotage to a political campaign. The junta confirmed the damage, and the prosecutor named the claimant group as the author. A single, high-value target and attacker publicity narrowed the gap. No source checked links the FPL claim to the Salkam attack.

AG-265.summary: An Azerbaijan Airlines Embraer E190 flying Baku-Grozny was struck as it approached Grozny during a Ukrainian drone attack. It was rerouted across the Caspian Sea and crashed near Aktau, Kazakhstan, on 25 December 2024, killing 38 of 67 on board. Early explanations included a bird strike (Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency) and a possible on-board oxygen tank explosion (Mangistau regional medical services). On 4 February 2025 Kazakhstan's Transport Ministry published a preliminary report finding that external objects had struck the aircraft, with damage consistent with missile strikes, without directly blaming Russia. On 9 October 2025 in Dushanbe, Putin told Aliyev that two Russian air-defense missiles had detonated about 10 meters from the aircraft.
AG-265.records:
Russian air-traffic control and air-defense units: the engagement record.
The pilot: a report of a bird strike to Russian controllers.
The Federal Air Transport Agency: the bird-strike version, which it adopted publicly.
Mangistau medical services: a report of a possible oxygen tank explosion.
The flight-tracking data: the aircraft's signal disappearing and reappearing, which reporters linked to possible GPS suppression.
The Kazakh government commission and the Transport Ministry: the investigation, in which they invited Azerbaijani officials and Embraer to take part. Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev led the commission.
An anonymous Azerbaijani government source: the account given to Reuters that a Russian Pantsir-S1 missile struck the aircraft.
AG-265.gap: The aircraft was hit in one state's airspace, crashed in a second state and belonged to a third. The engagement record (Russian military) and the wreckage record (Kazakh investigators) therefore sat in different jurisdictions. The Annex 13-style preliminary report stated physical findings and declined to name a cause. The state holding the air-defense record withheld it for about ten months.
AG-265.joining: Within days, Azerbaijan named Russian air defense through an anonymous government source. In 2024 Putin apologized for what the Kremlin called a 'tragic incident' in Russian airspace, without admitting a shoot-down. The Kazakh preliminary report described external damage only. On 9 October 2025 Putin acknowledged the missiles and promised compensation and a legal assessment of officials' actions. Acknowledgment came from the responsible state after months of Azerbaijani criticism, while the investigating authority's report stopped at physical damage.

AG-266.summary: On 17 and 18 November 2024 two Baltic fiber-optic cables were damaged off the Swedish islands of Gotland and Öland. One was the Arelion cable between Gotland and Lithuania; the other was the C-Lion1 cable between Helsinki and Rostock. The Chinese-flagged bulk carrier Yi Peng 3, which had left the Russian port of Ust-Luga on 15 November, was in the area at the time and then anchored in international waters in the Kattegat. A Reuters analysis of MarineTraffic data matched its positions to the breaches. On 19 December China allowed officials from Sweden, Germany, Finland and Denmark aboard. The ship sailed on 21 December, giving Egypt as its destination.
AG-266.records:
Swedish police: a preliminary investigation into suspected sabotage covering both breaks.
Finland's National Bureau of Investigation: a criminal investigation into the C-Lion1 break for aggravated criminal mischief and aggravated interference with communications.
MarineTraffic AIS data: the ship's track.
The Swedish Accident Investigation Authority (SHK): participation with maritime expertise in the 19 December inspection. It conducted no investigation of its own.
The police from Finland, Germany, Sweden and Denmark: observers at the inspection.
The Swedish Coast Guard: monitoring of the ship until it left.
AG-266.gap: Two cables ran to different states and were covered by separate national investigations. The breaks lay off Sweden, the ship flew China's flag, and it lay at anchor in international waters off Denmark, whose foreign minister said it would be able to sail on after the inspection. Chinese authorities conducted the on-board inspection and invited the others to observe. Swedish police said the visit formed no part of their investigation. The anchor could not be examined closely because it hung outside the hull. SHK's deputy director-general said the team had significant observations whose details he could not share.
AG-266.joining: Germany's defense minister said the damage appeared to be sabotage and that there was no proof yet. The Swedish prime minister said there was no accusation of any sort. In the sources checked, no joint finding was published and no state publicly named a perpetrator or established intent.

AG-267.summary: During the student-led quota reform protests, mobile internet was restricted in parts of Bangladesh on 15–16 July 2024. A broadband cut ran from 18 to 23 July, and mobile internet was blacked out from 17 to 28 July and again on 5 August. On 18 July the State Minister for Posts, Telecommunications and IT, Zunaid Ahmed Palak, said that mobile internet had been shut to curb misinformation. He then blamed protesters, saying that staff at data centres in Mohakhali had shut down servers for fear of attack, and attributed the blackout to a fire. After the government fell, a seven-member committee of the Posts and Telecommunications Division reported on 13 August that there had been no fire. The committee reported that Palak had ordered the shutdown verbally through the chairman of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC). In its account, the National Telecommunication Monitoring Centre (NTMC) had ordered the mobile blackout.
AG-267.records:
The BTRC's Engineering and Operations Department: the 15 July order 'via WhatsApp' to suspend mobile internet in specific areas of Dhaka, extended on 16 July to 59 universities. On 18 July, on Palak's orders, it instructed submarine-cable and international terrestrial cable providers to halt all bandwidth, disconnecting the country by 9 p.m.
The NTMC, under the Home Ministry: directives from 17 July to suspend platforms and mobile internet.
The ministry: approval of the BTRC decision without full consultation among the commissioners.
The minister: a verbal order through the BTRC chairman that bypassed the necessary administrative approval.
The operators: the instructions they received.
The public record: only the minister's statements blaming arson and fear of attack.
AG-267.gap: The orders that explained the outage passed through informal channels, verbal instructions and messaging apps, outside the necessary administrative approval. The records that contradicted the arson account therefore sat with a regulator, a security agency and private carriers. None of them published those records while the government that issued the orders stood.
AG-267.joining: About a week after the government fell, a seven-member committee of the interim government, headed by Additional Secretary A. K. M. Amirul Islam of the Posts and Telecommunications Division, joined the BTRC, NTMC and operator records. The committee found that Palak had 'misled the nation and engaged in deception'. The NTMC's director general, Major General Ziaul Ahsan, was removed on 6 August. Regime change supplied the authority to join the records.
AG-267.harm_found_later: No record checked measured the harm of the nationwide communications blackout during the protests, including lost access to emergency help and health services.

AG-268.summary: From June 2024 Finnish municipalities reported break-ins and attempted break-ins at water towers, pressure-boosting stations and intakes. Among them were the Tesoma water tower and a Hervanta booster station in Tampere, the Sipoo water tower and Porvoo's Linnamäki backup intake, the last two targeted on two consecutive nights. By mid-July Foreign Policy counted 11 attempts at water towers and treatment plants. The intruders stole nothing and did not reach sensitive parts of the plants. The National Police Board said the motive was unclear and the number of reports had grown. The National Emergency Supply Agency stated that the incidents would not affect security of supply. In October 2024 Interim Interior Minister Lulu Ranne said there was no clear proof of Russian involvement in the water-facility breaches but that circumstantial indications pointed to Russia. The Security and Intelligence Service (Supo) said there had been no indications of a state actor in the Finnish cases.
AG-268.records:
Each water utility and municipality: its own intrusion.
Different police units: the National Bureau of Investigation investigated the three Pirkanmaa cases. The East Uusimaa police investigated Sipoo and Porvoo.
The National Emergency Supply Agency: measured the incidents against security of supply and stated that "every organisation is responsible for securing its own infrastructure". The agency named the police as the primary channel for suspected crimes, with the National Cyber Security Centre and Supo as further channels.
The ELY Centre of South Savo: monitors water plants' preparedness. ELY tasks under the Water Services Act were centralized to it.
Supo: commented only in general terms, saying the threat of intelligence gathering and influence against critical infrastructure had increased.
AG-268.gap: Many small utilities and municipalities recorded the break-ins. Each break-in stayed below the threshold of the agency that saw it, because nothing was taken and supply was never interrupted. Police handled the cases in different districts, the supply agency judged them by security of supply, and the security service declined to comment on specific cases. When the records were compared at national level, the interior ministry and the security service reached opposite public conclusions. The pooling of the reports therefore did not supply a common standard for deciding whether they amounted to an attack.
AG-268.joining: The National Police Board followed the cases nationally and asked the public to report unfamiliar people or drone flights near water and energy sites. Tomi Vuori, director general of the interior ministry's police department, said of several incidents that "there is no other explanation than the fact that there is some state actor behind them." Supo declined to attribute. No authority named an attacker, and the sources checked report no suspects apprehended.

AG-269.summary: On 21 February 2024 Change Healthcare detected a ransomware attack that disrupted claims, eligibility checks and pharmacy processing across the United States. The company, a UnitedHealth Group subsidiary, says it completes 15 billion health care transactions a year. On 1 May 2024 UnitedHealth's chief executive, Andrew Witty, told the Senate Finance Committee that the intrusion began on a server without multifactor authentication and that the company paid a $22 million ransom. The number of people affected, as reported to HHS, rose from an initial 500, the minimum for posting on the HHS breach portal (19 July 2024), to about 192.7 million (31 July 2025).
AG-269.records:
Change Healthcare: the intrusion records, and the breach report to HHS's Office for Civil Rights.
The covered entities (providers, health plans): remained 'ultimately responsible' for notifications but could delegate them to Change.
Pharmacies: failed refills, and patients paying out of pocket when co-pay assistance cards failed.
Physician practices: unpaid claims. In an informal AMA survey of more than 1,400 respondents reported on 10 April 2024, 80 percent reported lost revenue and 55 percent used personal funds to cover practice expenses.
CMS: guidance relaxing prior authorization and allowing advance payments.
OCR: investigations of Change and UnitedHealth focused on HIPAA compliance.
AG-269.gap: Change Healthcare was a single target. Recognition was immediate, but the harm fell on thousands of downstream recorders whose records are financial and administrative (unpaid claims, unfilled prescriptions) and contain no clinical outcome field. The federal breach record measures exposed data, a category that does not register delayed care.
AG-269.joining: Congress joined the company's account in public testimony (Senate Finance and House Energy and Commerce, 1 May 2024). The AMA joined practice-level reports by survey; OCR joined breach notifications. Change Healthcare said the attacker 'represented itself to us as ALPHV/Blackcat,' and analysts at Recorded Future and Tenable pointed to a bitcoin wallet they linked to the group that received more than $22 million. No government attribution appears in the sources checked. Patient-level effects were joined only anecdotally, by journalists.
AG-269.harm_found_later: A pharmacist in Virginia told NBC News that patients were 'walking away from diabetes medicines, antipsychotics, ADHD medications'. The sources checked contain no systematic count of the resulting clinical harm, because each downstream record captured money or data and left patient outcomes unrecorded.

AG-270.summary: A faulty update to a configuration file (Channel File 291) for CrowdStrike's Falcon sensor crashed Windows hosts worldwide on 19 July 2024. Microsoft estimated that 8.5 million devices were affected. Airlines were grounded, broadcasters went off air, banks and UK doctors' booking systems failed, and federal agencies were affected. Within hours CrowdStrike's chief executive, Australia's National Cyber Security Coordinator, France's ANSSI and a UK government security source said that the outage was not a cyberattack. CISA, meanwhile, recorded threat actors exploiting the outage with phishing and malicious files.
AG-270.records:
Each affected operator (airlines, banks, broadcasters, health providers, police): its own outage.
The FAA: an update attributing the grounding of Delta, United and American flights to a 'communication issue'.
CrowdStrike: the update and deployment logs. It published a preliminary review on 24 July and a root cause analysis on 6 August.
Microsoft: the estimate of affected devices.
CISA: an alert issued and updated from 19 July to 6 August. It recorded both the non-malicious cause and the exploitation campaigns, including a malicious ZIP-file campaign aimed at CrowdStrike customers in Latin America.
AG-270.gap: One vendor held the single common cause and announced it, the failure was simultaneous, and national cyber agencies in several states issued matching statements, so the gap closed within hours. A residual separation remained between the outage record (a vendor fault) and the opportunistic attack record (phishing exploiting the outage), which CISA kept in one alert.
AG-270.joining: CrowdStrike joined the crash reports to its own update on the day. Its chief executive, George Kurtz, said the outage was not a 'security or cyber incident'. CISA, ANSSI and Australia's coordinator made matching statements. In September 2024 the House Homeland Security Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection examined the outage. At the hearing, Committee Chairman Mark Green quoted CISA Director Jen Easterly's description of it as 'a dress rehearsal for what China may want to do to us.' No attacker existed to name.
AG-270.harm_found_later: Harm to patients was recorded, if at all, by each health provider separately. No checked source joined it.

AG-271.summary: On 3 May 2024 a fire broke out at a Berlin factory of Diehl Metall, part of the Diehl group, which is known for its air-defense systems. German authorities first ruled the fire an accident. After an investigation by its insurers, Diehl Metall attributed it to a technical fault while saying that sabotage could in theory have contributed. In June 2024 Bild reported that a foreign intelligence service had passed information on Russian involvement to the German government. In March 2025 the Telegraph reported that German authorities had opened a new investigation. It also reported that searches from Russia before and after the fire had sought information on the site's fire engines and fire-safety protocols.
AG-271.records:
German authorities: the fire, recorded as an accident.
The insurers: an investigation that produced the technical-fault finding.
A foreign ally's intelligence service: the report of Russian involvement.
European security investigators: records of the online searches.
The Telegraph: a report that officials told the Wall Street Journal in June 2024 that the fire began in an area few people could access. According to the same report, the officials also told the Wall Street Journal that CCTV footage of that area was destroyed in the fire and that experienced professionals acting for Russia had set it.
CSIS: describes the plant as making IRIS-T missiles used in Ukraine. The Telegraph reports that it produces metals for various purposes.
AG-271.gap: Diehl Metall, its insurers and the first official inquiry each recorded the fire within a loss-and-cause framework that settled on a technical fault. The report that cast doubt on that finding came from a foreign service and appeared in none of their records. The loss of the CCTV footage removed the record that could have joined them on site.
AG-271.joining: On the basis of allied intelligence, German authorities opened a new investigation. In March 2025 a European security source told the Telegraph that the investigation had found no hard proof of Russian sabotage. The sources checked report no public attribution by a German authority. CSIS, a think tank, lists the fire among Russian attacks on European defense plants.

AG-272.summary: From mid-November 2024 residents and officials in New Jersey and neighboring states reported drones. The reports included sightings over Picatinny Arsenal and Naval Weapons Station Earle. The FBI told Congress it had received more than 3,000 tips. Stewart International Airport in New York shut its runways for about an hour on the night of 13 December. The FAA issued temporary flight restrictions over Picatinny and Bedminster. A Joint Staff spokesperson confirmed sightings at both installations and said there was no intelligence indicating a foreign actor. The spokesperson also said, "We have not been able to locate or identify the operators or the points of origin." The agencies had "not identified anything anomalous," according to a joint FBI, DHS, FAA and DoD statement of 16 December. On 28 January 2025 the White House said the drones had been "authorized to be flown by the FAA for research and various other reasons" or flown by hobbyists.
AG-272.records:
Residents, local police and state governments: sighting reports.
The FBI: the tip line.
The FAA: flight authorizations, and the restrictions it issued.
The military installations: their own observations.
AG-272.gap: The military has limited authority to investigate off its installations and may not conduct intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance operations in the United States, so its detections stopped at the fence. The local police could investigate off base but held only sighting reports. The FAA held the authorization records that could explain many flights. The federal joint statement came about four weeks after the first sightings.
AG-272.joining: The federal agencies joined tips with their own records and on 16 December described the activity as a combination of lawful commercial, hobbyist and law-enforcement drones that presented no national security or public safety risk. The White House repeated that classification in January 2025. In the Joint Staff's account, the incursions at the military installations remained unattributed.

AG-273.summary: The army said 'a number of suicide drones' hit Merowe Dam, about 350 km north of Khartoum, early on 13 January 2025. In Port Sudan, Atbara, Dongola and Omdurman, power outages followed. In November 2024 the army had accused the RSF of targeting the dam with 16 drones. From 4 to 6 May 2025 drones struck a military base near Port Sudan's airport, the city's fuel depots, the main power substation and a hotel near the army chief's offices. The national electricity company confirmed a citywide blackout. On 6 May the army-aligned government cut diplomatic ties with the UAE, accusing it of supplying weapons to the RSF.
AG-273.records:
The army: described the Merowe strike as part of a 'systematic campaign' against military sites and vital infrastructure. It had accused the RSF of the November 2024 attempt.
Military sources: blamed the RSF for the Port Sudan strikes.
The national electricity company: confirmed the hit on Port Sudan's main substation.
AFP journalists in Port Sudan and local media: the January outages.
The RSF: did not address the Port Sudan strikes. It repeated its claim that the army was backed by Iran and accused the army of targeting civilian infrastructure.
The UAE: has consistently denied backing the RSF.
UN experts: were investigating the allegations.
AG-273.gap: Each strike hit a single, visible, high-value target, so the aggregation problem did not arise. The open question was the supply chain behind long-range drones, which no civilian recorder could address.
AG-273.joining: Sudan's army and government named the RSF and, by severing relations, the UAE as its supplier. The attacker did not claim the strikes. The visibility of single targets narrowed the gap; the attribution to a state sponsor stayed contested.

AG-274.summary: Drought left Ecuador's hydroelectric reservoirs critically low in early 2024 and forced power cuts of up to 13 hours in April. On 16 April President Noboa declared an energy-sector emergency and asked Energy Minister Andrea Arrobo to resign. He also announced an investigation into sabotage within the government. On 17 April Arturo Félix Wong, Secretary of Public Administration, filed a criminal complaint against 21 people, including Arrobo and her predecessors, for paralysis of a public service and treason. The complaint alleged that from late March she had hidden essential information from the President with signs of 'a criminal purpose tied to a political alliance' (finalidad delincuencial por alianza política). Before the Assembly's oversight committee on 31 October 2024, Arrobo said that she had alerted the highest authorities on 1 April. She also said she had visited the grid operator Cenace with Félix Wong on 12 April.
AG-274.records:
The complaint: reservoir data (2% capacity at Coca Codo Sinclair, no usable storage at Paute, Sopladora and Mazar) and a forecast energy deficit of 20–25% from April.
Arrobo: the void tender for a power barge, declared on 22 November 2023 under the previous government.
The National Assembly: admitted an impeachment request against Arrobo for failure to perform her duties in May 2024.
The Attorney General's office: a criminal investigation, in which Arrobo filed her account.
AG-274.gap: Reservoir levels and the drought were matters of technical record. The 'sabotage' claim concerned the flow of warnings between the ministry and the Presidency, a question that no technical record could settle.
AG-274.joining: The executive joined reservoir data and internal correspondence into a sabotage complaint that named its own former officials. Arrobo attributed the crisis to an atypical drought, a rupture of the heavy-crude pipeline that temporarily shut Coca Codo Sinclair, a surge in demand during a heat wave, and underinvestment by earlier governments. No outcome of the criminal complaint was found.

AG-275.summary: The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a multi-agency system, issued successive analyses of the Gaza Strip during the war, each reviewed by its Famine Review Committee (FRC). On 25 June 2024 the FRC found that 'the available evidence does not indicate that Famine is currently occurring'. It did not endorse a FEWS NET analysis finding it possible that famine had been under way in northern Gaza in April. On 22 August 2025 the FRC determined that 'Famine (IPC Phase 5) is currently occurring in Gaza Governorate,' and projected famine thresholds to be crossed in Deir al-Balah and Khan Younis. It called the famine 'entirely man-made.' Prime Minister Netanyahu's office issued a statement calling the report 'an outright lie.'
AG-275.records:
The humanitarian programs: community-based MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference) screenings, which the FRC called 'the only quantitative anthropometric data available'. Seven organizations screened in Gaza Governorate in July 2025.
The Gaza Ministry of Health: a count of 240 deaths attributed to starvation, malnutrition or famine by 15 August 2025, including 107 children. The count sits within mortality data that 'focus mainly on trauma-related deaths'.
The remote-sensing and sector assessments cited by the FRC: 1.5 percent of original cropland undamaged and accessible in late July 2025, and almost three quarters of fishing facilities destroyed by late 2024.
The COGAT dashboard: tonnage figures for aid, about which the FRC noted concerns.
FEWS NET: a separate analysis.
A population survey of malnutrition: none could be conducted because of access limits and insecurity.
AG-275.gap: Each program screened its own caseload. The children diagnosed with malnutrition entered treatment and were not included in later screenings, which the IPC says likely underestimated severity. Mortality reporting ran through a ministry whose figures 'almost certainly underestimate the actual mortality on the ground,' the IPC said. The FRC recommended leaving North Gaza unclassified because data on that governorate were limited. In June 2024 the FRC could not determine whether thresholds had been crossed in April 'given the uncertainty and lack of convergence of the supporting evidence,' so two joining bodies, FEWS NET and the FRC, reached different conclusions from overlapping data.
AG-275.joining: Under the IPC review procedure, the FRC joined the fragments and classified Gaza Governorate in Phase 5 'with reasonable evidence,' stating that 'the scarcity of available data is in no way a reflection of actual mortality on the ground.' On 30 August 2025 the IPC published a response to 'several issues' raised after the classification (the MUAC threshold, screening design, mortality data, the non-involvement of the parties to the conflict) without naming who raised them. It also announced an addendum to the FRC report clarifying its acute malnutrition data. The IPC kept the parties out of the analysis 'to safeguard impartiality.' Israel's government rejected the finding.
AG-275.harm_found_later: Starvation deaths are recorded through ministry channels that the FRC says capture only a fraction of the true toll and miss much non-traumatic mortality. The mortality caused by the disruption of food and health services will therefore be established only by later reconstruction.

AG-276.summary: Late on January 22, 2024, attackers sent Modbus commands to ENCO heating controllers of Lviv's municipal heat supplier, Lvivteploenergo. They also made the controllers report inaccurate measurements, which stopped heating. Dragos reported that more than 600 apartment buildings lost central heating and that remediation took almost two days in sub-zero temperatures. In Dragos's judgment, the attackers had possibly entered the network in April 2023, likely through an internet-exposed MikroTik router that was not segmented from the controllers. The firm began analyzing the malware in April 2024 and first took it for a test tool. It later learned from the Cyber Security Situation Center of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) that the malware had been used in Lviv.
AG-276.records:
Lvivteploenergo: the outage record.
The local media: reported the disruption on January 23, 2024 in Sykhiv district, home to about 100,000 people.
The SBU: said the attackers had compromised the utility's infrastructure, causing a temporary shutdown of heating and hot water for more than 600 households. It said the consequences were quickly neutralized.
Ukraine's Security Council: also gave the figure of more than 600 households.
Dragos: a malware sample from April 2024 with no known victim until the CSSC told it of the Lviv use. It also held records of connections from Moscow-based IP addresses during the attack.
MITRE ATT&CK: catalogued the tool (S1165) and the incident (C0041) in November 2024.
AG-276.gap: Local reports in January 2024 recorded a heating disruption. A foreign firm found the malware separately, months later, without knowing it had been used. The sample and the incident file sat with different institutions in different countries until the CSSC told Dragos of the link. As a matter of policy, Dragos does not attribute attacks. The SBU described the consequences as quickly neutralized.
AG-276.joining: Between April and July 2024, Ukraine's CSSC linked its incident file to Dragos's sample. Dragos published on July 23, 2024, six months after the outage. The firm noted the Moscow IP addresses and named no attacker. No claim of responsibility was made.
AG-276.harm_found_later: Residents of more than 600 buildings were without heating for almost two days in January. The sources checked report no assessment of health effects.

AG-277.summary: On 9 May 2024 a suspect planted a timed device in the IKEA store in Vilnius. It ignited overnight and was put out quickly by employees and firefighters. A Ukrainian minor, Daniil Bardadim, was arrested a few days later while traveling toward Riga, where prosecutors said he was heading to carry out a similar attack. On 17 March 2025 the Lithuanian prosecutor general's office said it had reasonable grounds to believe that Russian military intelligence organized and funded the arson. On 24 November 2025 a Lithuanian court convicted Bardadim of a terrorist act and related offenses, sentencing him to three years and four months. He acted in the interests of Russia's military structures and security services, prosecutors said.
AG-277.records:
Store staff and firefighters: dealt with a small fire.
Lithuanian police and prosecutors: the arrest, the case file and the record of the suspect's agreement, made at a secret meeting in Poland, to burn and blow up shopping centers in Lithuania and Latvia for 10,000 euros and a BMW.
Lithuanian law enforcement: the file on the network behind the July 2024 parcel fires. It links the courier Aleksandras Šuranovas to this fire and to the Marywilska fire in Warsaw, and says he supplied the extra incendiary devices the suspect carried when arrested.
Polish authorities: the record of a second suspect arrested in Poland after setting fire to a shopping center.
AG-277.gap: A small store fire with no lasting damage sits below the level that draws national attention. Its significance depended on two records outside the case. One was the agreement made in Poland, which covered targets in two countries. The other was the courier's overlap with the parcel network and the Warsaw fire.
AG-277.joining: Lithuanian prosecutors announced the attribution to Russian military intelligence in March 2025. They said they had worked closely with law enforcement in Poland and other countries. The same day Tusk said that the Lithuanian investigation had confirmed Polish suspicions about the shopping-center fires in Vilnius and Warsaw. In September 2025 Lithuanian authorities concluded that the GRU was behind the courier-parcel arsons. The November 2025 judgment gave the IKEA case legal form.

AG-278.summary: After a failed attempt in late June 2024, parcels containing timed incendiary devices hidden in items such as massage pillows and cosmetic tubes were posted from Lithuania on 19 July 2024. One ignited at the DHL hub at Leipzig airport on 20 July, one in a DPD delivery truck near Warsaw on 21 July, and one at a DHL warehouse in Minworth near Birmingham on 22 July. Polish security services seized a fourth parcel. In October 2024 a Polish prosecutor stated that the shipments tested a channel for sending such parcels to the United States and Canada. In September 2025 Lithuanian prosecutors charged 15 people and said that suspects with ties to Russian military intelligence (GRU) had led the operation.
AG-278.records:
DHL and German authorities: the first record of the fire at Leipzig.
DPD and Polish investigators: the first record of the truck fire near Warsaw.
DHL and British counterterrorism police: the first record of the fire at Minworth.
Polish security services: the seized parcel.
Lithuanian prosecutors: the sender side, including the courier and the assembly of the devices in a rented apartment.
The German and British domestic intelligence services: threat assessments.
AG-278.gap: Taken one at a time, each event was a cargo fire in a logistics facility or vehicle. The fires occurred in three countries over three days and in two carriers' networks. The parcels' common origin lay in a fourth country. The prosecutors described the shipments as a test of a transfer channel, which implies that none of the fires needed to cause serious damage.
AG-278.joining: On the sender's side, the joining ran through criminal justice channels. Lithuanian prosecutors, working with police and intelligence services, carried out more than 30 searches in Lithuania, Poland, Latvia and Estonia. In September 2025 they charged 15 people of Russian, Lithuanian, Latvian, Estonian and Ukrainian citizenship, naming GRU-linked organizers. The Polish prosecutor Katarzyna Calów-Jaszewska disclosed the test-channel purpose on 25 October 2024. That autumn the head of Germany's domestic intelligence service, Thomas Haldenwang, told the Bundestag of aggressive action by Russian intelligence services. Also that autumn, the head of MI5, Ken McCallum, said the GRU was on a sustained mission to generate mayhem on British and European streets. A consortium of journalists from LRT, Delfi, Frontstory.pl, VSquare, Re:Baltica and The Insider reconstructed the network. Its questions led the Lithuanian Prosecutor General's Office to disclose details of the case early. Authorities linked the courier to the Marywilska fire in Warsaw and the IKEA fire in Vilnius.

AG-279.summary: Satellite networks at 5°E, 10°E, 13°E and 21.5°E suffered repeated harmful interference in the 13/14 GHz and 18 GHz ranges. The interference ranged from high-power unmodulated carriers to replicated signals that replaced the original content. The affected channels predominantly carried Ukrainian television and radio programs but also channels of the Netherlands. In 2024 Sweden, Luxembourg, France (also as notifying administration for Eutelsat), the Netherlands and Ukraine brought the cases to the ITU Radio Regulations Board.
AG-279.records:
Satellite operators: the interference. Two operators independently geolocated the sources to earth stations in the areas of Moscow, Kaliningrad and Pavlovka.
National spectrum administrations: submitted the cases to the ITU Radiocommunication Bureau and the Board.
The international space radio monitoring station at Leeheim, Germany: two separate sets of geolocation measurements.
Russia's administration: told France it had monitored and detected no emission that could cause the interference. It later told the Board it had found no interference present when it investigated.
AG-279.gap: The earth stations responsible were not recorded in the Master International Frequency Register. Russia later said details could not be shared because they were military radio installations. Each operator and administration held only its own satellite's record. The Board's procedure depends on the source administration's cooperation, and Russia did not provide the information the Board requested in June 2024.
AG-279.joining: The ITU Radio Regulations Board joined the complaints. In June 2024 it called the deliberate interference to French and Swedish networks 'extremely worrisome and unacceptable', asking Russia to cease. In March 2025 it noted two Leeheim reports reconfirming sources on Russian territory and the Crimean Peninsula, finding no dispute over the sources. In November 2025, after Bureau-organized meetings in October 2025, it recorded that interference to French and Swedish satellites originated from the operation of Russian military installations. It held that cases involving military installations were within its mandate and again strongly urged Russia to cease. Russia filed a counter-complaint about interference to its Yamal satellites since March 2022, which its monitoring attributed to Ukrainian territory.

AG-280.summary: On 20 March 2024 two units on the Cromwell industrial estate in Leyton, east London, were set alight, causing about £1 million in damage. Ukrainian-owned businesses used the units, which held humanitarian aid and Starlink equipment destined for Ukraine. Local Metropolitan Police officers in Waltham Forest first investigated the fire. On 8 July 2025 three men were convicted of aggravated arson. The organizers, Dylan Earl and Jake Reeves, had pleaded guilty, Earl to preparatory conduct and Reeves to agreeing to accept a material benefit from a foreign intelligence service. These were the first convictions under the National Security Act 2023. On 23 and 24 October 2025 the Old Bailey sentenced six men, Earl to 17 years.
AG-280.records:
Waltham Forest police: the original arson report.
Spain: a fire at a Madrid warehouse of the same Ukrainian company, a separate matter there.
The Met Counter Terrorism Command: the investigation after the takeover, including 56 GB of data from Earl's phone that showed contact with the Wagner Group on Telegram.
The Crown Prosecution Service and the court: the criminal case.
AG-280.gap: As a local warehouse fire, the event fell within ordinary criminal arson. The recruits who set it did not know they were working for Wagner. A second fire at the same company's warehouse in another country, the fact that turned it into a national-security case, sat in another state's records.
AG-280.joining: After officers learned of the Madrid fire, the Met Counter Terrorism Command took over. Prosecutors charged the organizers under the National Security Act 2023. Wagner recruited Earl and Reeves, according to the CPS. Counter Terrorism Policing describes Wagner as acting on behalf of the Russian state and described the attack as Russian-ordered.

AG-281.summary: In the early hours of 12 May 2024 a fire destroyed about 90 percent of the Marywilska 44 shopping center in Warsaw, which housed about 1,400 commercial units, many of them small family businesses. The center was closed and no casualties were reported. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on 21 May 2024 that Russian involvement was likely. On 11 May 2025 he stated that the fire was arson ordered by the Russian security services and coordinated by a person in Russia. Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski withdrew consent for the Russian consulate in Kraków on 12 May 2025, after Poland had closed the Poznań consulate in October 2024 over Russian sabotage and cyberattacks, including an attempted sabotage in Wrocław.
AG-281.records:
Polish police and prosecutors: the Marywilska criminal investigation. For a year dozens of prosecutors and police worked on it together with Lithuanian authorities.
Internal Security Agency (ABW): a separate case on a related act, against a Ukrainian man instructed over Telegram to set fire to a paint factory in Wrocław.
Separate file on a related act: the case of a Belarusian man, Stepan K., charged in March 2025 with a terrorist arson attack on a Warsaw store on Russia's behalf. That fire was set a month before Marywilska in a very similar way.
Lithuanian law enforcement: the file on a courier, Aleksandras Šuranovas, whom it links to both the Marywilska fire and the May 2024 IKEA fire in Vilnius.
AG-281.gap: A night fire in a large commercial building enters the record as a fire-safety and arson matter, in which no hostile state is presumed. Russian intelligence recruited people for such attacks, often Ukrainian and Belarusian immigrants, and instructed some of them over Telegram, so each local case resembled ordinary crime. The related cases ran separately in Poland, with part of the link to a foreign service coming from records held in Lithuania.
AG-281.joining: Tusk said in March 2025 that records from Lithuania also pointed to Russian involvement. In May 2025 the interior and justice ministers stated that investigators had in-depth knowledge of the arson and of how the perpetrators documented it. Tusk said that month that some perpetrators were in custody and that the rest had been identified and were sought. A year after the fire, while the criminal cases were still open, the government named the Russian security services and closed a consulate.

AG-282.summary: From late May 2024 North Korea launched more than 5,500 balloons carrying refuse into the South, some of which caused small fires. By late September runway closures at Incheon and Gimpo airports totaled 413 minutes over 20 days, including a 166-minute closure of all Incheon runways on 26 June. Seoul and Gyeonggi recorded 51 damage reports for bundles that landed between 28 May and 10 August. The combined damage exceeded 100 million won, but the law then in force gave the government no basis for compensation. On 14 November 2024 the National Assembly passed a revision of the civil defense law that allowed it.
AG-282.records:
South Korean officials: counted the launches.
Joint Chiefs of Staff: a spokesperson spoke publicly on the launches.
The airport authorities: runway closures at Incheon and Gimpo.
Seoul city and Gyeonggi provincial governments: the damage reports. They submitted them to Rep. Yang Bu-nam of the Democratic Party.
The interior ministry: said it would speed up processing of damage reports before the law was revised.
AG-282.gap: Because the launches were visible and continuous and the military attributed them from the outset, the gap lay in the harm. The vehicle damage, small fires and runway closures fell to municipalities, fire services and airports. There was no legal category for compensating damage caused by the North.
AG-282.joining: A legislator joined the municipal and provincial damage records, and the National Assembly created a basis for compensation. Attribution was never in doubt.
AG-282.harm_found_later: Owners had no legal route to state compensation until the November 2024 revision, although local governments already held the damage records.

AG-283.summary: Okhmatdyt, Ukraine's largest children's hospital, was hit during a Russian strike wave on 8 July 2024 that involved at least 38 cruise missiles and ballistic rockets. Two people were killed, including a doctor, and 32 were wounded. The next day Danielle Bell, head of the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, stated that video analysis and a site assessment indicated 'a high likelihood that the children's hospital suffered a direct hit rather than receiving damages due to an intercepted weapons system,' and that the factors suggested a Kh-101 missile launched by Russia. Russia's Defense Ministry stated that a falling Ukrainian air-defense missile caused the damage. Its UN envoy said at the Security Council that the missile was most likely fired from a Norwegian-supplied NASAMS system.
AG-283.records:
The UN monitoring mission: interviews with medical staff, parents and residents, and the observations of its military expert at the site. It also recorded the transfer of 600 children to other hospitals.
Security Service of Ukraine: reported fragments of a Kh-101 rear body with a serial number and part of the rudder. It opened criminal proceedings and reported further missile parts on 9 July.
Video footage: the weapon striking the hospital.
Russian Defense Ministry: asserted that photos and videos from the scene showed a falling Ukrainian air-defense missile.
AG-283.gap: Little aggregation gap arose: the case had one target, video footage and physical remnants. The disagreement concerned attribution between two parties, with the UN mission grading its finding as a likelihood that 'must be investigated.'
AG-283.joining: Within a day the UN monitoring mission joined video, site observation and testimony. It assessed a likely direct hit by a Russian Kh-101 while stating 'We haven't determined.' Russia's UN envoy, Vasily Nebenzya, presented the counter-account at a Security Council meeting on 9 July 2024.

AG-284.summary: A 26-year-old Colombian national, Andrés Alfonso de la Hoz de la Cruz, set fire to three Prague public-transport buses at a depot at night, filmed the act and left. The fire was extinguished by local workers. On 10 June 2024 Prime Minister Fiala announced the detention of a 26-year-old foreigner on suspicion of an attempted terrorist attack and later called the arson likely part of Russia's hybrid war. On 9 June 2025 the Prague Municipal Court approved a plea agreement and sentenced him to eight years: he had received the order through Telegram for a promised $3,000 and had planned a second arson. In July 2025 Poland's ABW announced that the same man had been charged with terrorism over fires at two building depots in Poland in May 2024. The ABW stated that the acts were 'commissioned, overseen and financed by an individual linked to the Russian intelligence services'.
AG-284.records:
Depot workers: put out the Prague fire.
Czech police and prosecutors: investigated the fire as a suspected attempted terrorist attack.
Czech court: convicted the man of arson and planning another arson on a plea agreement. It recorded the Telegram tasking and did not state a finding of Russian commissioning.
Czech government: made the political attribution.
ABW in Poland: attached the May 2024 depot fires to the same individual and to a Russian handler. It described Russian recruitment through Telegram of people with military backgrounds, especially from Latin America.
AG-284.gap: A depot fire with three damaged buses is recorded locally as arson. The link to a foreign service ran through a Telegram tasking channel and a single recruited person whose acts crossed a border. The Polish fires were joined to the Prague case about fourteen months after they occurred.
AG-284.joining: After the arrest, Czech authorities joined the bus fire to Telegram tasking. The Czech court recorded the tasking without its source. The Polish ABW joined the Polish depot fires to the same man and named an individual linked to Russian intelligence, without naming that individual publicly.

AG-285.summary: On 18 February 2024 a Houthi anti-ship ballistic missile struck the bulk carrier Rubymar off Yemen's west coast. The crew dropped anchor and abandoned the ship, which drifted for almost two weeks and sank on 2 March. In late February three cables in the same area were knocked offline: Seacom (also reported as Tata TGN-Eurasia), AAE-1 and EIG. HGC Global Communications estimated that they carried about 25 percent of the region's traffic. The Israeli site Globes alleged Houthi sabotage in an early report that offered no support. Houthi representatives denied targeting the cables, and Mohammed Ali al-Houthi blamed the United States.
AG-285.records:
The cable owners: recorded the faults.
Seacom's chief digital officer: said the cause could not be determined before inspection and that a dragged anchor seemed likely.
The Rubymar's location data before it lost power: showed that the ship passed close to the damaged cables.
US Central Command: recorded the missile strike and the sinking.
International Cable Protection Committee (ICPC): represents cable operators. It said it was 'generally accepted' that the Rubymar dropped an anchor when fired upon.
AG-285.gap: The military record of the strike and the operators' fault records sat with different holders. The cause lay across a crewless, war-damaged ship and parties to the conflict with opposed interests in the explanation. Seacom said repairs depended on a permit to work in Yemeni waters. The operators had to determine what insurance and security their maintenance contractors needed in a conflict zone.
AG-285.joining: US National Security Council spokesman John Kirby said the cables were cut 'most likely by an anchor dragging from the Rubymar as she sank'. The ICPC and Seacom gave the same likely cause before any inspection. Yemen's information minister, Moammar al-Eryani, said the Houthis were to blame because of their 'terrorist activities' in the Red Sea, even if they had not targeted the cables directly. The prevailing account classed the cable damage as an unintended effect of the attack on the ship.
AG-285.harm_found_later: Users of cables carrying about a quarter of regional traffic lost capacity through an anchor drag that followed from a missile strike. That causal route lies one step removed from the record of the strike.

AG-286.summary: A PRC state-linked campaign tracked as Salt Typhoon gained access to the networks of at least nine US telecommunications operators, to law enforcement wiretapping platforms and to dozens of telecom providers abroad. US and partner agencies announced in November 2024 that PRC-affiliated actors had compromised major telecom networks. On 17 January 2025 Treasury sanctioned Sichuan Juxinhe Network Technology and Yin Kecheng for 'direct involvement' in the campaign, describing Juxinhe as a contractor of the Ministry of State Security. On 27 August 2025 the FBI, NSA and CISA issued a joint advisory with agencies of 12 partner nations, stating that the threat was 'substantially greater than previously reported'.
AG-286.records:
Each carrier: its own intrusion data.
AT&T: said in December 2024 that it detected 'no activity by nation-state actors in our networks at this time'.
Verizon: said in December 2024 that it 'has contained the cyber incident'.
US officials: said they might never know whether the actors had been fully removed.
Anne Neuberger, White House deputy national security adviser: raised the count of affected US carriers from eight to nine.
Treasury's OFAC: the designation record.
Cyber Safety Review Board: was investigating when the White House disbanded it in January 2025.
Nine private contributors: took part in the August 2025 advisory. Among them were Microsoft, Google Mandiant, Cisco Talos and CrowdStrike.
AG-286.gap: The intruders worked inside each carrier's own network and the wiretapping platforms connected to it, so each operator saw activity confined to its network. The one federal body set up to produce a public reconstruction across companies was disbanded mid-investigation, a step that Rep. Doris Matsui said 'leaves in limbo' the government's investigation. Foreign carriers report to separate national regulators.
AG-286.joining: The records came together in stages, starting in November 2024 when US and partner agencies announced the campaign. Treasury named an MSS contractor in January 2025. The August 2025 advisory joined the observations of agencies from 13 countries and nine private contributors. The CSRB reconstruction was never completed.

AG-287.summary: The Rapid Support Forces besieged El Fasher, capital of North Darfur, from May 2024 according to a UN official. By October 2025 they had 'fully entrapped' the city behind a nearly continuous 57-km earthen berm. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab combined satellite and thermal imagery with open-source reports. On 8 October 2025 it corroborated damage at Abu Qurun market, where open sources reported an RSF drone attack on 27 September 2025 that killed at least 7 people. The lab also corroborated repeated bombardment of a building used as a shelter and community kitchen, as well as arson in Daraja Oula and Abu Shouk camp. In January 2025 WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus reported 70 deaths and 19 injuries among patients and companions in an attack on the Saudi Teaching Maternal Hospital, the city's only functional hospital, without naming the attacker.
AG-287.records:
Yale Humanitarian Research Lab: satellite and thermal imagery checked against open sources, UN P-codes and IOM displacement data.
WHO: the hospital attack toll.
Sudan's Foreign Ministry: blamed an RSF drone attack on the hospital's emergency ward.
The RSF: blamed the Sudanese army and its allies. It offered no support for the claim.
The UN: 782 civilians killed and more than 1,140 wounded by the siege, as of December 2024.
The open-source reports: casualties at the market and the shelter.
AG-287.gap: Under the siege, El Fasher lost its routine recorders. The lab itself notes that 'the information environment in Sudan does not have the breadth of data available in other locations'. It adds that there is 'likely a significant reporting bias' among open-source reporters, and that imagery coverage and resolution limit what damage analysts can see.
AG-287.joining: An academic remote-sensing lab joined imagery and open-source reports into a running account of attacks on civilian sites. WHO and UN officials issued counts and statements. The RSF was identified as the besieging force throughout, although WHO named no attacker for the hospital strike and the two belligerents blamed each other.
AG-287.harm_found_later: Casualty figures for attacks on markets and shelters rest on open-source reports that the lab could corroborate only in part. The sources checked did not count deaths from food deprivation under siege.

AG-288.summary: From the afternoon of 2 February 2024, Sudani and MTN Sudan connectivity fell to zero or near zero. When Zain went largely offline on 7 February, most of the country was left without mobile and internet service. The civil registry halted operations, the banking system was paralyzed, and civil-society groups said aid delivery was hindered. The state news agency SUNA and two telecommunications sources told Reuters that the RSF, which held the operators' facilities in Khartoum, had shut the two providers down while demanding restoration of service in Darfur. The regulator (TPRA) accused the RSF of shutting the Sudani and MTN data centers. The RSF denied responsibility and blamed the army for months of outages in Darfur, Kordofan and elsewhere.
AG-288.records:
Network measurement groups: the collapse by operator and time.
IODA: dated the drop to about 4:30 p.m. on 2 February.
NetBlocks: tracked each operator.
MTN Group: attributed the outage to the conflict.
Zain: cited 'circumstances outside of its control'.
Sudani: a representative declined to comment.
The TPRA: accused the RSF of shutting the data centers.
Civil-society groups (Hadhreen, SAMA, SIHA): blamed the RSF.
The Wad Madani Resistance Committees: blamed both belligerents.
Digital Rights Lab–Sudan, a watchdog: said sources confirmed that the RSF had taken over ISP data centers in Khartoum.
Earlier regional outages in Darfur and Kordofan: had lasted weeks or months. Their cause was not clear.
AG-288.gap: Because the outage was national and simultaneous, no aggregation was needed to see it. The record stayed divided on cause. The operators that knew what had happened in their facilities did not say, the regulator blamed the RSF, and the RSF answered by blaming the army for the earlier regional shutdowns. As of 9 February, according to Radio Dabanga, no official statement had explained the blackout.
AG-288.joining: The regulator and the state news agency named the RSF, which denied responsibility. No neutral body established the technical cause. A single, visible disruption removed the aggregation problem and left attribution contested.
AG-288.harm_found_later: Millions relied on online payments for food. Bankak and Fawry remained operational, but most people could not use them during the outage. No outage record captures that harm.

AG-289.summary: On 1 August 2024 the IPC Famine Review Committee concluded that famine conditions prevailed in parts of North Darfur, including Zamzam camp south of El Fasher, whose population it put at at least 500,000. On 23 December 2024 the acting agriculture minister, Abubakr El Bishri, suspended Sudan's participation in the IPC system, accusing it of "issuing unreliable reports that undermine Sudan's sovereignty and dignity." The IPC's famine findings for Abu Shouk camp, El Salam camp and parts of the Nuba Mountains were published the following day.
AG-289.records:
Famine Review Committee: reviewed analyses from FEWS NET and the Sudan IPC Technical Working Group. It recorded that restrictions on humanitarian access, "including intentional impediments imposed by the active parties to the conflict," had hindered aid delivery.
December 2024 IPC analysis: put at least 638,000 people in Phase 5 and projected famine in five further areas of North Darfur.
El Bishri, acting agriculture minister: had told Al Jazeera in September 2024 that talk of famine aimed to open borders for weapons smuggling.
UN Special Rapporteurs: stated on 26 June 2024 that "both the SAF and the RSF are using food as a weapon and starving civilians."
AG-289.gap: Famine classification requires household, nutrition and mortality data from the places under siege, which is where the parties blocked access. The government then removed itself from the system that produces the classification, so the national channel closed while the fighting continued. Each contributing body was left holding its fragment.
AG-289.joining: Under the IPC's own review procedure, the Famine Review Committee joined the fragments in August and December 2024, against the stated position of the state on whose territory the famine was found. In June 2024 UN experts named starvation as a method used by both the army and the Rapid Support Forces, without attributing the famine to one party.
