AG-290.summary: At the Luftwaffe barracks in Köln-Wahn on 14 August 2024, a technical alarm, a hole in the fence leading to its waterworks and a person seen leaving prompted suspicion that the drinking water had been tampered with. Quick tests showed abnormal values, and the plant was shut down. On the same day suspicious observations were reported at the NATO air base in Geilenkirchen. On 15 August the health office warned about 10,000 residents in Mechernich that tap water from a reservoir that also supplies a Bundeswehr site might be contaminated. Between 16 and 19 August the Köln-Wahn water was declared usable with no limits exceeded. In the same period the Mechernich water was found uncontaminated, and police concluded that the Mechernich fence damage had probably been caused by a wild animal.
AG-290.records:
Köln-Wahn investigators: police, military police, the Military Counterintelligence Service (MAD) and the police state-protection unit. They investigated, initially for trespass by unknown persons.
Bundeswehr's Territorial Command: declared the Köln-Wahn water usable on 16 August.
Health office: issued a boil-water notice at Mechernich, which the town lifted on 18 August.
Fire-service special team: tested the Mechernich water.
Euskirchen police: investigated property damage at Mechernich.
State-protection unit: closed its Mechernich inquiry with no indication of a politically motivated act.
Aachen prosecutor's office: filed a precautionary complaint against unknown persons for trespass at Geilenkirchen.
Der Spiegel: reported that two men who climbed the fence at the Wilhelmshaven naval base on 14 August were sailors from a nearby ship who wanted to look at German warships.
AG-290.gap: The alarms came within days at separate sites, each with its own owner (the Bundeswehr, a public water supplier, NATO) and its own investigators. A cluster of reports during a period of heightened alert produced a sabotage hypothesis that the separate tests did not support.
AG-290.joining: Within a week the Bundeswehr, police and local authorities resolved the water questions. They found water within limits at Köln-Wahn, no contamination and probably an animal at Mechernich, and sailors at Wilhelmshaven. In the sources checked, the trespass complaints at Köln-Wahn and Geilenkirchen stayed open against unknown persons. On 21 August the Bundeswehr was reported to have increased checks, patrols and fence inspections at its sites nationwide, although the Defence Ministry said the lowest of four security levels still applied.

AG-291.summary: Overnight into 13 October 2024 an intruder forced the door of Helsingevatten's high-level reservoir in the Bollnäs water tower. The utility issued a boil-water recommendation for Bollnäs and Freluga, and residents emptied shops of bottled water. SVT reported intrusions in recent years at Hofors and Robertsfors and drone flights over some facilities. On 2 March 2025 someone opened an electrical cabinet on Gotland and disconnected the power cable to a pump that supplies large parts of the island. The police opened a sabotage investigation, and Säpo confirmed the incident. No perpetrator was publicly identified in the cases checked.
AG-291.records:
Municipal water companies, among them Helsingevatten in Bollnäs: recorded intrusions, alarms, sampling and boil-water notices. On Gotland a technician answered a pump alarm and reconnected the cable.
The local police: recorded the crimes, in the Gotland case as suspected sabotage.
Säpo: confirmed the Gotland incident.
Livsmedelsverket: sets the protection rules for drinking-water facilities. Under these rules municipal utilities make their own risk assessments.
Must (military intelligence): had named water sabotage as a threat.
SVT: gave no national count of intrusions.
AG-291.gap: Sweden's more than 1,500 treatment plants and roughly 1,000 reservoirs are run by municipal utilities that each assess their own risks and choose their own measures. An incident therefore registers as a local water-quality event and a local police case. No agency named in the sources publishes a national series that would show whether the incidents form a pattern. SVT's reporting referred only to intrusions 'in recent years' without a figure.
AG-291.joining: Säpo confirmed the Gotland incident, which press coverage placed beside Baltic Sea cable incidents that many experts and political leaders attributed to Russian hybrid warfare. The incidents were not joined publicly, and no agency named an actor.

AG-292.summary: On 3 June 2024 a ransomware attack disabled Synnovis, the pathology provider for King's College Hospital, Guy's and St Thomas' and GP services in south east London. The press reported the attack as the work of the Qilin group. By 26 September 2024 NHS England London reported, as unvalidated management information, 10,152 acute outpatient appointments and 1,710 elective procedures postponed at the two trusts. A year later NHS managers confirmed some 170 incidents of patient harm. King's College Hospital stated that a long wait for a blood test result caused by the attack was one of several factors contributing to a patient's unexpected death.
AG-292.records:
Synnovis: the laboratory systems and the test backlog.
Each hospital trust: postponed activity and patient safety incidents, recorded in its own reporting system.
NHS England London: published weekly cumulative activity figures that reported no patient harm.
HSJ (18 June 2025): reported that NHS managers confirmed nearly 600 incidents linked to the attack. Of these, 170 involved harm to patient care: one severe, 14 moderate and 155 low.
Infosecurity Magazine (26 June 2025): reported two severe cases among the 170.
King's College Hospital's patient safety incident investigation: identified the attack's disruption to pathology as a contributing factor in one death.
AG-292.gap: The attack was recognized immediately and had a single target, so the gap concerned harm. Harm was recorded incident by incident in trust safety systems and classified by severity. It became a single figure only when the incidents were counted a year after the attack.
AG-292.joining: NHS England London joined activity data while the disruption lasted. Harm figures, confirmed by NHS managers and reported through the trade press (HSJ), were not found in any official publication. In June 2025 King's College Hospital disclosed the contributing role of the attack in one death. The criminal group was identified through press reporting, and no government attribution was reported in the sources checked.
AG-292.harm_found_later: A year after the event, patient safety reviews joined clinical outcomes to the outage. Only then did the death and the 170 harm incidents become attributable to the attack.

AG-293.summary: In January 2024 intruders broke into a remote login system for the industrial software controlling a water tank in Muleshoe, Texas (about 5,000 residents). The tank overflowed for about 30 to 45 minutes before officials took the system offline and switched to manual operation. Later, town officials said the overflow caused no service disruption. Tanks also overflowed in Abernathy, Lockney detected suspicious activity on its SCADA system, and Hale Center recorded failed attempts to get through its firewall. On 18 January the CyberArmyofRussia_Reborn persona (CARR) posted a Telegram video that it said showed the Muleshoe manipulation.
AG-293.records:
Town officials: each recorded a different kind of event (an overflow, suspicious activity, a blocked intrusion). They were Muleshoe city manager Ramon Sanchez, Lockney's Buster Poling and Hale Center's Mike Cypert.
FBI: investigating, according to one town official. It declined comment.
Mandiant (17 April 2024): found multiple links between Sandworm (APT44), a GRU unit, and infrastructure used by the CARR persona. It said, however, that it was unclear whether the GRU was behind the Muleshoe attack.
Joint fact sheet of 1 May 2024: "Some victims experienced minor tank overflow events," with no victims named and no state named. Its authors were CISA, FBI, NSA, EPA, DOE, USDA, FDA, MS-ISAC, Canada's Cyber Centre and UK NCSC.
US Treasury (19 July 2024): sanctions on CARR's leader Yuliya Pankratova and its "primary hacker" Denis Degtyarenko.
AG-293.gap: Each town filed its event under a different heading (operational overflow, suspicious activity, firewall noise). The joint federal record named no victims. Without the persona's own video, the Muleshoe overflow would have remained a local operational event in a town of 5,000. The step from persona to state was made by a private firm; the official records reviewed confirm effects and sanction individuals of the persona.
AG-293.joining: The attacker's publicity joined the towns' records first. Mandiant, a private firm, linked the persona to APT44 in April 2024. In May ten agencies generalized the pattern across water, dams, energy, and food and agriculture. They also recorded that such hacktivists "exaggerate their capabilities and impacts to targets". Treasury named two CARR members in July.

AG-294.summary: The remote-control system of Tureby-Alkestrup Vandværk, a small waterworks on the border between Køge and Faxe municipalities, was taken over by intruders in December 2024. On the first night the pumps dropped to zero, and consumers were without water for a few hours until the pumps were reset by hand. The intruders raised the pressure in the network less than 24 hours later, and three water pipes burst. The pro-Russian group Z-Pentest claimed the attack on X. On 18 December 2025 the Danish Defence Intelligence Service (FE) stated that Russia was behind a destructive cyberattack on a Danish water utility in 2024. FE said the attack was carried out by Z-Pentest, a group it assessed as having links to the Russian state.
AG-294.records:
The waterworks' chairman: first took the pump failure for a technical fault. He concluded that the system had been hacked when the supplier of the remote-control system found that it could not control the system either.
The operator: reset the pumps by hand.
The waterworks association: referred the chairman to the Danish Data Protection Agency.
Danish Data Protection Agency: referred him on to FE and to the police's Center for Cyberkriminalitet.
FE: held the attribution.
Danske Vandværker, an industry body: in autumn 2026 surveyed 691 consumer-owned waterworks and found that 12 percent had been targeted by a cyberattack at some point. The water sector comprises about 2,500 supply companies.
AG-294.gap: Denmark's water sector consists of about 2,500 supply companies, and at the time no fixed IT security requirements applied to waterworks. This waterworks had alarms on its pumps, boreholes and doors and had not covered electronic security. The first effect entered the record as a fault. The reporting route was improvised through the data-protection authority. The incident stayed a local outage until national intelligence attributed it a year later. Although the attacker's claim on X was public from the start, state attribution still took twelve months.
AG-294.joining: FE joined the incident to its assessment of Russian hybrid operations. Defence Minister Troels Lund Poulsen announced the attribution on 18 December 2025, together with FE's attribution to NoName057(16) of denial-of-service attacks on Danish websites before the November 2025 municipal and regional elections. FE's chief, Thomas Ahrenkiel, said the service was very sure that pro-Russian groups with ties to the Russian state were responsible. The foreign ministry said it would summon the Russian ambassador.

AG-295.summary: On 7 April 2025 intruders reached the remote control panel of a valve at the Risevatnet dam near Svelgen in Bremanger and set it fully open. For about four hours the valve released about 497 liters per second above the required minimum flow, more than 7 million liters in all. Then the owner, the property company Breivika Eigedom, whose dam supplies a smolt facility, found the irregularities and reversed the setting. The incident became public in June 2025. In August 2025 the head of the Police Security Service (PST), Beate Gangås, said at the Arendalsuka forum that pro-Russian hackers were believed to be behind it. Gangås added that the aim of such actors is to show what they are capable of, with destruction not necessarily intended.
AG-295.records:
The dam owner: the control-system records and the discovery.
The police and the National Criminal Investigation Service (Kripos): received the report of the incident.
NVE, the dam-safety regulator: knew of the incident. In June 2025 it declined to confirm who was responsible.
The attackers: posted a three-minute video of the control panel on Telegram. The video carried a watermark associated with a pro-Russian group.
PST: the counterintelligence assessment.
AG-295.gap: The physical effect was small, with no harm to fish, facilities or the environment. In a dam-safety record, therefore, the event was a minor flow deviation at a small private dam. The owner agreed with PST not to comment, which left attribution to a security-service speech four months later.
AG-295.joining: Kripos linked the incident to the attackers' Telegram video and reached its conclusion in June 2025. In August 2025 PST named pro-Russian actors in public without naming a Russian state body. The attackers' own publicity narrowed a gap that a four-hour valve opening would otherwise have left open.

AG-296.summary: In northern Chile on 25 February 2025, the forced disconnection of the 2×500 kV Nueva Maitencillo–Nueva Pan de Azúcar line, owned by Interchile, split the grid into two islands that both lost stability. The disaster agency Senapred counted 14 of 16 regions affected. The government declared a state of emergency and a 10 p.m.–6 a.m. curfew and deployed the armed forces. The Santiago Metro closed. Interior minister Carolina Tohá ruled out sabotage, and President Gabriel Boric blamed the private firms and said the state must hold them responsible. The Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional sent its final failure analysis to the regulator SEC in March 2025. The analysis found that Interchile staff had restarted a protection device's communications module without notifying the coordinator, an unauthorized intervention that coincided with the failure.
AG-296.records:
Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional: restoration under executive director Ernesto Huber, a failure analysis built from more than a thousand reports, and audits ordered of Interchile and Transelec.
Interchile: line owner. It reported the protection deactivated at 13:35 while its backup worked.
Transelec: SCADA and telecommunications problems that complicated restoration.
Interior Ministry: its own record.
Senapred: 14 of 16 regions affected.
Santiago Metro: its own record.
SEC: fuel and electricity regulator, recipient of the report.
AG-296.gap: On the first day the government attributed the outage to a failed transmission line in the north, and within about three weeks the coordinator traced it to unauthorized work on that line's protection. The gap was small.
AG-296.joining: The interior minister ruled out sabotage on the first day, although the state still invoked emergency powers and the military. Under its statutory role, the system coordinator joined the operators' reports into a failure analysis and sent it to the regulator. No attacker was suspected in the official statements found.

AG-297.summary: On 13 April 2026 Cornelio Valencia, assistant director general and spokesperson of the Philippine National Security Council, spoke at a press conference. He said that tests by the National Bureau of Investigation's Forensic and Scientific Research Service had conclusively established cyanide in ten yellow bottles that the Philippine Navy had seized from Chinese sampans near the grounded BRP Sierra Madre at Second Thomas Shoal in February and October 2025. Valencia called the use of cyanide sabotage intended to kill local fish and said it could damage the reef and compromise the stability of the ship. Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun called the claim a stunt and accused Philippine forces of harassing Chinese fishing boats and seizing fishermen's supplies.
AG-297.records:
Philippine Navy: the seizure records. Its spokesperson, Rear Admiral Roy Vincent Trinidad, gave the count of ten bottles.
National Bureau of Investigation's forensic service: the test results.
National Security Council: made the public claim at the Coast Guard's West Philippine Sea transparency office.
Chinese foreign ministry: issued the rebuttal.
AG-297.gap: The public account describes no reef survey, no fish kill and no chain of custody beyond the seizure and the laboratory test. The step from seized bottles to deliberate poisoning of the reef therefore rests on a security council's joining. No personnel aboard the ship tested positive for exposure, and each side keeps its own account of the surrounding waters.
AG-297.joining: Philippine security officials joined seizure and laboratory records into a sabotage claim, which China rejected. No independent scientific assessment was cited.

AG-298.summary: During the hostilities that followed the Pahalgam attack and India's Operation Sindoor, Pakistani media and social-media accounts claimed that a cyberattack had disabled about 70 percent of India's power grid. These accounts also claimed that the cyberattack had breached many Indian infrastructure systems. Pakistan's state broadcaster PTV reported attacks on sensitive Indian domains, including websites of the ruling BJP. The Indian government's PIB Fact Check labeled the power-grid claim fake. Maharashtra Cyber, the state police cyber unit, reported more than 1.5 million attacks by seven APT groups, of which 150 succeeded, and listed power outages, banking hacks and data theft from Mumbai airport among false claims.
AG-298.records:
PTV and Pakistani outlets: reported defaced Indian domains, a disabled grid, ten compromised SCADA systems in the energy sector and data stolen from more than 150 databases.
Profit (Pakistan Today): said it had not independently verified those claims.
PIB Fact Check: labeled the 70 percent grid claim fake, noting that it was attributed to the Pakistan Army 'without any credible source'.
Maharashtra Cyber's report 'Road of Sindoor': presented by Additional Director General Yashasvi Yadav. It counted attacks by type (malware, DDoS, GPS spoofing, defacement), named seven groups (among them APT 36 and Pakistan Cyber Force) and listed origins in Pakistan, Bangladesh, Indonesia, Morocco and the Middle East.
CERT-In: cautioned financial institutions and critical sectors.
Techniasanct, an Indian firm: reported DDoS attacks on the Income Tax Department, HAL, Indian Railways and BSNL.
An ORF analyst: later judged the Pakistani cyber operations to have had 'limited tangible impact'.
AG-298.gap: The two sides recorded different things. The claimants reported effects that no operator record checked here corroborates. The Indian police count joined 1.5 million attempts of every kind into one figure, of which the 150 successes were identified only in part (two website defacements among them). Neither record came from the operators of the grid, airports or banks, whose own outage and incident records were not published in the sources checked.
AG-298.joining: PIB's denials were, in the sources checked, the central government's public response during the fighting. Maharashtra Cyber, a state police body, produced the only joined Indian count. It named groups, some of them Pakistan-based or Pakistan-allied, and source countries, without attributing the activity to the Pakistani state. A think tank (ORF, 28 May 2025) provided an independent assessment. Attacker publicity in this case enlarged the claim beyond the record and left the gap unresolved.

AG-299.summary: On the night of 9 to 10 September 2025 Russian drones entered Polish airspace during an attack on Ukraine. Warsaw, Modlin, Lublin and Rzeszów-Jasionka airports were closed for unplanned military activity. Poland and its allies shot down several drones. A house in Wyryki-Wola near Włodawa was badly damaged. Poland reported at least 19 violations of its airspace and requested an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council, scheduled for 12 September. On 16 September the newspaper Rzeczpospolita reported, citing unnamed security officials, that the house had been hit by an AIM-120 missile fired from a Polish F-16 that failed to detonate.
AG-299.records:
The military: the records of its engagements.
The interior ministry: reported finding missile fragments along with drone wreckage.
The prosecutors in Lublin: the debris investigation. They said they had identified remains of 17 drones, while the object that hit the house remained unidentified pending an expert opinion.
A ministry: stated that the object had not been identified as a drone or drone fragments.
The residents: the damage.
The government: the account given to the UN.
AG-299.gap: The military knew which missiles it had fired; the prosecutors knew what had been recovered. The public account came from ministers who described the damage as a Russian provocation or its result. Joining the engagement records to the debris would have pointed to friendly fire. The first public join came from journalists relying on unnamed sources.
AG-299.joining: Rzeczpospolita joined the military and debris records through its sources. In response, politicians promised an explanation. A commentary in the same paper criticized how politicians and the military had handled the matter. The sources checked report no official confirmation of the missile's origin.

AG-300.summary: Several drones were reported near and on the grounds of Munich Airport on the evening of 2 October 2025. From 22:18 flight operations were suspended, and both runways closed from 22:35, causing 17 cancellations and 15 diversions. The perpetrators were not identified. On the evening of 4 November 2025 Brussels Airport suspended flights twice after drone sightings, with 40 cancellations. Liège Airport was disrupted, and drones were reported near the Kleine-Brogel, Florennes and Schaffen military sites. Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken called the incidents coordinated and deliberate. Belgian security services, according to anonymous sources cited by the news agency Belga, suspected a state actor, most likely Russia.
AG-300.records:
Federal Police, Munich Airport and Northern Upper Bavaria police headquarters: a joint statement setting out the division of responsibility at Munich.
DFS, state aviation-security authorities, state police and federal police: share drone detection and defense at commercial airports, each within its remit. DFS is the air navigation service.
Federal police: cover the airport grounds.
Bavarian police: cover the surroundings and the criminal investigation.
The local police in Belgium: confirmed sightings over military bases. They said the drones could not be intercepted.
Belgian National Crisis Center: activated to coordinate.
Belgian National Security Council: scheduled to meet on 6 November.
AG-300.gap: At Munich, different forces recorded sightings according to whether a drone was inside or outside the airport fence. The authorities withheld details of their detection systems for tactical reasons. In Belgium, civil airports and military bases recorded sightings separately. Police could confirm drones without capturing any. In neither country was a drone recovered or an operator identified in the sources checked, so the records could support only a pattern of sightings.
AG-300.joining: The records were joined at the political level. In Belgium this happened through the National Security Council and the defense minister's statements, in Germany through the joint statement of three authorities. Neither government named an attacker on the record in the sources checked.

AG-301.summary: On the evening of 22 September 2025 reported drone sightings halted flights at Copenhagen Airport for several hours. In the following days Aalborg Airport, which also serves the military, closed on two nights, and drones were reported near other airports and near Skrydstrup air base. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called the Copenhagen incident the most serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure to date. Copenhagen police described the operator as a capable actor. In June 2026 Copenhagen police closed their nine-month investigation without suspects and said they could not confirm drone activity in and around the airport. An Armed Forces report, however, concluded from soldiers' observations and technical information that drones had flown over military installations several times. On 1 October 2026, after media reports of contradicting witness accounts, the Armed Forces conceded that their account of one incident might have been mistaken.
AG-301.records:
Airport operators: recorded the closures.
Copenhagen police and other police districts: recorded sightings and ran the criminal investigation.
The Armed Forces: recorded soldiers' observations and technical data at military sites. At the Borris camp, a unit guarding Ukrainian trainees reported drones on 24, 25 and 28 September 2025.
The ministers: made the public characterizations.
AG-301.gap: The record-holders worked to different standards. The prime minister's characterization came within a day. The police needed proof of drone activity for a criminal case and did not find it. The military relied on soldiers' observations and technical information and left criminal investigation to the police. The sources show no body charged with reconciling the military and police records before the government spoke in public.
AG-301.joining: The records were never joined into a single finding. The government described an attack at once, and the police later declined to confirm drones at Copenhagen. The Armed Forces confirmed drones over military sites. After journalists gathered witness accounts and Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus asked for a review, the Armed Forces conceded a possible error on one incident. Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen said that it is part of the nature of hybrid warfare that the adversary does not reveal itself. No attacker was named, and Russia denied involvement.

AG-302.summary: An explosion and fire hit the Port of Shahid Rajaee, Iran's largest commercial port, on 26 April 2025. The local authorities first reported 70 dead, and the judiciary later revised the toll to at least 57, with more than 1,000 injured. The New York Times, citing a person with ties to the Revolutionary Guards, reported that the material was sodium perchlorate, an ingredient of solid missile fuel, which a Defense Ministry spokesman denied. Supreme Leader Khamenei told security and judicial authorities to 'detect if there's been any negligence or deliberate acts,' and two days after the blast Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni attributed it to negligence as well as failure to observe safety measures.
AG-302.records:
Port and customs operators: the cargo declarations.
A crisis-management spokesman: said on 27 April that the blast appeared to result from poor storage of chemicals in containers.
The open-source data: suggested that chemical ingredients for missile fuel had arrived from China at the port in February and March.
Defense Ministry spokesman Reza Talaei-Nik: said no military fuel cargo had been imported, exported or present in the area.
Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni: cited 'shortcomings, including incompliance with safety precautions and negligence in terms of passive defense' and said 'some culprits have been identified and summoned'.
The judiciary: revised the death toll after finding that some bodies counted separately were one.
An investigating committee: found that 'false declarations (of goods) were made in some cases.'
AG-302.gap: A press report of a missile-fuel ingredient and the Defense Ministry's denial disagreed over the cargo record most relevant to the cause. The investigating committee found that some goods had been falsely declared, so the commercial record itself was unreliable. Sabotage remained a possibility that the Supreme Leader's instruction named.
AG-302.joining: Within days the state joined the records under its own interior, judicial and investigative apparatus and settled on negligence. On 4 May state television reported the arrest of a government manager and a private-sector manager. No public final report or named hostile actor appears in the sources checked.

AG-303.summary: On the night of 15 to 16 November 2025 an explosive device damaged the track near Mika, about 100 km southeast of Warsaw, on the line from Warsaw through Lublin toward the Ukrainian border. On the same weekend about 60 meters of overhead line were damaged and a metal clamp was found fixed to the track in the Puławy area. A long-distance train with 475 passengers made an emergency stop there. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the Mika explosion an unprecedented act of sabotage most likely meant to blow up a train. On 18 November Tusk said that two Ukrainian citizens who had long cooperated with Russian services were suspected and were believed to have left for Belarus. Poland then ordered the closure of the last Russian consulate, in Gdańsk.
AG-303.records:
A train driver: reported track irregularities early on 16 November.
The police: found a rail section so badly damaged that traffic was halted.
The train crews and the rail infrastructure manager: recorded the damage at both sites.
The investigators: secured nearby CCTV footage.
A special team: set up from prosecutors, the Central Bureau of Police Investigation (CBŚP) and the Internal Security Agency (ABW).
The Mazovian branch of the National Prosecutor's Office: opened an investigation into acts of sabotage of a terrorist nature carried out for foreign intelligence.
A court in Lviv: had convicted one suspect of sabotage in May 2025.
The defense minister: announced that the army would inspect about 120 km of the line toward Hrubieszów.
AG-303.gap: The damage was found when a train driver reported track irregularities the next morning. Once it was found, the gap closed fast. One line, two nearby sites and a confirmed explosive device left little room for an accident category.
AG-303.joining: Prosecutors, police and the ABW joined the records within three days. The interior minister said there had beyond any doubt been a detonation of an explosive device. On 18 November the prime minister named Russian services, and the government followed with the consulate closure. Public attribution came about two days after the damage was found.

AG-304.summary: The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's alert AL25-016 of 29 October 2025 described three recent incidents in which internet-accessible control devices were manipulated. At a water facility, tampering with pressure values degraded service to the community. At an oil and gas company, manipulation of an automated tank gauge triggered false alarms. On a farm, altered temperature and humidity in a grain-drying silo created potentially unsafe conditions.
AG-304.records:
The victims: local operational records.
The Cyber Centre and the RCMP: received "multiple reports of incidents involving internet-accessible ICS" over recent weeks.
The local police of jurisdiction: the alert directs victims to them. It notes that "not every complaint will result in an active criminal investigation."
AG-304.gap: On its own, each incident resembles an instrument fault or a nuisance alarm. The victims are small operators in three sectors. The alert names no victims, dates or group. It urges provinces and territories to work with municipalities to inventory and protect services in sectors that lack cybersecurity regulatory oversight. Its examples of such sectors are water, food and manufacturing.
AG-304.joining: The Cyber Centre and the RCMP joined the reports into one public alert. It attributes the activity to hacktivists seeking "to gain media attention, discredit organizations, and undermine Canada's reputation," without naming a group or state.

AG-305.summary: On 22 February 2025 the Togo-registered Hong Tai 58 (also named Hong Tai 168), with eight Chinese crew, entered a restricted zone about five nautical miles offshore. At about 03:00 on 25 February, as the ship was leaving, Chunghwa Telecom reported an outage on the Taiwan–Penghu No. 3 cable. The Coast Guard intercepted the ship and directed it to port, and Taiwan detained it. In June 2025 a district court in southern Taiwan sentenced the captain, surnamed Wang, to three years for violating the Telecommunications Management Act. The other seven crew were sent back to China for insufficient evidence.
AG-305.records:
Chunghwa Telecom: recorded the outage and spent about US$578,572 on repair.
The Coast Guard: monitored the ship's movements. It told the court that the ship dragged its anchor directly over the cable before moving in a zigzag pattern around it.
Prosecutors: argued intent.
The ship: had used several names and had one cargo record in the past year.
The captain: at first refused to give ownership details.
Beijing: called the incident a 'common maritime accident' and Taiwan's accounts 'exaggerated'.
AG-305.gap: The Coast Guard intercepted the vessel in the act, so the record reached a court with the ship and its master in custody. The ownership behind the flag of convenience stayed unresolved.
AG-305.joining: A district court joined the Coast Guard's track records and the operator's outage report into a criminal conviction of the master. The conviction was for willfully anchoring in a prohibited zone and damaging the cable. The court named no state sponsor, and the owner was not identified in the sources consulted.

AG-306.summary: Continental Spain and Portugal lost power at 12:33 CEST on 28 April 2025, for up to ten hours. Spain had lost 15 gigawatts, about 60 percent of its supply, in five seconds. Red Eléctrica (REE) ruled out a cyberattack by 29 April. National Court judge José Luis Calama, however, opened preliminary proceedings to test the hypothesis of computer sabotage against critical infrastructure, which could constitute terrorism. The judge ordered reports from the National Cryptologic Center, REE and the National Police. On 17 June 2025 Ecological Transition Minister Sara Aagesen presented the government report, prepared with analysts from the national security agencies. It found no indications of cyber-sabotage by foreign actors and attributed the collapse to technical and planning errors. The ENTSO-E expert panel's final report of 20 March 2026 named oscillations, gaps in voltage and reactive-power control and cascading generator disconnections in Spain among several causes.
AG-306.records:
REE and the Portuguese operator REN: the transmission-system data.
The National Cryptologic Center: reviewed the computer records of REE and private operators.
The National Court: a criminal file on possible cyber sabotage, with a preliminary report from the National Police.
The government commission: prepared the national report. It was led by the Ministry for Ecological Transition with cybersecurity bodies and the regulator CNMC.
The National Security Council: met three times in 24 hours and asked the European Commission's Electricity Coordination Group for an independent report.
ENTSO-E's 49-member panel: experts from transmission operators, a regional coordination center, ACER and national regulators (CNMC, BNetzA, CRE and URE among them). It was led by Klaus Kaschnitz (APG, Austria) and Richard Balog (MAVIR, Hungary), from systems not directly affected.
AG-306.gap: Joining was fast, but it ran on parallel tracks that asked different questions. A criminal court asked about cyber sabotage and terrorism. The cryptologic center asked about intrusion into operators' systems. The government commission asked about cause and security, and the transnational panel about system physics. The security verdict came in seven weeks and the panel's causal account in almost eleven months.
AG-306.joining: On 17 June 2025 the government commission set aside the attack hypothesis, and Aagesen blamed 'the poor planning' of grid operators. The ENTSO-E panel, led by experts from unaffected systems, issued its final report on 20 March 2026. ENTSO-E's president, Damian Cortinas, said, 'There is no single cause,' and the report faulted operators such as REE for lacking real-time monitoring as voltage approached critical thresholds. No attacker was named because none was found.

AG-307.summary: From early September 2025 JNIM attacked fuel convoys on the roads to Bamako, including the route from Senegal. Bellingcat verified six attacks in the Kayes, Koulikoro and Sikasso regions between 14 September and 6 November, two of them less than 70 km from the capital. It counted more than 130 tankers destroyed since September. Human Rights Watch reported attacks on hundreds of tankers and the abduction or assault of drivers. Night-light imagery showed Bamako dimming. On 26 October the education minister suspended classes nationwide until 10 November because of disruptions in fuel supply.
AG-307.records:
JNIM: publicized its campaign on its own channels, including ChirpWire.
Colonel Assimi Goïta, the junta leader: in a televised address on 22 September, urged people to 'resist disinformation campaigns orchestrated by armed terrorist groups'.
The education ministry: announced the school closure as a fuel-supply measure.
Human Rights Watch: documented the effect on schooling and electricity.
Héni Nsaibia, ACLED's senior West Africa analyst: described the campaign as an escalation of JNIM's economic warfare aimed at undermining the regime's legitimacy.
AG-307.gap: JNIM publicized the campaign, so recognition did not depend on joining records. The government limited public admission: state-aligned media showed convoys reaching Bamako under heavy escort. Because connectivity was limited and access for journalists restricted, independent counting was left to open-source analysts.
AG-307.joining: Open-source analysts at Bellingcat joined geolocated social-media footage, satellite imagery, NASA fire detections and night-light data into a verified count, with commentary from ACLED's West Africa analyst. JNIM's own publicity removed the aggregation problem. The junta's public statements framed the campaign as disinformation, while state media showed fuel getting through.
AG-307.harm_found_later: Nsaibia noted that the blockade caused severe economic and social harm without a high death toll. The rise in food prices and the closure of schools and universities are not recorded as casualties of the conflict.

AG-308.summary: On Sunday 26 January 2025 damage was discovered on a communication cable between Sweden and Latvia, and Swedish prosecutors opened an investigation into gross sabotage. Swedish police seized the Maltese-flagged cargo ship Vezhen, whose Bulgarian operator said the ship might have struck the cable with its anchor but denied any malicious intent. At the request of Latvian authorities, police in Tromsø, with the Norwegian Coast Guard, seized the Silver Dania, a ship of the Silver Sea group with an all-Russian crew.
AG-308.records:
The Swedish Prosecution Authority's National Security Unit: led the investigation.
The Security Police: conducted the investigation with assistance from the Coast Guard, the Police Authority and the Armed Forces.
Latvian authorities: requested the Silver Dania's seizure.
Tromsø police: held the Silver Dania.
The owners of both ships: issued statements.
AG-308.gap: Two ships under different jurisdictions were detained on the same suspicion within days of the break. Sweden detained one, Norway the other at Latvia's request.
AG-308.joining: Tromsø police released the Silver Dania late on Friday 31 January, saying no findings linked it to the damage. The Swedish prosecutor said investigators had looked at the Norwegian ship and dismissed its involvement. On 3 February the Swedish prosecutor said the investigation 'clearly shows that it is not a case of sabotage'. The prosecutor attributed the break to a combination of weather conditions and deficiencies in equipment and seamanship. The prosecutor also confirmed that the Vezhen had caused it. The seizure was lifted, and the investigation continued into whether other crimes could be suspected.

AG-309.summary: Near Los Yébenes and Manzaneque (Toledo), signaling cable was cut and removed at five points on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line on the late afternoon of 4 May 2025, a week after the Iberian blackout. The early reports combined the theft with a separate catenary fault and counted more than 30 trains and over 10,000 passengers affected. Transport Minister Óscar Puente called it 'a serious act of sabotage'. On 7 May unnamed sources close to the Guardia Civil investigation told The Objective that sabotage had been ruled out and that a local copper-theft gang was suspected. On 4 July 2025 the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of two men living near the sites, with prior police records for similar thefts, for continuing theft with force of copper cable. It put the theft's effect at 21 trains and about 6,300 passengers.
AG-309.records:
Adif (infrastructure manager): recorded the signaling failure, prepared a legal complaint and estimated the damage at about €25,000.
Renfe's president: attributed most of the delay to a separate incident in which an Iryo train dragged the catenary.
The Transport Ministry: issued the public sabotage framing.
The Guardia Civil's judicial police: investigated on instructions from an investigating court, supported by the UCO, the Technical Judicial Police Unit and the information service.
An internal Guardia Civil log of 4 May: already largely ruled out sabotage, according to The Objective.
AG-309.gap: Within hours the political recorder (the minister) and the criminal recorder (the Guardia Civil) applied different categories to the same cut cable. The minister classified intent from the effect on a national artery shortly after a blackout. The Guardia Civil classified method and motive against the routine pattern of copper theft by gangs operating in the area.
AG-309.joining: Through forensic and technical work the Guardia Civil joined the five cut points to one local group. The case closed as property crime two months later, with no hostile actor named. According to The Objective, the government later acknowledged that it may have acted hastily.

AG-310.summary: A fire at National Grid's North Hyde substation in Hayes on the night of 20 to 21 March 2025 cut one of Heathrow's three supply points. The airport closed to all flights on 21 March until about 6 p.m. By early estimates about 200,000 passengers were disrupted, and by the later count more than 270,000 passenger journeys. The Metropolitan Police Counter Terrorism Command led the inquiry into the cause until the Met said on 25 March that it was no longer treating the fire as a potentially criminal matter. NESO's final report of 2 July 2025 found that the fire most likely began when moisture entered a transformer bushing. It also found that an elevated moisture level measured in July 2018 had not been acted on, and that a 2022 review had found the site's fire suppression system inoperable. Ofgem opened an enforcement investigation into National Grid Electricity Transmission. Heathrow's own review under Ruth Kelly concluded that the airport had made the right decisions.
AG-310.records:
National Grid: the asset and maintenance records, including the 2018 oil sample and the 2022 decision to defer maintenance.
NESO: the review commissioned by the energy department and Ofgem.
Ofgem: the enforcement investigation.
The Counter Terrorism Command: the criminal inquiry.
Heathrow: its operational review.
SSEN Distribution: recorded 66,919 directly supplied customers cut off, among 71,655 in total. The outage also affected roads, rail and Hillingdon Hospital.
AG-310.gap: The police examined the question of crime, the airport its closure decision, NESO the grid and the cross-sector dependencies, and Ofgem the operator's compliance, each within its remit. According to NESO, the energy companies did not know of Heathrow's dependence on each supply point for some operationally critical systems. NESO also reported that network operators generally do not know whether their connected customers are critical national infrastructure. As a result, no record held the dependency itself in full.
AG-310.joining: The Counter Terrorism Command closed the criminal question within five days. NESO's review joined the grid, distribution and airport records and settled the event as an equipment failure that maintenance had not prevented.

AG-311.summary: On 29 December 2025 attackers struck more than 30 wind and photovoltaic farms. They also struck a large combined heat and power (CHP) plant supplying heat to almost half a million customers, and a private manufacturing company. At the farms' grid-connection substations the attacks damaged remote terminal units, local HMIs, protection relays and communication devices. The damage cut communication with the distribution system operator and remote control without stopping generation. At the large CHP plant the organization's EDR software blocked the wiper, and heat supply was not disrupted. CERT Polska's follow-up report of 8 August 2026 disclosed an attack on a second, smaller CHP plant (heat for about 50,000 residents). There a steam turbine and the system producing process water were shut down for a short time. That event had not previously been disclosed publicly.
AG-311.records:
The 30-plus renewable farm operators: each held its own record of lost remote control.
The distribution system operator: lost communication with the farms.
The CHP plants: endpoint (EDR) and OT logs.
CERT Polska (the national CSIRT at NASK): compiled the incident report (30 Jan 2026) and the follow-up (8 Aug 2026).
ESET, a private firm: linked the wiper, named DynoWiper, to Sandworm.
Prime Minister Tusk: announced the government's attribution at a press conference.
AG-311.gap: Because the renewable side of the grid consists of many small operators, the disturbance arrived as dozens of separate communication losses. There was no production loss, so no supply-side threshold was crossed. Polish officials named two CHP plants among the targets in January 2026. But the shutdown at the smaller plant stayed outside the public record for more than seven months, until a forensic investigation of more than three months reconstructed the attack path through a misconfigured private APN.
AG-311.joining: Within a month CERT Polska joined the farm, CHP and manufacturer incidents into one campaign, and it later added the shutdown at the second CHP plant. Attribution split by recorder: ESET linked the wiper to Sandworm (GRU). Prime Minister Tusk said that 'everything indicates' the attacks were prepared by groups 'directly linked to the Russian services'. CERT Polska found that the infrastructure overlapped with the cluster tracked as Static Tundra, Berserk Bear, Ghost Blizzard and Dragonfly, and its follow-up named no actor. The attacker did not publicize the act.

AG-312.summary: Chunghwa Telecom reported to Taiwan's Coast Guard Administration shortly before 13:00 on 3 January 2025 that a vessel had snagged and dragged its Trans-Pacific Express cable near Keelung. The traffic was rerouted through other cables with minimal disruption. The suspected ship, the Shunxin-39 (also Xing Shun-39), was flagged to Cameroon and Tanzania. Its owner was the Hong Kong company Jie Yang Trading Limited, whose sole director is a Chinese citizen. It carried two sets of AIS equipment. The Coast Guard intercepted it but could not board in rough weather. The ship continued toward Busan, and Taiwan asked South Korea for assistance.
AG-312.records:
Chunghwa Telecom: recorded the damage and reported it to the Coast Guard.
Taiwanese authorities: collected radar data and navigation records for prosecutors.
Open-source analysts: AIS histories. Stanford's SeaLight reported that the ship had used as many as six AIS numbers and at least two names over six months.
The Coast Guard: said it could not rule out gray-zone harassment by a Chinese vessel. On 6 January it drove away the Mongolia-flagged Baoshun, which had moved in a zigzag pattern near cables off New Taipei.
Herming Chiueh, deputy digital minister: told the Wall Street Journal that the cutting was likely intentional.
AG-312.gap: Cable redundancy kept the damage below the threshold of a service outage. The ship's identity was split across transponders and flags. Because the vessel left Taiwanese waters before it could be boarded, the next step fell to a foreign port state.
AG-312.joining: Only part of the record was joined: Taiwanese authorities compiled track records for prosecutors, and open-source analysts joined AIS histories. The sources consulted report no prosecution and no official naming of a state.

AG-313.summary: From October 2025 helium balloons launched from Belarus, many carrying contraband cigarettes, entered Lithuanian airspace and forced Vilnius Airport to close at least six times that month. A closure on the night of 21 to 22 October lasted more than eight hours and affected more than 4,000 travelers. One group of recovered balloons carried more than 18,000 packs of cigarettes. Lithuanian officials described the balloons as a hybrid threat that combined criminal smuggling with political pressure. Prime Minister Inga Ruginienė announced the closure of the border crossings with Belarus until 30 November, and the military was authorized to shoot balloons down if necessary. Belarus retaliated by blocking more than 1,000 Lithuanian trucks. Lithuania reopened the border less than three weeks later under pressure from logistics companies. The airport closures continued, including one of 11 hours in late November.
AG-313.records:
Air-navigation services and the airport: recorded the intrusions and closures.
The aviation authorities: counted at least 60 balloons launched in one night, 40 of which reached areas critical for aviation safety. They reported that the balloons appeared to be sent at regular intervals toward the runways.
The smuggling records: the recovered balloons and their cargo.
The government, the foreign ministry and the military: handled the response.
AG-313.gap: Belarusian smugglers often use balloons to carry contraband into the EU. Each balloon was in the first place a smuggling matter. The balloons themselves could not settle whether the closures served a state purpose. The cumulative effect appeared in airport records, outside the smuggling category in which each balloon was recorded.
AG-313.joining: The Lithuanian government joined smuggling and aviation records into a hybrid-threat finding. It responded with a border closure and shoot-down authority without waiting for any criminal attribution to the Belarusian state. The deputy foreign minister, Taurimas Valys, later called the balloons a cynical hybrid attack against the economy, aviation security and the entire nation. Alexander Lukashenko had said Belarus would apologize if its involvement was established.

AG-314.summary: All four major operators (M1, SIMBA Telecom, Singtel and StarHub) were targeted. The operators that detected the activity notified the regulator IMDA and the Cyber Security Agency (CSA). On 18 July 2025 Coordinating Minister for National Security K. Shanmugam said the actor UNC3886 had been detected attacking critical infrastructure, giving no details for operational security reasons. The next day Shanmugam called suggested China links 'speculative'. On 9 February 2026 CSA and IMDA disclosed Operation Cyber Guardian, in which over 100 cyber defenders countered an actor. The actor had gained access to some parts of the operators' networks, in one case limited access to critical systems, and had exfiltrated a small amount of mainly network-related technical data. CSA and IMDA reported no disruption of services.
AG-314.records:
The operators: detection records.
IMDA (sector regulator) and CSA (national cyber agency): received notifications.
Operation Cyber Guardian: the Centre for Strategic Infocomm Technologies, the Digital and Intelligence Service, GovTech and the Internal Security Department took part.
Mandiant, a private firm: assigned the tracking name UNC3886. It describes UNC3886 as 'a group with a China nexus'.
The Chinese embassy in Singapore: objected to that description.
AG-314.gap: The aggregation problem was small: four operators each notified two central agencies in a single jurisdiction, and a multi-agency operation followed. The open decision concerned naming. Government statements used the vendor's tracking label and named no state.
AG-314.joining: CSA and IMDA joined the operators' records under a single operation and published a public account. The government declined to name a state sponsor.

AG-315.summary: A cyberattack that began on 23 March 2025 (24 March in some reports) took down the online ticketing website and app of Ukraine's state railway, Ukrzaliznytsia. The station ticket offices, whose core ticketing system withstood the attack, sold tickets in an 'enhanced mode'. The company's chairman said no train was stopped. Ukrzaliznytsia, which called it the largest cyberattack it had faced, restored online sales on 27 March after 89 hours of work. On 1 April Yevheniia Nakonechna, head of the State Cyber Protection Centre of the SSSCIP, relayed CERT-UA's finding that the tactics were 'characteristic of Russian intelligence services' and called the attack 'an act of terrorism'.
AG-315.records:
Ukrzaliznytsia: the operational record. It stated that no train was stopped and no sensitive data leaked.
CERT-UA (within the SSSCIP): investigated and attributed the attack by its tactics and by malware built for the targeted infrastructure.
The SBU's cybersecurity department: assisted investigation and recovery.
AG-315.gap: Little gap opened: one national operator was the single target, and the outage was visible to every passenger. The joining institution (CERT-UA) sat inside the state cyber agency with authority to attribute.
AG-315.joining: About nine days after the attack began, CERT-UA and the SSSCIP joined the forensic record and named Russian intelligence services. No group claimed the attack in the sources checked. A single target and a wartime attribution practice narrowed the gap.

AG-316.summary: During the US military operation of 3 January 2026 that ended with the capture of Nicolás Maduro, parts of Caracas lost power and internet connectivity. At a press conference at Mar-a-Lago, President Trump said 'the lights of Caracas were largely turned off due to a certain expertise that we have'. Joint Chiefs chairman Gen. Dan Caine said US Cyber Command, Space Command and other combatant commands 'began layering different effects' to 'create a pathway' for US forces, without describing them. Whether the outage came from a cyber operation, electronic warfare or kinetic strikes has not been publicly established.
AG-316.records:
NetBlocks: recorded loss of internet connectivity in parts of Caracas coinciding with the operation. Its founder, Alp Toker, said its data 'doesn't expose or indicate the use of any specific cyber capability' and that the timing and geolocation 'match up closely with the kinetic force' of the operation.
The White House and both commands: did not respond to requests for comment.
A Venezuelan government video: purportedly showed a Caracas substation physically damaged by an explosion (unconfirmed, per Truesec).
PDVSA: in December 2025 had separately accused the United States of a cyberattack that disrupted its operations.
AG-316.gap: The United States announced the effect but withheld the means. The operator's own records (Corpoelec) were not published in the sources checked. Outside monitors observe effects without causes.
AG-316.joining: Private analysts and journalists (NetBlocks, Truesec, Dark Reading, Cyber Daily) combined official statements with connectivity data. Truesec judged it 'likely that U.S. Cyber command was part of the attack'. It also said 'it is still not possible to determine exactly how, or if it really was a cyberattack' that caused the blackout. No Venezuelan technical account was found.

AG-317.summary: On 4 August 2026 a drone carrying explosives and a detonator was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The airport closed temporarily while bomb-disposal teams secured the device, which did not explode. A US intelligence source said its explosives and structure were typical of Russian military intelligence (GRU) and that its trigger had been disconnected. Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany had increasingly become a target for hybrid attackers. On 1 September 2026 the German government blamed Russia: Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were known from other Russian hybrid operations. Germany ordered the Russian consulate in Bonn closed and summoned the Russian ambassador.
AG-317.records:
Airport operations and the federal police: the discovery and the closure.
The bomb-disposal units: the device.
German security and intelligence agencies, working with US counterparts: the forensic assessment.
The government: an attribution resting on police investigations and intelligence findings.
US officials: counted 18 drone incidents that had disrupted air traffic at the airport since January 2026.
AG-317.gap: A single intact device at one site left little dispersion. The open question was attribution, which rested on forensic comparison with devices from other Russian operations.
AG-317.joining: German security agencies, with US support, joined the forensic record to earlier Russian designs. Within four weeks the government attributed the attempt to Russian state entities without naming a specific service. Dobrindt said the planning showed a high degree of technical expertise, while execution appeared to have been left to low-level agents. Russia's foreign ministry rejected the attribution and promised a fitting response.

AG-318.summary: Around 6 a.m. on 7 February 2026, the day after the opening ceremony of the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics, electric cables were cut in a manhole near Bologna Centrale on the Bologna-Padua high-speed line. A rudimentary device was found and removed on a switch of the ordinary Bologna-Padua line. An electric cabin beside the tracks near Pesaro on the Ancona-Rimini line was set on fire. Anadolu reported a further device on the Bologna-Ancona line that failed to detonate. High-speed, Intercity and regional trains were delayed by up to 150 minutes in Bologna and Pesaro. Infrastructure and Transport Minister Salvini said prosecutors were investigating on suspicion of terrorism. Bologna prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation by 9 February. On 10 February ANSA reported an anarchist post on the platform La Nemesi that claimed the Pesaro and Bologna actions as a protest against the Games.
AG-318.records:
RFI, the infrastructure manager: repaired the lines, in Pesaro only after judicial checks.
The firefighters: put out the Pesaro fire.
The scientific police: inspected the Pesaro site.
Polfer and DIGOS: conducted the investigation.
The Bologna prosecutors: a file against unknown persons for terrorist association and attack on transport safety.
The investigators in Ancona: also examined the case.
The Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport: called the incidents 'serious episodes of sabotage' and said it would seek damages.
The claimants: published their own account.
AG-318.gap: The state classified three incidents from the same morning, on a symbolic date, as sabotage on the same day. The claim followed within three days, so the gap barely opened.
AG-318.joining: On 7 February the Ministry of Infrastructure and Transport joined the incidents as sabotage. Bologna prosecutors opened a terrorism file. The anarchist claim named the actor as a movement without naming individuals. Attacker publicity and simultaneity narrowed the gap. No arrests were reported in the sources checked.

AG-319.summary: In the Israeli–US war against Iran, under way from 28 February 2026, Israel struck more than 30 oil processing and storage facilities across Iran, including four sites in and around Tehran on 7–8 March. The Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia and Fujairah port in the UAE were damaged in strikes reportedly by Iranian drones. Iran accused the United States of attacking a desalination plant on Qeshm Island, affecting the water supply of 30 villages. The next day Bahrain accused Iran of damaging a desalination plant in a drone strike. The Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) identified over 300 incidents by 10 March.
AG-319.records:
Each state: recorded damage on its own territory and issued accusations.
Israel and the United States: Israel said the oil facilities were being used for 'military purposes,' and the United States later questioned the scale and rationale of those strikes.
The IAEA, whose inspections in Iran had been restricted since 2025: at first said it had no sign of strikes on nuclear facilities. It later confirmed damage to entrance buildings at the Natanz Fuel Enrichment Plant.
CEOBS: logged incidents from social and traditional media and verified them with satellite imagery.
AG-319.gap: In an open war each attack is recognized. But the records of what was hit and with what effect were dispersed among belligerents that accused each other, an international agency with restricted access, and an NGO working from social media. CEOBS warned that incidents are 'largely identified through social media monitoring' and that 'many additional incidents will need to be retrospectively added.'
AG-319.joining: CEOBS, an NGO without any official mandate, joined the incidents into a risk-assessed dataset (232 of over 300 assessed by 10 March). Online analysts working from satellite imagery identified minor damage at Natanz before the IAEA confirmed it. The counter-accusations over desalination plants were not resolved in the sources checked.
AG-319.harm_found_later: After the Tehran depot fires, CEOBS reported risks of 'toxic acid rain' over the city. The city's average fine-particle (PM2.5) levels already exceed WHO guidelines by up to 4.5 times. CEOBS noted that 'no direct observations are available due to the black-out'. The health effect will be visible only through later reconstruction.
